title: Improving OCR Faithfulness via Gated and Attenuated On-Policy Distillation
summary: Vision-language models may rewrite anomalous text in images into linguistically plausible expressions, compromising OCR transcription faithfulness. Sequence-level task rewards and local teacher guidance are complementary, but guidance from the same teacher may not remain equally effective as the student improves. Offline analysis shows that supervision from a fixed teacher becomes progressively less favorable as the student improves, both across training checkpoints and across response groups with different task rewards. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GAD-RL, which adaptively regulates teacher supervision during joint post-training according to the student's current task performance and local distributions. A frozen teacher conditions on reference transcriptions and student-generated prefixes. GAD-RL disables distillation for response groups containing an output with task reward at least 0.95 and continuously attenuates distillation strength as group-mean reward increases. It also weights forward KL by the student's probability of the teacher's Top-1 token, moderating local auxiliary updates when student support for that candidate is low. On Qwen3.5-2B, GAD-RL achieves 59.92% Micro Recall on CHAOS-Bench, surpassing GRPO and GRPO+OPD (fixed-weight) by 8.45 and 4.43 percentage points, respectively, while achieving an Overall score of 91.18 on OmniDocBench v1.6.

AI.tldr: GAD-RL adaptively regulates teacher distillation during joint post-training of vision-language models, disabling or attenuating supervision based on student task performance and token-level support, yielding large OCR accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models may rewrite anomalous text in images into plausible expressions, harming OCR transcription faithfulness. Sequence-level task rewards and local teacher guidance are complementary, but a fixed teacher's supervision effectiveness degrades as the student improves, making uniform distillation suboptimal.
AI.method: The paper first performs offline analysis showing fixed-teacher supervision becomes less favorable across training checkpoints and across response groups with different task rewards. It then proposes GAD-RL, which uses a frozen teacher conditioned on reference transcriptions and student-generated prefixes, disables distillation for response groups containing an output with task reward at least 0.95, continuously attenuates distillation strength as group-mean reward rises, and weights forward KL by the student's probability of the teacher's Top-1 token.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5-2B, GAD-RL achieves 59.92% Micro Recall on CHAOS-Bench, surpassing GRPO and GRPO+OPD (fixed-weight) by 8.45 and 4.43 percentage points, respectively, and reaches an Overall score of 91.18 on OmniDocBench v1.6.
AI.conclusion: Adaptively regulating teacher supervision according to student performance and local distributions improves joint post-training for faithful OCR transcription, outperforming fixed-weight distillation baselines.

title: AREX-2: Advancing Self-Improving Agents through Long-Horizon Reflective Tasks
comment: Code will be released at https://github.com/VectorSpaceLab/AREX-2 and models at https://huggingface.co/collections/BAAI/arex-2
summary: We present AREX-2, an effort to advance the self-improving capability of LLM agents, which we define as the ability to iteratively refine a solution at test time. This ability rests on two complementary capabilities: reflection, which produces a solution better than the current one, and long-horizon execution, which keeps the iteration effective over many rounds. We hypothesize that both capabilities are domain-agnostic, and can therefore be learned in scenarios that are well suited for supervision. Accordingly, we synthesize long-horizon improvement trajectories from machine learning and algorithmic programming tasks, two domains that offer verifiable feedback and reward sustained iteration. Trained on this data, our agent, built on Qwen3.8-27B, achieves strong results on MLE-bench Lite (81.8) and Frontier-CS (70.7), transfers to deep research with 84.0 on BrowseComp, 52.6 on HLE, 92.2 on GAIA, and 93.8 on DeepSearchQA, and keeps improving as its budget of rounds grows. These results show that long-horizon reflective data is an effective route toward self-improving agents.

AI.tldr: AREX-2 trains an LLM agent (on Qwen3.8-27B) with synthesized long-horizon improvement trajectories from ML and algorithmic programming to learn domain-agnostic reflection and sustained iteration, yielding strong verified gains on ML/CS benchmarks and transfer to deep research tasks.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to advance the self-improving capability of LLM agents, defined as iteratively refining a solution at test time. This capability is decomposed into reflection (producing a better solution than the current one) and long-horizon execution (sustaining effective iteration over many rounds). The hypothesis is that both are domain-agnostic and can thus be learned in scenarios well suited for supervision.
AI.method: Synthesize long-horizon improvement trajectories from two domains—machine learning and algorithmic programming—chosen because they provide verifiable feedback and reward sustained iteration. Train an agent built on Qwen3.8-27B on this data to internalize reflection and long-horizon execution.
AI.result: The trained agent reaches 81.8 on MLE-bench Lite and 70.7 on Frontier-CS, and transfers to deep research with 84.0 on BrowseComp, 52.6 on HLE, 92.2 on GAIA, and 93.8 on DeepSearchQA. Performance continues to improve as the budget of rounds increases.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon reflective data is an effective route toward self-improving agents; because reflection and long-horizon execution are domain-agnostic, training in verifiable-feedback domains enables transfer and continued gains with more iteration rounds.

title: MoFlow: Multi-Objective Agentic Workflow Generation
summary: We study the generation of agentic workflows that jointly optimize multiple objectives, such as accuracy, cost, latency, robustness, and consistency. Existing methods for workflow generation typically optimize accuracy alone or a weighted sum of objectives, so each trained generator commits to one fixed trade-off and must be retrained from scratch when preferences change. To alleviate this, we propose MoFlow, which generates workflows optimized across varied preferences. Specifically, MoFlow formulates workflow generation as a multi-objective Markov decision process and solves it by leveraging Convex-Hull Monte Carlo Tree Search with optimistic set-valued backups, where every node stores a set of reachable trade-offs rather than one weighted score. A single search thus approximately covers the Pareto front, from which MoFlow can return a workflow for any preference by lookup without retraining. We evaluate MoFlow against six strong baselines on six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code, and question answering. Since the baselines are single-scalar optimizers by design, an apples-to-apples comparison is difficult. We instead adopt an evaluation setup that favors the baselines, in that they are rerun for each testing preference, which MoFlow never sees. Even under this stringent setup, MoFlow achieves the highest average hypervolume.

AI.tldr: MoFlow generates agentic workflows that cover the Pareto front across multiple objectives (accuracy, cost, latency, robustness, consistency) via a single multi-objective MDP search, returning any preference by lookup without retraining, and achieves the highest average hypervolume against six baselines on six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing workflow generators optimize accuracy alone or a weighted sum, so each trained generator commits to one fixed trade-off and must be retrained from scratch when preferences change.
AI.method: MoFlow formulates workflow generation as a multi-objective Markov decision process and solves it with Convex-Hull Monte Carlo Tree Search using optimistic set-valued backups, where each node stores a set of reachable trade-offs rather than a single weighted score, so one search approximately covers the Pareto front.
AI.result: Evaluated against six strong baselines on six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code, and question answering, under a setup favoring baselines (rerun per testing preference unseen by MoFlow), MoFlow still attains the highest average hypervolume.
AI.conclusion: A single Pareto-front-covering search enables preference-agnostic workflow generation without retraining, and demonstrates superior multi-objective performance even under baseline-favoring evaluation.

title: AI Agents are Vulnerable to Radicalization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can influence people's beliefs, yet little is known about whether and how they can manipulate each other. To investigate this, we simulate conversations between two agents: a target LLM that role-plays a human persona based on demographic and psychological attributes, and an influencer LLM that aims to make the target's beliefs more extreme. We examine radicalization along two pathways: resonance, where the influencer reinforces a target's pre-existing belief, and persuasion, where the influencer promotes a belief the target initially considers unimportant. Across affective and behavioral metrics, we find that both mechanisms radicalize the target. However, resonance produces consistently stronger effects than persuasion. Different influence tactics, such as using sycophancy and unverified claims, produce different levels of radicalization, but not consistently across metrics. We further show that resonance propagates to related beliefs, suggesting interconnected belief structures within AI agents. These findings indicate that AI agents are susceptible to radicalization, particularly when messages align with their existing beliefs, raising concerns about the vulnerability of personalized AI agents and multi-agent AI ecosystems.

AI.tldr: This study simulates conversations between LLM agents to test whether AI agents can radicalize each other. Both resonance (reinforcing existing beliefs) and persuasion (promoting unimportant beliefs) radicalize targets, but resonance is consistently stronger and propagates to related beliefs.
AI.motivation: LLMs can influence people's beliefs, but it is unknown whether and how they can manipulate each other. Understanding this is important given the growing use of personalized AI agents and multi-agent AI ecosystems.
AI.method: Two LLM agents converse: a target that role-plays a human persona based on demographic and psychological attributes, and an influencer that aims to make the target's beliefs more extreme. Radicalization is examined along two pathways—resonance (reinforcing pre-existing beliefs) and persuasion (promoting initially unimportant beliefs)—measured across affective and behavioral metrics, with varying influence tactics such as sycophancy and unverified claims.
AI.result: Both resonance and persuasion radicalize the target, but resonance produces consistently stronger effects. Different influence tactics yield different radicalization levels, though not consistently across metrics. Resonance also propagates to related beliefs.
AI.conclusion: AI agents are susceptible to radicalization, especially when messages align with their existing beliefs. This suggests interconnected belief structures within AI agents and raises concerns about the vulnerability of personalized AI agents and multi-agent AI ecosystems.

title: Optimize, Learn, Refine: Whole-Body Grasping and Pick-and-Throw with a Spiral Soft Robot
summary: Soft continuum robots can exploit distributed compliance for whole-body manipulation, but synthesizing behavior through changing contacts remains difficult. We address whole-body grasping and pick-and-throw from an initially ungrasped state through outcome-based actuation-space optimization. Grasping is quantified by tip angular sweep and body-object enclosure, while throwing further incorporates release-direction alignment and minimum release speed. These objectives allow grasping, acceleration, and release to emerge from compliant interaction without prescribing contact forces, contact locations, or body configurations. Because the resulting actuation-to-outcome mapping is nonsmooth, we utilize derivative-free CMA-ES within an optimize-learn-refine framework. CMA-ES generates solutions for sampled conditions, a task-conditioned predictor learns warm starts, and CMA-ES refines them for unseen conditions. In simulation, the method achieves 492/500 successful grasps (98.4%) and success rates of 98%, 97%, and 94% across three directional throwing trials. Learned initialization increases grasping success from 78.6% to 98.4% while reducing the median rollout count from 1184 to 816 in CMA-ES. Hardware experiments achieve a 100% grasping success rate across 50 executions and a 100% pick-and-throw success rate across 30 executions, with 10 repetitions per direction. Together, these simulation and hardware results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework across both simulated and physical whole-body manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper enables whole-body grasping and pick-and-throw in soft continuum robots via outcome-based actuation-space optimization using CMA-ES within an optimize-learn-refine framework, achieving strong simulation (98.4% grasping) and hardware (100%) success rates.
AI.motivation: Soft continuum robots can exploit distributed compliance for whole-body manipulation, but synthesizing behavior through changing contacts remains difficult. The paper targets whole-body grasping and pick-and-throw from an initially ungrasped state without prescribing contact forces, contact locations, or body configurations.
AI.method: The method formulates outcome-based actuation-space optimization. Grasping is quantified by tip angular sweep and body-object enclosure; throwing adds release-direction alignment and minimum release speed. Because the actuation-to-outcome mapping is nonsmooth, the authors use derivative-free CMA-ES within an optimize-learn-refine framework: CMA-ES generates solutions for sampled conditions, a task-conditioned predictor learns warm starts, and CMA-ES refines them for unseen conditions.
AI.result: In simulation, the method achieves 492/500 successful grasps (98.4%) and success rates of 98%, 97%, and 94% across three directional throwing trials. Learned initialization raises grasping success from 78.6% to 98.4% while reducing median rollout count from 1184 to 816. Hardware experiments achieve 100% grasping success over 50 executions and 100% pick-and-throw success over 30 executions (10 repetitions per direction).
AI.conclusion: Grasping, acceleration, and release emerge from compliant interaction through outcome objectives alone, and the simulation and hardware results jointly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed optimize-learn-refine framework for whole-body manipulation in both simulated and physical tasks.

title: CARAT: Do Materials LLMs Reason or Recite?
summary: When a materials LLM answers a question about crystal structure, does it reason from the structure or copy an answer already printed in its input? Accuracy cannot tell: a structural description often prints the very field it is scored against. CARAT holds question and gold answer fixed across eight matched views, names each structural relation separately in GraphSpace, and adds matched fine-tuning, answer masking, evidence injection, paired inference, and a rule that can withhold claims. First, on the benchmark's hardest families the grounded view is worth 17.3 points over formula inputs. Second, we turn that scrutiny on ourselves. GraphSpace beats a plain periodic graph by 19.3 points, but that margin is two effects at once: where the plain rendering carries everything the question needs it is 1.96 points, and where it omits those fields entirely, 46.7 points. The headline mostly measures what the baseline lacked, not how evidence is presented. Third, we attack our own benchmark. A rule that skips the link and reads the list directly answers four of seven hardened families, so we rebuilt it until eleven such shortcuts sat near chance. The frozen model quotes that link yet answers the same when we redirect it, on 95.6% of paired cases: it repeats the relation without using it. After matched supervision it reaches 99.8%, and deleting the link drops it to 23.4%, below the 27.0% the best shortcut reaches: both steps are learnable.

AI.tldr: CARAT separates whether a materials LLM reasons from crystal structure or copies printed answers, using eight matched views with fixed question and gold answer, introducing GraphSpace. Grounded structure yields +17.3 points over formula inputs; GraphSpace beats a plain periodic graph by 19.3 points but this splits into 1.96 and 46.7 points, showing the margin mostly reflects baseline deficiencies. A hardened benchmark with eleven shortcuts near chance shows the model repeats a relation without using it (95.6% of paired cases); after supervision it reaches 99.8%, and deleting the link drops it to 23.4%.
AI.motivation: Accuracy alone cannot distinguish reasoning from structure versus copying a field already printed in the input, since a structural description often prints the very field it is scored against.
AI.method: CARAT holds question and gold answer fixed across eight matched views, names each structural relation separately in GraphSpace, and adds matched fine-tuning, answer masking, evidence injection, paired inference, and a rule that can withhold claims. The benchmark is also attacked with shortcut rules and rebuilt until shortcuts sit near chance.
AI.result: On the hardest families the grounded view is worth 17.3 points over formula inputs. GraphSpace beats a plain periodic graph by 19.3 points, decomposing into 1.96 points where the plain rendering carries everything and 46.7 points where it omits those fields. A rule skipping the link answers four of seven hardened families, so it was rebuilt until eleven shortcuts sat near chance. The frozen model quotes the link but answers the same when redirected on 95.6% of paired cases; after matched supervision it reaches 99.8%, and deleting the link drops it to 23.4%, below the 27.0% best shortcut.
AI.conclusion: The headline margin mostly measures what the baseline lacked, not how evidence is presented. Parroting and genuine structural use are separable and both steps are learnable.

title: Fiatlux: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Humanoid Ladder Climbing and Light-Bulb Replacement
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables, 2 figures. Project page: https://fiatlux-bench.github.io
summary: Existing benchmarks evaluate tabletop manipulation, flat-floor household activity, or humanoid locomotion and manipulation as separate task groups; none scores vertical mobility and dexterous work on a fragile payload in one long-horizon episode. We present Fiatlux, a light-bulb replacement benchmark built on NVIDIA Isaac Lab. In one episode, a Unitree G1 humanoid positions a step ladder under a ceiling or wall fixture, climbs it, exchanges a spent bulb in a socket for a fresh one, and leaves the spent one in a disposal crate. We decompose the episode into twelve subtask environments scored on difficulty-weighted gates. The goal is a successful replacement, with the fresh bulb seated, the spent one disposed of, neither dropped, and a fragility bound not crossed. Runs that fall short can earn partial credit. Observations are split into a standard mode (signals a physical robot could sense or estimate) and a privileged mode (exact simulator state). We specify the evaluation protocol and provide reference baseline implementations spanning RSL-RL PPO, zero-shot NVIDIA GR00T N1.7 Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, and whole-body controllers. Additionally, we provide the teleoperated recordings used to specify and check the success gates. The benchmark code and the teleoperated recordings are available at fiatlux-bench.github.io.

AI.tldr: Fiatlux is a long-horizon Isaac Lab benchmark for a Unitree G1 humanoid that must position and climb a step ladder to replace a ceiling or wall light bulb, combining vertical mobility, dexterous manipulation, and fragile-payload handling in one episode scored via twelve difficulty-weighted subtask gates with partial credit.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate tabletop manipulation, flat-floor household activity, or humanoid locomotion and manipulation as separate task groups. None scores vertical mobility and dexterous work on a fragile payload within a single long-horizon episode, leaving this integrated capability unmeasured.
AI.method: Built on NVIDIA Isaac Lab, the benchmark defines one episode in which a Unitree G1 humanoid positions a step ladder under a ceiling or wall fixture, climbs it, exchanges a spent bulb in a socket for a fresh one, and disposes of the spent bulb in a crate. The episode is decomposed into twelve subtask environments scored on difficulty-weighted gates, with a fragility bound and partial credit for incomplete runs. Observations are provided in standard mode (robot-sensible or estimable signals) and privileged mode (exact simulator state). Reference baselines span RSL-RL PPO, zero-shot NVIDIA GR00T N1.7 Vision-Language-Action models, and whole-body controllers, and teleoperated recordings specify and validate the success gates.
AI.result: The work delivers the Fiatlux benchmark, its evaluation protocol, twelve difficulty-weighted subtask environments, dual observation modes, reference baseline implementations (RSL-RL PPO, zero-shot GR00T N1.7 VLA, whole-body controllers), and teleoperated recordings for gate specification and checking. Success requires a seated fresh bulb, a disposed spent bulb, no drops, and adherence to the fragility bound, with partial credit available for shortfall runs. Code and recordings are released at fiatlux-bench.github.io.
AI.conclusion: Fiatlux fills a gap in humanoid evaluation by scoring vertical mobility and dexterous fragile-payload work in a single long-horizon episode, offering a standardized protocol, baseline results, and open resources to drive progress on integrated whole-body household task performance.

title: Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses
summary: When a student is stuck, a tutor faces the assistance dilemma: help given too early can hinder productive struggle, while help withheld too long leaves the student in a frustrating, persistent impasse (i.e., wheel spinning). Generative AI tutors increasingly use guardrails restricting answer-giving, yet little is known about how such tutors behave once an impasse persists. We analyze 20,462 student turns from 1,260 authentic sessions with a guided LLM chemistry tutor, identifying 6,630 impasse turns of three major types: conceptual errors, expressed uncertainty, or help-seeking. We then used these impasses to simulate three tutoring conditions to study variation in AI tutor guidance through impasses: baseline, no-direct-answer, and guided tutor. For a sample of 150 impasses, prompt specificity changed pedagogy: a baseline tutor provided the answer directly in 50.7% of responses, a no-direct-answer tutor asked a follow-up question every time, and the guided tutor responded in a wide variety of ways depending on the context. We then analyzed impasse trajectories in authentic interactions, finding that each additional impasse turn lowered the odds of next-turn recovery by 12.7% (AOR = 0.873, p < .001), and early dropouts were caught in recursive concept elicitation before reaching execution. The benefit of questioning decayed as impasses persisted (scripted question x depth AOR = 0.78; follow-up x depth AOR = 0.83), whereas addressing the student's error grew more beneficial (AOR = 1.14); after a failed scripted question, repeating it was followed by recovery in 28.1% of cases, compared with 39.8% when the tutor addressed the error instead. For learning analytics, these findings identify impasse depth and type as observable, turn-level dialogue signals that analytics can use to trigger graduated, state-sensitive assistance in real time.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 20,462 student turns from 1,260 authentic sessions with a guided LLM chemistry tutor, identifying 6,630 impasse turns of three types (conceptual errors, expressed uncertainty, help-seeking). Simulating three tutoring conditions on 150 impasses revealed that prompt specificity shapes pedagogy. Trajectory analysis showed each additional impasse turn lowered next-turn recovery odds by 12.7%, and that questioning's benefit decayed with impasse depth while addressing the student's error grew more beneficial.
AI.motivation: Tutors face an assistance dilemma: helping too early can hinder productive struggle, while withholding help too long leaves students in frustrating, persistent impasse (wheel spinning). Although generative AI tutors increasingly use guardrails restricting answer-giving, little is known about how such tutors behave once an impasse persists. The study aims to understand AI tutor guidance through persistent impasses and to identify observable dialogue signals for triggering graduated, state-sensitive assistance.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 20,462 student turns from 1,260 authentic sessions with a guided LLM chemistry tutor, identifying 6,630 impasse turns of three types: conceptual errors, expressed uncertainty, and help-seeking. They simulated three tutoring conditions (baseline, no-direct-answer, and guided tutor) on a sample of 150 impasses to study variation in AI tutor guidance, then analyzed impasse trajectories in authentic interactions.
AI.result: Prompt specificity changed pedagogy: a baseline tutor provided the answer directly in 50.7% of responses, a no-direct-answer tutor asked a follow-up question every time, and the guided tutor responded in a wide variety of context-dependent ways. Each additional impasse turn lowered the odds of next-turn recovery by 12.7% (AOR = 0.873, p < .001), and early dropouts were caught in recursive concept elicitation before reaching execution. The benefit of questioning decayed as impasses persisted (scripted question x depth AOR = 0.78; follow-up x depth AOR = 0.83), whereas addressing the student's error grew more beneficial (AOR = 1.14). After a failed scripted question, repeating it was followed by recovery in 28.1% of cases, versus 39.8% when the tutor addressed the error instead.
AI.conclusion: For learning analytics, impasse depth and type are observable, turn-level dialogue signals that analytics can use to trigger graduated, state-sensitive assistance in real time.

title: SynIL: Leveraging Synergy for Offline Imitation Learning from Imperfect Demonstration Datasets
summary: Imitation learning enables robots to acquire complex skills directly from massive demonstration datasets, but its performance degrades severely when datasets are contaminated with suboptimal or noisy demonstrations. While prior quality-assessment methods attempt to filter or reweight data, they typically rely on manual pre-selection of expert reference data or task-specific heuristics, limiting scalability. To address this challenge, we introduce SynIL (Synergy-based Imitation Learning), a novel framework for automated, label-free demonstration quality assessment in offline reinforcement learning. Grounded in neuroscientific evidence that motor synergy, a low-dimensional coordinated structure in movement, correlates directly with motor proficiency, SynIL algorithmically quantifies synergy manifestation to generate dense, transition-level reward signals via self-supervised reward regression. Comprehensive evaluations on D4RL locomotion benchmarks and multi-human Robomimic manipulation datasets demonstrate that synergy-derived rewards correlate strongly with ground-truth rewards. Furthermore, SynIL substantially outperforms Behavior Cloning (BC) and achieves performance comparable to, and in sparse-reward human teleoperation scenarios, superior to, offline reinforcement learning trained on true environment rewards.

AI.tldr: SynIL is a label-free framework that assesses demonstration quality in offline RL by quantifying motor synergy to generate dense, transition-level rewards via self-supervised reward regression, outperforming BC and matching or surpassing offline RL with true rewards.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning degrades when demonstration datasets contain suboptimal or noisy data. Prior quality-assessment methods rely on manual pre-selection of expert references or task-specific heuristics, which limits scalability.
AI.method: Grounded in neuroscientific evidence linking motor synergy (low-dimensional coordinated movement structure) to motor proficiency, SynIL algorithmically quantifies synergy manifestation and produces dense, transition-level reward signals through self-supervised reward regression, requiring no labels or manual expert references.
AI.result: On D4RL locomotion benchmarks and multi-human Robomimic manipulation datasets, synergy-derived rewards correlate strongly with ground-truth rewards. SynIL substantially outperforms Behavior Cloning and achieves performance comparable to offline RL trained on true environment rewards, exceeding it in sparse-reward human teleoperation scenarios.
AI.conclusion: SynIL offers a scalable, automated, label-free solution for demonstration quality assessment, using motor synergy as a robust proxy for proficiency and enabling effective offline RL without ground-truth reward supervision.

title: Beyond Mode Collapse: Generating Diverse Synthetic Expert Conversations via Generative Flow Networks
summary: High quality synthetic data is central to post training LLMs for adaptive AI applications that represent the diverse expert strategies and decisions in conversations. Prompting LLMs directly or conditioning them on end use scenarios yields low diversity data that collapses onto dominant modes. We propose a method to generate diverse high quality synthetic data using Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). We show that training GFlowNets to generate latent conversation structure using a Gaussian mixture density over key interaction features (e.g., confusion episode dynamics, scaffolding directive balance) enables sampling expert strategies in proportion to their prevalence in the training data. Across two structurally distinct domains, tutoring and emotional support dialogues, our GFlow based synthetic data generation approach offers a better balance of fidelity, mode coverage and authenticity than reinforcement-learning and end to end LLM baselines, without copying training data. Evaluated on three downstream outcome prediction tasks, classifiers trained on synthetic GFlowNet generated conversations provide a stronger training signal than competitive synthesis baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) to generate diverse, high-quality synthetic conversation data for post-training LLMs, sampling latent conversation structures via a Gaussian mixture density over key interaction features to match expert strategy prevalence.
AI.motivation: High-quality synthetic data is central to post-training LLMs for adaptive AI applications that must represent diverse expert strategies and decisions in conversations. However, prompting LLMs directly or conditioning them on end-use scenarios yields low-diversity data that collapses onto dominant modes.
AI.method: The authors train GFlowNets to generate latent conversation structure using a Gaussian mixture density over key interaction features (e.g., confusion episode dynamics, scaffolding directive balance), enabling sampling of expert strategies in proportion to their prevalence in the training data.
AI.result: Across two structurally distinct domains—tutoring and emotional support dialogues—the GFlowNet-based approach achieves a better balance of fidelity, mode coverage, and authenticity than reinforcement-learning and end-to-end LLM baselines, without copying training data. On three downstream outcome prediction tasks, classifiers trained on synthetic GFlowNet-generated conversations provide a stronger training signal than competitive synthesis baselines.
AI.conclusion: GFlowNet-based synthetic data generation offers a superior balance of fidelity, mode coverage, and authenticity for post-training LLMs, and produces synthetic conversations that yield stronger training signals for downstream outcome prediction compared to competitive synthesis baselines.

title: A Two-Echelon Covering Tour Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones for Post-Disaster Relief
summary: We introduce the two-echelon covering tour vehicle routing problem (2E-CTVRP) for the distribution of relief supplies after a disaster. In the first echelon, a fleet of trucks transports supplies and drones from a central depot to satellites at the periphery of the affected area. In the second echelon, drones launched in parallel from the satellites deliver the supplies to the centroids of victim clusters, which are obtained by clustering the victim locations, and each truck waits at a satellite until its drones have returned. The problem combines the assignment of satellites to trucks, the sequencing of the truck routes, and the assignment of clusters to satellites, and minimizes the sum of the arrival times of the trucks at the satellites and at the depot. We formulate the 2E-CTVRP as a mixed integer linear program and propose a hybrid metaheuristic, GRASP-ILS-PR, which combines greedy randomized construction, a single-trajectory search, and periodic path relinking on the assignment of clusters to satellites. On a new benchmark set of 110 instances, GRASP-ILS-PR finds all known optimal solutions within 30 seconds, matches or improves on the one-hour solutions of a commercial solver on most larger instances, and improves on them by up to 11% for instances with 50 satellites. It clearly outperforms a conventional GRASP with evolutionary path relinking and yields more consistent results than a simulated annealing algorithm that uses the same search components. An analysis of two fleet configurations shows that few large trucks minimize the cumulative arrival time in most instances, whereas many small trucks deliver supplies to the victims earlier and more equitably in every instance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the two-echelon covering tour vehicle routing problem (2E-CTVRP) for post-disaster relief distribution, formulates it as a mixed integer linear program, and proposes a hybrid metaheuristic (GRASP-ILS-PR) that outperforms benchmark solvers on 110 instances.
AI.motivation: Efficient routing of trucks and drones for delivering relief supplies to disaster victims is a critical logistics challenge. Existing routing models rarely address the combined assignment, sequencing, and coverage decisions across two echelons in this humanitarian context.
AI.method: A mixed integer linear program (MILP) formulation of the 2E-CTVRP, and a hybrid metaheuristic GRASP-ILS-PR combining greedy randomized construction, a single-trajectory (iterated local search) procedure, and periodic path relinking applied to the cluster-to-satellite assignment. A new benchmark set of 110 instances was used for evaluation against a commercial solver, a conventional GRASP with evolutionary path relinking, and a simulated annealing algorithm.
AI.result: GRASP-ILS-PR finds all known optimal solutions within 30 seconds, matches or improves upon one-hour solutions of a commercial solver on most larger instances, and improves them by up to 11% for instances with 50 satellites. It clearly outperforms conventional GRASP with evolutionary path relinking, and yields more consistent results than simulated annealing. Analysis of two fleet configurations shows few large trucks minimize cumulative arrival time in most instances, while many small trucks deliver supplies earlier and more equitably in every instance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GRASP-ILS-PR is an effective and efficient method for solving the 2E-CTVRP, delivering high-quality, consistent solutions. The fleet configuration analysis provides managerial insights showing a trade-off between minimizing cumulative arrival time and achieving earlier, more equitable delivery.

title: Can an AI Agent Rediscover a Blaschke-Curve Invariant?
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI). 8 pages, 1 figure. Code and data: https://github.com/yezeytuncu/blaschke-ai-rediscovery
summary: We study generalized Blaschke curves as a controlled environment for AI-assisted mathematical rediscovery. For one fixed degree-four Blaschke product, an agent receives numerical coordinates of the six pair-lines determined by each of 80 boundary configurations. The target theorem is withheld from the task instructions. The saved research log reports rejected geometric hypotheses and a homogeneous cubic fitted to polygon sides. Its frozen coefficients predict 480 lines from 80 unseen parameter values, with a recorded RMS scale-free residual of $8.88\times10^{-17}$. Discovery-set diagonals provide an out-of-fit consistency check, not a fully held-out test. A separate one-configuration run reports insufficient evidence for invariance. A post-review deterministic degree-search baseline also recovers the cubic, so the experiment does not establish an advantage over polynomial fitting. We present this single-instance case study as a protocol for separating conjecture, numerical validation, and proof, with explicit limitations concerning agent metadata, prior knowledge, and reproducibility.

AI.tldr: A single-instance case study uses degree-four Blaschke curves as a controlled testbed for AI-assisted mathematical rediscovery, where an agent recovers a homogeneous cubic from numerical data, but the experiment lacks evidence of advantage over straightforward polynomial fitting.
AI.motivation: To provide a controlled environment for studying AI-assisted mathematical rediscovery, separating conjecture, numerical validation, and proof, while making limitations explicit.
AI.method: Fix a degree-four Blaschke product; give an agent numerical coordinates of six pair-lines across 80 boundary configurations, withholding the target theorem. Record the research log of rejected hypotheses and a homogeneous cubic fitted to polygon sides; test prediction on 80 unseen parameter values and use discovery-set diagonals as an out-of-fit consistency check; additionally run a one-configuration invariance test and a post-review deterministic degree-search baseline.
AI.result: The frozen cubic predicts 480 lines from 80 unseen parameter values with RMS scale-free residual 8.88e-17. The one-configuration run gives insufficient evidence for invariance. The deterministic degree-search baseline also recovers the cubic, so no advantage over polynomial fitting is established. Discovery-set diagonals serve only as an out-of-fit check, not a fully held-out test.
AI.conclusion: The work is presented as a protocol for separating conjecture, numerical validation, and proof, with explicit limitations regarding agent metadata, prior knowledge, and reproducibility; it does not establish an AI advantage over polynomial fitting.

title: TALK-Dem: Benchmarking Embodied Task Planning under Dementia-Associated Communication Patterns
summary: Existing LLM-driven robot task planners rely on a taken-for-granted assumption of an ideal user whose instructions are clear, complete, and task-focused. However, when interacting with real-world users, especially those experiencing cognitive impairments, such as people living with dementia (PLWD), the planners often make mistakes and even pose physical safety risks. We proposed TALK-Dem (Talking Attributes and Linguistic Knowledge in Dementia), the first benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven robot task planning under dementia-associated verbal communication. TALK-Dem contains 4,800 instructions and covers five typical communication patterns, including Referential Imprecision, Object Substitution, Empty Speech, Topic Drift, and Intrusion, at three intensity levels. Experiments across six open-weight LLMs reveal a substantial robustness gap. Across communication patterns, open-weight models exhibited performance drops of up to 22.3 percentage points compared to ideal instructions. This revealed a critical gap and even danger for real-world applications, especially in assistive robotics, where locally deployable models are necessary due to privacy concerns and connectivity constraints. To mitigate this issue, we proposed the Context-Aware Retrieval from Experience (CARE) method, which retrieves relevant previously resolved tasks to provide task-specific interpretation and planning context. CARE generally outperformed standard prompting baselines across the six open-weight models, improving average task success by 18.1 percentage points over the vanilla prompt. These results highlighted the importance of both evaluating communication robustness and developing effective adaptation strategies for locally deployable assistive robots. The TALK-Dem dataset is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TALK-Dem-A6B3/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TALK-Dem, the first benchmark evaluating LLM-driven robot task planning under dementia-associated verbal communication, revealing a robustness gap up to 22.3 points, and proposes CARE, a context-aware retrieval method improving task success by 18.1 points.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-driven robot task planners assume an ideal user with clear, complete, task-focused instructions. Real users, especially people living with dementia (PLWD), violate this assumption, causing planner mistakes and physical safety risks. There is a need to evaluate robustness under atypical communication and to develop adaptation strategies for locally deployable assistive robots.
AI.method: Proposes TALK-Dem (Talking Attributes and Linguistic Knowledge in Dementia), a benchmark with 4,800 instructions covering five dementia-associated communication patterns (Referential Imprecision, Object Substitution, Empty Speech, Topic Drift, Intrusion) at three intensity levels. Evaluates six open-weight LLMs. Also proposes CARE (Context-Aware Retrieval from Experience), which retrieves relevant previously resolved tasks to supply task-specific interpretation and planning context.
AI.result: Across communication patterns, open-weight models showed performance drops of up to 22.3 percentage points versus ideal instructions. CARE generally outperformed standard prompting baselines across the six models, improving average task success by 18.1 percentage points over the vanilla prompt.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of evaluating communication robustness and developing effective adaptation strategies for locally deployable assistive robots. The TALK-Dem dataset is publicly released.

title: Self-Evolving Harness on Multiple Tasks with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer
summary: A harness is the code around a language-model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks never used during evolution. We frame the evolution process as deep-learning training with two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harness obtained at the end of the first stage improves the average score by 4.48 points on the in-distribution benchmarks and by 12.64 points on the out-of-distribution benchmarks, surpassing Codex on the former and matching it on the latter. In the second stage, continued evolution on Claw-Eval, one of the out-of-distribution benchmarks, further raises the score on that benchmark from 66.17 to 68.06, exceeding Codex. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms that emerged during evolution, including output truncation, history compaction, and independent review.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a recursive-self-improvement-style framework where the same frozen model acts first as solver then as proposer to directly edit its own harness, evolving across multi-domain tasks with staged multi-task pretraining and continual training, achieving gains over Codex on in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving harness methods rely on a separate proposer with a human-designed harness and evolve a distinct harness per benchmark, which fails to cover the diverse, multi-domain nature of real-world tasks in both evolution and evaluation. The work aims for a setup closer to recursive self-improvement and better generalization.
AI.method: A harness is the code around a language-model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. The same frozen model, on the same harness version, first solves tasks as solver, then as proposer reads complete run records and directly edits that harness. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks across domains. Training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, with five OOD benchmarks never used in evolution. Evolution is framed as deep-learning training with two stages: multi-task pretraining and continual training.
AI.result: From a 49-line seed harness, the first stage improves the average score by 4.48 points on in-distribution benchmarks and 12.64 points on out-of-distribution benchmarks, surpassing Codex on the former and matching it on the latter. In the second stage, continued evolution on Claw-Eval (an OOD benchmark) raises its score from 66.17 to 68.06, exceeding Codex.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables effective self-evolution of an agent harness by a single frozen model acting as both solver and proposer, generalizing across domains and outperforming or matching Codex. Analysis of emerged mechanisms, including output truncation, history compaction, and independent review, provides insight into how harnesses self-improve.

title: GestAdapt: Workspace-Conditioned Co-Speech Gesture Generation for Humanoid Robots
summary: Co-speech gestures for robots must adapt not only to speech and embodiment, but also to the workspace available for performing the motion. Since the same speech can be accompanied by different gestures, a robot can respond to workspace constraints, e.g., gestures for speech next to a wall. In these scenarios, the robot should gesture in a suitable motion rather than simply correcting an unconstrained one. To achieve this goal, we present GestAdapt, a workspace-conditioned framework that conditions co-speech gesture generation on a prescribed wrist workspace. The GestAdapt framework learns from six complementary co-speech corpora through a shared motion representation and supports retargeting to different robot embodiments. Quantitative evaluation shows that generated motions remain close to the real-motion distribution while respecting the workspace. In a user study, gestures generated under modified workspace constraints receive a mean quality score of 3.24/5, above our no-workspace variant (2.43/5) and below the reference motions (3.68/5). In a real robot evaluation, all compared motions are retargeted to the Reachy2 humanoid robot under identical workspace constraints. Motions generated with our framework rank first in 69.7\% of comparisons, higher than our no-workspace variant baseline and retargeted ground-truth motions constrained afterward. Overall, the results support adapting gestures to the available workspace during generation, rather than modifying unconstrained trajectories afterward to satisfy workspace constraints, potentially compromising gesture naturalness.

AI.tldr: GestAdapt is a workspace-conditioned framework that generates co-speech robot gestures constrained to a prescribed wrist workspace, learning from six corpora via a shared motion representation and supporting embodiment retargeting.
AI.motivation: Robot co-speech gestures must adapt to speech, embodiment, and the available workspace (e.g., gesturing near a wall). Since the same speech can pair with different gestures, robots should generate motion that is intrinsically suitable for the constrained workspace rather than generating unconstrained motion and correcting it afterward, which may compromise naturalness.
AI.method: GestAdapt conditions co-speech gesture generation on a prescribed wrist workspace. It learns from six complementary co-speech corpora through a shared motion representation and supports retargeting to different robot embodiments.
AI.result: Quantitative evaluation shows generated motions remain close to the real-motion distribution while respecting the workspace. In a user study, gestures under modified workspace constraints score 3.24/5 mean quality, above the no-workspace variant (2.43/5) and below reference motions (3.68/5). On the Reachy2 humanoid under identical constraints, GestAdapt motions rank first in 69.7% of comparisons, beating the no-workspace baseline and retargeted ground-truth motions constrained afterward.
AI.conclusion: Results support adapting gestures to the available workspace during generation rather than modifying unconstrained trajectories afterward to satisfy workspace constraints, which can compromise gesture naturalness.

title: Aligned Data Can Induce Misalignment via Context Confusion
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are frequently updated for various use cases, where filtering out misaligned training samples is a common practice for preventing post-update misalignment. However, alignment is inherently context-dependent: a recommendation that is aligned in one context may be inappropriate in another. For example, in response to the question "What should a researcher do with the research data?", recommending that the researcher preserve the data for reproducibility is aligned. In contrast, recommending data saving in response to "What should a mobile-app developer do with users' sensitive data?" may be inappropriate from a privacy perspective. Starting from this observation, we identify a post-training phenomenon where aligned training induces misaligned behavior in other contexts. We call this phenomenon **context confusion**. We demonstrate context confusion across three domains: (1) Gender Equality, (2) Privacy, and (3) Physical Safety. We further show that context confusion causes narrow misalignment, in contrast to emergent misalignment, and is not effectively reduced by injecting general alignment data, but can be substantially reduced by including targeted alignment data for the misaligned domain or providing in-context learning examples during inference. Lastly, we provide a mechanistic explanation of *context confusion*. We observe that queries from different domains can undergo similar representational shifts during the fine-tuning. Consequently, a query from a different domain may activate the same behavioral feature learned during fine-tuning, which causes the behavior to transfer to a context where it is misaligned. Based on our findings, we argue that it is difficult to predict the alignment state of a model after training by inspecting the training data alone, which highlights the importance of comprehensive post-training alignment evaluations.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and names "context confusion," a post-training phenomenon where alignment fine-tuning on one context causes misaligned behavior in another context, demonstrating it across Gender Equality, Privacy, and Physical Safety, and providing a mechanistic explanation.
AI.motivation: Model updates commonly filter out misaligned training samples to prevent post-update misalignment, but alignment is context-dependent: the same recommendation can be appropriate in one context and inappropriate in another. The authors aim to show that this context dependence makes context-specific alignment fine-tuning cause misalignment elsewhere, and that inspecting training data alone cannot predict a model's post-training alignment state.
AI.method: The authors investigate the phenomenon across three domains—(1) Gender Equality, (2) Privacy, and (3) Physical Safety—by fine-tuning on aligned training data and observing resulting behavior in other contexts. They test mitigations such as injecting general alignment data, including targeted alignment data for the misaligned domain, and providing in-context learning examples at inference. They also provide a mechanistic analysis of representational shifts of queries during fine-tuning and the activation of behavioral features.
AI.result: Aligned training induces misaligned behavior in other contexts (context confusion) across all three domains. Context confusion causes narrow misalignment, in contrast to emergent misalignment, and is not effectively reduced by injecting general alignment data, but is substantially reduced by including targeted alignment data for the misaligned domain or by providing in-context learning examples during inference. Mechanistically, queries from different domains undergo similar representational shifts during fine-tuning, so a query from a different domain can activate the same behavioral feature learned during fine-tuning, transferring the behavior to a context where it is misaligned.
AI.conclusion: The alignment state of a model after training is difficult to predict by inspecting the training data alone, which underscores the importance of comprehensive post-training alignment evaluations.

title: Memorize, Adapt, Ignore: Diagnosing Robot Learning Mechanisms under Training Data Variation
summary: Training data variation, whether through designing a domain randomization (DR) scheme in simulation or curating demonstrations for imitation learning, is a primary lever for improving the robustness of robotic manipulation policies. Yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, and practitioners typically select randomization parameters through expensive trial and error. We investigate these mechanisms through a series of case studies, randomizing object size, color, and type as well as scene lighting and linguistic prompts across settings including pick-and-place RL in ManiSkill and fine-tuning of vision-language-action (VLA) models on LIBERO and RoboTwin. We examine both model behavior and internal representations, using the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) as our primary diagnostic tool. We show that the NTK distinguishes a shift in the internal learning mechanism from \textit{memorizing} different situations with insufficient variation (e.g.\ learning what to do for a large cube, and what to do for a small cube) to \textit{adapting} to the situation at hand with sufficient variation. An NTK-based signal-to-noise ratio also helps distinguish when policies have learned to \emph{ignore} task-irrelevant factors (e.g.\ treating blue and red cubes identically, instead of learning a blue sub-policy and a red sub-policy). We use these diagnostics to develop practical guidance for designing DR schemes, selecting models, and detecting shortcut learning. We further compare different kinds of representations and validate our findings with real-world hardware experiments using ACT-based imitation learning.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how training data variation affects robotic manipulation policy robustness, using the empirical NTK to distinguish memorization from adaptation and to detect when policies ignore task-irrelevant factors, yielding practical guidance for domain randomization design.
AI.motivation: Training data variation (e.g., domain randomization in simulation or curated demonstrations for imitation learning) is a key lever for improving robustness of robotic manipulation policies, but its underlying mechanisms are poorly understood, and practitioners select randomization parameters via expensive trial and error.
AI.method: Case studies randomizing object size, color, and type, plus scene lighting and linguistic prompts, across pick-and-place RL in ManiSkill and fine-tuning of vision-language-action (VLA) models on LIBERO and RoboTwin. Both model behavior and internal representations are examined, using the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) as the primary diagnostic tool.
AI.result: The NTK distinguishes a shift in the internal learning mechanism from memorizing different situations under insufficient variation to adapting to the situation at hand under sufficient variation. An NTK-based signal-to-noise ratio distinguishes when policies ignore task-irrelevant factors rather than learning separate sub-policies. These diagnostics inform guidance for DR design, model selection, and shortcut learning detection. Comparisons across representation types and validation with real-world hardware experiments using ACT-based imitation learning support the findings.
AI.conclusion: The empirical NTK provides effective diagnostics for understanding and designing training data variation in robotic manipulation, enabling principled domain randomization scheme design, model selection, and detection of shortcut learning, validated in both simulation and real-world settings.

title: Fine-Tuning Diffusion Language Models with Context Selection and Target Weighting
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Main text 10 pages, references and appendix follow. Project page with interactive visualizations: https://loaym.github.io/GoldiMask/
summary: Supervised fine-tuning of discrete diffusion language models masks some response tokens and trains the model to recover their original values from the visible context. The masking pattern therefore determines both the context available to the model and the tokens it learns to predict. Uniform random masking does not explicitly account for the interaction between these choices. We introduce GoldiMask, which selects tokens to reveal as context by approximately maximizing a submodular objective. This objective uses model signals to balance the benefit of revealing tokens against their value as prediction targets. GoldiMask then weights the remaining targets according to how they benefit from the selected context and their remaining learning potential. Across three backbones and three training datasets, GoldiMask achieves the highest average accuracy in most evaluated settings, demonstrating gains on both reasoning and code generation. Component ablations show that both context selection and target weighting contribute to the gains. GoldiMask also reduces decoding iterations on GSM8K and MATH-500 under confidence-threshold parallel decoding, while maintaining comparable accuracy at higher confidence thresholds.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GoldiMask, a masking strategy for supervised fine-tuning of discrete diffusion language models that jointly optimizes which tokens to reveal as context and which to use as prediction targets via a submodular objective, improving accuracy on reasoning and code tasks.
AI.motivation: In supervised fine-tuning of discrete diffusion language models, masking determines both the visible context and the prediction targets, but uniform random masking ignores the interaction between these two roles, leaving performance on the table.
AI.method: GoldiMask selects context tokens by approximately maximizing a submodular objective that uses model signals to balance the benefit of revealing tokens against their value as prediction targets, then weights the remaining targets by how much they benefit from the selected context and their remaining learning potential.
AI.result: Across three backbones and three training datasets, GoldiMask attains the highest average accuracy in most settings, with gains on reasoning and code generation, and ablations confirm both context selection and target weighting contribute. It also reduces decoding iterations on GSM8K and MATH-500 under confidence-threshold parallel decoding while keeping comparable accuracy at higher confidence thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing context selection and target weighting via a submodular, model-signal-driven masking strategy yields consistent accuracy and efficiency improvements for fine-tuning discrete diffusion language models.

title: Draft: A Parametric Tool for Robot Design Exploration
summary: Robot performance is often limited by the cost of iterating on morphology and control together, since every computer-aided design (CAD) change has to be carried into a simulation-ready model before control work begins. Co-design methods attempt to close this gap, but each uses a model generator written for a single platform or lack the use of real-world data to suggest that designs are plausible. We present Draft, a parametric generation tool whose generalized engine compiles any parametric tree of serial chains into a simulation-ready MJCF model, without CAD. It allows engineers to explore design tradeoffs through easily adjustable models and evaluate how changes influence controller performance. Draft grounds the free parameters of each design using trends fitted to a survey of $114$ actuators and $49$ published robot descriptions, so that a generated robot is anchored to real-world hardware. We validate those trends wholistically by building twins of four off-the-shelf robots, whose masses agree to $1.10\times$ geometric mean fold error. Finally, we demonstrate how Draft exposes design tradeoffs by evaluating three quadrupeds through a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum.

AI.tldr: Draft is a parametric generation tool that compiles any tree of serial chains into a simulation-ready MJCF model without CAD, uses actuator and robot survey data to ground design parameters in real hardware, validates via twins of four commercial robots, and demonstrates design tradeoffs by evaluating three quadrupeds under an RL curriculum.
AI.motivation: Robot performance is constrained by the high cost of iterating on morphology and control jointly, since every CAD change must be converted to a simulation-ready model before control work can proceed. Existing co-design methods are limited: each relies on a model generator built for a single platform, and they lack real-world data to establish that generated designs are plausible.
AI.method: Draft employs a generalized engine that compiles any parametric tree of serial chains into a simulation-ready MJCF model without CAD. It enables exploration of design tradeoffs through easily adjustable models and assessment of how changes affect controller performance. Free design parameters are grounded using trends fitted to a survey of 114 actuators and 49 published robot descriptions.
AI.result: Whole-perspective validation was performed by building twins of four off-the-shelf robots whose masses agree with a 1.10x geometric mean fold error. Design tradeoffs were then exposed by evaluating three quadrupeds through a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum.
AI.conclusion: Draft provides a platform-agnostic, CAD-free pipeline for morphology-control co-design that anchors generated robots to real-world hardware via empirical trends, and it effectively surfaces design tradeoffs for controller evaluation.

title: Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill: A Model-Free Controller and Its Generalization Limits
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Includes negative generalization results for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, and two-GPU tensor parallelism
summary:
Concurrent autoregressive inference creates a fundamental interference problem: prefilling a newly arrived long prompt can delay tokens for requests that are already decoding. Fixed prefill chunks reduce this interference, but the best chunk size depends on the model, hardware, load, and latency objective. We introduce Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill (DLFP), a model-free controller that changes only prefill work that overlaps active decodes. After a guarded scheduling cycle, DLFP uses the observed interval as proportional feedback to resize the next prefill chunk; isolated prefills remain unrestricted.
  We implement DLFP in vLLM and evaluate it with open-loop Poisson arrivals, exact token accounting, raw request traces, and NVIDIA telemetry. On Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 on one A100 80 GB GPU, three paired 100-request trials reduce P99 inter-token latency by 24.8%, 30.1%, and 28.2% (mean 27.7%, paired 95% confidence interval 21.0% to 34.3%) with exact output agreement, no failures, and unchanged SLO compliance. The benefit is not free: mean P99 time to first token increases 34.8% while remaining inside the declared SLO.
  Crucially, the mechanism does not generalize to Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, or a two-GPU tensor-parallel configuration. We trace the failure to an asynchronous scheduler-call interval that is only a proxy for completed GPU iteration time. This negative result defines the boundary of the contribution and motivates a completion-timed controller for concurrent CPU and on-device inference. We do not claim mobile-device performance; the present work is a reproducible proof-of-concept and generalization study.

AI.tldr: DLFP is a model-free feedback controller in vLLM that dynamically resizes overlapping prefill chunks to cut decode latency interference, achieving ~27.7% lower P99 inter-token latency on Qwen3-0.6B but failing to generalize to larger models and tensor-parallel setups.
AI.motivation: Concurrent autoregressive inference suffers an interference problem: prefilling a newly arrived long prompt delays already-decoding requests. Fixed prefill chunk sizes mitigate this but their optimal value varies with model, hardware, load, and latency objective, so a static setting is inadequate.
AI.method: Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill (DLFP), a model-free controller that restricts only prefill work overlapping active decodes. After a guarded scheduling cycle, it uses the observed interval as proportional feedback to resize the next prefill chunk, while isolated prefills remain unrestricted. It is implemented in vLLM and evaluated with open-loop Poisson arrivals, exact token accounting, raw request traces, and NVIDIA telemetry.
AI.result: On Qwen3-0.6B (BF16, one A100 80 GB GPU), three paired 100-request trials reduced P99 inter-token latency by 24.8%, 30.1%, and 28.2% (mean 27.7%, paired 95% CI 21.0%-34.3%), with exact output agreement, no failures, and unchanged SLO compliance. Mean P99 time to first token rose 34.8% but stayed within SLO. Benefits did not generalize to Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, or a two-GPU tensor-parallel config, traced to an asynchronous scheduler-call interval that only approximates completed GPU iteration time.
AI.conclusion: DLFP is a reproducible proof-of-concept yielding substantial decode-latency gains in one setting, but the negative result defines the boundary of its contribution and motivates a completion-timed controller for concurrent CPU and on-device inference. No mobile-device performance is claimed.

title: PneuTac: Tactile Manipulation with Soft Pneumatic Robots via Unified MPM-Gaussian Splatting Simulation
summary: Soft robots and tactile sensors have demonstrated great potential in delicate manipulation tasks. Soft pneumatic robots enable safe contact through compliance, and vision-based tactile sensors offer high-resolution touch perception. However, learning tactile manipulation with compliant robots has been challenging, bottlenecked by the lack of efficient simulation. Existing simulators typically model them in isolation, and exhibit large calibration gaps that are difficult to overcome efficiently. We present PneuTac, a unified framework for tactile-feedback manipulation with soft pneumatic robots. We leverage the material point method (MPM) for modelling the dynamics of the soft robot and the deformable tactile membrane, and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) for rendering. Real-to-sim modelling is done with a simple vision-based method, to then train action and perception networks for efficient simulation with surrogate models. We use the framework to drive a tactile-guided pipeline to collect demonstrations in simulation. Through experiments on a custom-designed pneumatic soft finger with a tactile sensing tip, together with additional cross-device evaluations, we show that PneuTac is capable of accurately modelling soft robots with tactile sensors, and that policies trained with simulation-augmented demonstrations outperform baselines trained on the same real data on three real-world contact-rich compliant manipulation tasks, making it a practical framework for tactile manipulation on compliant hardware.

AI.tldr: PneuTac is a unified simulation framework that couples the material point method (MPM) with 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) to jointly model soft pneumatic robots and vision-based tactile sensors, enabling simulation-augmented policy learning for contact-rich compliant manipulation.
AI.motivation: Soft pneumatic robots provide safe contact via compliance, and vision-based tactile sensors provide high-resolution touch perception, but learning tactile manipulation on compliant hardware is bottlenecked by inefficient simulation. Existing simulators model the robot and sensor in isolation and exhibit large calibration gaps that are hard to overcome efficiently.
AI.method: PneuTac uses MPM to model the dynamics of both the soft robot and the deformable tactile membrane, and 3DGS for rendering. Real-to-sim modelling is performed with a simple vision-based method, after which action and perception networks are trained to serve as efficient surrogate models. The framework drives a tactile-guided pipeline that collects demonstrations in simulation.
AI.result: Experiments on a custom-designed pneumatic soft finger with a tactile sensing tip, plus cross-device evaluations, show that PneuTac accurately models soft robots with tactile sensors, and that policies trained with simulation-augmented demonstrations outperform baselines trained on the same real data across three real-world contact-rich compliant manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: PneuTac is a practical framework for tactile manipulation on compliant hardware, showing that unified, accurate soft-robot-plus-tactile-sensor simulation can effectively augment real demonstrations and improve real-world policy performance.

title: MetaPersona: Task-Grounded Synthetic Populations from Empirical Social Science
summary: Personas used to seed LLM social simulations face a cold-start problem: existing methods lack a principled basis for deciding which attributes to include and how to assign their values. As a result, synthetic populations may misrepresent the demographic composition, latent attributes, and dependency structure that shape downstream behavior. We introduce MetaPersona-DB, a dataset of 11,000+ empirical human-subjects studies annotated with task-relevant variables, reported relationships, and aggregate-level population statistics. Building on this resource, we propose MetaPersona, a framework that retrieves task-relevant evidence, constructs literature-derived persona dependency graphs, and samples synthetic populations from empirical priors linking demographics, latent attributes, and outcomes. Across three downstream case studies, three baselines, and three frontier models, results vary by task and model: MetaPersona performs strongly on misinformation belief and AI-tool sentiment, while results on income redistribution are mixed. It also reduces persona-construction cost to under $0.5 per task using GPT-5.2. Finally, we present MetaPersona-Studio, a prototype interactive interface for empirically grounded persona generation.

AI.tldr: MetaPersona-DB and MetaPersona address the cold-start problem in LLM social simulations by grounding persona construction in empirical priors retrieved from over 11,000 studies, enabling evidence-based synthetic population sampling that performs strongly on some tasks but mixed on others, at under $0.5 per task.
AI.motivation: Personas that seed LLM social simulations suffer from a cold-start problem: current methods lack a principled basis for selecting which attributes to include and how to assign their values. This leads to synthetic populations that may misrepresent demographic composition, latent attributes, and dependency structure, thereby distorting downstream behavior.
AI.method: The authors introduce MetaPersona-DB, a dataset of 11,000+ empirical human-subjects studies annotated with task-relevant variables, reported relationships, and aggregate-level population statistics. Building on it, they propose MetaPersona, a framework that retrieves task-relevant evidence, constructs literature-derived persona dependency graphs, and samples synthetic populations from empirical priors linking demographics, latent attributes, and outcomes. They also present MetaPersona-Studio, a prototype interactive interface for empirically grounded persona generation.
AI.result: Across three downstream case studies, three baselines, and three frontier models, performance varies by task and model: MetaPersona performs strongly on misinformation belief and AI-tool sentiment, while results on income redistribution are mixed. Persona-construction cost is reduced to under $0.5 per task using GPT-5.2.
AI.conclusion: Grounding persona generation in empirical literature-derived priors and dependency graphs offers a principled, low-cost alternative to ad hoc persona construction, though its benefits are task- and model-dependent rather than uniformly superior.

title: A Reachability-based Safety Certificate for Dynamical System Motion Policies
summary: Dynamical Systems (DS) are reactive motion policies representing vector fields trained with theoretical guarantees of stability and convergence. To ensure safety during deployment in unknown environments they must be locally reshaped, either through modulation or geometric control barrier function strategies. However, depending on the geometry of the obstacles and the complexity of the DS, these local strategies can lead the system to unavoidable collisions or spurious attractors. In this work, we certify safety with a value function drawn from the notion of backward reachability tube, which measures the worst-case safety along a rollout trajectory of the nominal DS. Usually, such a value function is intractable for a controlled system due to curse of dimensionality. We show that in the DS-based learning-from-demonstration setting, the absence of a control input collapses the reachability problem to a deterministic rollout, and the presence of certain stability conditions truncates the infinite horizon to a finite one, resulting in a well-defined value function. We further show that the value function we devised is the maximal forward-invariant subset of the obstaclefree region for the nominal DS flow. The application of this certificate function is validated across five DS constructions - analytical, Neural ODE, diffeomorphic latent space, LPV-DS, SE(3)and validate it on a Franka manipulator. Modulation and geometric CBFs also suffer from saddle point in cases of headon approach towards an unsafe zone. We show that CBF-on-V avoids this pitfall entirely.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a value function derived from backward reachability to certify safety of Dynamical Systems motion policies, exploiting the deterministic rollout and stability conditions to make the infinite-horizon problem tractable, and shows this certificate defines the maximal forward-invariant subset of the obstacle-free region.
AI.motivation: Dynamical Systems trained with stability and convergence guarantees still require local reshaping (modulation or geometric CBF) for safe deployment in unknown environments. These local strategies can cause unavoidable collisions or spurious attractors depending on obstacle geometry and DS complexity, and they suffer from saddle points during head-on approaches to unsafe zones, so a global safety certificate is needed.
AI.method: The authors define a value function based on the backward reachability tube that measures worst-case safety along a rollout of the nominal DS. They show that the absence of a control input collapses the reachability problem into a deterministic rollout, and that stability conditions truncate the infinite horizon to a finite one, yielding a well-defined value function. They then apply this certificate (CBF-on-V) to ensure safety.
AI.result: The value function is proven to be the maximal forward-invariant subset of the obstacle-free region for the nominal DS flow. The certificate is validated across five DS constructions: analytical, Neural ODE, diffeomorphic latent space, LPV-DS, and SE(3), and validated on a Franka manipulator. CBF-on-V is shown to avoid the saddle-point pitfall that modulation and geometric CBFs suffer from during head-on approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed backward-reachability-tube value function provides a tractable global safety certificate for DS-based learning-from-demonstration, characterizing the maximal forward-invariant safe set and overcoming the saddle-point limitations of modulation and geometric CBF strategies, as demonstrated across multiple DS constructions and on a Franka manipulator.

title: SimTrace: Grounded Multimodal User Trajectories Generation for Online User Modeling
summary: Virtual clients offer a cost-effective approach to support applications such as A/B testing, recommender system development, and interface evaluation. However, building them requires access to large-scale, semantically faithful, fine-grained online user trajectories. These data are difficult to obtain because proprietary logs are subject to privacy restrictions and small businesses often lack sufficient traffic. Consequently, existing public datasets either abstract away fine-grained user interaction details or preserve rich context but remain platform-specific and small-scale. To address this gap, we propose SimTrace, a framework that generates faithful, fine-grained synthetic multimodal clickstreams through a computer-use client agent that is grounded in real user trajectories and the given web environment. SimTrace anonymizes real interactions and constructs a simulated twin of the given web environment, then uses both to generate synthetic interaction trajectories. Each action is paired with its corresponding web observations and user context, yielding a shareable alternative to confidential logs for developing computer-use agent-style virtual clients. We apply SimTrace to an e-commerce setting and evaluate both its fidelity and downstream utility. SimTrace outperforms competing baselines on 7 out of 8 fidelity metrics. Models trained on synthetic data achieve performance comparable to those trained on real data on downstream tasks such as purchase prediction and recommendation.
