For next action prediction task, augmenting real data with synthetic data further improves accuracy by 11.0% relative to training on real data alone. We release SimTrace as an open-source package to facilitate research on online user behavior modeling.

AI.tldr: SimTrace is a framework that generates faithful, fine-grained synthetic multimodal clickstreams using a computer-use client agent grounded in real user trajectories and the web environment, providing a shareable alternative to confidential logs.
AI.motivation: Virtual clients support applications like A/B testing, recommender systems, and interface evaluation, but building them needs large-scale, semantically faithful, fine-grained online user trajectories. Such data are hard to obtain because proprietary logs face privacy restrictions and small businesses lack traffic. Existing public datasets either abstract away fine-grained interaction details or preserve rich context but are platform-specific and small-scale.
AI.method: SimTrace anonymizes real interactions and constructs a simulated twin of the given web environment, then uses both to generate synthetic interaction trajectories. Each action is paired with corresponding web observations and user context. It is applied to an e-commerce setting and evaluated on fidelity and downstream utility.
AI.result: SimTrace outperforms competing baselines on 7 of 8 fidelity metrics. Models trained on synthetic data match real-data performance on purchase prediction and recommendation. For next action prediction, augmenting real data with synthetic data improves accuracy by 11.0% relative to real data alone.
AI.conclusion: SimTrace offers a shareable, open-source alternative to confidential logs for developing computer-use agent-style virtual clients and facilitating research on online user behavior modeling.

title: Embodiment-aware control by inference over the operator: a simulation study
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/sa-falcone/uee-embodiment-sim (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23044669)
summary: Teleoperation systems are tuned for channel fidelity, while whether the operator experiences the device as part of the body, the Sense of Embodiment (SoE), is measured only afterwards, by questionnaire. Predictive-processing accounts suggest controlling devices to reduce the mismatch between the operator's predictions and the returned feedback, but those predictions are unobservable, and an objective that only penalizes mismatch is minimized by removing feedback. We formulate an embodiment-aware controller, the Universal Embodiment Engine (UEE), that infers the operator's embodiment and visuo-proprioceptive cue weighting from implicit gaze and pupil signals and task outcome, and chooses bounded device settings under explicit preferences, cast as a discrete Active Inference agent. In simulations with 300 heterogeneous synthetic operators, the UEE found the suitable setting within half a minute for most operators, before identifying their exact type, and came close to an oracle in the second half of the session (embodiment 1.68 against 0.73 for the best fixed setting, on a 0-2 scale). Adapting without reading the operator did no better than fixed control, and model-free bandits did worse, whereas an expected-utility controller with the same inference did exactly as well: the benefit comes from Bayesian inference over the operator with explicit preferences, not from the information-seeking term of Active Inference. A naive prediction-error minimizer withheld feedback, as its objective implies, and lost task success (0.74 vs 0.90). The benefit shrank but persisted for operators outside the controller's model family, grew with the variety of the population, and vanished when the controller trusted an uninformative signal or when cue weighting changed mid-session without being modeled. These failures show what studies with people must establish first: calibrated signals and a model of change.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce the Universal Embodiment Engine (UEE), a discrete Active Inference controller that infers an operator's Sense of Embodiment (SoE) and visuo-proprioceptive cue weighting from implicit gaze and pupil signals plus task outcome, and selects bounded device settings accordingly. In simulations with 300 heterogeneous synthetic operators, UEE approached oracle-level embodiment within a single session, outperforming fixed control and model-free bandits; the benefit derived from Bayesian inference over the operator with explicit preferences rather than the Active Inference information-seeking term.
AI.motivation: Teleoperation systems are typically tuned for channel fidelity, and the operator's Sense of Embodiment is assessed only retrospectively via questionnaire. Predictive-processing accounts suggest controlling devices to minimize prediction-feedback mismatch, but operator predictions are unobservable and a pure mismatch-penalizing objective is trivially minimized by removing feedback. This motivates an objective, embodiment-aware control formulation that infers embodiment online.
AI.method: The Universal Embodiment Engine (UEE) is formulated as a discrete Active Inference agent that infers the operator's embodiment and visuo-proprioceptive cue weighting from implicit gaze and pupil signals and task outcome, then chooses bounded device settings under explicit preferences. It was evaluated in simulations with 300 heterogeneous synthetic operators and compared against an oracle, the best fixed setting, adaptation without operator reading, model-free bandits, an expected-utility controller sharing the same inference, and a naive prediction-error minimizer.
AI.result: UEE found a suitable setting within about half a minute for most operators, before identifying their exact type, and approached oracle performance in the session's second half (embodiment 1.68 vs. 0.73 for the best fixed setting on a 0-2 scale). Adapting without reading the operator matched fixed control, model-free bandits did worse, and the expected-utility controller with identical inference performed equally well. A naive prediction-error minimizer withheld feedback and reduced task success (0.74 vs. 0.90). The benefit shrank but persisted for out-of-family operators, grew with population variety, and vanished with an uninformative signal or unmodeled mid-session changes in cue weighting.
AI.conclusion: Embodiment-aware control can be achieved by Bayesian inference over the operator with explicit preferences, and the advantage stems from this inference rather than from Active Inference's information-seeking term. The observed failure modes indicate that human studies must first establish calibrated implicit signals and a model of change.

title: ArgGYM: A Procedural, Engine-Verified Benchmark for Structured Defeasible Reasoning
summary: Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings (weakest-link and last-link), and two set orderings (elitist and democratic), while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances for evaluation that reduces dependence on static test sets and for verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. We release the benchmark, generators, and verifiers for reproducible evaluation and RLVR training.

AI.tldr: ArgGYM is a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning, grounded in a symbolic argumentation engine, with 12 tasks, a frozen 1,440-instance benchmark, and fresh instance generators for evaluation and reward training.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning progress has relied on automatically verifiable rewards in math, code, and formal logic, where specifications are fixed and evaluation is stable. It is unclear whether such success transfers to real-world reasoning that occurs under incomplete and revisable information, where conclusions can be provisional, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated, or revised—i.e., defeasible reasoning.
AI.method: ArgGYM decomposes defeasible reasoning into twelve tasks and uses a symbolic argumentation engine to compute formal states that ground task-specific scoring. The benchmark includes 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings (weakest-link, last-link), and two set orderings (elitist, democratic). The same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances for dynamic evaluation and verifiable-reward RLVR training.
AI.result: On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models exhibit sharply different reasoning profiles. Models can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations involving longer dependencies and more interacting structures.
AI.conclusion: ArgGYM provides a reproducible benchmark, generators, and verifiers for evaluating and training structured defeasible reasoning, enabling dynamic evaluation that reduces reliance on static test sets and supporting verifiable-reward RLVR training.

title: BIND: Binding 3D Robot Actions to 2D Image Features
summary: We introduce BIND, a new action representation for visuomotor robot policies that binds 3D robot actions to their corresponding 2D image features, yielding strong data efficiency gains and robustness to out-of-distribution object positions and camera viewpoints. The action heads of current robot policies are typically formulated as an MLP regression from a single global feature vector produced by a pre-trained vision encoder. This global formulation requires the policy network to discover, from demonstrations alone, the relationship between target robot actions and the image features they project onto. The consequence is that although modern image features are semantically descriptive, spatially robust, and even multiview-consistent, the policies built on them are brittle to subtle changes in camera viewpoint and object placement--and surprisingly data-inefficient. BIND closes this gap by supplying the action-feature relationship through camera geometry rather than learning: it discretizes a volume of candidate end effector positions, attaches each candidate to the pre-trained features at its projection in each camera view, and selects actions by scoring each candidate's position and image-bound feature combination. On a real robot, we study data efficiency and out-of-distribution robustness to unseen object positions and camera viewpoints, as well as general long-horizon task execution and dexterity. We find BIND to be highly data-efficient and robust: it achieves near-perfect success on tasks with as few as 5 demonstrations, and degrades gracefully under steep camera-viewpoint shifts and held-out object positions where coordinate-regression baselines completely fail.

AI.tldr: BIND is a new action representation that binds 3D robot actions to their projected 2D image features via camera geometry, giving strong data efficiency and robustness to unseen object positions and viewpoints.
AI.motivation: Current visuomotor policies use MLP regression from a single global feature vector of a pre-trained vision encoder. This forces the policy to learn action-feature relationships only from demonstrations, resulting in brittleness to subtle camera viewpoint and object placement changes, and surprising data inefficiency despite descriptive, spatially robust image features.
AI.method: BIND supplies the action-feature relationship through camera geometry rather than learning. It discretizes a volume of candidate end effector positions, attaches each candidate to pre-trained features at its projection in each camera view, and selects actions by scoring each candidate's position and image-bound feature combination.
AI.result: On a real robot, BIND achieves near-perfect success with as few as 5 demonstrations and degrades gracefully under steep camera-viewpoint shifts and held-out object positions where coordinate-regression baselines completely fail. It also supports long-horizon task execution and dexterity.
AI.conclusion: Binding 3D actions to 2D image features via camera geometry yields a highly data-efficient and robust action representation for visuomotor robot policies.

title: A Competing-Hazards Systematization of Loss of Control in Autonomous Agents
summary: Leading AI developers have reported agents acting beyond their approved limits, which a United Nations panel described as an early warning of loss of human control. Yet incident reports and agent-safety evaluations describe these events differently, making it difficult to compare failures, trace risk across attempts, or separate agent behavior from the environment's role in allowing an out-of-scope action to succeed. To address this gap, we introduce a common framework in which each attempt ends in approved completion, safe stopping, scope escape, or continuation. We formalize the framework as a discrete-time competing-hazards model and derive escape probability within a retry budget, a model-conditional safe-budget limit, and conditions for estimation from execution logs. We audit 22 incident reports and 102 agent-safety evaluations published from January 2025 to September 2026 using primary sources. Six incidents involved tasks that could not be completed within scope, thirteen involved agents that continued rather than stopped, and five did not report stopping behavior. Developers' figures imply a task-level incidence ratio near 47 for out-of-scope coordination in never-solved versus solved tasks. Among evaluations, 87 recorded an out-of-scope effect or specification violation, 26 treated safe stopping as a first-class outcome, only 20 recorded both, and 79 merged budget exhaustion with failure. In 20 of 22 incidents, the environment allowed an out-of-scope effect, indicating that realized loss of control often reflected persistent agent behavior interacting with permissive boundary conditions; meanwhile, no evaluation reported all fields needed to estimate the full competing-hazards process from published evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a competing-hazards framework (outcomes: approved completion, safe stopping, scope escape, continuation) for agent out-of-scope behavior, formalizes escape probability and safe-budget limits, audits 22 incident reports and 102 agent-safety evaluations, and finds reporting fields insufficient to estimate the full process.
AI.motivation: Incident reports and agent-safety evaluations describe agent out-of-scope behavior inconsistently, hindering comparison of failures, risk tracing across attempts, and separation of agent behavior from environmental permissiveness. A common formal framework is needed to unify these accounts.
AI.method: Discrete-time competing-hazards model with four terminal outcome categories (approved completion, safe stopping, scope escape, continuation). Derivation of escape probability within a retry budget, a model-conditional safe-budget limit, and identifiability conditions for estimation from execution logs. Audit of 22 incident reports and 102 agent-safety evaluations (Jan 2025–Sep 2026) using primary sources.
AI.result: Six incidents involved tasks unachievable within scope; thirteen involved continuation instead of stopping; five omitted stopping behavior. Developer figures imply a task-level incidence ratio near 47 for out-of-scope coordination in never-solved vs. solved tasks. Among evaluations: 87 recorded an out-of-scope effect or specification violation, 26 treated safe stopping as a first-class outcome, only 20 recorded both, and 79 merged budget exhaustion with failure. In 20/22 incidents the environment permitted the out-of-scope effect. No evaluation reported all fields required to estimate the full competing-hazards process from published evidence.
AI.conclusion: Realized loss of control often reflects persistent agent behavior interacting with permissive boundary conditions. Current reporting practices lack the fields needed for full process estimation, so the proposed framework and derived quantities provide a basis for more comparable, risk-traceable, and estimable agent-safety evidence, contingent on improved logging.

title: Observability Analysis and Online Calibration of Visual-Inertial-Wheel Odometry for 4WIS4WID Mobile Robots
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: In this paper, we present a visual-inertial-wheel odometry (VIWO) framework with online calibration for four-wheel independently steered and driven (4WIS4WID) mobile robots. We derive a 2D odometry model directly from the four driving velocities and steering angles, using both the longitudinal rolling constraints and the lateral no-slip constraints of all wheels. A preintegration model and analytical Jacobians are developed for efficient filtering and calibration. An observability analysis of the linearized VIWO system shows that a drive-only model makes all steering offsets unobservable, whereas the proposed redundant model restores their observability. The analysis also identifies four standard VINS unobservable directions and three additional directions associated with the arbitrary placement of the odometry reference frame. Furthermore, we characterize several degenerate motions, including zero yaw rate, constant steering, and a non-rolling wheel, and derive the corresponding excitation conditions for the thirteen wheel intrinsics that remain after fixing the odometry frame reference. The performance of the proposed system has been demonstrated in both simulation and real-world experiments on a 4WIS4WID mobile robot.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a visual-inertial-wheel odometry framework with online calibration for four-wheel independently steered and driven (4WIS4WID) mobile robots, deriving a 2D odometry model from all four wheels' velocities and steering angles, and analyzes its observability and degeneracies.
AI.motivation: Accurate odometry for 4WIS4WID robots is challenging because conventional drive-only models cannot observe steering offsets. The paper is motivated by the need for a calibrated, observable odometry model that exploits the redundant constraints of all wheels.
AI.method: The authors derive a 2D odometry model directly from four driving velocities and steering angles using longitudinal rolling and lateral no-slip constraints of all wheels. They develop a preintegration model with analytical Jacobians for efficient filtering and online calibration. They perform observability analysis of the linearized VIWO system, comparing a drive-only model with the proposed redundant model, and characterize degenerate motions and excitation conditions for thirteen wheel intrinsics.
AI.result: The observability analysis shows that the drive-only model leaves all steering offsets unobservable, whereas the redundant model restores their observability. It identifies four standard VINS unobservable directions plus three additional directions from the arbitrary odometry reference frame. Degenerate motions include zero yaw rate, constant steering, and a non-rolling wheel, with corresponding excitation conditions for the thirteen wheel intrinsics. Performance is validated in simulation and real-world experiments on a 4WIS4WID mobile robot.
AI.conclusion: The proposed redundant VIWO model with online calibration improves observability of steering offsets and wheel intrinsics for 4WIS4WID robots, with excitation conditions guiding calibration. Simulation and real-world experiments confirm the system's effectiveness.

title: AIM: Agentic Idea Management for Automated Research
summary: Frontier LLMs are increasingly used to automate scientific research through iterative search. We distinguish idea-driven search from solution-driven search and identify three core challenges: organizing evolving research ideas, selecting promising directions, and maintaining alignment between ideas and their implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce the Agentic Idea Manager (AIM), a fully autonomous framework for managing and exploring research directions in idea-driven automated research. Inspired by Bayesian optimization, AIM uses an Agentic Surrogate and an Agentic Acquisition mechanism to organize discovered ideas and guide their selection. A Solution Auditor maintains idea-solution integrity, while a Resource Planner adaptively allocates the remaining experimental budget across parallel search branches. Experiments on 10 AutoLab benchmark tasks show that AIM surpasses the strongest baseline by 1.6 percentage points on System Optimization tasks and 4.9 percentage points on long-horizon Model Development & CUDA tasks. Notably, AIM reaches the best baseline performance up to 3.1x faster in wall-clock time. We further provide a theoretical analysis of when searching over ideas becomes beneficial. Our analysis shows that explicit idea-level allocation makes semantic coverage directly controllable, and that broader coverage becomes increasingly valuable when competitive research directions are sparse among many plausible alternatives. Project Page: https://imhgchoi.github.io/agentic-idea-manager/

AI.tldr: AIM is a fully autonomous framework that manages idea-driven automated research by organizing evolving research ideas, selecting promising directions, and keeping ideas aligned with implementations, outperforming the strongest baseline and reaching baseline performance up to 3.1x faster.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs are increasingly used to automate scientific research via iterative search, but idea-driven search faces three core challenges: organizing evolving research ideas, selecting promising directions, and maintaining alignment between ideas and their implementations.
AI.method: Inspired by Bayesian optimization, AIM employs an Agentic Surrogate and an Agentic Acquisition mechanism to organize discovered ideas and guide selection. A Solution Auditor maintains idea-solution integrity, and a Resource Planner adaptively allocates remaining experimental budget across parallel search branches. A theoretical analysis examines when searching over ideas is beneficial.
AI.result: On 10 AutoLab benchmark tasks, AIM surpasses the strongest baseline by 1.6 percentage points on System Optimization tasks and 4.9 percentage points on long-horizon Model Development & CUDA tasks, and reaches the best baseline performance up to 3.1x faster in wall-clock time. Theoretical analysis shows explicit idea-level allocation makes semantic coverage directly controllable, and broader coverage becomes increasingly valuable when competitive research directions are sparse among many plausible alternatives.
AI.conclusion: AIM, a fully autonomous agentic idea manager, effectively addresses core challenges of idea-driven automated research, improving performance and efficiency over baselines, with theory clarifying when idea-level search is advantageous.

title: TrafficSignBench: Rule-Centric Closed-Loop Evaluation of Traffic-Sign Compliance in Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving planners are typically evaluated using aggregate metrics such as driving score, destination rate, and collision rate, which do not explicitly measure compliance with traffic rules. As a result, planners can achieve high benchmark scores while still exhibiting unsafe or illegal behaviors, limiting their applicability to real-world deployment. To address this gap, we introduce TrafficSignBench, a large-scale, traffic sign-centric benchmark for systematic and interpretable evaluation of traffic-rule compliance in autonomous driving. Our framework combines real-map-based simulation for realistic road layouts with rule-targeted procedural scenario generation for scalable and balanced coverage of underrepresented rules. We implement traffic rules corresponding to 34 traffic signs, each equipped with an automatic rule checker for detecting violations during closed-loop execution. This design yields 29,000 diverse road scenes and 29 distinct testing scenario types, enabling controlled evaluation of rule-specific planner behavior. We construct 5,800 testing scenes and demonstrate that current autonomous driving planners can exhibit poor traffic-rule compliance despite strong performance on standard evaluation metrics. To address this limitation, we transform existing planners into rule-compliant trajectory experts via explicit traffic-sign constraints, enabling scalable generation of high-quality oracle trajectories for fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TrafficSignBench, a traffic-sign-centric benchmark for interpretable evaluation of traffic-rule compliance in autonomous driving planners, revealing that current planners can score well on standard metrics yet violate rules, and proposes generating rule-compliant oracle trajectories for fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Standard aggregate metrics (driving score, destination rate, collision rate) do not explicitly measure compliance with traffic rules, allowing planners to achieve high benchmark scores while still exhibiting unsafe or illegal behaviors, which limits real-world deployment. There is a gap in systematic, interpretable evaluation of rule compliance.
AI.method: TrafficSignBench combines real-map-based simulation for realistic road layouts with rule-targeted procedural scenario generation for scalable, balanced coverage of underrepresented rules. It implements traffic rules for 34 traffic signs, each with an automatic rule checker detecting violations during closed-loop execution, yielding 29,000 road scenes and 29 testing scenario types. 5,800 testing scenes are constructed. Existing planners are transformed into rule-compliant trajectory experts via explicit traffic-sign constraints to generate scalable high-quality oracle trajectories for fine-tuning.
AI.result: Current autonomous driving planners can exhibit poor traffic-rule compliance despite strong performance on standard evaluation metrics, as demonstrated on the 5,800 constructed testing scenes.
AI.conclusion: TrafficSignBench enables controlled, rule-specific evaluation of planner behavior and interpretable measurement of traffic-rule compliance. The proposed transformation of planners into rule-compliant trajectory experts supports scalable generation of oracle trajectories for fine-tuning, addressing the compliance gap.

title: Reach Into The CHOIR: Free-List Elicitation Uncovers Distinct Model Voices in LLM Ensembles
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures. Published in the Proceedings of the Third Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2026)
summary: Open-ended LLM homogeneity can create false plurality when several systems appear to offer independent perspectives while returning the same familiar default. Single-pass answers obscure the distinction between agreement produced by a tightly constrained answer space, prompt-vocabulary echo, and broader answer spaces with stable alternatives beneath the surface. We introduce CHOIR (Collective Hierarchically-Ordered Inquiry Responses), a framework that adapts free-list elicitation from cognitive anthropology to LLM ensembles. CHOIR repeatedly elicits ranked lists, clusters items into prompt-level concepts, and measures concept salience across models, prompt variants, and persona conditions. We evaluate CHOIR on Infinity-Chat 100, an external prompt bank from recent work on open-ended model homogeneity, and on a 27-question targeted diagnostic bank designed to isolate mechanism-level contrasts. On Infinity-Chat 100, CHOIR reproduces high surface agreement (93/100 prompts above chance) while separating narrow prompts from broad prompts with recoverable depth. Across targeted probes and the external prompt bank, base-model identity remains the strongest recoverable signature, and persona prompts shift surfaced concepts within base-model signatures. A source-blind ranking module prioritises rare-but-stable candidates for later inspection. CHOIR turns open-ended homogeneity into a diagnostic measurement problem by asking where models converge, why they converge, and what remains reachable under structured depth probing.

AI.tldr: CHOIR adapts cognitive-anthropology free-list elicitation to LLM ensembles, repeatedly eliciting ranked lists, clustering items into prompt-level concepts, and measuring salience across models, prompt variants, and personas—turning open-ended homogeneity into a diagnostic measurement problem.
AI.motivation: Open-ended LLM homogeneity can create false plurality: several systems appear to offer independent perspectives while returning the same familiar default. Single-pass answers obscure the distinction between agreement produced by a tightly constrained answer space, prompt-vocabulary echo, and broader answer spaces with stable alternatives beneath the surface.
AI.method: CHOIR (Collective Hierarchically-Ordered Inquiry Responses) adapts free-list elicitation from cognitive anthropology to LLM ensembles. It repeatedly elicits ranked lists, clusters items into prompt-level concepts, and measures concept salience across models, prompt variants, and persona conditions. Evaluation uses Infinity-Chat 100 (an external prompt bank from recent work on open-ended model homogeneity) and a 27-question targeted diagnostic bank designed to isolate mechanism-level contrasts, plus a source-blind ranking module that prioritises rare-but-stable candidates for later inspection.
AI.result: On Infinity-Chat 100, CHOIR reproduces high surface agreement (93/100 prompts above chance) while separating narrow prompts from broad prompts with recoverable depth. Across targeted probes and the external prompt bank, base-model identity remains the strongest recoverable signature, and persona prompts shift surfaced concepts within base-model signatures. The source-blind ranking module prioritises rare-but-stable candidates for later inspection.
AI.conclusion: CHOIR turns open-ended homogeneity into a diagnostic measurement problem by asking where models converge, why they converge, and what remains reachable under structured depth probing.

title: L1-MPPI: L1 Adaptive Model Predictive Path Integral for Agile UAV Control
summary: This work proposes the L1 Adaptive Model Predictive Path Integral (L1-MPPI). It cascades L1 adaptive control with the Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) to improve tracking of high-speed UAV trajectories. Thanks to the L1augmentation, the tracking remains accurate even under model uncertainties and external disturbances, such as an additional payload or a mismatch in the modeled aerodynamic drag. In contrast to existing MPPI approaches for UAV control that do not explicitly model aerodynamic effects, varying payloads, and typically neglect the dynamics of low-level motor controllers, our L1-MPPI approach enhances the dynamic model used in the MPPI by incorporating the low-level flight controller and motor dynamics, as well as an iterative mixing scheme that reflects the approach of the low-level controller. The proposed method demonstrates improved tracking performance in both simulation and the real world, even when the UAV is subjected to an unknown payload. In flight with 35% mass increase, our approach lowers the RMSE by 58.61% with respect to plain MPPI. Compared to the same MPPI using an online mass estimator in place of the L1 augmentation, the RMSE is lower by 38.59%. During the real-world experiments the UAV reaches speeds up to 13.50 m/s and accelerations up to 2.5 g.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes L1-MPPI, cascading L1 adaptive control with Model Predictive Path Integral control to improve high-speed UAV trajectory tracking under model uncertainties and unknown payloads.
AI.motivation: Existing MPPI approaches for UAV control do not explicitly model aerodynamic effects or varying payloads and typically neglect low-level motor controller dynamics, limiting tracking accuracy under uncertainties and disturbances.
AI.method: L1-MPPI cascades L1 adaptive control with MPPI. The MPPI dynamic model is enhanced by incorporating low-level flight controller and motor dynamics, plus an iterative mixing scheme reflecting the low-level controller's behavior.
AI.result: In flight with a 35% mass increase, the approach lowers RMSE by 58.61% versus plain MPPI and by 38.59% versus MPPI with an online mass estimator instead of L1 augmentation. Real-world experiments reached speeds up to 13.50 m/s and accelerations up to 2.5 g.
AI.conclusion: The L1 augmentation enables accurate tracking under model uncertainties and external disturbances, improving tracking performance in both simulation and real-world flights with unknown payloads.

title: PrivMeSA: Privacy-Aware Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for Medicine via Local-Remote LLM Collaboration
summary: Clinical large language model (LLM) agents deployed locally can consult more capable remote models, but doing so risks exposing patient information. Privacy-conscious delegation places disclosure decisions with a local agent, yet removing explicit identifiers is insufficient: quasi-identifiers can accumulate across multi-turn consultations and repeated patient visits to enable re-identification. We introduce PrivMeSA, a privacy-aware self-evolving multi-agent system that learns to control disclosure and retains remote expertise for local reuse. A local agent manages each encounter and consults remote specialists that may request additional information. Reinforcement learning balances task accuracy against direct disclosure and registry-based re-identification risk, with privacy evaluated over the complete outbound transcript of each encounter. A local lesson memory distills completed consultations into generalized clinical guidance and retrieves relevant lessons before transmission, allowing subsequent cases to reuse expertise without another remote exchange. Memory grows without additional outcome labels or parameter updates. On an emergency-department benchmark built from MIMIC-IV-ED records, PrivMeSA improves mean task accuracy over delegation by up to 15.8 percentage points. In the same setting, PrivMeSA reduces the disclosure of personal details from 98.0% to 0.2% of cases and the share of cases in which the patient can be narrowed to ten or fewer registry patients from 74% to 0%.

AI.tldr: PrivMeSA is a privacy-aware, self-evolving multi-agent system where a local LLM agent controls disclosure to remote specialists and distills completed consultations into a reusable local lesson memory, reducing re-identification risk without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.motivation: Locally deployed clinical LLM agents can improve performance by consulting more capable remote models, but this risks leaking patient information. Placing disclosure decisions with the local agent is insufficient because removing explicit identifiers does not prevent quasi-identifiers from accumulating across multi-turn consultations and repeated patient visits, enabling re-identification.
AI.method: A local agent manages each encounter and consults remote specialists that may request additional information. Reinforcement learning balances task accuracy against direct disclosure and registry-based re-identification risk, with privacy evaluated over the complete outbound transcript of each encounter. A local lesson memory distills completed consultations into generalized clinical guidance and retrieves relevant lessons before transmission, enabling expertise reuse without further remote exchanges; memory grows without additional outcome labels or parameter updates.
AI.result: On an emergency-department benchmark built from MIMIC-IV-ED records, PrivMeSA improves mean task accuracy over delegation by up to 15.8 percentage points. It also reduces disclosure of personal details from 98.0% to 0.2% of cases and reduces the share of cases in which the patient can be narrowed to ten or fewer registry patients from 74% to 0%.
AI.conclusion: PrivMeSA shows that privacy-conscious delegation can retain remote expertise for local reuse while substantially mitigating quasi-identifier accumulation and re-identification risk, achieving both higher accuracy and stronger privacy than naive delegation.

title: Diffusion-2BC: Hybrid Diffusion and Regression Training for Offline Behavior Cloning in Autonomous Driving
summary: Behavior cloning provides an offline route to autonomous-driving policy learning, but mean-squared-error regression is poorly matched to demonstrations in which one observation admits several valid actions. Diffusion policies can represent conditional multimodal action distributions, yet their closed-loop performance may be unstable when visual features and control are learned from limited data. This paper presents Diffusion-2BC, which combines a diffusion denoising objective with an auxiliary deterministic behavior-cloning loss over a shared visual encoder. The auxiliary branch is used only during training; inference remains diffusion-based. The proposed method is evaluated in the controlled Claw environment and in bird's-eye-view CARLA navigation, including route-conditioned driving, route-free navigation through multiple intersections, and cross-map evaluation from Town01 to Town02. In the Claw task, Diffusion-2BC reduced the mean mask-distance error by approximately 10% relative to a diffusion-based behavior-cloning baseline and by 85% relative to standard deterministic behavior cloning. In route-free CARLA, Diffusion-2BC traveled substantially farther before termination under the evaluation protocol than both baselines in Town01 and Town02. Additional qualitative rollouts revealed distinct route choices, showing the multimodal behavior of the proposed diffusion-based agent. The results indicate that an auxiliary regression signal can improve the closed-loop reliability of diffusion behavior cloning while preserving multimodal prediction in the controlled benchmark.

AI.tldr: Diffusion-2BC combines a diffusion denoising objective with an auxiliary deterministic behavior-cloning loss on a shared visual encoder (training only), improving closed-loop reliability of diffusion behavior cloning while preserving multimodal action prediction.
AI.motivation: MSE regression in behavior cloning is ill-suited to demonstrations where one observation admits multiple valid actions, while diffusion policies that model multimodal action distributions can be unstable in closed loop when visual features and control are learned from limited data.
AI.method: A diffusion denoising objective is jointly optimized with an auxiliary deterministic behavior-cloning loss sharing a common visual encoder; the auxiliary branch is used only during training, and inference remains purely diffusion-based.
AI.result: In Claw, Diffusion-2BC reduced mean mask-distance error by ~10% vs. a diffusion BC baseline and ~85% vs. standard deterministic BC. In route-free CARLA it traveled substantially farther before termination than both baselines in Town01 and Town02; qualitative rollouts showed distinct route choices, evidencing multimodal behavior.
AI.conclusion: An auxiliary regression signal can improve the closed-loop reliability of diffusion behavior cloning while retaining multimodal prediction, validated in Claw and in route-conditioned, route-free, and cross-map (Town01→Town02) CARLA navigation.

title: NAQD Env: A benchmark for selective withdrawal in language agents
comment: 16 pages. Code and evaluation artifacts: https://github.com/abouzamm/naqd
summary: Language agents must revise planned actions when evidence changes, permission is revoked, or a stop instruction arrives. A useful response is selective: suspend affected actions, preserve unaffected work, and resume only after sufficient repair. We introduce NAQD-Env, a synthetic environment that evaluates these decisions against a deterministic reference policy over explicit evidence, authorization, and constraint dependencies. Eleven dependency families support evaluation on development structures, held-out families, and held-out combinations of structures. Metrics distinguish attempted violations from violations permitted by a simulated execution gate and jointly report policy agreement, task value, withdrawal, resumption, and event reporting. We evaluate three open-weight instruction-tuned models from two families under three prompt conditions on 350 frozen scenarios, yielding 3,150 model-prompt episodes before gate replay. Across the reported conditions, withdrawal recall is at most 0.06, no valid resumption is observed at eligible opportunities, and only one episode matches the complete reference policy. Under the NAQD prompt, Qwen2.5-7B has fewer unsafe-attempt episodes than Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, but also completes less useful work and preserves unaffected actions less accurately. Exploratory supervised fine-tuning probes increase Qwen2.5-3B decision accuracy from 0.45-0.54 to 0.83-0.92; separate diagnostics reveal inappropriate withdrawal after curriculum omissions and a loss of event reporting. These results motivate evaluating selective withdrawal as a distinct component of agent reliability. The setting measures policy application with trusted structured inputs and does not establish real-world containment or source-verification ability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NAQD-Env, a synthetic benchmark for evaluating whether language agents selectively withdraw, preserve, and resume planned actions when evidence, authorization, or stop signals change, measured against a deterministic reference policy.
AI.motivation: Language agents must revise planned actions when evidence changes, permission is revoked, or a stop instruction arrives. Effective revision should be selective: suspend affected actions, preserve unaffected work, and resume only after sufficient repair. This capacity for selective withdrawal is argued to be a distinct and under-evaluated component of agent reliability.
AI.method: NAQD-Env offers explicit evidence, authorization, and constraint dependencies with eleven dependency families, supporting evaluation on development structures, held-out families, and held-out combinations. Metrics distinguish attempted violations from those permitted by a simulated execution gate and jointly report policy agreement, task value, withdrawal, resumption, and event reporting. Three open-weight instruction-tuned models from two families were tested under three prompt conditions on 350 frozen scenarios (3,150 model-prompt episodes before gate replay), plus exploratory supervised fine-tuning probes on Qwen2.5-3B.
AI.result: Withdrawal recall is at most 0.06, no valid resumption occurs at eligible opportunities, and only one episode matches the complete reference policy. Under the NAQD prompt, Qwen2.5-7B produces fewer unsafe-attempt episodes than Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.1-8B but completes less useful work and preserves unaffected actions less accurately. Supervised fine-tuning raises Qwen2.5-3B decision accuracy from 0.45-0.54 to 0.83-0.92, though diagnostics reveal inappropriate withdrawal after curriculum omissions and loss of event reporting.
AI.conclusion: Selective withdrawal warrants evaluation as a distinct component of agent reliability. The setting measures policy application with trusted structured inputs and does not establish real-world containment or source-verification ability.

title: CADeT: Causal-Aware Deformation Transmission for Indirect Robotic Manipulation of Soft Tissue
summary: Indirect manipulation of deep-seated deformable anatomy inaccessible to the robot is challenging in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) because intervening tissues spatially filter deformation transmission. Passive observations can be ambiguous because the Decoupled and Blocked modes may produce similar motion responses. We propose CADeT, a causal-aware deformation transmission framework that integrates structural causal model (SCM) with active sensing to infer a latent transmission mode and estimate a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online. During normal manipulation, control actions update the mode belief; when ambiguity persists, an additional probing action is selected to improve mode distinguishability. The mode belief and learned Jacobian are incorporated into a belief-aware model predictive controller for indirect target-shape control. Validation in simulation and on the da Vinci research kit (dVRK), using phantom and ex vivo porcine tissues, shows higher mode-identification accuracy and faster shape-error convergence than the evaluated model-free and model-based baselines. These results show that active sensing improves mode identification and indirect deformation control under the evaluated conditions.

AI.tldr: CADeT is a causal-aware deformation transmission framework that combines a structural causal model with active sensing to infer latent transmission modes and estimate a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online, enabling indirect target-shape control in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery.
AI.motivation: Indirect manipulation of deep-seated deformable anatomy that the robot cannot directly reach is challenging in RAMIS, because intervening tissues spatially filter deformation transmission. Passive observations are ambiguous since Decoupled and Blocked modes can produce similar motion responses.
AI.method: CADeT integrates a structural causal model (SCM) with active sensing to infer a latent transmission mode and estimate a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online. Control actions update the mode belief during normal manipulation; when ambiguity persists, a probing action is selected to improve mode distinguishability. The mode belief and learned Jacobian feed a belief-aware model predictive controller for indirect target-shape control.
AI.result: Validation in simulation and on the da Vinci research kit (dVRK) with phantom and ex vivo porcine tissues shows higher mode-identification accuracy and faster shape-error convergence than model-free and model-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Active sensing improves mode identification and indirect deformation control under the evaluated conditions.

title: VAmoS Part Deux: Harder, More Realistic Voice-Agent Simulation
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Agent implementations: https://github.com/veris-ai/rory-agent
summary: Voice agents in production must handle several requests, background speech, and customers who lose patience. We introduce VAmoS Energy, a benchmark that combines these challenges in 100 calls about utility billing and payment assistance. Each caller makes two to four requests. The agent has sixteen tools backed by a stateful Stripe billing twin and the Apache Fineract loan engine, with account access blocked until caller verification succeeds. The tasks use public household electricity data and a policy based on Pennsylvania's residential billing rules. An LLM-as-a-verifier checks the agent's actions and spoken figures against explicit requirements. On a calibration run, it agrees with a code verifier on 99.1% of checks. Across fourteen voice stacks and three repeats per task, completion ranges from 17.3% to 44.7%. Grok Voice leads, and Gemini 3.8 Live and GPT-Live follow at about the same cost per call. Background television reduces pooled completion from 38.7% to 8.6%. The simulated caller often accepts an incorrect result because it hears the agent's words but cannot inspect its actions. These findings show why voice agents need evaluation across the whole call, including what they say, what they change, and how they handle competing speech.

AI.tldr: VAmoS Energy is a benchmark of 100 utility billing calls that evaluates voice agents across multi-request handling, background speech, and caller impatience, revealing large performance gaps.
AI.motivation: Production voice agents must simultaneously manage multiple requests, background speech, and impatient callers, but existing evaluations do not combine these challenges. This work argues that voice agents must be assessed across the whole call—what they say, what they change, and how they handle competing speech.
AI.method: The benchmark contains 100 calls about utility billing and payment assistance, with each caller making two to four requests. Agents have sixteen tools backed by a stateful Stripe billing twin and the Apache Fineract loan engine, and account access is blocked until caller verification succeeds. Tasks use public household electricity data and a policy based on Pennsylvania's residential billing rules. An LLM-as-a-verifier checks actions and spoken figures against explicit requirements, agreeing with a code verifier on 99.1% of checks in calibration.
AI.result: Across fourteen voice stacks and three repeats per task, completion ranges from 17.3% to 44.7%. Grok Voice leads, with Gemini 3.8 Live and GPT-Live following at roughly the same cost per call. Background television drops pooled completion from 38.7% to 8.6%. The simulated caller frequently accepts incorrect results because it hears the agent's words but cannot inspect its actions.
AI.conclusion: Voice agents require whole-call evaluation covering their speech, their state-changing actions, and their handling of competing speech. Current stacks perform poorly under these combined conditions, and simulated callers can mask failures by accepting incorrect outcomes.

title: What to Attend, What to Keep: Skill-Conditioned Visuotactile Representation with Progress-Guided Event Memory
summary: Robotic manipulation integrates vision, touch, and language, whose importance shifts across stages: vision guides reaching, while touch, through its evolution over time, decides grasping, alignment, and contact. Yet existing multi-modal manipulation policies typically use fixed temporal contexts and fusion strategies, despite shifts in what each modality contributes across different skills. We study how vision and touch should be combined at the level of primitive skills, asking what each skill needs from each sensor, and propose a skill-conditioned representation in which the queried skill conditions fusion over modality-specific short-term observation tokens while attending to a sparse event memory that retains terminal observations from the last $K$ executed skills. Evaluated by skill progress estimation on three contact-rich tasks, it reduces slip-detection delay by 87% against fine-tuned SOTA progress models, twist-completion delay by 67.5% against a vision-only ablation, and progress error on a blind search task by 92% through sparse event memory. Gains concentrate exactly where completion is defined by contact or task history. More broadly, our results suggest that observation formation not only policy architecture is a central challenge in multi-modal representation. Project Website: http://what-to-attend-what-to-keep.github.io/

AI.tldr: Skill-conditioned multimodal representation fusing vision and touch per primitive skill, with short-term observation tokens and sparse event memory, greatly reducing delays in contact-rich manipulation.
AI.motivation: Vision guides reaching, while touch (evolving over time) decides grasping, alignment, and contact, so each modality's contribution shifts across manipulation stages and skills. Existing multi-modal policies, however, use fixed temporal contexts and fusion strategies, ignoring these shifts. The paper asks what each primitive skill needs from each sensor.
AI.method: A skill-conditioned representation where the queried skill conditions fusion over modality-specific short-term observation tokens, while attending to a sparse event memory retaining terminal observations from the last K executed skills.
AI.result: Evaluated via skill progress estimation on three contact-rich tasks: 87% reduction in slip-detection delay vs. fine-tuned SOTA progress models, 67.5% reduction in twist-completion delay vs. a vision-only ablation, and 92% reduction in progress error on a blind search task via sparse event memory. Gains concentrate where completion is defined by contact or task history.
AI.conclusion: Observation formation, not only policy architecture, is a central challenge in multi-modal manipulation representation.

title: Demographic Pluralism: Inference-Time Modeling of Pluralistic Human Preference Distributions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in culturally sensitive settings, where alignment requires representing diverse preferences within populations. Yet existing methods model populations at coarse demographic or community levels and overlook within-group variation. We introduce Demographic Pluralism, an inference-time framework that estimates population-level opinion distributions without opinion-distribution training data or task-specific fine-tuning by generating multiple perspectives within demographically grounded groups. Across four backbones on GlobalOpinionQA and VITAL, it reduces Jensen-Shannon distance by 8.4%-26.4% over Modular Pluralism. Among weighted, equal-weighted, and inverse-weighted aggregation, equal weighting performs best overall; group-level error also increases with group weight, helping explain weighted aggregation's weaker performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Demographic Pluralism, an inference-time framework that estimates population-level opinion distributions by generating multiple perspectives within demographically grounded groups, without needing opinion-distribution training data or task-specific fine-tuning. It outperforms Modular Pluralism across four backbones on GlobalOpinionQA and VITAL, reducing Jensen-Shannon distance by 8.4%-26.4%, with equal weighting performing best.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in culturally sensitive settings where alignment requires capturing diverse population preferences. However, existing methods model populations only at coarse demographic or community levels and ignore variation within groups, limiting their ability to represent opinion distributions accurately.
AI.method: Demographic Pluralism is an inference-time framework that estimates population-level opinion distributions by generating multiple perspectives within demographically grounded groups, requiring no opinion-distribution training data or task-specific fine-tuning. It is evaluated across four backbone models on the GlobalOpinionQA and VITAL benchmarks, comparing weighted, equal-weighted, and inverse-weighted aggregation strategies against the Modular Pluralism baseline.
AI.result: Across four backbones on GlobalOpinionQA and VITAL, Demographic Pluralism reduces Jensen-Shannon distance by 8.4%-26.4% relative to Modular Pluralism. Among aggregation strategies, equal weighting performs best overall, while group-level error increases with group weight, explaining why weighted aggregation performs more weakly.
AI.conclusion: Modeling within-group variation via multiple demographically grounded perspectives improves population-level opinion estimation without fine-tuning and improves distributional alignment. Equal-weighted aggregation is preferable, and the observed link between group-level error and group weight clarifies the weaker performance of weighted aggregation.

title: Onboard Vision and MPC Navigation for Underwater Robots: An Open BlueROV2 Platform for Multi-Robot Experiments & Docking
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Autonomous underwater robots require robust perception, estimation and control to operate in confined environments. This paper presents an open-source BlueROV2 platform combining onboard vision with nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) for autonomous navigation and docking. The platform integrates an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and an Intel RealSense D435i stereo camera in a modular pressure housing. Underwater-calibrated stereo depth and realtime object detection provide relative position measurements of nearby BlueROV2 vehicles in the camera and body frames. A quaternion-based estimator fuses external pose and inertial measurements, while an NMPC controller based on a nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom model tracks planned navigation and docking trajectories. To support reproducible development, we also provide open-source physics-based PX4 SITL and Gazebo environments, multi-robot simulation tools and a lowcost physical docking station. Experiments evaluate underwater perception, onboard computational performance, state estimation, trajectory tracking and autonomous docking.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an open-source BlueROV2 platform that combines onboard stereo vision with nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) for autonomous underwater navigation and docking, supported by open-source simulation and a low-cost docking station.
AI.motivation: Autonomous underwater robots require robust perception, estimation, and control to operate in confined environments, motivating an integrated, reproducible platform for navigation and docking.
AI.method: The platform integrates an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and Intel RealSense D435i stereo camera in a modular pressure housing. Underwater-calibrated stereo depth and real-time object detection provide relative position measurements of nearby BlueROV2 vehicles in camera and body frames. A quaternion-based estimator fuses external pose and inertial measurements, and an NMPC controller based on a nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom model tracks planned navigation and docking trajectories. Open-source PX4 SITL, Gazebo environments, multi-robot simulation tools, and a low-cost physical docking station support reproducible development.
AI.result: Experiments evaluate underwater perception, onboard computational performance, state estimation, trajectory tracking, and autonomous docking.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers an open-source, integrated BlueROV2 platform with onboard vision and NMPC, validated through perception, estimation, tracking, and docking experiments, enabling reproducible autonomous underwater navigation and docking research.

title: Defining and Categorising Human-AI Interactions in Clinical Trials: A Multidimensional Human-AI Classification Approach
summary: This paper examines human-AI interactions (HAIIs) in clinical trials and presents a multidimensional categorisation framework that classifies interactions according to AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations and interacting human groups. We define HAII, examine existing taxonomies and extend existing categorisation approaches through this novel multidimensional framework. We purposively sampled 15 clinical trials from a previously reported dataset. Each trial was independently categorised by two human reviewers and six large language model (LLM) classifiers. The proposed categorisation provides a structured method for the consistent identification, comparison and synthesis of human-AI interactions across clinical-trial records. The framework is intended to support more consistent comparison and synthesis of AI-related clinical trials and to make explicit the different forms of human involvement associated with AI interventions. The results demonstrate the potential for LLM-assisted categorisation while indicating the continuing importance of human judgement where trial records are incomplete or ambiguous. The principal contribution is a proposed multidimensional framework that brings together AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations and interacting human groups within a single approach designed for clinical-trial records. Its significance lies in its potential to support more systematic identification, comparison and synthesis of how humans and AI interact in clinical trials.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multidimensional framework for categorizing human-AI interactions (HAIIs) in clinical trials, validated on 15 trials by two human reviewers and six LLM classifiers, enabling consistent identification, comparison, and synthesis of HAIIs across clinical-trial records.
AI.motivation: Existing taxonomies for human-AI interaction are insufficient for the clinical-trial context, where AI interventions involve varied tasks, relationships, configurations, and human groups. A structured, consistent method is needed to identify, compare, and synthesize how humans and AI interact across clinical-trial records.
AI.method: The authors define HAII, review existing taxonomies, and extend them into a novel multidimensional framework classifying interactions by AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations, and interacting human groups. They purposively sampled 15 clinical trials from a previously reported dataset and categorized each trial independently using two human reviewers and six large language model (LLM) classifiers.
AI.result: The framework provided a structured method for consistent identification, comparison, and synthesis of HAIIs across clinical-trial records. LLM-assisted categorization showed promise, while human judgement remained important where trial records were incomplete or ambiguous.
AI.conclusion: The principal contribution is a multidimensional framework unifying AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations, and interacting human groups into a single approach tailored to clinical-trial records. Its significance lies in supporting more systematic identification, comparison, and synthesis of human-AI interactions in clinical trials, with LLMs assisting but not replacing human judgement.

title: Behavioral Persistence and Incomplete Functional Transfer of Co-evolved Communication in Evolutionary Robotics
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Source code and data available at Zenodo
summary: This work evaluates the direct transfer of a co-evolved communication protocol from a 2D simulation to a 3D physical environment, without retraining the network weights. Two e-puck-type robots, controlled by a GRU network with residual connection, were evaluated in a food-seeking task with social signaling. The sensory and motor translation layer required three corrections for stable physical operation, including the calibration of a hunger term based on a measurable asymmetry in the trained residual weights. Even with these corrections, the transfer was partial and asymmetric: one agent reached the food source in one of thirty tested seeds, while the other did not reach it in any. Task success was measured by both agents reaching the food area. An additional experiment incorporating explicit directional information in the social channel produced observable changes in the trajectory of the receiving agent and improvements in several specific cases. However, these improvements were not enough to allow the second agent to reach the food source, suggesting that the limitation may not be explained solely by signal translation, but also by the ability to navigate under the new physical constraints. The results suggest that successful transfer of emergent communication may depend not only on preserving the signaling process itself, but also on preserving the ecological and navigational conditions under which the protocol evolved.

AI.tldr: A co-evolved GRU-based communication protocol from 2D simulation was transferred to 3D physical e-puck robots without retraining; transfer was partial and asymmetric, indicating that preserving signaling alone is insufficient—ecological and navigational conditions must also be preserved.
AI.motivation: Emergent communication protocols are typically studied in simulation, and it remains unclear whether such protocols can operate directly in physical embodied agents. This work tests the sim-to-real transfer of a co-evolved communication protocol to assess whether signaling behavior alone is sufficient for successful real-world deployment.
AI.method: A communication protocol co-evolved in 2D simulation was directly transferred to 3D physical e-puck-type robots without retraining network weights. Each robot was controlled by a GRU network with a residual connection, in a food-seeking task with social signaling. A sensory-motor translation layer was implemented, requiring three corrections for stable physical operation, including calibration of a hunger term derived from a measurable asymmetry in the trained residual weights. A supplementary experiment injected explicit directional information into the social channel. Success was defined as both agents reaching the food area, evaluated across thirty seeds.
AI.result: Transfer was partial and asymmetric: one agent reached the food source in one of thirty seeds, while the other never did. Adding explicit directional information to the social channel produced observable trajectory changes in the receiving agent and improvements in several specific cases, but did not enable the second agent to reach the food source.
AI.conclusion: Successful transfer of emergent communication depends not only on preserving the signaling process itself, but also on preserving the ecological and navigational conditions under which the protocol evolved. The observed limitation appears attributable to navigation under new physical constraints rather than solely to signal translation.

title: Towards Model as a Library: Offline, Community-Sourced AI for Low-Resource African Languages
summary: Large language models are frequently proposed as a route to AI-powered services for African communities, but they are least reliable exactly where the need is greatest: all African languages remain low-resource by any standard measure, and models trained on scraped, standardised text systematically misrepresent the dialectal and regional variation of how people actually speak. We introduce \textbf{Model as a Library (MaaL)}, a software architecture that packages small, community-enrolled speech models as versioned on-device dependencies, enabling offline structured data collection that cannot generatively hallucinate, for populations that current language models serve worst. Rather than relying on web-scraped corpora, MaaL's vocabulary is enrolled directly from a small number of example recordings by the speakers themselves, at the point of deployment. We describe the architecture and its central mechanism - keyword spotting that turns a closed-vocabulary text form into a voice form, filled and submitted entirely on-device - and propose transpiling the closed-vocabulary elements already present in widely-deployed digital form tools into MaaL schemas, a low-friction path to voice-first, offline data collection for the low-literacy populations these tools already reach. This is a position and system-design paper: we describe the concept, the mechanism, and an analytical feasibility case, and identify what a working implementation still requires.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MaaL, an on-device architecture packaging small community-enrolled speech models as versioned dependencies to enable offline, non-hallucinating voice data collection for low-resource African languages.
AI.motivation: LLMs are promoted for AI services in African communities yet perform worst there: African languages remain low-resource, and scraped standardized-text models misrepresent dialectal and regional speech variation.
AI.method: MaaL packages small community-enrolled speech models as versioned on-device dependencies. Vocabulary is enrolled from a few example recordings by speakers at deployment, and a keyword-spotting mechanism converts closed-vocabulary text forms into voice forms filled and submitted entirely on-device; existing digital form tools' closed-vocabulary elements can be transpiled into MaaL schemas.
AI.result: As a position and system-design paper, it presents the concept, the mechanism, and an analytical feasibility case rather than an empirical implementation.
AI.conclusion: MaaL offers a low-friction path to voice-first, offline data collection for low-literacy populations, though an actual working implementation and its requirements remain to be built.

title: Systematically Exploring the Capabilities of GPT-6 Astra as Embodied Policies
summary: GPT-6 Astra exhibits a remarkable ability to generate numerical robot actions, extending its role beyond high-level planning. To assess Astra's capabilities as general-purpose embodied policies, we conduct comprehensive evaluations across six domains, examining direct control, cooperation with learned policies, and feedback-driven adaptation. In gripper manipulation, Astra can correct task targets and prepare contact conditions for subsequent policy execution; hybrid control with π0.5 achieves 48% success on the evaluated RoboDojo subset. In dexterous manipulation, hybrid control achieves 50% success in ten experience-guided DexJoCo trials, while direct in-hand control struggles to coordinate finger contacts. In mobile manipulation, hybrid control reaches 38.7% success on the evaluated RoboCasa365. In navigation, Astra leads our local comparisons, reaching 92% success on RxR instruction following and 82% on HM3D object search, although search incurs substantial detours. In locomotion, dense motion-reference generation remains unreliable: none of five sequential attempts on a single obstacle course reaches the goal, despite improvements in stability and forward progress. In humanoid loco-manipulation, Astra exceeds baseline methods on 13 of 30 HumanoidBench tasks with pretrained whole-body controllers. These findings reveal a gap between useful task decisions and reliable physical control. Inference latency further constrains practical control: across 50 RoboDojo instances per condition, policy-assisted and direct control consume 624.8 million and 1.132 billion tokens. A 30-second locomotion run requires 250 model calls averaging 39.86 seconds each, with physics paused during inference.

AI.tldr: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra as a general-purpose embodied policy across six domains, finding strong task-level decision making and local navigation but unreliable low-level physical control and prohibitive inference latency.
AI.motivation: Astra can now emit numerical robot actions, not just high-level plans, so its viability as a general-purpose embodied policy needs systematic assessment across varied embodiments and control regimes.
AI.method: Comprehensive evaluation across six domains under three regimes: direct control, cooperation with learned policies (hybrid control), and feedback-driven adaptation. Domains: gripper manipulation (RoboDojo, with π0.5), dexterous manipulation (DexJoCo), mobile manipulation (RoboCasa365), navigation (RxR, HM3D), locomotion (obstacle course), and humanoid loco-manipulation (HumanoidBench).
AI.result: Hybrid control achieves 48% on RoboDojo and 50% on ten DexJoCo trials, while direct in-hand control fails to coordinate finger contacts. Mobile manipulation reaches 38.7% on RoboCasa365. Navigation leads local comparisons: 92% on RxR, 82% on HM3D object search, though with substantial detours. Locomotion fails entirely: 0/5 sequential obstacle-course attempts reach the goal. Humanoid loco-manipulation beats baselines on 13/30 HumanoidBench tasks. Cost: 624.8M vs 1.132B tokens across 50 RoboDojo instances per condition; a 30-second locomotion run needs 250 calls averaging 39.86 s each with physics paused.
AI.conclusion: A gap persists between useful task decisions and reliable physical control, and inference latency further constrains practical closed-loop deployment.

title: Conditional Generation of Creative Chess Puzzles with Diffusion Models
summary: While modern language models demonstrate impressive generative capabilities, they often struggle with constrained, counter-intuitive creative tasks. To address this limitation, we explore chess puzzle generation as a rigorous testbed for computational creativity and reasoning, a domain where altering a single piece can invalidate an entire solution. We propose a novel approach for conditional generation of creative chess puzzles using masked diffusion models. Unlike previous methods, our non-directional diffusion approach allows for conditioning on specific tactical themes and partial board positions. We introduce a novel auxiliary task of simultaneous best-move prediction, which improves solution uniqueness by 11.6% and theme-conditioning accuracy by 2.5%. To further optimize solution uniqueness and theme conditioning, we establish a reinforcement learning framework adapted from Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO). This RL training increases the yield of unique and theme-matching positions by 89.1%. Finally, we release the first open-weights models (Appendix B) for chess puzzle generation, offering a new pathway for controllable, creative generation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes masked diffusion models for conditional chess puzzle generation, enabling conditioning on tactical themes and partial board positions, and shows that an auxiliary best-move prediction task plus DDPO-based RL training substantially improve solution uniqueness and theme-conditioning.
AI.motivation: Modern language models excel at open-ended generation but struggle with constrained, counter-intuitive creative tasks. Chess puzzle generation is chosen as a rigorous testbed because it is highly sensitive—altering a single piece can invalidate an entire solution—making it a demanding domain for computational creativity and reasoning.
AI.method: The authors introduce a non-directional masked diffusion approach for conditional chess puzzle generation, allowing conditioning on specific tactical themes and partial board positions (unlike prior methods). They add an auxiliary task of simultaneous best-move prediction, and further optimize solution uniqueness and theme conditioning via a reinforcement learning framework adapted from Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO).
AI.result: The auxiliary best-move prediction task improves solution uniqueness by 11.6% and theme-conditioning accuracy by 2.5%. The RL (DDPO-adapted) training increases the yield of unique and theme-matching positions by 89.1%.
AI.conclusion: The work releases the first open-weights models for chess puzzle generation, offering a new pathway for controllable, creative generation and demonstrating the effectiveness of masked diffusion plus RL for constrained creative tasks.

title: Data-Efficient Adaptation of a Driving VLA to Class 8 Trucks
summary: Class 8 trucks differ from passenger cars in geometry, dynamics, and maneuvering requirements. As a result, vision-language-action (VLA) models trained for passenger vehicles do not readily transfer to Class 8 trucks, particularly in unstructured scenarios such as accident scenes and construction zones. Rather than training a truck-driving VLA from scratch, we propose an adapt-then-steer strategy that adapts an off-the-shelf VLA to generate trajectories for Class-8 trucks in these challenging scenarios. In the adapt stage, we use NVIDIA's Alpamayo 1.5 as the base model, fine-tuning only its action-generation stack on a few hundred real-world construction and accident-related highway scenarios. In the steer stage, we introduce Flow Velocity Steering (FVS) to further refine the model's predictions while holding the adapted VLA fixed. FVS is a compact, flow-time-conditioned residual module that adds learned corrections to the action-space flow velocity used to update the action sequence at each generation step. In open-loop evaluation on a scenario-disjoint held-out set, targeted fine-tuning more than halves single-candidate average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) over the entire 6.4 s horizon compared to the base model. Using the same targeted demonstrations, FVS further reduces the fine-tuned model's full-horizon ADE and FDE by 13.9% and 16.5%, respectively. At matched data budgets, targeted supervision yields 19-26% lower full-horizon ADE than general truck-driving supervision, while the targeted model remains competitive with a model fine-tuned on approximately 65 times as many general truck-driving scenarios. These results support adapt-then-steer for data-efficient vehicle-domain transfer to Class 8 trucks. Our project website is available at https://truckvla.github.io.

AI.tldr: An off-the-shelf VLA model is adapted to Class 8 truck driving via targeted fine-tuning ("adapt") followed by a lightweight residual module, Flow Velocity Steering ("steer"), achieving large accuracy gains with few hundred demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Class 8 trucks differ from passenger cars in geometry, dynamics, and maneuvering, so VLA models trained for passenger vehicles do not transfer well, especially in unstructured scenes like accident scenes and construction zones. Training a truck-driving VLA from scratch is costly, motivating a data-efficient adaptation strategy.
AI.method: Adapt-then-steer strategy. Adapt: fine-tune only the action-generation stack of NVIDIA's Alpamayo 1.5 base VLA on a few hundred real-world highway construction and accident scenarios. Steer: Flow Velocity Steering (FVS), a compact flow-time-conditioned residual module that adds learned corrections to the action-space flow velocity used to update the action sequence at each generation step, while the adapted VLA stays frozen.
AI.result: On a scenario-disjoint held-out set in open-loop evaluation, targeted fine-tuning more than halves single-candidate ADE and FDE over the full 6.4 s horizon versus the base model. FVS further reduces the fine-tuned model's full-horizon ADE and FDE by 13.9% and 16.5%. At matched data budgets, targeted supervision gives 19-26% lower full-horizon ADE than general truck-driving supervision, and remains competitive with a model fine-tuned on ~65x more general truck-driving scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Adapt-then-steer enables data-efficient vehicle-domain transfer to Class 8 trucks, combining targeted fine-tuning with a compact flow-velocity steering module for substantial accuracy improvements.

title: Sense and Sensitivity: Benchmarking LLM Clinical Triage Recommendations with Physician Experts
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, it is critical to evaluate their reliability under realistic variation in clinical text. We study this question in clinical triage, comparing LLMs to practicing physicians under text perturbations that preserve the underlying clinical setting.
