We introduce a benchmark of over 6,000 clinical scenarios, 7,000 physician annotations, and 225,000 model responses. Using this benchmark, we make two key observations. First, LLMs are more likely than physicians to recommend unnecessary care at baseline, and this tendency increases under perturbed inputs. Further, we find that LLM recommendations are more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human recommendations. Together, these results demonstrate that LLMs can vary under clinically irrelevant textual changes, highlighting the need for deployment-oriented evaluations grounded in expert physician behavior.

AI.tldr: LLMs in clinical triage are compared to physicians under clinically irrelevant text perturbations using a large benchmark (6,000+ scenarios, 7,000 physician annotations, 225,000 model responses). LLMs recommend unnecessary care more than physicians at baseline, and this tendency grows with perturbations; LLM recommendations are also more sensitive to gender and tone changes than human ones.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in clinical settings, yet their reliability under realistic variation in clinical text is underexplored. The authors argue that evaluations must reflect clinically irrelevant textual changes and be grounded in expert physician behavior to assess deployment readiness.
AI.method: The authors build a clinical triage benchmark comprising over 6,000 clinical scenarios, 7,000 physician annotations, and 225,000 model responses. They compare LLM recommendations against practicing physicians under text perturbations that preserve the underlying clinical setting (e.g., gender and tone perturbations).
AI.result: LLMs are more likely than physicians to recommend unnecessary care at baseline, and this tendency increases under perturbed inputs. LLM recommendations are more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human recommendations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can vary under clinically irrelevant textual changes, revealing a robustness gap relative to physicians. This underscores the need for deployment-oriented evaluations grounded in expert physician behavior.

title: Drone Soccer: Learning to Manipulate with Multicopter Downwash
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, IROS 2026 Workshop (Sim2Real and Classical Control)
summary: Although multicopter drones are traditionally designed for "perception-only" tasks, like mapping and exploration, recent work has sought to develop Unmanned Aerial Manipulators (UAMs) to solve mobile manipulation tasks. Aerial manipulation performance can be impacted by "downwash," the airflow produced by propellers, but current state-of-the-art UAMs either ignore downwash or treat it as a disturbance. Instead, is it possible to actively use downwash as a tool during manipulation? We design a drone soccer task to explore the feasibility of downwash-based manipulation. Specifically, we develop a simplified downwash dynamics model which we use to train an RL policy to dribble a soccer ball. We further demonstrate that our policy transfers to real world deployment. This work provides key insights into novel manipulation capabilities for multicopters.

AI.tldr: This work explores using propeller downwash as an active manipulation tool for drones, training an RL policy with a simplified downwash model to dribble a soccer ball and demonstrating sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Multicopter drones are traditionally "perception-only," and Unmanned Aerial Manipulators (UAMs) extend them to mobile manipulation. However, current UAMs either ignore downwash or treat it as a disturbance. The authors hypothesize that downwash could instead be actively exploited as a manipulation tool.
AI.method: They design a drone soccer task to test downwash-based manipulation. They build a simplified downwash dynamics model and use it to train an RL policy for dribbling a soccer ball, then deploy the policy in the real world.
AI.result: The trained RL policy achieves ball-dribbling behavior in simulation and successfully transfers to real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: The results validate the feasibility of downwash-based manipulation, offering key insights into novel manipulation capabilities for multicopters.

title: When Scientific Contradictions Are Lost in Translation
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 AI for Science Workshop: Verification in the Age of AI Scientists. This version is not included in the official NeurIPS proceedings
summary: Two scientific findings can disagree without contradicting each other. Determining whether they conflict requires knowing whether they describe comparable measurements. We study how language models behave at this decision point. In a controlled task, we generate an unsatisfiable XOR constraint system and translate its constraints into scientific reports from different laboratories. One assignment satisfies more constraints, while another satisfies fewer but better matches expected biology. This creates a simple dilemma: does the model choose the assignment that best fits the constraints, or the one that better matches biological expectations? When the constraints are stated directly, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 recover the best-supported assignment in 90% and 96% of cases, respectively. In scientific prose, however, the models behave differently. Claude Opus 5 often prefers the biologically expected assignment. Removing that biological preference increases recovery of the better-supported assignment from 27% to 79% (p<.001); recovery reaches 92% when the same Biology-favored record is accompanied by a formalization request and an explicit paired-design cue (p<.001). GPT-5.6 Sol is less sensitive, with neither corresponding change reaching statistical significance. These results suggest that reliable scientific verification depends not only on formal reasoning, but also on how models decide which findings should be compared and what relations they imply.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how language models decide whether two scientific findings conflict, using a controlled XOR-constraint task where a better-supported assignment competes with a biologically expected one, and finds that in scientific prose, prior biological expectations can override formal constraint satisfaction.
AI.motivation: Two scientific findings can disagree without logically contradicting each other; determining conflict requires judging whether the findings describe comparable measurements. The authors ask how language models behave at this decision point, since reliable scientific verification may depend on such comparability judgments rather than only on formal reasoning.
AI.method: A controlled task is constructed: an unsatisfiable XOR constraint system is generated, and its constraints are translated into scientific reports attributed to different laboratories. One assignment satisfies more constraints, while another satisfies fewer but better matches expected biology, creating a dilemma between constraint fit and biological expectation. Models are tested with constraints stated directly and with constraints embedded in scientific prose, including manipulations that remove the biological preference and that add a formalization request plus an explicit paired-design cue.
AI.result: With directly stated constraints, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 recover the best-supported assignment in 90% and 96% of cases, respectively. In scientific prose, Claude Opus 5 often prefers the biologically expected assignment; removing that biological preference raises recovery of the better-supported assignment from 27% to 79% (p<.001), and recovery reaches 92% when the Biology-favored record is accompanied by a formalization request and an explicit paired-design cue (p<.001). GPT-5.6 Sol is less sensitive, with neither corresponding change reaching statistical significance.
AI.conclusion: Reliable scientific verification depends not only on formal reasoning but also on how models decide which findings should be compared and what relations they imply. Biological expectations and presentation format can substantially shift model judgments, with effects varying across models.

title: FAST-Sync: Fast Group Synchronization for any Matrix Lie Group
summary: Group synchronization (GS) is the problem of estimating a set of $N$ unknown elements $g_1,\ldots, g_N \in \mathcal{G}$ in a group $\mathcal{G}$, given noisy measurements of a subset of their pairwise ratios $g_i^{-1} g_j$. GS problems lie at the core of many state estimation tasks in robotics and computer vision, including 3D vision, robotic mapping, inertial navigation, and molecular reconstruction. Unfortunately, GS problems are typically both high-dimensional and non-convex, and therefore hard to solve in general. In this paper, we present Fast-Sync, a fast linear approximation method for GS that is suitable for initializing local manifold-based optimizers or certifiable global methods. Our approach generalizes chordal initialization to arbitrary matrix Lie groups, and additionally proposes two new key algorithmic enhancements: we show how to exploit both the Kronecker-product structure in the problem data matrix and the topology of the synchronization graph to improve speed, scalability, and accuracy. Experimental evaluation across several GS tasks demonstrates that Fast-Sync provides high-quality initializations that enable local optimizers to efficiently recover globally optimal GS solutions, achieving high success rates even with considerable measurement noise.

AI.tldr: Fast-Sync is a fast linear approximation method for group synchronization that generalizes chordal initialization to arbitrary matrix Lie groups and exploits Kronecker-product structure and graph topology to provide high-quality initializations for global optimizers.
AI.motivation: Group synchronization (GS) underlies many state estimation tasks in robotics and computer vision (3D vision, robotic mapping, inertial navigation, molecular reconstruction), but GS problems are typically high-dimensional and non-convex, making them hard to solve in general.
AI.method: Fast-Sync is a fast linear approximation method for GS suitable for initializing local manifold-based optimizers or certifiable global methods. It generalizes chordal initialization to arbitrary matrix Lie groups, and introduces two algorithmic enhancements: exploiting the Kronecker-product structure in the problem data matrix, and leveraging the topology of the synchronization graph to improve speed, scalability, and accuracy.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation across several GS tasks shows that Fast-Sync provides high-quality initializations that enable local optimizers to efficiently recover globally optimal GS solutions, achieving high success rates even with considerable measurement noise.
AI.conclusion: Fast-Sync delivers high-quality initializations for GS that let local optimizers efficiently attain globally optimal solutions, with high success rates under significant measurement noise.

title: Component-Aware Feedback for Self-Evolving Programs
summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search can discover complex programs, but existing methods mostly only save candidate programs and fitness scores while discarding which component edits produced which fitness metric changes. Existing methods force the mutator LLM to infer the effect of prior edits from cluttered histories, making program search slow and unstable. This is especially true for locally servable LLMs to evolve multi-component systems. We introduce component-aware feedback, which compares each evaluated program with its parent, identifies the components that changed, and logs them with the associated metric differences into an attribution memory that later mutations read. The memory keeps each change in two reference frames, local against the parent it came from and global against the seed program, which shows both the immediate effect of a change and the cumulative progress made since the seed. We study this on LLM reranking, a multi-objective optimization problem where a multi-stage pipeline must balance quality against serving cost. Across twelve \textsc{Bright} datasets, our method reaches the strongest baseline's final quality after a median of one third of the search budget and ends 7.2\% higher in held-out nDCG@10, and under a cost-aware objective it finds pipelines that are on average more accurate while using 11\% fewer tokens per query, showing component-aware feedback to be a promising direction for more efficient self-evolving systems.

AI.tldr: Component-aware feedback improves LLM-guided evolutionary program search by logging which component edits caused which metric changes, enabling faster and better multi-objective optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-guided evolutionary search methods retain only candidate programs and fitness scores, discarding edit-to-metric attribution. This forces the mutator LLM to infer edit effects from cluttered histories, making search slow and unstable, especially for locally servable LLMs evolving multi-component systems.
AI.method: The paper introduces component-aware feedback: each evaluated program is compared with its parent, changed components are identified, and these are logged with associated metric differences into an attribution memory read by later mutations. Each change is stored in two reference frames—local (against its parent) and global (against the seed program)—capturing both immediate effects and cumulative progress since the seed.
AI.result: Evaluated on LLM reranking, a multi-objective problem balancing quality against serving cost. Across twelve Bright datasets, the method reaches the strongest baseline's final quality after a median of one third of the search budget and ends 7.2% higher in held-out nDCG@10. Under a cost-aware objective, it finds pipelines that are on average more accurate while using 11% fewer tokens per query.
AI.conclusion: Component-aware feedback is a promising direction for more efficient self-evolving systems, improving both search efficiency and final solution quality.

title: Correcting WHERE, Preserving HOW: Compositional Generalization for Vision-Language-Action Models via Referential Guidance
summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable flexible action generation, their generalization across diverse environmental elements, including manipulated objects, destinations, and backgrounds, is limited by the lack of diversity in robotic training data. Trained end-to-end on such data, VLAs tend to exploit visual shortcuts, associating actions with task-irrelevant visual features rather than the intended task semantics. These shortcuts block recomposition of elements already seen by the policy, that is, compositional generalization. Existing approaches mitigate such entanglement through task-relevant perception or targeted data diversification, but offer no explicit mechanism for unseen recomposition and require backbone-specific modifications with retraining. We observe that under such recomposition, VLAs often fail at global grounding while retaining local manipulation skills that recover near the correct target in familiar configurations. Therefore, we propose Referential Guidance (ReGuide), a training-free wrapper that, given object poses from a grounding module, combines semantic and geometric rebinding to guide the end-effector into demonstration-supported configurations of the instructed referent, where the frozen policy can resume execution. Experiments in simulation across multiple VLA backbones as well as on a real robot show that ReGuide improves success rates under compositional shifts by up to 56.8 and 75.0 percentage points, respectively, while preserving standard-task performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ReGuide, a training-free wrapper for VLA models that restores compositional generalization under novel element recompositions by combining semantic and geometric rebinding to steer the end-effector into demonstration-supported configurations of the instructed referent, where the frozen policy resumes execution.
AI.motivation: VLA models trained end-to-end on limited-diversity robotic data exploit visual shortcuts, associating actions with task-irrelevant visual features rather than task semantics. This blocks compositional generalization—recombining already-seen objects, destinations, and backgrounds. Existing mitigations rely on task-relevant perception or data diversification but provide no explicit mechanism for unseen recomposition and require backbone-specific modification with retraining.
AI.method: The authors observe that under recomposition, VLAs fail at global grounding while retaining local manipulation skills that recover near the correct target in familiar configurations. Building on this, they propose Referential Guidance (ReGuide), a training-free wrapper that, given object poses from a grounding module, combines semantic and geometric rebinding to guide the end-effector into demonstration-supported configurations of the instructed referent, at which point the frozen policy resumes execution.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation across multiple VLA backbones and on a real robot show that ReGuide improves success rates under compositional shifts by up to 56.8 and 75.0 percentage points, respectively, while preserving standard-task performance.
AI.conclusion: ReGuide provides an explicit, training-free, backbone-agnostic mechanism for compositional generalization that leverages the persistent local manipulation competence of frozen VLAs, substantially improving performance under compositional shifts without degrading standard tasks.

title: ChartRevise: A Dataset and Evaluation Protocol for Exact Chart Editing via Code
summary: Chart editing requires cross-modal edit grounding, realizing a requested visual change in the code that draws it, with necessary related updates and without altering unrelated content. Existing benchmarks emphasize either code executability or chart quality, but their metrics do not clearly distinguish request completion from missed coupled updates and gratuitous changes. We introduce ChartRevise, a structured dataset and evaluation protocol for exact program-grounded chart editing. For dataset construction, we build on the grammar of graphics to systematically cover chart-editing operations, using source-program checks to verify their applicability across chart types and libraries. To improve edit exactness, our pipeline checks individual requirements and guides repair or exclusion when they are unmet. The resulting dataset contains 92,438 records covering 344 edit types across 20 chart types and three plotting libraries. For evaluation, our reference-free protocol separately measures atomic requirement completion, identifies gratuitous changes, and detects missed coupled updates. These checks are combined with successful execution and rendering to determine exact-edit success. Across five models and four external benchmarks, fine-tuning yields relative gains of 16\% in mean requirement recall and 22\% in mean exact-edit rate.

AI.tldr: ChartRevise introduces a dataset and reference-free evaluation protocol for exact program-grounded chart editing, separating requirement completion, gratuitous changes, and missed coupled updates, with fine-tuning yielding notable gains.
AI.motivation: Chart editing demands cross-modal edit grounding: turning a requested visual change into the code that produces it, including necessary related updates while avoiding changes to unrelated content. Existing benchmarks emphasize either code executability or chart quality, but their metrics fail to distinguish request completion from missed coupled updates and gratuitous changes.
AI.method: The authors build ChartRevise using the grammar of graphics to systematically cover chart-editing operations, verifying applicability across chart types and libraries via source-program checks. A pipeline checks individual requirements and guides repair or exclusion when unmet. The evaluation protocol is reference-free and separately measures atomic requirement completion, identifies gratuitous changes, and detects missed coupled updates, combined with successful execution and rendering to determine exact-edit success.
AI.result: The dataset contains 92,438 records covering 344 edit types across 20 chart types and three plotting libraries. Across five models and four external benchmarks, fine-tuning yields relative gains of 16% in mean requirement recall and 22% in mean exact-edit rate.
AI.conclusion: ChartRevise provides a structured dataset and a fine-grained, reference-free evaluation protocol that better captures exact chart-editing success, demonstrating substantial improvements in requirement recall and exact-edit rate after fine-tuning.

title: Dense Temporal Motion Retargeting for Legged Robots
summary: Legged robots can learn expressive whole-body skills from the motions of humans and animals. Due to the morphology gap between the source and the robot, however, the motion must be tailored to the dynamic properties of the robot. In particular, dynamic motions such as a jump require careful adjustment, since their timing and control are interdependent. We propose dense temporal motion retargeting (DTMR), which jointly optimizes timing and control within a single optimization, where dense means that the timing is adjusted for every control step. This dense formulation enables DTMR to deform only the parts of the motion that need a change in timing. The problem is solved with sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) in parallel on a GPU. We evaluate DTMR against baselines on two hours of human motion with four humanoid robots, where the results show that DTMR outperforms baseline methods, particularly on dynamic motions. We also show that allowing more temporal deformation yields more precise retargeting. We further compare DTMR with a baseline that optimizes the temporal dimension, where the result shows that DTMR retargets more precisely under the same deformation budget while being ~19x faster. Lastly, policies trained on our references transfer to a real humanoid robot.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Dense Temporal Motion Retargeting (DTMR), a method that jointly optimizes timing and control at every control step within a single optimization to retarget human/animal motion onto legged robots, solved via GPU-parallel sampling-based MPC, and shown to outperform baselines especially on dynamic motions.
AI.motivation: Legged robots can acquire expressive whole-body skills from human and animal motions, but the morphology gap between the source and the robot requires tailoring the motion to the robot's dynamic properties. Dynamic motions like jumps are especially challenging because their timing and control are interdependent, demanding careful adjustment.
AI.method: DTMR jointly optimizes timing and control within a single optimization, with "dense" meaning timing is adjusted for every control step. This dense formulation lets DTMR deform only the parts of the motion needing a timing change. The problem is solved with sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) parallelized on a GPU.
AI.result: Evaluated against baselines on two hours of human motion with four humanoid robots, DTMR outperforms baselines, particularly on dynamic motions. Allowing more temporal deformation yields more precise retargeting. Compared to a baseline that optimizes the temporal dimension, DTMR retargets more precisely under the same deformation budget while being ~19x faster. Policies trained on DTMR references transfer to a real humanoid robot.
AI.conclusion: DTMR achieves more precise and faster motion retargeting than temporal-optimization baselines under equivalent deformation budgets, benefits from greater temporal deformation, and produces references whose policies transfer to real humanoid hardware.

title: AgBench: Agentic AI Benchmarks for Personal AI Devices
summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on cloud-hosted large language models for planning, tool use, and iterative execution, raising concerns about API cost and data exposure. Advances in personal AI devices enable agents to execute locally, but limited resources on device may affect task success and performance. Existing benchmarks are inadequate for systematically characterizing these trade-offs across devices, workloads, and deployment architectures. We present AgBench, a benchmark suite and open artifacts for reproducible evaluation of agentic AI on personal devices. Using AgBench, we evaluate local, hybrid, and cloud execution across agentic workloads, examining task success, latency, cloud API cost, and data exposure. Our results, drawn from over 162.07 million data points, show that personal AI devices can complete many agent tasks locally, but local-only execution generally has lower task success and longer completion times than cloud-only execution, especially as concurrency increases. Local-only execution eliminates cloud model API costs and sensitive-information exposure to cloud agents. Hybrid execution can improve task success, but its cloud cost and data exposure depend on how agents divide work and share information. No single architecture performs best across task success, goodput, cloud cost, and data exposure; deployment choices should reflect the intended workload and device capabilities. AgBench is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AgBench-2777.

AI.tldr: AgBench is a benchmark suite for reproducible evaluation of agentic AI on personal devices, comparing local, hybrid, and cloud execution across task success, latency, cloud API cost, and data exposure using over 162 million data points.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems increasingly depend on cloud-hosted LLMs for planning, tool use, and iterative execution, raising API cost and data exposure concerns. Personal AI devices can enable local execution, but limited on-device resources may affect task success and performance. Existing benchmarks cannot systematically characterize these trade-offs across devices, workloads, and deployment architectures.
AI.method: The authors present AgBench, a benchmark suite and set of open artifacts for reproducible evaluation of agentic AI on personal devices. Using AgBench, they evaluate local, hybrid, and cloud execution across agentic workloads, measuring task success, latency, cloud API cost, and data exposure.
AI.result: Based on over 162.07 million data points, personal AI devices can complete many agent tasks locally, but local-only execution generally yields lower task success and longer completion times than cloud-only execution, especially as concurrency increases. Local-only execution eliminates cloud model API costs and sensitive-information exposure to cloud agents. Hybrid execution can improve task success, but its cloud cost and data exposure depend on how agents divide work and share information. No single architecture performs best across task success, goodput, cloud cost, and data exposure.
AI.conclusion: No single deployment architecture is optimal across task success, goodput, cloud cost, and data exposure; deployment choices should reflect the intended workload and device capabilities. AgBench is publicly available for reproducible evaluation.

title: Yggdrasil: a Layer-First 3D Scene Graph for Real-Time Querying
summary:
Robotic agents use 3D scene graphs (3DSG) to perform tasks ranging from scene understanding to scene interaction. Although an extensive body of work addresses scene graph generation, little attention has been paid to optimizing the graph for consumption, which leaves state-of-the-art perception pipelines to work around their own scene graph and to pay a latency cost that does not fit the real-time budget a perception loop runs on.
  We present Yggdrasil, the first 3D scene graph designed to be efficient for both generation and consumption: a layer-first hierarchical graph built from generic nodes, edges, and layers, which expresses the representations existing pipelines already produce, indoor or outdoor, flat or hierarchical, while natively answering the positional and semantic queries downstream tasks issue.
  Against a published DSG baseline, Yggdrasil answers queries up to $121\times$ faster, and every query we measure falls between 2 and 127 microseconds, three to five orders of magnitude inside the 200 microsecond keyframe budget a 3DSG consumer lives in, on both a workstation and embedded class device. We integrate Yggdrasil into three published pipelines spanning human trajectory prediction, object-goal navigation, and human-aware motion planning, where it removes up to 99% of the time each spends on its scene graph. The implementation, benchmark harness, and all three integrations are available online.

AI.tldr: Yggdrasil is a layer-first hierarchical 3D scene graph that is efficient for both generation and consumption, answering downstream queries 2–127 microseconds (up to 121× faster than a DSG baseline) and cutting scene-graph time by up to 99% across three robotic pipelines.
AI.motivation: Robotic agents rely on 3D scene graphs (3DSG) for scene understanding and interaction. Prior work focuses on scene graph generation, but little attention has been paid to optimizing the graph for consumption. This forces state-of-the-art perception pipelines to work around their own scene graphs and incur latency that does not fit the real-time budget of a perception loop.
AI.method: The authors introduce Yggdrasil, a layer-first hierarchical graph built from generic nodes, edges, and layers. It expresses the representations existing pipelines already produce—indoor or outdoor, flat or hierarchical—while natively answering the positional and semantic queries issued by downstream tasks. It is integrated into three published pipelines: human trajectory prediction, object-goal navigation, and human-aware motion planning.
AI.result: Against a published DSG baseline, Yggdrasil answers queries up to 121× faster; every measured query takes 2 to 127 microseconds, three to five orders of magnitude inside the 200 microsecond keyframe budget of a 3DSG consumer, on both workstation and embedded-class devices. In the three pipelines, it removes up to 99% of the time each spends on its scene graph.
AI.conclusion: Yggdrasil is presented as the first 3D scene graph designed for efficient generation and consumption, providing substantial latency improvements suitable for real-time robotic perception. The implementation, benchmark harness, and all three integrations are available online.

title: EvoSteer: Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration via Reference-Anchored Credit Assignment
summary: In recent years, LLM-based multi-agent systems have been widely applied to orchestrate tool-using agents into executable communication graphs. However, existing self-evolving orchestration still faces key challenges, including post-hoc evolution that revises the team only after the trajectory ends, credit diffusion that gives every action the same terminal advantage under confounded baselines, and skill admission that is uncalibrated and never retired. To address these challenges, we propose EvoSteer, a new paradigm of Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration -- the orchestrator builds a running team and repairs its plausible but failing steps from execution features and a learned value estimate. To support this paradigm, we introduce Anchored Trajectory Balance (AnchorTB), a regression-style flow-matching loss that assigns each orchestration action a coefficient by balancing subtrajectories against a frozen reference. Built on the learned flow, we further propose Validated Skill Admission, in which a candidate skill is tried before promotion and promoted only if paired evidence passes a sequential test under a shared nominal testing budget. Moreover, AnchorTB combines measured task-level reference reward statistics with prefix-dependent corrections. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that EvoSteer significantly outperforms baselines across question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive decision making. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/evosteer.

AI.tldr: EvoSteer introduces online self-evolving graph orchestration for LLM multi-agent systems, using Anchored Trajectory Balance and Validated Skill Admission to enable real-time team repair and calibrated skill promotion.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving orchestration suffers from three limitations: post-hoc evolution that only revises the team after a trajectory ends, credit diffusion that assigns identical terminal advantage to every action under confounded baselines, and uncalibrated skill admission with no retirement mechanism.
AI.method: The paper proposes EvoSteer, an Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration paradigm where the orchestrator builds a running team and repairs plausible-but-failing steps using execution features and a learned value estimate. It introduces Anchored Trajectory Balance (AnchorTB), a regression-style flow-matching loss assigning per-action coefficients by balancing subtrajectories against a frozen reference, and combines measured task-level reference reward statistics with prefix-dependent corrections. It further proposes Validated Skill Admission, where candidate skills are tried before promotion and promoted only if paired evidence passes a sequential test under a shared nominal testing budget.
AI.result: Across twelve datasets spanning question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive decision making, EvoSteer significantly outperforms baselines.
AI.conclusion: EvoSteer offers an online, credit-aware, and calibration-driven approach to self-evolving multi-agent orchestration, with code publicly released.

title: TERRA: Terrain-Aware Reconstruction, Retargeting and Control for Musculoskeletal Locomotion
summary: Recent advances in musculoskeletal modeling and reinforcement learning have enabled muscle-actuated agents to reproduce increasingly complex human motions. Yet these capabilities remain largely confined to flat ground, in part because motion datasets rarely include aligned terrain geometry and because retargeting terrain interactions to complex musculoskeletal bodies is challenging. We present TERRA, an end-to-end pipeline for terrain-aware retargeting and control of musculoskeletal locomotion. From kinematic trajectories alone, TERRA combines terrain priors, estimated contacts, and negative free-space evidence to recover task-relevant support geometry. TERRA further considers anatomical, tendon-continuity, and contact constraints during retargeting. Using the resulting motion-terrain pairs from five datasets, we successfully train a single muscle-actuated control policy on 9.4 hours of diverse locomotion. Across reconstruction, retargeting, and held-out tracking benchmarks, TERRA improves terrain accuracy, sharply reduces anatomical and interaction violations, and achieves the highest observed completion rate over supported terrain families. Overall, TERRA provides a practical route from scene-less motion data to muscle-actuated locomotion over diverse non-flat terrain. Project website: https://cnai.epfl.ch/terra/

AI.tldr: TERRA is an end-to-end pipeline that retargets scene-less human motion data onto musculoskeletal bodies and recovers terrain geometry, enabling a single muscle-actuated policy to produce complex locomotion over diverse non-flat terrain.
AI.motivation: Musculoskeletal modeling and reinforcement learning now let muscle-actuated agents reproduce complex human motion, but this largely works only on flat ground. Two obstacles: motion datasets rarely contain aligned terrain geometry, and retargeting terrain interactions onto complex musculoskeletal bodies is difficult.
AI.method: From kinematic trajectories alone, TERRA combines terrain priors, estimated contacts, and negative free-space evidence to recover task-relevant support geometry. During retargeting it enforces anatomical, tendon-continuity, and contact constraints. Motion-terrain pairs derived from five datasets are then used to train a single muscle-actuated control policy.
AI.result: Trained on 9.4 hours of diverse locomotion, TERRA improves terrain accuracy across reconstruction, retargeting, and held-out tracking benchmarks, sharply reduces anatomical and interaction violations, and attains the highest observed completion rate across supported terrain families.
AI.conclusion: TERRA offers a practical route from scene-less motion data to muscle-actuated locomotion over diverse non-flat terrain.

title: Where Scientific Search Agents Fail: Decision-Checkpoint Auditing of Exposure and Inspection Attempts
summary: Final-answer accuracy does not reveal whether a scientific-search agent failed to encounter a target paper, attempt to inspect it, or return an accepted answer after inspection. We introduce decision checkpoints that record observations and tool actions without benchmark labels during inference, then join target identities and evaluator labels to assign outcome categories from recorded events. Across five conditions on 540 answerable AutoResearchBench Deep questions in a fixed, target-enriched environment, keyword search achieves 24.6\% accuracy, compared with 17.8\% for raw search. The keyword condition has fewer incorrect answers with neither target exposure nor inspection, but more incorrect answers after the target is exposed and left uninspected. Compared with keyword search, read-first has 27.4\% more recorded evidence-search calls. Target inspection attempts occur on 199 questions under read-first and 191 under keyword search; both conditions achieve 24.6\% accuracy. The checkpoint protocol makes these question-level differences explicit, distinguishing target exposure and inspection from aggregate accuracy and total tool use.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "decision checkpoints" that log a scientific-search agent's observations and tool actions during inference without using benchmark labels, then join them with target identities and evaluator labels to classify question-level outcomes. This protocol shows that equal final accuracy can mask different failure modes (target never encountered vs. exposed but not inspected).
AI.motivation: Final-answer accuracy is an aggregate metric that cannot reveal whether a search agent failed to encounter a target paper at all, chose not to inspect a paper it did encounter, or inspected it yet returned an accepted answer. This obscures the actual behavioral causes of failures and differences between search conditions.
AI.method: Decision checkpoints record observations and tool actions during inference without benchmark labels; target identities and evaluator labels are then joined post hoc to assign outcome categories (e.g., no target exposure, target exposed but uninspected, inspected) from the recorded events. Evaluated across five conditions on 540 answerable AutoResearchBench Deep questions in a fixed, target-enriched environment.
AI.result: Keyword search achieves 24.6% accuracy versus 17.8% for raw search. The keyword condition yields fewer incorrect answers with neither target exposure nor inspection, but more incorrect answers where the target was exposed yet left uninspected. Read-first records 27.4% more evidence-search calls than keyword search. Target inspection attempts occur on 199 questions under read-first and 191 under keyword search, yet both conditions reach 24.6% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The checkpoint protocol makes question-level behavioral differences explicit, separating target exposure and inspection from aggregate accuracy and total tool use, revealing that identical accuracy can arise from distinct underlying failure mechanisms.

title: Residual Wrench Certification and Margin-Aware Control Synthesis for Aerial Physical Interaction
summary: We develop a task-relative framework for certifying residual wrench authority after hover and contact loading in multirotors with bounded actuators. Using convex geometry, we derive signed margins for prescribed convex reserves, including Euclidean balls and weighted ellipsoids. We obtain computable reserve certificates from actuator-interiority bounds to support slack-maximizing allocation. To preserve the required reserve, we propose command projection onto a tightened feasible set. We then connect the available reserve to structured gain synthesis and certify a local tracking region that respects actuator limits. Within this region, we establish nominal exponential convergence and robust ultimate boundedness. For the prescribed task and morphology family, we show that the optimized octarotor attains a larger margin than the optimized hexarotor at equal total thrust. We evaluate the proposed framework in closed-loop simulations of sustained rigid-wall contact using a fixed-geometry octarotor and a variable-tilt quadrotor with matched installed thrust. The quadrotor's local certificate admits a higher normalized push limit for the prescribed task family. In tests beyond the realizability boundaries, we observe the predicted loss of authority through rotor-thrust limits for the octarotor and tilt-servo limits for the quadrotor.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a task-relative framework using convex geometry to certify residual wrench authority for multirotors with bounded actuators after hover and contact loading, deriving signed margins, computable reserve certificates, and local tracking guarantees, and comparing optimized octarotor, hexarotor, and variable-tilt quadrotor designs.
AI.motivation: Multirotors with bounded actuators lose wrench authority after hover and contact loading, so a rigorous, task-relative means of certifying the remaining control authority (residual reserve) is needed.
AI.method: A task-relative certification framework is built on convex geometry, deriving signed margins for prescribed convex reserves (Euclidean balls, weighted ellipsoids) and computable reserve certificates from actuator-interiority bounds. Slack-maximizing allocation is supported via command projection onto a tightened feasible set. The available reserve is linked to structured gain synthesis, yielding a certified local tracking region; nominal exponential convergence and robust ultimate boundedness are established within it.
AI.result: For the prescribed task and morphology family, the optimized octarotor attains a larger margin than the optimized hexarotor at equal total thrust. Closed-loop simulations of sustained rigid-wall contact compare a fixed-geometry octarotor and a variable-tilt quadrotor with matched installed thrust: the quadrotor's local certificate admits a higher normalized push limit. Beyond realizability boundaries, authority loss occurs via rotor-thrust limits (octarotor) and tilt-servo limits (quadrotor), as predicted.
AI.conclusion: The framework certifies residual wrench authority, supports reserve-preserving allocation and gain synthesis with local tracking guarantees, and predicts morphology-dependent authority limits validated in simulation.

title: Concept-Grounded Attention: A Controlled Evaluation of Graph-Injected Attention, Temporal Versioning, and Epistemic Status
summary: Knowledge-intensive language-model systems typically represent external knowledge as text chunks or static graphs, with limited support for concept evolution, point-in-time reasoning, and distinctions between validated and inferred knowledge. We introduce the Concept Lifecycle Model (CLM), which represents concepts as persistent, graph-grounded, temporally versioned entities with explicit provenance and epistemic status, and Concept-Grounded Attention (CGA), which injects concept-graph structure into transformer computation through graph-biased self-attention (Form A) and gated cross-attention over concept nodes (Form B). We evaluate the framework in controlled settings using disabled-mechanism baselines. On 200 MuSiQue and HotpotQA questions with retrieval fixed, concept-graph retrieval recovers explicit multi-hop paths but does not improve evidence recall. Form A appears to steer attention, with 2.76 times more attention on gold than distractor concepts, but the same ratio occurs when Form A is disabled; the learned bias is negligible and no answers change. An identity-preserving Form B improves F1 from 0.188 to 0.221, but control concepts yield 0.213, indicating that most of the gain reflects added capacity. On LongMemEval, explicit temporal representation improves answer accuracy by 13 to 25 points across all tested generators, up to 122B parameters, while simplified CLM version resolution performs similarly to dated serialization because concept identity is not established reliably. On a synthetic source-independence task, protocol-derived epistemic status reduces unsupported assertions from 28% to 0.1% in a fine-tuned small model and from 19-68% to 0-5% in 72-122B models. Overall, the results support making temporal validity and epistemic status explicit, while showing that graph-attention diagnostics are not informative without disabled-mechanism controls.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Concept Lifecycle Model (CLM) and Concept-Grounded Attention (CGA) for knowledge-intensive systems, representing concepts as temporally versioned, provenance-tagged graph entities and injecting concept structure into transformer computation. Controlled ablations show that explicit temporal representation and epistemic status yield real gains, while graph-attention benefits are largely explained by added capacity and vanish under disabled-mechanism controls.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge-intensive systems represent external knowledge as text chunks or static graphs, which poorly support concept evolution, point-in-time reasoning, and separating validated from inferred knowledge. The paper aims to make temporal validity and epistemic status explicit and to test whether concept-graph structure actually improves transformer attention.
AI.method: CLM represents concepts as persistent, graph-grounded, temporally versioned entities with explicit provenance and epistemic status. CGA injects concept-graph structure via graph-biased self-attention (Form A) and gated cross-attention over concept nodes (Form B). Evaluation uses controlled, disabled-mechanism baselines on 200 MuSiQue/HotpotQA questions with fixed retrieval, LongMemEval, a synthetic source-independence task, and models from small fine-tuned to 122B generators.
AI.result: Concept-graph retrieval recovers explicit multi-hop paths but does not improve evidence recall. Form A shows 2.76x more attention on gold than distractor concepts, yet the same ratio appears with Form A disabled; learned bias is negligible and no answers change. Identity-preserving Form B raises F1 from 0.188 to 0.221, but control concepts reach 0.213, indicating most gain is added capacity. On LongMemEval, explicit temporal representation improves accuracy by 13-25 points across generators up to 122B. On source-independence, protocol-derived epistemic status cuts unsupported assertions from 28% to 0.1% (small fine-tuned) and 19-68% to 0-5% (72-122B).
AI.conclusion: The framework supports making temporal validity and epistemic status explicit, yielding consistent gains. However, graph-attention diagnostics are uninformative without disabled-mechanism controls, and simplified CLM version resolution matches dated serialization because concept identity is not reliably established.

title: CEER2: Directional and Tunable End-Effector and Root Compliance for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Humanoids are increasingly capable of tracking complex whole-body motions, but physical interaction introduces a different challenge. When a robot makes contact with a person or the environment, it needs to respond to external forces while preserving the motion needed for the task. This response can vary across directions in the end-effectors and on the body. For example, an end effector may need to accommodate contact force in one direction while maintaining motion accuracy in another, while the robot body may resist an external force or move with it. We present a compliance framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines directional and tunable end-effector (EE) compliance with selectable root compliance for external force rejection or force following. A hierarchical reinforcement learning controller modulates a fixed whole-body tracking policy through high-level EE and root commands, while interaction forces are estimated from proprioceptive history. Our simulation and real-world experiments on a humanoid demonstrate directional stiffness control, online stiffness adjustment, distinct root compliance, compliant manipulation, and collaborative carrying.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical RL compliance framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines directional, tunable end-effector compliance with selectable root compliance, enabling external-force rejection or following during physical interaction.
AI.motivation: Humanoids can track complex whole-body motions, but physical interaction poses a distinct challenge: upon contact with a person or the environment, the robot must respond to external forces while preserving task-required motion. Compliance needs can differ across directions and body sites—an end effector may need to accommodate force in one direction yet maintain motion accuracy in another, while the root may resist or yield to external forces.
AI.method: The authors design a compliance framework combining directional and tunable end-effector (EE) compliance with selectable root compliance for force rejection or force following. A hierarchical reinforcement learning controller modulates a fixed whole-body tracking policy via high-level EE and root commands, with interaction forces estimated from proprioceptive history.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world humanoid experiments demonstrate directional stiffness control, online stiffness adjustment, distinct root compliance behaviors, compliant manipulation, and collaborative carrying.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables flexible, direction- and site-specific compliance for humanoid loco-manipulation, supporting both compliant manipulation and physically collaborative tasks such as carrying.

title: GATE-ST: Gene-Aware Text-image Encoder for Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Spatial transcriptomics enables spatially resolved gene expression analysis from slide-level images while preserving morphological features, providing valuable information for studying disease mechanisms and developing treatments. However, spatial gene expression profiling typically requires expensive and time-consuming tests. While existing image-based prediction optimizations mostly revolve around including positional embeddings and further image-based changes, text-based optimizations remain relatively unexplored. We present GATE-ST, which incorporates text-based inputs into image-based spatial gene expression predictions. With this approach, generated text descriptions of genes are utilized to better spatial transcriptomics prediction results. Gene summaries are put through a text encoder, generating embeddings that integrate with image embeddings through cross-attention layers to align with morphological features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of such text inputs by benchmarking performance against random gene embeddings and multiple other image-text fusion architectures, and show that GATE-ST outperforms these alternatives. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of GATE-ST in pathology imaging, which may greatly reduce the time and cost of accurate spatial transcriptomic predictions, proving the potential of text-guided spatial gene expression prediction.

AI.tldr: GATE-ST augments image-based spatial gene expression prediction by incorporating text descriptions of genes, fusing text embeddings with image embeddings via cross-attention to improve spatial transcriptomics prediction accuracy and reduce reliance on costly profiling.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics provides spatially resolved gene expression while preserving morphology, valuable for disease research and treatment development. However, spatial gene expression profiling is expensive and time-consuming. Existing image-based prediction optimizations mainly focus on positional embeddings and image-based modifications, leaving text-based optimization relatively unexplored.
AI.method: GATE-ST incorporates text-based inputs into image-based spatial gene expression prediction. Generated gene text descriptions (gene summaries) are encoded by a text encoder, producing text embeddings that are integrated with image embeddings through cross-attention layers to align with morphological features.
AI.result: Benchmarking against random gene embeddings and multiple other image-text fusion architectures shows that GATE-ST outperforms these alternatives.
AI.conclusion: GATE-ST is effective in pathology imaging, potentially greatly reducing the time and cost of accurate spatial transcriptomic predictions and demonstrating the potential of text-guided spatial gene expression prediction.

title: Path-Following Control and Terramechanics Analysis for Planetary Rovers Under Wheel-to-Wheel Traction Asymmetry
comment: Author's version of a manuscript accepted at the International Conference on Space Robotics 2026 (iSpaRo 2026). (c) IEEE
summary: This paper proposes a control strategy for path following that is model-free and relies solely on deceleration for skid-steering planetary rovers navigating deformable loose terrain under continuously imposed traction asymmetry. While conventional controllers that are based on kinematics frequently cause slip-sinkage entrapment by accelerating the wheels during path correction, the proposed approach prevents this failure by setting an upper limit on the maximum commanded velocity. Heading correction is achieved solely through the selective deceleration of the outer wheels, which are located on the outside of the turn, driving them into a negative slip regime to act as a mechanical anchor. The system was evaluated using the four-wheel independent-drive rover EX1 under an asymmetric wheel configuration with different left and right grouser heights that induces significant deviations from the path. Experimental results demonstrate that this deceleration-only control successfully suppresses accumulated lateral drift across various velocity regimes up to 0.7 m/s without causing sinkage. Crucially, direct force measurements from onboard multi-axis sensors provide important empirical evidence of the underlying terramechanics, proving that the targeted deceleration establishes dynamic load equalization across the chassis and completely restores the native thrust capability of the opposite driving wheel.

AI.tldr: A model-free, deceleration-only path-following controller for skid-steering planetary rovers on deformable terrain under persistent traction asymmetry avoids slip-sinkage entrapment by capping commanded velocity and correcting heading only via selective deceleration of outer wheels.
AI.motivation: Kinematics-based controllers tend to accelerate wheels during path correction, which on deformable loose terrain can cause slip-sinkage entrapment. A strategy is needed that follows paths under continuously imposed traction asymmetry without inducing sinkage.
AI.method: The approach is model-free and relies solely on deceleration. It imposes an upper limit on maximum commanded velocity, and performs heading correction exclusively by selectively decelerating the outer wheels. This drives them into negative slip so they act as a mechanical anchor, rather than accelerating inner or opposite wheels. Validation used the four-wheel independent-drive rover EX1 with an asymmetric wheel configuration (different left and right grouser heights) that induces significant path deviations.
AI.result: The deceleration-only controller suppressed accumulated lateral drift across velocity regimes up to 0.7 m/s without causing sinkage. Onboard multi-axis force sensors confirmed that targeted deceleration produced dynamic load equalization across the chassis and fully restored the native thrust capability of the opposite driving wheel.
AI.conclusion: Deceleration-only, model-free path following is effective for skid-steering rovers on deformable terrain under sustained traction asymmetry, mitigating entrapment risk while improving load distribution and thrust recovery.

title: Budget Boundary Effects in Test-Time Mathematical Reasoning
comment: Accepted as a poster at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI), NeurIPS 2026. 11 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Includes additional post-acceptance accounting and selection diagnostics
summary: A cumulative token cap can fall inside a mathematical derivation, forcing a test-time controller to choose between stopping at the cap (strict) and allowing the current attempt to finish (advisory). We measure this boundary choice with paired offline replays of 19,200 public traces: 120 AIME, BrUMO and HMMT problems and two archive configurations of one model. Candidate order and a 16-attempt cap are fixed, and answer selection is blind to reference answers and correctness labels. Three findings emerge. First, at the 4k cap, most advisory accuracy gains replace abstention with a correct answer; strict stopping pays for an unfinished prefix that the completed-only selector cannot use. Second, comparisons along realized cost differ from same-cap comparisons: advisory 4k in low has higher accuracy than strict 8k at comparable mean completion cost, while in high its observed accuracy is 0.42 points below strict 32k using 59% of its mean tokens. These aggregate comparisons do not establish equal-compute superiority or accuracy equivalence. Third, increased candidate coverage does not guarantee higher answer accuracy: a log-probability selector loses accuracy while coverage rises, including after a source-grade consistency repair. Same-cap majority-accuracy differences shrink below 1.3 percentage points at 32k. Budget curves should jointly state the cap, realized cost, eligible candidates, stopping rule and selector information.

AI.tldr: Paired offline replays of 19,200 public traces compare strict versus advisory stopping at a cumulative token cap, showing that advisory stopping mainly converts abstentions into correct answers, that same-cap and realized-cost comparisons diverge, and that higher candidate coverage does not guarantee higher accuracy.
AI.motivation: A cumulative token cap can fall inside a mathematical derivation, forcing a test-time controller to either stop exactly at the cap (strict) or let the current attempt finish (advisory). This boundary choice is under-measured, and its effect on accuracy, realized cost, and candidate selection is unclear.
AI.method: Paired offline replays of 19,200 public traces: 120 AIME, BrUMO, and HMMT problems under two archive configurations of one model. Candidate order and a 16-attempt cap are fixed; answer selection is blind to reference answers and correctness labels. Comparisons are made both at the same cap and along realized cost.
AI.result: At the 4k cap, most advisory accuracy gains replace abstention with a correct answer, whereas strict stopping pays for an unfinished prefix the completed-only selector cannot use. Advisory 4k (low) exceeds strict 8k at comparable mean completion cost, while in high the observed accuracy is 0.42 points below strict 32k using 59% of its mean tokens—aggregate comparisons that do not establish equal-compute superiority or accuracy equivalence. A log-probability selector loses accuracy as candidate coverage rises, even after a source-grade consistency repair; same-cap majority-accuracy differences shrink below 1.3 percentage points at 32k.
AI.conclusion: Budget curves should jointly state the cap, realized cost, eligible candidates, stopping rule, and selector information. Realized-cost and same-cap comparisons answer different questions, and increased candidate coverage does not guarantee higher answer accuracy.

title: FlapKAD: A Simulation Dataset of Coupled Wing Kinematics and Aerodynamic Dynamics for Flapping-Wing Aerial Vehicles
summary: Experimental investigation and modeling of flapping-wing aerial vehicles are limited by the scarcity of large-scale records that temporally align wing kinematics, aerodynamic responses, and flight states. Existing datasets are often limited in scale and affected by measurement noise and temporal misalignment between rapidly varying wing motion and the associated dynamic response, particularly during high-frequency flapping. We introduce FlapKAD, an episode-structured simulation dataset comprising 2,000 rigid-wing flight episodes and 720,152 valid time steps, with bilateral wing kinematics, aerodynamic responses, and flight states recorded synchronously within a common clock. FlapKAD supports a unified bidirectional sequence-prediction benchmark constructed from the same temporally aligned episodes. The forward task predicts future vertical force coefficients and body vertical velocity from histories of realized flap and twist angles, whereas the inverse task reconstructs future flap- and twist-angle trajectories from the corresponding response histories. A benchmark of eight representative time-series architectures across multiple prediction horizons reveals direction- and horizon-dependent model behavior, systematically higher reconstruction errors for twist angle than for flap angle, and no consistent advantage from increased architectural complexity. FlapKAD provides a reproducible dataset and benchmark for studying coupled wing-kinematic, aerodynamic, and flight-state dynamics in flapping-wing aerial vehicles.

AI.tldr: FlapKAD is a temporally aligned, episode-structured simulation dataset of 2,000 rigid-wing flapping flight episodes (720,152 time steps) that synchronizes bilateral wing kinematics, aerodynamic responses, and flight states, together with a bidirectional sequence-prediction benchmark over eight time-series architectures.
AI.motivation: Research on flapping-wing aerial vehicles is constrained by the scarcity of large-scale records that temporally align wing kinematics, aerodynamic responses, and flight states; existing datasets suffer from limited scale, measurement noise, and temporal misalignment between rapidly varying wing motion and its dynamic response, especially at high flapping frequencies.
AI.method: The authors introduce FlapKAD, an episode-structured simulation dataset with 2,000 rigid-wing flight episodes and 720,152 valid time steps, recording bilateral wing kinematics, aerodynamic responses, and flight states synchronously on a common clock. From the same aligned episodes they construct a unified bidirectional sequence-prediction benchmark: a forward task predicting future vertical force coefficients and body vertical velocity from histories of realized flap and twist angles, and an inverse task reconstructing future flap- and twist-angle trajectories from response histories. Eight representative time-series architectures are benchmarked across multiple prediction horizons.
AI.result: Benchmarking reveals direction- and horizon-dependent model behavior, systematically higher reconstruction errors for twist angle than for flap angle, and no consistent advantage from increased architectural complexity.
AI.conclusion: FlapKAD offers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for studying coupled wing-kinematic, aerodynamic, and flight-state dynamics in flapping-wing aerial vehicles.

title: Staying on Task: Testing the Foundations of Long-Horizon Agent Reliability
summary: Long-horizon agentic workflows require models to sustain repeated state-dependent actions all while the context grows, sub-task complexity changes, and new data arrives. Each situation represents an independent axis along which an agent may fail. An agent reconciling a long ledger, for example, must repeatedly read its state, update the correct record, and preserve alignment across thousands of outputs. A model may accept the entire ledger yet lose its place or stop applying the operation consistently as generation proceeds. We introduce Long-Transduction, a controlled diagnostic that tests a model's ability to stay on task during long generation while continuously reading, mutating, and outputting input-context dependent operations such as arithmetic, sorting, variable lookups, and table transformations. Long-Transduction evaluation independently varies local task complexity, input data formatting, and context length isolate failures along each axis. We evaluate seven open-weight models, finding a 62.8\% decrease when scaling context length from 4-128K, a 36.5\% decrease when varying input format, and a 39.9\% decrease by increasing local task complexity. Together, these failures represent critical liabilities in long-horizon agentic workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Long-Transduction, a controlled diagnostic benchmark that tests whether models can sustain repeated state-dependent operations during long generation. It independently varies context length, input format, and local task complexity to isolate distinct failure axes, finding open-weight models degrade substantially along all three.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agentic workflows require models to perform repeated, state-dependent actions as context grows, sub-task complexity changes, and new data arrives. Each of these is an independent axis of potential failure: a model may accept a long input yet lose its place or stop applying an operation consistently as generation proceeds. Existing evaluations do not cleanly separate these axes, so the sources of long-horizon failures remain poorly isolated.
AI.method: The authors propose Long-Transduction, a controlled diagnostic in which a model must continuously read, mutate, and output input-context-dependent operations (e.g., arithmetic, sorting, variable lookups, table transformations) during long generation. The design independently varies three factors—context length, input data formatting, and local task complexity—so that performance degradation can be attributed to each axis separately. Seven open-weight models are evaluated.
AI.result: Scaling context length from 4K to 128K produces a 62.8% decrease in performance; varying input format produces a 36.5% decrease; increasing local task complexity produces a 39.9% decrease. These results hold across seven open-weight models.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon reliability in agentic workflows is limited by multiple independent axes of failure—context length, input formatting, and local task complexity—each of which degrades model performance substantially even when other factors are held fixed. These failures constitute critical liabilities for long-horizon agentic workflows and motivate more targeted evaluation and modeling of sustained state-dependent generation.

title: Bounded Channel-Adaptive Spectral Learning for Forward-Consistent Inverse Flapping-Wing Aerodynamics
summary: Flapping-wing vehicles regulate aerodynamic forces and moments through coordinated variations in stroke, deviation, and pitch motion. Because the resulting loads depend on both the instantaneous wing configuration and its preceding motion history, recovering suitable wing kinematics from a desired aerodynamic trajectory is a challenging inverse problem. Existing sequence models capture temporal dependencies, while spectral methods can exploit the periodic structure of flapping motion. However, unrestricted frequency-domain augmentation may interfere with temporal representations and produce inconsistent corrections across kinematic variables and prediction horizons. We propose the Bounded Channel-Adaptive Spectral Residual Gated Recurrent Unit (BCS-GRU), which retains recurrent temporal prediction as its primary representation and restricts spectral information to a controlled output-specific correction. We further introduce a causally aligned forward-consistency objective that evaluates predicted kinematics through a separately trained and frozen aerodynamic surrogate. Experiments under a unified episode-level protocol show that BCS-GRU improves inverse prediction over recurrent and adaptive-spectral baselines, with greater benefits at longer prediction horizons. Forward-consistent fine-tuning further improves surrogate-based aerodynamic consistency while maintaining mean kinematic accuracy. These results demonstrate that controlled spectral correction and forward-consistent learning provide an effective framework for history-aware inverse modelling of flapping-wing aerodynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BCS-GRU, a model for inverse aerodynamic modeling of flapping-wing vehicles that combines recurrent temporal prediction with bounded, channel-adaptive spectral corrections and a forward-consistency fine-tuning objective.
AI.motivation: Recovering suitable wing kinematics from a desired aerodynamic trajectory is a challenging inverse problem because aerodynamic loads depend on both the instantaneous wing configuration and its preceding motion history. Existing sequence models capture temporal dependencies but spectral methods that exploit periodic flapping structure can interfere with temporal representations when applied without restriction, producing inconsistent corrections across kinematic variables and prediction horizons.
AI.method: The proposed Bounded Channel-Adaptive Spectral Residual Gated Recurrent Unit (BCS-GRU) keeps recurrent temporal prediction as the primary representation and restricts spectral information to a controlled, output-specific correction. Additionally, a causally aligned forward-consistency objective is introduced that evaluates predicted kinematics through a separately trained and frozen aerodynamic surrogate. Experiments use a unified episode-level protocol.
AI.result: BCS-GRU improves inverse prediction over recurrent and adaptive-spectral baselines, with greater benefits at longer prediction horizons. Forward-consistent fine-tuning further improves surrogate-based aerodynamic consistency while maintaining mean kinematic accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Controlled spectral correction and forward-consistent learning provide an effective framework for history-aware inverse modeling of flapping-wing aerodynamics.

title: UniEvo-VL: An On-policy Self-Distillation Training Recipe for Multimodal Model Self-improvement
summary: Modern multimodal models bring generation and understanding into a single unified system, which enables them to provide and learn from their own feedback. Motivated by this unified capacity, we introduce UniEvo-VL, a self-evolving framework for multimodal models to learn from this constructive self-correction feedback during test-time compute. Instead of relying on a separate, often larger, teacher, we leverage their self-critiques as privileged information and ask a single multimodal model to act as both teacher and student with different contexts. The student only sees the vanilla question, while the teacher conditions on the privileged critique. Then training minimizes the per-state divergence between their denoising diffusion distributions over the student's own sampling trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that UniEvo-VL improves the image generation capabilities of multimodal models, while maintaining their sensitivity to additional reflection information. Specifically, we build on top of the open-source Qwen-image-2512 and observe a significant performance gain from 0.747 to 0.808 on GenEval and from 32.97 to 35.53 on GenEval2 Soft-TIFA. Moreover, attempts with more powerful external critics (e.g., GPT5.6-Luna) show that multimodal models with strong judge capabilities can anticipate a higher self-evolving ceiling. Last but not least, mixed text-rendering outcomes show that our self-improvements may not be uniform across different tasks. Our study aims to shed light on the current hot recursive self-improvement research line to enhance the user experience when using multimodal models without external supervision or guidance.

AI.tldr: UniEvo-VL is a self-evolving test-time framework in which a single multimodal model acts as both teacher and student, using its own self-critiques as privileged information to minimize per-state divergence between their denoising diffusion distributions, improving image generation without external supervision.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal models can generate and understand, so they can produce and learn from their own feedback. The authors want to exploit this capacity for recursive self-improvement at test-time compute, avoiding dependence on a separate (often larger) external teacher or external supervision/guidance.
AI.method: The single multimodal model is used in two roles with different contexts: the student sees only the vanilla question, while the teacher additionally conditions on the model's self-generated critique (privileged information). Training minimizes the per-state divergence between the teacher's and student's denoising diffusion distributions along the student's own sampling trajectories. Built on Qwen-image-2512; also tested with stronger external critics such as GPT5.6-Luna.
AI.result: GenEval improves from 0.747 to 0.808 and GenEval2 Soft-TIFA from 32.97 to 35.53. Models with stronger judge capabilities—via more powerful external critics—show a higher self-evolving ceiling. Results are not uniform across tasks, with mixed text-rendering outcomes observed.
AI.conclusion: Self-critique-as-privileged-information enables effective self-evolving multimodal generation while preserving sensitivity to reflection information. The work contributes to recursive self-improvement research and aims to improve user experience with multimodal models without external supervision or guidance, while noting task-dependent, non-uniform gains.

title: AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ICRA 2027. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Desk-based learning and creative activities benefit from handwritten engagement. However, current generative AI tools deliver guidance through a separate screen, creating a gap between where users think and where assistance appears. To address this, in this work we design AIfred, a desk-based robotic arm with a projector mounted at the end-effector that places AI-generated guidance alongside handwritten work. AIfred combines workspace perception, context-aware content generation, and robot-mediated projection to support math assignments, image generation, and drawing tasks. In a user study (n = 36), we compared AIfred against ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Luna) running on a laptop. Both tools performed comparably while assistance was available during the math assignment (6.7 vs. 7.3/10, p = .41), but AIfred improved short-term learning transfer by 60% once assistance was withdrawn (7.0 vs. 4.4/10, p = .003). In addition, independent art and design professors ranked drawings produced with AIfred better in 33 of 36 cases. Our findings indicate that spatially co-located AI assistance benefits tasks whose guidance shares a spatial frame with the work.

AI.tldr: AIfred is a desk-based robotic arm with an end-effector projector that spatially co-locates AI-generated guidance with handwritten work; versus laptop ChatGPT it matched in-task math performance but improved short-term learning transfer by 60% after assistance was withdrawn, and produced better-ranked drawings in 33/36 cases.
AI.motivation: Handwritten and creative desk activities benefit from physical engagement, yet current generative AI tools deliver guidance on a separate screen, creating a spatial gap between where users work/think and where assistance appears.
AI.method: Designed AIfred, a robotic arm with a projector mounted at the end-effector that projects AI guidance directly onto the workspace, integrating workspace perception, context-aware content generation, and robot-mediated projection for math assignments, image generation, and drawing tasks. Evaluated in a user study (n = 36) against ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Luna) on a laptop, plus expert ranking of drawings by independent art and design professors.
AI.result: During assisted math, performance was comparable (6.7 vs. 7.3/10, p = .41). After assistance was withdrawn, AIfred improved short-term learning transfer by 60% (7.0 vs. 4.4/10, p = .003). Art/design professors ranked AIfred drawings better in 33 of 36 cases.
AI.conclusion: Spatially co-located AI assistance benefits tasks whose guidance shares a spatial frame with the work, improving transfer and creative output quality.

title: Code to Control: Synthesizing Parameterized Reactive Controllers
summary: Recent LLM-based approaches to control either invoke a language model to select actions or synthesize world models that require planning at every decision, introducing latency that can limit real-time use. We introduce Code to Control, an approach that synthesizes Python controllers which execute directly as policies. Code to Control separates program structure from parameters. An LLM synthesizes the controller structure, while derivative-free search fits its parameters for continuous control using feedback from the environment. Once learned, the resulting controllers require neither LLM inference nor planning at decision time, enabling real-time gameplay and, under our timing protocol, faster action selection than a PPO policy. Across a suite of Atari games, Flappy Bird, and MuJoCo tasks, Code to Control outperforms planning-based program synthesis methods, remains competitive with deep reinforcement learning while using fewer environment interactions, transfers across substantial changes in environment dynamics, and scales to complex locomotion tasks.

AI.tldr: Code to Control synthesizes Python controllers as direct policies, separating LLM-generated structure from derivative-free parameter fitting, achieving real-time control without LLM inference or planning.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based control methods either call a language model for each action selection or synthesize world models requiring planning at every decision, introducing latency that limits real-time use.
AI.method: The approach separates program structure from parameters: an LLM synthesizes the controller structure, and derivative-free search fits its parameters for continuous control using environment feedback. The learned controllers then execute directly as policies, requiring neither LLM inference nor planning at decision time.
AI.result: Across Atari games, Flappy Bird, and MuJoCo tasks, it outperforms planning-based program synthesis, stays competitive with deep RL using fewer environment interactions, transfers across substantial changes in environment dynamics, and scales to complex locomotion. It also enables real-time gameplay with faster action selection than a PPO policy under the timing protocol.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling LLM-synthesized controller structure from derivative-free parameter optimization yields efficient, real-time-capable controllers that avoid inference and planning overhead while remaining competitive and transferable.

title: HALO: Heterogeneous Allocation Via Localized Observations for the Vehicle Routing Problem
comment: 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted.
