Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary:
Scalable robotic fleets have become increasingly popular for various applications such as package delivery, warehouse management, and military operations. Prior fleet control algorithms solve centralized routing problems with up to $1{,}000$ tasks in controlled environments, yet they fail to consider realistic constraints such as limited observation and communication ranges typical of decentralized fleets. Thus, deploying existing fleet control algorithms into real-world settings is currently infeasible.
  To tackle this, we propose Heterogeneous Allocation via Localized Observations (HALO) to solve the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP). HALO is a hybrid method that splits the VRP into allocation and routing portions to provide onboard, real-time solutions to robots in dynamic environments. During the allocation phase, HALO utilizes a heterogeneous graph neural network framework with unique message passing layers to explicitly separate the learning of spatial distributions and task-to-robot compatibility.
  Evaluation results on a partially observable, online variant of the VRP show HALO significantly outperforms the heuristic baseline while maintaining similar solution quality to an all-knowing offline variant of HALO. While HALO is explicitly designed for partially observable environments, it imposes no strict upper bound on the observation space allowing us to test HALO on the traditional static, single-depot VRP. Here, HALO outperforms state-of-the-art architectures strictly optimized for the static variant of the VRP by up to $14.06\%$. Throughout all testing, this framework maintains the quickest execution times which emphasizes its potential for large-scale, real-time deployment.

AI.tldr: HALO is a hybrid, decentralized vehicle routing framework that splits VRP into allocation and routing, using a heterogeneous graph neural network with specialized message passing to handle limited observation and communication in robotic fleets.
AI.motivation: Scalable robotic fleets (delivery, warehousing, military) need decentralized control, but prior fleet control algorithms solve centralized routing with up to 1,000 tasks in controlled settings and ignore realistic constraints like limited observation and communication ranges, making real-world deployment infeasible.
AI.method: HALO (Heterogeneous Allocation via Localized Observations) is a hybrid method that decomposes VRP into allocation and routing to deliver onboard, real-time solutions in dynamic environments. Its allocation phase uses a heterogeneous graph neural network framework with unique message passing layers that explicitly separate learning of spatial distributions from task-to-robot compatibility.
AI.result: On a partially observable, online VRP variant, HALO significantly outperforms the heuristic baseline while matching the solution quality of an all-knowing offline HALO variant. Tested on the traditional static, single-depot VRP despite being designed for partial observability (no strict upper bound on observation space), HALO beats state-of-the-art architectures strictly optimized for the static variant by up to 14.06%. It also maintains the quickest execution times across all tests.
AI.conclusion: HALO provides high-quality, real-time, decentralized VRP solutions under realistic partial observability and communication limits, with speed and scalability supporting large-scale real-world fleet deployment.

title: Learning to Route in Visual Space via Multi-Step Embedding Retrieval
summary: LLM agents rely on retrieval tools to access external knowledge, yet visual agentic search remains severely bottlenecked by standard single-step retrievers. In current pipelines, the agent must issue text queries for every intermediate step, struggling when visual clues are difficult to describe or when the retriever fails to surface necessary intermediate evidence within its top results. We hypothesize that offloading multi-step navigation across the entire embedding space directly to the retrieval tool resolves this performance bottleneck. To study this systematically, we introduce VHOP, a flexible data generation framework and benchmark with five core difficulty levels testing both visual matching and search planning. Using this framework, we develop VHOP-Router, an end-to-end training pipeline---combining supervised fine-tuning, online imitation learning, and reinforcement learning---that transforms a standard embedding model into an autoregressive multi-step retriever. Operating directly in the visual latent space, VHOP-Router retrieves linked image chains in a single tool call without requiring the agent to formulate intermediate text queries. Experiments show VHOP-Router boosts retrieval performance from under 5\% to 76.3\%. In agentic search, it improves task success rates by 52.7\% and reduces the average token length by 61\% from 1886 to 728, whereas upgrading the agent yields only a 3.7\% gain. Compared to a strong baseline where the agent retrieves the top 50 results per step, VHOP-Router maintains superior performance while reducing in-context images by $23\times$ and cutting the cumulative API payload by $35\times$. The models also generalize robustly to unseen difficulty levels and realistic test sets. Ultimately, VHOP and VHOP-Router provide an efficient and effective solution for visual agentic search that leaves native LLM capabilities entirely intact.

AI.tldr: VHOP is a benchmark and data generation framework for visual agentic search, paired with VHOP-Router, an autoregressive multi-step retriever trained via SFT, online imitation, and RL that navigates the visual latent space to retrieve image chains in a single tool call, dramatically improving retrieval and agentic search efficiency.
AI.motivation: Visual agentic search is bottlenecked by standard single-step retrievers: agents must issue text queries at every intermediate step, fail when visual clues are hard to describe, and miss necessary intermediate evidence in top results.
AI.method: The authors introduce VHOP, a data generation framework and benchmark with five difficulty levels testing visual matching and search planning. Using it, they develop VHOP-Router, an end-to-end training pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, online imitation learning, and reinforcement learning, which turns a standard embedding model into an autoregressive multi-step retriever operating directly in the visual latent space.
AI.result: VHOP-Router raises retrieval from under 5% to 76.3%, improves agentic task success by 52.7%, and cuts token length 61% (1886 to 728), versus only a 3.7% gain from upgrading the agent. Against a top-50-per-step baseline it maintains superior performance while reducing in-context images by 23x and API payload by 35x, generalizing to unseen difficulty levels and realistic test sets.
AI.conclusion: VHOP and VHOP-Router offer an efficient, effective solution for visual agentic search that offloads multi-step navigation to the retrieval tool while leaving native LLM capabilities entirely intact.

title: PhaseSync-Exo: Human Clock Anchored Reference Adaptation for Dynamic Gait Tracking
summary: Human-aware exoskeleton walking requires reconstructing gait, tracking diverse motions under dynamic constraints, and preserving human timing. We present PhaseSync-Exo, which combines two-IMU CNN-Transformer reconstruction, factorized amplitude-cadence retargeting with curriculum-trained recurrent control, and a human-clock-anchored adapter (HCA). HCA combines human-clock attraction with robot-relative feedback to adjust reference rate while preserving forward progression and continuity. The reconstruction module achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.24 degrees on a held-out recording, and the frozen tracking policy completes 356 of 357 amplitude-frequency trials. Two complementary dynamic comparisons isolate HCA's timing benefit without retraining. Against robot-relative correction, HCA reduces human-clock phase MAE from 95.55 degrees to 10.99 degrees, limiting reference drift. When human and delivered phases initially differ, it reduces phase MAE from 72.02 degrees to 13.90 degrees versus fixed-clock continuation. Compared with immediate phase reset, HCA reduces transient reference-tracking hip RMSE by 22.7% without reference jumps. All 420 timing rollouts complete without falls. These simulation results support continuous phase acquisition and sustained alignment to an independent human clock.

AI.tldr: PhaseSync-Exo is a human-aware exoskeleton control framework combining two-IMU CNN-Transformer gait reconstruction, factorized amplitude-cadence retargeting with curriculum-trained recurrent control, and a human-clock-anchored adapter (HCA) that aligns robot timing to an independent human clock in simulation.
AI.motivation: Human-aware exoskeleton walking requires reconstructing gait, tracking diverse motions under dynamic constraints, and preserving human timing. Maintaining alignment to the human's own timing (rather than a robot-relative clock) while ensuring forward progression and continuity is a key unmet need.
AI.method: The framework has three components: (1) a two-IMU CNN-Transformer reconstruction module; (2) factorized amplitude-cadence retargeting paired with a curriculum-trained recurrent tracking policy; and (3) a human-clock-anchored adapter (HCA) that combines human-clock attraction with robot-relative feedback to adjust the reference rate while preserving forward progression and continuity.
AI.result: The reconstruction module achieves 3.24 degrees MAE on a held-out recording, and the frozen tracking policy completes 356 of 357 amplitude-frequency trials. Two retraining-free dynamic comparisons isolate HCA's timing benefit: versus robot-relative correction, HCA reduces human-clock phase MAE from 95.55 degrees to 10.99 degrees, limiting reference drift; versus fixed-clock continuation with initially differing human and delivered phases, it reduces phase MAE from 72.02 degrees to 13.90 degrees; versus immediate phase reset, it cuts transient reference-tracking hip RMSE by 22.7% without reference jumps. All 420 timing rollouts complete without falls.
AI.conclusion: Simulation results support continuous phase acquisition and sustained alignment to an independent human clock, indicating that the human-clock-anchored adapter effectively preserves human timing while maintaining tracking performance and stability.

title: Self-Evolving Algorithm-Design Agents: Escaping In-Context Evolutionary Stagnation via Population-Curated Policy Optimization
summary: Large language models are increasingly participating in complex real-world tasks in the form of algorithm-design agents, designing and refining algorithms. Many successful algorithm-design agents adopt pure in-context evolutionary frameworks, but they may quickly plateau in domains that require specialized knowledge. Parametric adaptation offers a way to internalize specialized knowledge, but conventional training requires abundant domain-specific corpora while high-quality algorithms are scarce in complex algorithm-design scenarios. In this paper, we propose sample-efficient parametric self-evolution where agents can explore and learn from self-generated algorithms. First, we characterize in-context evolutionary stagnation and analytically propose the Improvement Chain proposition, showing how learning successive self-generated algorithms can locally increase the likelihood of neighboring algorithms. Motivated by this local-transfer perspective, we further propose Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO) to utilize a global population and a hybrid policy update scheme for retaining and reusing high-quality, diverse self-generated algorithms, shifting the policy towards stronger algorithms. In the task of learning rate schedule design for global placement in electronic design automation, trained only on 4 chip cases, PCPO outperforms the state-of-the-art in-context evolutionary methods (e.g., OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve) on average across 16 chip cases. With an 8B-size base model, PCPO achieves competitive performance compared to frontier closed-source models such as GPT-5.5. PCPO also reduces inference-time token cost by internalizing grounded domain knowledge and prompt distillation. Moreover, PCPO achieves significant speedups on four GPU kernel designs, with an average of 8.27$\times$ speedup against the PyTorch Eager baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes sample-efficient parametric self-evolution for algorithm-design agents, introducing the Improvement Chain proposition to explain in-context evolutionary stagnation and Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO) to internalize self-generated algorithms, achieving strong results on EDA learning-rate scheduling and GPU kernel design.
AI.motivation: Algorithm-design agents built on pure in-context evolutionary frameworks quickly plateau in domains requiring specialized knowledge. Parametric adaptation can internalize such knowledge, but conventional training needs abundant domain-specific corpora, which are scarce because high-quality algorithms are rare in complex design scenarios.
AI.method: The authors characterize in-context evolutionary stagnation and propose the Improvement Chain proposition, which shows that learning successive self-generated algorithms locally increases the likelihood of neighboring algorithms. Motivated by this local-transfer perspective, they propose Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO), which uses a global population and a hybrid policy update scheme to retain and reuse high-quality, diverse self-generated algorithms and shift the policy toward stronger ones.
AI.result: In learning rate schedule design for global placement in electronic design automation, PCPO trained on only 4 chip cases outperforms state-of-the-art in-context evolutionary methods (e.g., OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve) on average across 16 chip cases. With an 8B base model, it is competitive with frontier closed-source models such as GPT-5.5. It also reduces inference-time token cost via internalizing grounded domain knowledge and prompt distillation, and achieves an average 8.27x speedup over the PyTorch Eager baseline on four GPU kernel designs.
AI.conclusion: Sample-efficient parametric self-evolution with PCPO enables algorithm-design agents to internalize specialized domain knowledge from self-generated algorithms, overcoming in-context evolutionary stagnation while improving performance, reducing inference cost, and generalizing across EDA and GPU kernel design tasks.

title: Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS): Scaling Coral Recruit Monitoring Through Robotics and Computer Vision
summary: Climate change is the largest threat to coral reefs, with increasing global impacts accelerating the need for scalable reef restoration technologies. Large-scale reef restoration depends on the mass production of corals, such as through coral aquaculture. Coral seeding with recruits grown in aquaculture facilities is a feasible restoration approach, but effective production requires consistent, high-frequency monitoring of tens of thousands of macroscopic (0.5-2mm diameter) recruits, making conventional manual assessment prohibitively labor-intensive. To address this monitoring bottleneck, we introduce the Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS) which combines robotic imaging and computer vision to automate data acquisition, perform multi-species detection and counting of corals, and evaluate coral health. CGRAS automatically extracts coral growth, survival and spatial distribution metrics, with the aim of providing timely feedback to operators for optimizing production, grow-out and deployment workflow processes. We demonstrate CGRAS in a large aquaculture facility on standardized coral settlement tiles, reducing the time and labor costs by a factor of 9.6 as compared to manual monitoring, whilst achieving 96.4% agreement for Acropora kenti corals relative to expert counts.

AI.tldr: Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS) combines robotic imaging and computer vision to automate multi-species detection, counting, and health evaluation of coral recruits in aquaculture, cutting monitoring labor by 9.6x while achieving 96.4% agreement with expert counts for Acropora kenti.
AI.motivation: Climate change is the largest threat to coral reefs, so scalable restoration via coral aquaculture and seeding is needed. However, effective production requires high-frequency monitoring of tens of thousands of tiny (0.5-2mm) recruits, and conventional manual assessment is prohibitively labor-intensive—creating a monitoring bottleneck.
AI.method: CGRAS integrates robotic imaging with computer vision to automate data acquisition and perform multi-species detection and counting of coral recruits, while also evaluating coral health. It automatically extracts coral growth, survival, and spatial distribution metrics to provide timely feedback for optimizing production, grow-out, and deployment workflows.
AI.result: Demonstrated in a large aquaculture facility on standardized coral settlement tiles, CGRAS reduced monitoring time and labor costs by a factor of 9.6 compared to manual monitoring, and achieved 96.4% agreement with expert counts for Acropora kenti corals.
AI.conclusion: CGRAS addresses the coral aquaculture monitoring bottleneck by combining robotic imaging and computer vision for scalable, automated assessment, delivering substantial labor savings and high counting accuracy, thereby supporting scalable reef restoration efforts.

title: PathAnchor: Path-Structured Evidence for Scientific Agents
summary: Scientific agents can retrieve relevant passages yet still lose functional order, mix evidence across sources, or state conclusions that exceed the retrieved record. We introduce PathAnchor, a bounded scientific reasoning system built on path-structured evidence workspaces. Instead of treating passages or extracted concepts as independent units, the system retrieves source-linked Material-Sensor-Signal-System trajectories that preserve role, direction, and the evidence supporting each transition. A controller uses three read-only tools to search paper-specific trajectories, trace paths across candidate sources, and open exact evidence before producing a claim-cited answer and an explicit evidence boundary. On 120 single- and cross-paper flexible-sensor questions, PathAnchor scores 82.6% and leads six evaluated systems. Under a matched controller, corpus, and six-call budget, replacing unordered concept graphs with path-structured records raises source recall from 61.3% to 82.9%, increases answers whose claims all cite opened evidence from 69.2% to 90.0%, and reduces tool calls. These results show that evidence organization affects retrieval and citation completeness under fixed agent resources.

AI.tldr: PathAnchor is a bounded scientific reasoning system that uses path-structured evidence workspaces—source-linked Material-Sensor-Signal-System trajectories—so an agent can search, trace, and open exact evidence before answering; it scores 82.6% on 120 flexible-sensor questions and outperforms six systems.
AI.motivation: Scientific agents often retrieve relevant passages but still lose functional order, mix evidence across sources, or state conclusions that exceed the retrieved record. The paper argues that treating passages or concepts as independent units is insufficient.
AI.method: The system retrieves path-structured records: source-linked Material-Sensor-Signal-System trajectories that preserve role, direction, and supporting evidence per transition. A controller with three read-only tools searches paper-specific trajectories, traces paths across candidate sources, and opens exact evidence to produce claim-cited answers and an explicit evidence boundary. A matched comparison replaces unordered concept graphs with path-structured records under identical controller, corpus, and six-call budget.
AI.result: On 120 single- and cross-paper flexible-sensor questions, PathAnchor scores 82.6% and leads six evaluated systems. Under matched settings, path-structured records raise source recall from 61.3% to 82.9%, increase fully cited answers from 69.2% to 90.0%, and reduce tool calls.
AI.conclusion: Evidence organization, not just retrieval, drives retrieval and citation completeness under fixed agent resources.

title: Locomotion-Grounded Humanoid Soccer: Task-Gated Reinforcement Learning of a Multi-Directional Kicking Library
summary: Recent humanoid soccer systems make motion tracking the substrate and derive locomotion from it, typically by steering a motion-reference anchor toward the ball. This yields strong shooting results, but locomotion is trained only on the narrow, deterministic command distribution ball approach induces, never evaluated as a capability in its own right. We invert the stack: a general, command-conditioned locomotion policy is trained first as the substrate, and N motion-guided kicking skills are added on top as task-gated layers, so the reachable gait space is set by the locomotion curriculum rather than any reference clip. Because every skill starts from and returns to this same commandable state, locomotion also becomes a composition hub (O(N) transitions rather than O(N^2)), and post-strike stabilisation is handed back to the trained controller rather than scripted per clip. We instantiate this on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 with seven retargeted kicking skills spanning 259.5 degrees of nominal aim direction, including lateral, rearward and weak-foot strikes a single forward-facing reference cannot express, and report shooting accuracy alongside command-tracking, terrain and push-recovery results with the full skill library attached, an axis prior humanoid soccer systems do not report. The library is validated on hardware across forward, lateral, rearward and commanded approaches.

AI.tldr: The authors invert the standard humanoid soccer stack by training a general command-conditioned locomotion policy first as the substrate, then layering task-gated motion-guided kicking skills on top, yielding a composable skill library with O(N) transitions and validated shooting plus locomotion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Prior humanoid soccer systems use motion tracking as the substrate and derive locomotion from it, typically by steering a motion-reference anchor toward the ball. This gives strong shooting but trains locomotion only on the narrow, deterministic command distribution induced by ball approach, so locomotion is never evaluated as a capability in its own right.
AI.method: A general, command-conditioned locomotion policy is trained first as the substrate; N motion-guided kicking skills are added as task-gated layers. The reachable gait space is therefore set by the locomotion curriculum rather than any reference clip. Each skill starts from and returns to the same commandable state, making locomotion a composition hub (O(N) transitions instead of O(N^2)); post-strike stabilisation is handled by the trained controller rather than scripted per clip. Instantiated on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 with seven retargeted kicking skills spanning 259.5 degrees of nominal aim direction.
AI.result: Seven retargeted kicking skills span 259.5 degrees of nominal aim direction, including lateral, rearward, and weak-foot strikes that a single forward-facing reference cannot express. The paper reports shooting accuracy alongside command-tracking, terrain, and push-recovery results with the full skill library attached—an axis prior humanoid soccer systems do not report. The library is validated on hardware across forward, lateral, rearward, and commanded approaches.
AI.conclusion: Treating command-conditioned locomotion as the substrate and kicking as task-gated layers enables a broadly aimable, composable skill library that preserves locomotion competence, with hardware-validated skating, kicking, and recovery behaviour.

title: Action Conditioned Bisimulation For GUI Agent Memory
summary: An agent that remembers what it did on a web page must decide when two pages count as the same. Memories built on observation similarity merge pages that look alike but behave differently, and GUIs are full of such pages: two tabs of one widget or two rows of one menu answer the same click differently. We define the merge rule as an action-conditioned bisimulation over the empirical predictive state graph a frozen agent fills as it acts. Two states merge only when their shared actions lead to agreeing outcomes and successor blocks under an affordance label. Observation similarity never enters the rule, and nothing is trained. It replaces the merge rule of an existing outcome-value memory, so a closed-loop comparison isolates it. On MiniWoB++ it raises success rate over a memoryless agent, while a control taking identical exploratory detours, the prior successor-representation merge, and the same criterion without action conditioning change nothing.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a page-merge rule for web-agent memory as an action-conditioned bisimulation over the empirical predictive state graph, merging states only when shared actions yield agreeing outcomes and successor blocks under an affordance label, with no observation similarity and no training.
AI.motivation: An agent that remembers its actions on a web page must decide when two pages are the same. Memory built on observation similarity wrongly merges pages that look alike but behave differently, a common situation in GUIs where two tabs of a widget or two rows of a menu respond differently to the same click.
AI.method: The merge rule is formalized as an action-conditioned bisimulation over the empirical predictive state graph that a frozen agent fills as it acts. Two states merge only when their shared actions lead to agreeing outcomes and successor blocks under an affordance label. Observation similarity is excluded from the rule and nothing is trained. The rule replaces the merge rule of an existing outcome-value memory, enabling a closed-loop comparison that isolates its effect.
AI.result: On MiniWoB++, the proposed rule raises success rate over a memoryless agent. Control conditions—an agent taking identical exploratory detours, the prior successor-representation merge, and the same criterion without action conditioning—produce no change.
AI.conclusion: Action-conditioned bisimulation over the empirical predictive state graph provides a training-free, behavior-based merge criterion for web-agent memory, improving task success where similarity-based and non-action-conditioned alternatives fail.

title: Online Evolution Strategy for Flow-Matching VLA Policies via Self-Supervised Trajectory Distribution Optimization
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models based on generative frameworks, such as Flow Matching, have recently achieved impressive performance in robotic manipulation. Unlike deterministic policies, Flow Matching enables VLA models to learn conditional action trajectory distributions, where latent noise vectors induce different actions under the same task scenario. However, we observe that these distributions are often ill-formed, with successful and failed behaviors coexisting while considerable probability mass remains in unfavorable regions. To this end, we propose Online-ES, an online adaptation framework for Flow Matching VLAs based on Evolution Strategy (ES), which refines the learned action trajectory distribution through interaction feedback. Instead of pruning the latent noise space, our method performs evolutionary exploration directly in the action trajectory space, where diverse trajectories generated by Flow Matching provide candidate solutions for adaptation. By perturbing sampled trajectories and evaluating their execution outcomes, we derive a self-supervised MSE objective that transfers the evolution direction from trajectory space into model parameter space. Mathematically, we prove that the proposed objective provides an unbiased estimator of the optimal evolution direction. Moreover, we also incorporate failure experiences as negative feedback to regularize the evolution direction, steering the policy away from previously explored failure regions. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that Online-ES achieves policy improvement comparable to reinforcement fine-tuning, without learning a value model or computing advantages.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Online-ES, an online adaptation framework for Flow Matching VLA models that refines action trajectory distributions via Evolution Strategy using execution feedback, achieving reinforcement-finetuning-level improvement without a value model or advantage computation.
AI.motivation: Flow Matching VLAs learn conditional action trajectory distributions where latent noise vectors produce different actions under the same task, but these distributions are often ill-formed: successful and failed behaviors coexist, and considerable probability mass lies in unfavorable regions.
AI.method: Rather than pruning the latent noise space, Online-ES performs evolutionary exploration directly in the action trajectory space, using diverse Flow Matching-generated trajectories as candidates. It perturbs sampled trajectories, evaluates their execution outcomes, and derives a self-supervised MSE objective that transfers the evolution direction from trajectory space into model parameter space. The objective is proven to be an unbiased estimator of the optimal evolution direction, and failure experiences are used as negative feedback to regularize the direction and steer the policy away from previously explored failure regions.
AI.result: Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments show that Online-ES achieves policy improvement comparable to reinforcement fine-tuning, without learning a value model or computing advantages.
AI.conclusion: Online-ES offers an effective, value-model-free approach for online adaptation of Flow Matching VLA policies by refining action trajectory distributions through evolutionary exploration in trajectory space.

title: Persona and Persuasive Framing in AI Voice Agents: A $2\times2$ Field Experiment with Children
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-60), 2027
summary: Conversational agents increasingly interact with children, yet evidence on how their design shapes children's susceptibility to persuasion comes almost entirely from the lab. We report a $2\times2$ randomized field experiment embedded in a public German Santa Claus telephone hotline. Children's calls were randomly routed to one of four LLM voice agents varying persona (Santa, high authority, vs. Helper, low authority) and framing (persuasive nudges toward prosocial wishes vs. neutral). Of 1,072 logged calls, 89 conversations (median age 6) met inclusion criteria. Persuasive framing raised the probability of a prosocial wish from 11.6% to 45.7%, robust to controls. Persona authority showed a near-zero effect: Santa did not outperform the Helper. Persona instead shaped engagement; children hung up on the Helper far more often within the first minute (65% vs. 39%). Where context already lends an agent legitimacy, how it speaks shapes children's compliance more than who it claims to be.

AI.tldr: A 2×2 field experiment on a German Santa hotline found that persuasive framing nearly quadrupled children's prosocial wishes, while the agent's authority persona had little effect on persuasion but strongly affected engagement (children hung up on the low-authority Helper more).
AI.motivation: Conversational agents increasingly interact with children, but evidence on how their design shapes children's susceptibility to persuasion comes almost entirely from lab settings, leaving real-world effects unclear.
AI.method: A 2×2 randomized field experiment embedded in a public German Santa Claus telephone hotline. Children's calls were randomly routed to one of four LLM voice agents crossing persona (Santa, high authority vs. Helper, low authority) with framing (persuasive nudges toward prosocial wishes vs. neutral). Of 1,072 logged calls, 89 conversations (median age 6) met inclusion criteria.
AI.result: Persuasive framing raised the probability of a prosocial wish from 11.6% to 45.7%, robust to controls. Persona authority had a near-zero effect: Santa did not outperform the Helper. However, persona shaped engagement: children hung up on the Helper far more often within the first minute (65% vs. 39%).
AI.conclusion: Where context already lends an agent legitimacy, how it speaks shapes children's compliance more than who it claims to be.

title: Plan-Conditioned Imitation for Robust Object Retrieval under Self-Occlusion in Dense Clutter
summary: Retrieving objects from dense clutter requires rearrangement during which the manipulator can occlude objects while moving them. Repeated arm withdrawals to restore visibility interrupt execution. We introduce TRACE, a plan-conditioned imitation framework for retrieval under self-occlusion. A single unoccluded observation initializes a digital twin, where a privileged teacher generates a fixed nominal rollout. A recurrent student combines local rollout context, partial object observations, and proprioception to select actions that can correct deviations from the prediction. Behavior cloning initializes the student; DAgger refines it with teacher labels on student-visited states. The rollout remains fixed throughout execution, so the deployed student needs neither online teacher queries nor additional simulator rollouts during pushing. On 511 simulation test scenes, TRACE achieves 90.7% success versus 43.4% for nominal replay and 96.7% for the privileged closed-loop teacher. At a matched 26,373-label budget, student-state supervision achieves 87.8% versus 66.7% for expert-only cloning, demonstrating gains beyond additional labels. On a UR5e, TRACE achieves 90.0% success versus 95.0% for the closed-loop teacher, while reducing total execution time from 192.7 s to 67.3 s. It avoids the teacher's 16.8 sensing-related arm retractions per trial during pushing, retaining a final withdrawal for graspability evaluation. Code and data will be released at: https://trace-retrieval.github.io.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a plan-conditioned imitation framework for clutter retrieval under self-occlusion, using a fixed privileged rollout plus a recurrent student corrector to avoid repeated sensing-driven arm retractions.
AI.motivation: Retrieving objects from dense clutter requires rearrangement, and the manipulator can occlude objects while moving them. Repeated arm withdrawals to restore visibility interrupt execution and slow retrieval, so a method is needed that handles self-occlusion without frequent visibility-restoring motions.
AI.method: A single unoccluded observation initializes a digital twin, in which a privileged teacher generates a fixed nominal rollout. A recurrent student combines local rollout context, partial object observations, and proprioception to select actions correcting deviations from the predicted rollout. Behavior cloning initializes the student, and DAgger refines it with teacher labels on student-visited states. The rollout stays fixed throughout execution, so deployment requires no online teacher queries or additional simulator rollouts during pushing.
AI.result: On 511 simulation test scenes, TRACE reaches 90.7% success versus 43.4% for nominal replay and 96.7% for the privileged closed-loop teacher. At a matched 26,373-label budget, student-state supervision reaches 87.8% versus 66.7% for expert-only cloning. On a UR5e, TRACE reaches 90.0% success versus 95.0% for the closed-loop teacher, while cutting total execution time from 192.7 s to 67.3 s, avoiding the teacher's 16.8 sensing-related arm retractions per trial during pushing and retaining a final withdrawal for graspability evaluation.
AI.conclusion: TRACE enables efficient, plan-conditioned retrieval under self-occlusion by combining a fixed privileged rollout with a recurrent student corrector, achieving high success while eliminating repeated sensing-related arm retractions and substantially reducing execution time.

title: Positive Ratings, Hidden Concerns: Employee Voice Disclosure in AI-Mediated Organizational Listening
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-60), 2027
summary: Organizations started listening to employees through conversational AI agents alongside structured surveys. Little is known about what these channels change in what employees say when disclosure carries hierarchical risk. We report a field study inside a global management consulting firm whose process pairs a pre-survey with an adaptive AI voice interview on the same themes within one session. Across 44 first-session interviews (132 matched theme observations), 20-41% of sessions showed a favorable rating co-occurring with a substantive concern voiced later, depending on the favorability threshold. The Gioia analysis drew on 158 protective quotes from 65 eligible sessions. Disclosure rarely arrived unguarded: employees softened concerns, deflected accountability, and bounded how far they went, and this protective work tracked the perceived legitimacy of the listening structure. We develop a grounded model of bounded disclosure and derive four propositions for voice, channel and listening research. Silence, we argue, can persist inside expression.

AI.tldr: A field study in a global consulting firm pairing a pre-survey with an adaptive AI voice interview on the same themes reveals "bounded disclosure": 20–41% of first sessions showed a favorable rating co-occurring with a substantive concern voiced later, and employees rarely disclosed without protective work (softening concerns, deflecting accountability, bounding scope) that tracked the perceived legitimacy of the listening structure.
AI.motivation: Organizations increasingly use conversational AI agents alongside structured surveys to listen to employees, yet little is known about how these channels change what employees say when disclosure carries hierarchical risk. The paper addresses this gap by examining whether added expressive channels reduce silence or merely relocate it.
AI.method: Field study inside a global management consulting firm whose process pairs a pre-survey with an adaptive AI voice interview on the same themes within one session. Analysis covers 44 first-session interviews (132 matched theme observations) with varying favorability thresholds, and a Gioia analysis drawing on 158 protective quotes from 65 eligible sessions.
AI.result: 20–41% of sessions showed a favorable rating co-occurring with a substantive concern voiced later, depending on the favorability threshold. Disclosure rarely arrived unguarded: employees softened concerns, deflected accountability, and bounded how far they went, and this protective work tracked the perceived legitimacy of the listening structure.
AI.conclusion: The paper develops a grounded model of bounded disclosure and derives four propositions for voice, channel, and listening research. Its central claim is that silence can persist inside expression.

title: Efficient Multi-Modal Planning with Reward-Guided Preference Optimization for Autonomous Driving
summary: Safe and efficient trajectory planning is essential in autonomous driving. However, existing end-to-end approaches often fall short in both computational efficiency and safety guarantees. Methods based on imitation learning suffer from causal confusion, while rule-based scoring approaches often incur heavy computational overhead and suffer from objective misalignment. Additionally, preference-based methods rely on strict pairwise annotations, limiting data utilization. To overcome these limitations, we propose EMPlan, an efficient multi-modal trajectory planning method powered by reward-guided fine-tuning. We design a hybrid architecture that combines sparse anchors with an offset refinement module for efficient multi-modal trajectory prediction. Sparse anchors provide coarse trajectory candidates with low latency, which are subsequently refined by the offset module for higher prediction accuracy. To enhance safety without incurring additional inference costs, we adopt a two-stage training paradigm consisting of pretraining and reward-guided fine-tuning. During fine-tuning, we leverage rule-based reward signals and unpaired preference supervision to refine the pretrained policy toward safer trajectory selection. We evaluate EMPlan on the non-reactive NAVSIM benchmark, where it strikes a favorable balance between planning accuracy and efficiency, demonstrating superior performance under real-time constraints.

AI.tldr: EMPlan is an efficient multi-modal trajectory planning method for autonomous driving that combines sparse anchors with an offset refinement module and uses reward-guided fine-tuning (rule-based rewards plus unpaired preference supervision) to improve safety without extra inference cost, achieving a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off on the NAVSIM benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end trajectory planning approaches fall short in computational efficiency and safety guarantees. Imitation learning suffers from causal confusion; rule-based scoring incurs heavy computational overhead and objective misalignment; preference-based methods require strict pairwise annotations, limiting data utilization.
AI.method: EMPlan uses a hybrid architecture combining sparse anchors with an offset refinement module for efficient multi-modal trajectory prediction: sparse anchors yield coarse low-latency candidates that the offset module refines for higher accuracy. A two-stage training paradigm (pretraining followed by reward-guided fine-tuning) refines the pretrained policy toward safer trajectory selection using rule-based reward signals and unpaired preference supervision, avoiding additional inference costs.
AI.result: Evaluated on the non-reactive NAVSIM benchmark, EMPlan strikes a favorable balance between planning accuracy and efficiency, demonstrating superior performance under real-time constraints.
AI.conclusion: EMPlan addresses efficiency and safety limitations of prior planners through sparse-anchor-based multi-modal prediction and reward-guided fine-tuning, proving effective for real-time autonomous driving trajectory planning.

title: GraphCert: Bootstrap Agentic Graph Reasoning with Certified Evidence Rubrics
summary: Graph agents extend large language models (LLMs) with the ability to actively explore and reason over knowledge graphs through multi-step interactions with graph tools. However, training capable graph agents typically requires large collections of question-answer pairs and reasoning trajectories, whose manual construction is costly and difficult to scale. Moreover, employing proprietary LLMs to generate such supervision further risks exposing sensitive graph data to external services. Therefore, we propose GraphCert to bootstrap agentic graph reasoning with certified evidence rubrics during post-training. Specifically, the Bootstrapped Graph Quizzer guided by generation controls produces graph-grounded QA pairs and marks supporting evidence, which undergo execution certification and semantic curation. The accepted evidence is then canonicalized into certified evidence rubrics that later reward Graph Solver evidence alignment alongside answer correctness during GRPO training. Experiments on five graph reasoning domains in GRBENCH demonstrate that GraphCert consistently outperforms substantially larger LLM agents and post-training method. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the learned policy transfers robustly across heterogeneous graph domains, suggesting that GraphCert acquires reusable graph-reasoning capabilities rather than domain-specific patterns. These results establish executable self-certification as an effective approach to self-training compact graph reasoning agents. Our code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: GraphCert bootstraps compact graph-reasoning agents via self-generated, execution-certified evidence rubrics used to reward evidence alignment during GRPO post-training, outperforming larger LLM agents across five GRBENCH domains.
AI.motivation: Training capable graph agents normally needs large collections of QA pairs and reasoning trajectories that are costly to build manually and hard to scale. Using proprietary LLMs to generate such supervision also risks exposing sensitive graph data to external services.
AI.method: GraphCert bootstraps agentic graph reasoning with certified evidence rubrics during post-training. A Bootstrapped Graph Quizzer guided by generation controls produces graph-grounded QA pairs and marks supporting evidence, which then undergo execution certification and semantic curation. Accepted evidence is canonicalized into certified evidence rubrics that reward Graph Solver evidence alignment alongside answer correctness during GRPO training.
AI.result: Experiments on five graph reasoning domains in GRBENCH show GraphCert consistently outperforms substantially larger LLM agents and prior post-training methods. The learned policy also transfers robustly across heterogeneous graph domains.
AI.conclusion: GraphCert acquires reusable graph-reasoning capabilities rather than domain-specific patterns, establishing executable self-certification as an effective approach to self-training compact graph reasoning agents.

title: DODGER: Safety-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Robot Navigation Among Dynamic Obstacles
comment: The first three authors contributed equally to this work. Project Page: https://psh0823.github.io/dodger-homepage
summary: Robots operating in human-centered environments must safely navigate among multiple dynamic obstacles to avoid collisions with people and surrounding infrastructure. Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide an effective mechanism for safety filtering, and recent CBF-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods embed such safety information into learned policies. However, executing only safety-filtered actions during training can restrict policy exploration, a limitation that becomes particularly consequential in dynamic scenes where safety depends on relative robot-obstacle motion. We propose DODGER, a safety-guided RL framework that directly executes policy-generated actions to drive training rollouts while using CBF-filtered references and constraint violations to shape the policy toward collision-avoidance behavior. We evaluate DODGER through a Dubins-car safety analysis and demonstrate goal-directed navigation among multiple dynamic obstacles in full-order humanoid simulation and real-world humanoid experiments using LiDAR-based perception, without a runtime safety filter.

AI.tldr: DODGER is a safety-guided reinforcement learning framework that executes policy-generated actions during training rollouts (instead of safety-filtered actions) while using CBF-filtered references and constraint violations to shape a collision-avoidance policy, enabling safe dynamic-obstacle navigation for a humanoid robot.
AI.motivation: Robots in human-centered environments must avoid collisions with people and infrastructure while navigating multiple dynamic obstacles. Existing CBF-based RL methods embed safety into the policy but execute only safety-filtered actions during training, which restricts policy exploration. This is especially problematic in dynamic scenes where safety depends on relative robot-obstacle motion.
AI.method: DODGER executes policy-generated actions directly to drive training rollouts, rather than safety-filtered ones. It uses CBF-filtered references and constraint violations as signals to shape the policy toward collision-avoidance behavior. The approach is analyzed via a Dubins-car safety analysis and requires no runtime safety filter at deployment.
AI.result: Goal-directed navigation among multiple dynamic obstacles is demonstrated in full-order humanoid simulation and real-world humanoid experiments using LiDAR-based perception, without a runtime safety filter.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling training-time exploration from safety filtering—by executing unfiltered policy actions while using CBF information as shaping signals—yields a collision-avoidance policy that transfers to real-world humanoid navigation among dynamic obstacles.

title: When Reasoning Goes Astray: Attention Dynamics of Uncontrolled Reasoning
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve performance on complex tasks through extended reasoning, yet the same process can degenerate into redundant verification and persistent generation loops. Such uncontrolled reasoning increases inference cost and creates risks of resource exhaustion and service degradation. However, existing mitigations largely truncate long outputs or react to surface repetition, and thus fail to distinguish normal thinking from uncontrolled reasoning or explain how benign reasoning degenerates into harmful behavior. In this paper, we operationalize LRM generation as four states and further introduce Reasoning-state Analysis via Dynamic Attention Responses (RADAR), which identifies the current reasoning state in real time and characterizes how effective reflection can develop into uncontrolled generation. Guided by RADAR's analysis, we further realign abnormal attention distributions toward patterns observed in normal requests and examine how this correction affects excessive reflection and persistent looping. Temporal analyses show that uncontrolled reasoning is characterized by attention distributions that deviate from normal generation, with abnormal trends becoming detectable before repetition begins. Correcting these deviations through Attention Realignment consistently reduces looping while largely preserving benign performance. Together, RADAR provide a mechanistic account of how reasoning becomes uncontrolled, offering actionable guidance for identifying critical failure stages and designing targeted runtime interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RADAR (Reasoning-state Analysis via Dynamic Attention Responses), which models LRM generation as four states and uses attention dynamics to detect uncontrolled reasoning (redundant verification and looping) in real time, before surface repetition appears.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance through extended reasoning, but the same process can degenerate into redundant verification and persistent generation loops, raising inference cost and risking resource exhaustion and service degradation. Existing mitigations truncate long outputs or react to surface-level repetition, so they neither distinguish normal thinking from uncontrolled reasoning nor explain how benign reasoning turns harmful.
AI.method: The authors operationalize LRM generation as four states and introduce RADAR, which identifies the current reasoning state in real time and characterizes how effective reflection develops into uncontrolled generation via dynamic attention responses. Guided by RADAR, they realign abnormal attention distributions toward patterns observed in normal requests (Attention Realignment) and examine its effect on excessive reflection and persistent looping.
AI.result: Temporal analyses show uncontrolled reasoning is marked by attention distributions deviating from normal generation, with abnormal trends detectable before repetition begins. Correcting these deviations via Attention Realignment consistently reduces looping while largely preserving benign performance.
AI.conclusion: RADAR offers a mechanistic account of how reasoning becomes uncontrolled and provides actionable guidance for identifying critical failure stages and designing targeted runtime interventions.

title: Benchmarking and Enhancing Skill-Level Memory for Partially Observable Robotic Manipulation
summary: Recent advances in robot learning have enabled manipulation policies to perform increasingly diverse tasks and generalize across environments. However, reliable execution often depends on hidden task states that cannot be determined from current observations alone, making interaction history essential. We introduce $HIDE$, a benchmark for evaluating manipulation memory under partial observability. HIDE comprises 15 tasks covering repetition counting, historical-state recall, and execution-progress tracking, with randomized initial configurations and decision points where similar observations require different actions depending on prior events. We further propose $SEEK$, a framework combining three complementary memory mechanisms to retain historical evidence and track execution state. Evaluations reveal substantial limitations in existing policies on HIDE, while memory augmentation improves task success in both simulation and real-world experiments. Individual mechanisms benefit some tasks but can degrade others; their combination achieves the highest average success rate on HIDE among the evaluated configurations. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining internal representations of hidden task states and matching memory design to task-specific information requirements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HIDE, a benchmark of 15 manipulation tasks testing memory under partial observability, and SEEK, a framework combining three memory mechanisms; evaluations show existing policies struggle, while memory augmentation improves success in simulation and real-world settings.
AI.motivation: Reliable manipulation policy execution often relies on hidden task states that cannot be inferred from current observations alone, making interaction history critical. Existing robot learning advances lack systematic evaluation of memory under partial observability, motivating a dedicated benchmark and memory framework.
AI.method: HIDE benchmark: 15 tasks spanning repetition counting, historical-state recall, and execution-progress tracking, with randomized initial configurations and decision points where similar observations demand different actions based on prior events. SEEK: a framework integrating three complementary memory mechanisms to retain historical evidence and track execution state.
AI.result: Existing policies show substantial limitations on HIDE. Memory augmentation improves task success in both simulation and real-world experiments. Individual memory mechanisms help some tasks but degrade others; their combination yields the highest average success rate among evaluated configurations.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining internal representations of hidden task states is essential, and memory design should be matched to task-specific information requirements.

title: Whose Voice Survives the Summary? A Voice-Retention Audit of LLM Employee Listening
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS 2027)
summary: Organizations increasingly route employee feedback to leaders through large language model (LLM) summaries, an unaudited layer that silences already-spoken voice. We introduce a Voice Retention / Representation Ratio metric for representational bias in summarization and apply it to a bilingual (English/German) corpus of 2,586 free-text responses from a global professional service company. First, employees supply criticism more reliably than praise (withholding praise is 82 times more common). Second, across 45 leader-summaries the pipeline filters by popularity, not sentiment: criticism survives, yet a concern voiced once is dropped 86% of the time, with short and German-only content lost on the same axis (theme retention 0.14 vs 0.74; German directional). Controlling for frequency, sentiment has no independent effect; the harm is prevalence-driven, which sentiment-only audits miss. A targeted prompt recovers only named themes. We contribute the metric, field evidence, and a disaggregated voice-retention card.

AI.tldr: LLM summarization pipelines used to route employee feedback to leaders exhibit prevalence-driven representational bias: rare concerns, short responses, and German-only content are systematically dropped, while criticism survives as reliably as frequent content—a pattern that sentiment-only audits miss.
AI.motivation: Organizations increasingly insert LLM-generated summaries between employees and leaders, creating an unaudited layer that can silence voice even after it has been spoken. Existing auditing approaches focus on sentiment, leaving representational bias in summarization unmeasured and therefore invisible to organizations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Voice Retention / Representation Ratio metric for quantifying representational bias in summarization. They apply it to a bilingual (English/German) corpus of 2,586 free-text employee responses from a global professional service company, analyzed across 45 leader-summaries, correlating retention with frequency, sentiment, response length, and language. A targeted prompt intervention is also tested.
AI.result: Employees withhold praise far more than criticism (82x). The summarization pipeline filters by popularity rather than sentiment: criticism survives, but a concern voiced only once is dropped 86% of the time. Short and German-only content is lost along the same axis (theme retention 0.14 vs 0.74, German directional). Controlling for frequency, sentiment has no independent effect. A targeted prompt recovers only named themes.
AI.conclusion: Representational harm in LLM feedback summarization is prevalence-driven rather than sentiment-driven, meaning sentiment-only audits systematically miss it. The paper contributes a measurable metric (Voice Retention / Representation Ratio), field evidence of the bias, and a disaggregated voice-retention card for organizational auditing.

title: PRICE the Action Chunks: Physical Relational Credit Assignment for Embodied Reinforcement Learning
summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) post-trains vision--language--action policies using terminal success signals, but assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to every action chunk. A failed episode can thus penalize useful early actions as if they caused the failure. Existing approaches seek finer-grained feedback through learned evaluators, adding task-specific supervision or additional model training. We explore, for the first time to our knowledge, whether physical relations across trajectories can provide action-chunk credit in embodied RL from terminal outcomes alone, without an auxiliary evaluator. The key insight is that rollouts reaching corresponding physical situations can serve as references for one another: their terminal outcomes provide evidence for assessing local progress. We introduce Physical Relations for Inferring Credit from Episodes(PRICE), with two components: (i) a physical relational graph that pools current and historical outcomes at corresponding chunk boundaries to estimate success potentials; and (ii) confidence-gated credit assignment that uses changes in these potentials to refine trajectory-level supervision. Our analysis connects oracle potential changes to the terminal-success objective and provides a finite-sample directional bound for outcome-independent evidence pools. Independent continuation tests show that PRICE's retained credits align with local progress, while experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real robots demonstrate improved task success over outcome-based baselines and faster learning.

AI.tldr: PRICE assigns finer-grained credit to action chunks in outcome-based embodied RL by exploiting physical relations across trajectories, using a relational graph over corresponding chunk boundaries and confidence-gated potential-difference credit, without auxiliary evaluators.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based RL post-trains vision-language-action policies using only terminal success signals, assigning the same trajectory-level advantage to every action chunk. This coarse credit means a failed episode can penalize useful early actions as though they caused the failure. Prior fixes rely on learned evaluators, requiring task-specific supervision or extra model training. The paper asks whether physical relations across trajectories can supply action-chunk credit from terminal outcomes alone.
AI.method: The key insight is that rollouts reaching corresponding physical situations can serve as mutual references, with their terminal outcomes providing evidence about local progress. PRICE has two components: (i) a physical relational graph that pools current and historical outcomes at corresponding chunk boundaries to estimate success potentials, and (ii) confidence-gated credit assignment that uses changes in these potentials to refine trajectory-level supervision. Theoretical analysis links oracle potential changes to the terminal-success objective and gives a finite-sample directional bound for outcome-independent evidence pools.
AI.result: Independent continuation tests show PRICE's retained credits align with local progress. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real robots show improved task success over outcome-based baselines and faster learning.
AI.conclusion: PRICE demonstrates that physical relations across trajectories can provide action-chunk credit in embodied RL from terminal outcomes alone, without an auxiliary evaluator, yielding better and faster learning than outcome-based baselines.

title: More Choices, Fewer Decisions: Ordinal-Scale Bias in JEV-like Direct-Decision Models
summary: Direct-decision models turn text into low-latency structured labels and scores, making them attractive for classification and automatic evaluation. Yet reliability requires more than accuracy: a model must also use the ordinal decision scale supplied by the user faithfully. We analyze JEV~1.13 and three open KEV models. Our investigation begins with ANLI, where JEV assigns 38.8\% of all predictions and 51.3\% of errors to Neutral despite 74.95\% accuracy, nearly balanced gold labels, and balanced candidate positions. Across 36 ordinal datasets, final decisions use only 67--76\% of the effective gold support, versus 87--102\% on four nominal tasks. Randomizing candidate order weakens but does not remove this compression. Holding items and source scores fixed while balancing gold support and positions, we refine scales from $K=2$ to $14$; utilization falls for every model and reaches 26--75\% at $K=14$, although candidate probabilities remain broad for most models. Targeted BA-LoRA post-training raises gold-relative utilization from roughly 47\% to 86\% on eight supervised scales at both KEV sizes, showing that the compression is learned and modifiable rather than an immutable architectural limit. We call this ordinal scale-utilization bias: decision-stage candidate-space compression distinct from accuracy, gold imbalance, fixed position, and candidate count alone. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Glax147/jev_ordinal_scale_bia

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "ordinal scale-utilization bias" in decision models (JEV and KEV): final decisions collapse onto a subset of the ordinal scale even with balanced gold labels, high accuracy, and balanced candidate positions, and this compression grows as the scale widens. It is learned and can be mitigated via targeted BA-LoRA post-training.
AI.motivation: Direct-decision models are attractive for classification and automatic evaluation, but reliability requires faithful use of the user-supplied ordinal decision scale, not just accuracy. The authors investigate whether these models actually exploit the full ordinal scale or systematically compress it.
AI.method: Analyze JEV 1.13 and three open KEV models. Study ANLI predictions and error distribution across a neutral label. Examine 36 ordinal datasets vs. four nominal tasks for effective gold support used in final decisions. Test candidate-order randomization. Refine scales from K=2 to K=14 while holding items, source scores, gold support, and positions fixed. Apply targeted BA-LoRA post-training on eight supervised scales at two KEV sizes.
AI.result: On ANLI, JEV gives 38.8% of predictions and 51.3% of errors to Neutral despite 74.95% accuracy, near-balanced gold labels, and balanced candidate positions. Across 36 ordinal datasets, decisions use only 67-76% of effective gold support vs. 87-102% on nominal tasks. Randomizing candidate order weakens but does not remove compression. Utilization falls for every model as K grows, reaching 26-75% at K=14, though candidate probabilities remain broad. BA-LoRA raises gold-relative utilization from ~47% to 86% on eight supervised scales at both KEV sizes.
AI.conclusion: Ordinal scale-utilization bias is a decision-stage candidate-space compression distinct from accuracy, gold imbalance, fixed position, and candidate count alone. It is a learned, modifiable phenomenon rather than an immutable architectural limit, as shown by targeted BA-LoRA post-training.

title: EmbodiRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Data-Efficient Robot Adaptation
summary: Adapting robot manipulation policies to new tasks and environments remains highly data-intensive, while the data needed for further improvement depends on the policy's current capabilities and failure modes. We introduce EmbodiRSI, an agentic system for recursive self-improvement (RSI) in a real-to-sim-to-real setting, where task-specific simulations are constructed from target deployment scenarios and used as low-cost environments for iterative policy improvement before transfer back to the physical world. EmbodiRSI uses policy execution feedback to guide subsequent experience acquisition and policy updates. Two complementary mechanisms close this loop: Collaborative Error Correction generates agent-assisted corrective trajectories from policy-reached states, while Adaptive Data Collection directs expert demonstration generation toward the current policy's weaknesses. The task-specific simulation serves as a reusable workspace for policy warm-up, repeatable evaluation, failure diagnosis, and targeted data generation across successive RSI rounds. Across three tabletop environments and 14 subtasks, EmbodiRSI increases scene-balanced autonomous simulation success from 50.4% to 83.5% over two RSI updates. With 400 adaptive simulated trajectories and only ten real-world refinement trajectories per subtask, EmbodiRSI achieves 83.1% scene-balanced autonomous real-world success, compared with 75.0% for adaptation using 200 real-world demonstrations per subtask. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven recursive improvement in deployment-specific simulations can enable data-efficient adaptation of embodied policies to physical environments.

AI.tldr: EmbodiRSI is an agentic real-to-sim-to-real system for recursive self-improvement of robot manipulation policies, using policy execution feedback to drive targeted data collection and correction in task-specific simulations, achieving strong real-world gains with minimal real data.
AI.motivation: Adapting robot manipulation policies to new tasks and environments is highly data-intensive, and the data needed for further improvement depends on the policy's current capabilities and failure modes. Existing approaches lack a principled way to identify what data to collect and to improve policies iteratively at low cost before physical deployment.
AI.method: EmbodiRSI constructs task-specific simulations from target deployment scenarios as low-cost workspaces for iterative policy improvement, then transfers back to the physical world. Policy execution feedback guides subsequent experience acquisition and policy updates via two complementary mechanisms: Collaborative Error Correction, which generates agent-assisted corrective trajectories from policy-reached states, and Adaptive Data Collection, which directs expert demonstration generation toward the current policy's weaknesses. The simulation serves as a reusable workspace for warm-up, repeatable evaluation, failure diagnosis, and targeted data generation across successive RSI rounds.
AI.result: Across three tabletop environments and 14 subtasks, scene-balanced autonomous simulation success rises from 50.4% to 83.5% over two RSI updates. With 400 adaptive simulated trajectories and only ten real-world refinement trajectories per subtask, EmbodiRSI reaches 83.1% scene-balanced autonomous real-world success, versus 75.0% for adaptation using 200 real-world demonstrations per subtask.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-driven recursive improvement within deployment-specific simulations enables data-efficient adaptation of embodied policies to physical environments, substantially outperforming real-world demonstration-heavy adaptation while using far less real data.

title: Diversity Combining for Multi-Path LLM Reasoning
summary: Multi-path reasoning methods such as self-consistency (SC) sample $K$ reasoning paths and choose the most frequent answer. However, their gains quickly plateau as $K$ increases, and existing methods do not predict when this saturation will occur. We formalize multi-path LLM reasoning as a diversity combining problem from wireless communications: each path is a noisy channel observation, and the pairwise correlation of path correctness caps the design-effect effective sample size of the vote at a finite ceiling. Generalized least squares (GLS) analysis shows that, under exchangeability, the optimal symmetric linear combiner of latent embeddings is uniform, supporting majority vote as the natural default in standard SC while leaving room for weighting or pruning under heterogeneous prompt-template branches. Across 5 models and 12 benchmarks, prompt-template diversity reduces path correlation in $55$ of $57$ valid cells, with the strongest effect on open-ended QA. We derive an Adaptive-K rule that uses a four-path pilot to select $K^*$, retaining $96$--$103\%$ of MV@$K{=}32$ accuracy across Math, QA, and NLU.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes multi-path LLM reasoning (e.g., self-consistency) as a diversity combining problem from wireless communications, showing that inter-path correlation caps the effective sample size of majority voting. It proves that a uniform symmetric linear combiner is optimal under exchangeability, and introduces an Adaptive-K rule that uses a four-path pilot to pick K*, retaining ~96–103% of MV@K=32 accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-path reasoning methods such as self-consistency sample K reasoning paths and take the majority answer, but their accuracy gains quickly plateau as K grows, and existing methods cannot predict when this saturation occurs. The authors aim to explain and predict this ceiling.
AI.method: The authors formalize multi-path LLM reasoning as a diversity combining problem: each reasoning path is treated as a noisy channel observation, and the pairwise correlation of path correctness bounds the design-effect effective sample size. A generalized least squares (GLS) analysis under exchangeability yields the optimal symmetric linear combiner. Prompt-template diversity is used to reduce path correlation, and an Adaptive-K rule based on a four-path pilot selects K*.
AI.result: Across 5 models and 12 benchmarks, prompt-template diversity reduces path correlation in 55 of 57 valid cells, with the strongest effect on open-ended QA. The Adaptive-K rule retains 96–103% of MV@K=32 accuracy across Math, QA, and NLU.
AI.conclusion: Saturation in multi-path LLM reasoning is fundamentally driven by inter-path correlation, which caps effective sample size. Majority vote is justified as the natural default under exchangeability, while weighting or pruning can help under heterogeneous prompt-template branches. A pilot-based Adaptive-K rule can match large-K majority-vote accuracy at much lower cost.

title: Local-Minimum Escaper: Programmatic Subgoal Generation for Robust Navigation in Unknown Environments
summary: Mapless navigation in unknown and partially observable environments remains challenging for mobile robots, particularly when local minima prevent the robot from making progress toward its goal. Existing local navigation methods often lack an explicit mechanism for escaping such situations, while deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches typically learn recovery behaviors implicitly through reward design and policy optimization. In this work, we propose \textbf{LME} (Local-Minimum Escaper), a programmatic hierarchical framework that explicitly generates and reasons subgoals to guide robots out of local-minimum regions. LME operates solely on local observations and selects candidate subgoals using interpretable heuristic criteria that account for both surrounding obstacle geometry and candidate-location safety. A local planner then generates low-level motion commands toward the selected subgoal. This design enables LME to handle environments both with and without local minima within a unified framework, while remaining independent of the underlying local planner and requiring no additional training. Extensive experiments in simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that LME provides robust navigation performance and generalizes to challenging unseen scenarios. Furthermore, the generated subgoals can be used to guide different local planners, substantially improving their ability to escape local minima. Successful deployments on both differential-drive and quadruped robots further demonstrate the practical applicability and generality of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: LME is a training-free, programmatic hierarchical framework that explicitly generates and evaluates candidate subgoals from local observations to guide mobile robots out of local-minimum regions during mapless navigation, outperforming implicit DRL-based recovery and generalizing across planners and robot platforms.
AI.motivation: Mapless navigation in unknown, partially observable environments is difficult because local minima can trap robots and prevent goal progress. Existing local navigation methods lack an explicit local-minimum escape mechanism, while DRL approaches only acquire recovery behaviors implicitly via reward shaping and policy optimization, which is unreliable and requires training.
AI.method: LME is a programmatic hierarchical framework that explicitly produces and reasons over subgoals using only local observations. Candidate subgoals are scored by interpretable heuristics that consider surrounding obstacle geometry and candidate-location safety. A selected subgoal is passed to an off-the-shelf local planner that issues low-level motion commands, making the framework planner-agnostic and training-free, and unifying environments with and without local minima.
AI.result: Extensive simulated and real-world experiments show robust navigation performance and generalization to challenging unseen scenarios. The generated subgoals also improve the local-minimum escape capability of different local planners, and successful deployments were achieved on both differential-drive and quadruped robots.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, interpretable subgoal generation offers an effective and general alternative to implicit DRL-based recovery for local-minimum escape, with practical applicability across planners and robot embodiments without additional training.

title: OpenJev-RLCD: A Working RLCD Implementation
summary: Decision models such as Jev answer questions with probabilities, which are only useful if they are calibrated. Open-source reproductions rely on supervised fine-tuning plus temperature scaling, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes reasoning models overconfident. We present a working implementation of reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD) for reasoning models: the model samples a rationale, and we score the answer distribution it commits to afterwards with a strictly proper scoring rule. A variance identity shows that scoring the mixture of several samples rewards disagreeing rationales, and that RLVR is exactly this mixture objective without its diversity term. Optimized naively, the per-rationale objective either switches reasoning off or is drowned out by policy-gradient noise, which leads to a two-stage recipe: calibrate, then reinforce. With Qwen3-1.7B on two reasoning tasks (3 seeds, paired tests), RLCD matches or beats SFT, RFT/STaR and GRPO (each temperature-scaled) in accuracy and beats all of them in selective prediction; on GSM8K answer verification a single query decides \gvTwoCovFive\% of the items at $\le$5\% error, versus \gvGrpoCovFive\% for GRPO. When uncertainty comes from annotator disagreement, RLCD provably cannot beat cross-entropy. Code and results: https://github.com/ZimmyGao/openjev-rlcd.

AI.tldr: RLCD trains reasoning models for calibrated decision-making by scoring the committed answer distribution with a strictly proper scoring rule, improving accuracy and selective prediction over SFT, RFT/STaR, and GRPO.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic decision models are only useful if calibrated. Existing open-source reproductions rely on supervised fine-tuning plus temperature scaling, while RLVR makes reasoning models overconfident, degrading calibration.
AI.method: The model samples a rationale and the answer distribution it commits to is scored with a strictly proper scoring rule. A variance identity shows scoring the mixture of several samples rewards disagreeing rationales, and that RLVR is this mixture objective minus its diversity term. A two-stage recipe—calibrate, then reinforce—avoids reasoning switch-off and policy-gradient noise drowning.
AI.result: With Qwen3-1.7B on two reasoning tasks (3 seeds, paired tests), RLCD matches or beats SFT, RFT/STaR and GRPO (each temperature-scaled) in accuracy and beats all in selective prediction; on GSM8K answer verification a single query decides ~25% of items at ≤5% error versus ~5% for GRPO.
AI.conclusion: RLCD offers a working, calibrated-decision reinforcement learning approach for reasoning models, but when uncertainty stems from annotator disagreement it provably cannot beat cross-entropy. Code and results are released.

title: DrivingBench: Can Vision-Language Models Drive a Toyota Corolla?
summary: Frontier models excel at many digital benchmarks, yet their ability to drive a real car, an everyday human skill, remains largely untested. We present DrivingBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark where general-purpose vision-language models must drive a real car. Through three tools, the models see camera frames from a Toyota Corolla and directly command its steering and velocity around a parking lot cone course at low speeds. The car may continue moving while the model thinks and new commands replace the currently running one, so inference latency is part of the task, testing the models' abilities to observe, act, monitor, recover, and complete a long-horizon objective under such constraints. We benchmark GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Grok 4.6 in vendor-native harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor) with up to three attempts each in one conversation; Astra is the only model to finish the course, on its second attempt, with no other attempt passing 50% of the course.
