Two of the four models improved materially across attempts with retained context. We also detail the design principles behind our action interface, and show how the tool output format and the framing of the task combined to determine whether models would drive at all or refuse. We release our harness, prompts, course map, and traces with video and telemetry for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: DrivingBench is introduced as the first benchmark requiring general-purpose vision-language models to drive a real car, where models process camera frames from a Toyota Corolla to control steering and velocity around a parking-lot cone course, with inference latency embedded in the task.
AI.motivation: Frontier models perform well on many digital benchmarks, but their capacity to perform an everyday physical skill such as driving a real car remains largely untested.
AI.method: Through three tools, models view camera frames from a Toyota Corolla and directly command steering and velocity around a low-speed parking-lot cone course. The car keeps moving while the model reasons, and new commands replace the currently executing one, making inference latency part of the task and requiring observation, action, monitoring, recovery, and long-horizon completion. GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Grok 4.6 are evaluated in vendor-native harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor) with up to three attempts each in one conversation. The paper also details action-interface design principles and how tool output format and task framing determined whether models drove or refused.
AI.result: Astra is the only model to finish the course, doing so on its second attempt, while no other attempt passed 50% of the course. Two of the four models improved materially across attempts with retained context.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose vision-language models remain far from reliable real-car driving under the benchmark's latency-constrained, long-horizon conditions, and driving behavior is highly sensitive to interface design and task framing. The harness, prompts, course map, and traces with video and telemetry are released for reproducibility.

title: When Context Changes: Understanding Update Failures in LLMs
summary: As preferences, goals, and facts change, LLM agents must use the current state while earlier versions remain in context. Yet they can answer with an old value of the same variable, a failure that we call stale binding. To study when models use outdated information and why, we introduce Controlled In-Context Memory (CICM), a benchmark for tracking and using updated information in conversations and agent logs. We observe that even frontier reasoning models can fail to recover the current state. We find that in open-source models probes can still recover the updated value when the model answers with an old one, pointing to a failure to select information that remains available. Component tests in Qwen and Pythia identify a mechanism for this selection failure: attention drift, where attention favors old values over the current one when producing an answer. We study a one-layer transformer to mathematically understand how this phenomenon happens: when attention scores are similar, several old values can together receive more attention than the current value. Guided by this explanation, we redirect attention toward the current value without further training. When the current value is requested directly, adjusting this intervention for each input corrects most old-value errors across various model families while preserving nearly all initially correct answers. Reliable context management therefore requires more than remembering updated information: models must use it to guide their answers.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "stale binding," where LLM agents answer with old values of a variable despite updated values remaining in context, and traces it to attention drift, which can be corrected at inference time.
AI.motivation: As preferences, goals, and facts change in conversations and agent logs, LLM agents must use the current state while earlier versions remain in context. However, they frequently answer with outdated values of the same variable—a failure the authors call stale binding. The goal is to determine when and why models rely on outdated information.
AI.method: The authors introduce Controlled In-Context Memory (CICM), a benchmark for tracking and using updated information in conversations and agent logs. They use probing on open-source models, run component tests in Qwen and Pythia, and mathematically analyze a one-layer transformer to explain the selection failure. They then design a training-free intervention that redirects attention toward the current value, adjusted per input.
AI.result: Even frontier reasoning models can fail to recover the current state. Probes can still recover the updated value when open-source models answer with an old one, indicating a selection failure rather than a memory failure. Component tests identify attention drift: attention favors old values over the current one when producing an answer. The one-layer analysis shows that when attention scores are similar, several old values collectively out-attend the current value. The per-input adjusted attention intervention corrects most old-value errors across various model families while preserving nearly all initially correct answers.
AI.conclusion: Reliable context management requires more than remembering updated information: models must use it to guide their answers. The reported failures stem from information selection, specifically attention drift, which can be mitigated without further training.

title: Video2SwimFish: An Automated Pipeline for Reconstructing Controllable Fish Models and Biological Locomotion from Real Fish Videos
summary: We present Video2SwimFish, an automated pipeline and benchmark for building controllable fish assets from real-fish videos for underwater embodied AI. Given synchronized multi-view videos of an individual fish, the pipeline reconstructs a metrically scaled deformable mesh from a VLM-selected canonical frame, generates internal articulation adapted to that individual's morphology through a VLM actor-critic loop, and extracts a Biological Locomotion Manifold (BLM) from the fish's observed midline curvature. The BLM provides a low-dimensional action space bounded by real-fish motion, enabling an individual swimming policy to be learned for each reconstructed fish. We release two paired datasets: synchronized top- and front-view recordings of 120 individual fish across 6 species, and the controllable assets and individual swimming policies derived from them. Because every asset is tied to the animal it came from, the dataset supports a benchmark that evaluates locomotion learning not only on task success but on fidelity to that individual in trajectory shape, body curvature, and tail-beat frequency, across trajectory following, reward-free swimming behavior transfer from video, and a downstream case study in which a simulated BlueROV underwater robot captures one of the assets. We find that task success and locomotion fidelity do not necessarily improve together: the method achieving the highest task completion is not the method achieving the highest locomotion fidelity, and we identify faithful reproduction of individual animal locomotion as an open challenge for the community. Project website: https://hangongchen.github.io/video2swimfish-web/.

AI.tldr: Video2SwimFish is an automated pipeline and benchmark that converts real-fish multi-view videos into metrically scaled, individually controllable deformable fish assets with learned swimming policies, and shows that task success and locomotion fidelity do not improve together.
AI.motivation: Underwater embodied AI needs controllable fish assets that faithfully reproduce the locomotion of specific real animals, but existing assets are typically generic, not tied to individual morphology or motion, and benchmarks rarely measure biological fidelity alongside task success.
AI.method: From synchronized multi-view videos of an individual fish, the pipeline reconstructs a metrically scaled deformable mesh from a VLM-selected canonical frame, generates internal articulation adapted to that individual's morphology via a VLM actor-critic loop, and extracts a Biological Locomotion Manifold (BLM) from the observed midline curvature. The BLM defines a low-dimensional action space bounded by real-fish motion, from which an individual swimming policy is learned. Two paired datasets are released: top- and front-view recordings of 120 individuals across 6 species, plus the derived controllable assets and policies.
AI.result: The dataset supports a benchmark evaluating locomotion learning on task success and on fidelity to the individual in trajectory shape, body curvature, and tail-beat frequency, across trajectory following, reward-free swimming behavior transfer from video, and a downstream case study where a simulated BlueROV captures one of the assets. Task completion and locomotion fidelity are found not to improve together: the highest task-completion method is not the highest-fidelity method.
AI.conclusion: Faithful reproduction of individual animal locomotion is identified as an open challenge for the community, with the benchmark and released assets providing a foundation for progress.

title: Talk2Agent: Benchmarking Voice Interfaces for Text Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) computer-use agents are typically evaluated with clean written instructions, despite speech being an increasingly popular interface for interacting with such systems. Speech input introduces an additional failure point: transcription errors can alter task-critical entities, constraints, or targets before the agent begins reasoning, while conventional ASR metrics do not directly measure whether the information required for successful execution has been preserved. We introduce Talk2Agent, a benchmark for evaluating how effectively voice interfaces convey human-spoken instructions to LLM-based computer-use agents. Talk2Agent builds human-spoken versions of tasks from WildClawBench and OSWorld and evaluates a range of voice interfaces, including dedicated ASR models, audio-capable LLMs, contextual biasing, and LLM-based ontology repair. Because repeatedly executing long-horizon computer-use tasks is costly and stochastic, we further propose an execution-free, task-conditioned evaluation framework that projects the original task grader onto prompt-addressable intentions and measures how much task-relevant information is retained after the voice interface. On WildClawBench, Talk2Agent's execution-free native projection provides a practical, execution-grounded measure of voice-interface quality, correlating with downstream task completion and improving Pearson correlation by 0.246 over WER/CER on 32 hours of real human speech.

AI.tldr: Talk2Agent is a benchmark that evaluates how well voice interfaces preserve task-critical information when conveying spoken instructions to LLM-based computer-use agents, using an execution-free, task-conditioned evaluation framework.
AI.motivation: LLM computer-use agents are typically evaluated with clean written instructions, even though speech is an increasingly common interface. Speech introduces a distinct failure point: transcription errors can corrupt task-critical entities, constraints, or targets before the agent reasons. Conventional ASR metrics (WER/CER) do not directly measure whether the information needed for successful execution is preserved.
AI.method: The authors build Talk2Agent using human-spoken versions of tasks from WildClawBench and OSWorld, and evaluate multiple voice interfaces including dedicated ASR models, audio-capable LLMs, contextual biasing, and LLM-based ontology repair. To avoid costly, stochastic execution of long-horizon tasks, they propose an execution-free, task-conditioned evaluation framework that projects the original task grader onto prompt-addressable intentions and quantifies retained task-relevant information after the voice interface.
AI.result: On WildClawBench, Talk2Agent's execution-free native projection provides an execution-grounded measure of voice-interface quality that correlates with downstream task completion and improves Pearson correlation by 0.246 over WER/CER on 32 hours of real human speech.
AI.conclusion: Talk2Agent offers a practical, execution-grounded benchmark for assessing voice-interface quality in LLM-based computer-use agents, showing that task-conditioned, execution-free evaluation better predicts downstream task success than conventional ASR metrics.

title: SimEX: Simulation-Integrated Robotics AutoResearch
summary: Coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable abilities to autonomously reason about and achieve goals in the digital world. However, bringing this success to the physical world remains challenging. On the one hand, direct generation methods (e.g., Code as Policies) often suffer from the LLMs' insufficient understanding of robots and physical environments. On the other hand, iterative trial-and-error tuning in the physical world (e.g., physical autoresearch) induces significant experimental cost and safety concerns. We introduce SimEX: Simulation-Integrated Robotics AutoResearch, an autoresearch framework that tightly integrates simulated experimentation, enabling coding agents to efficiently acquire physical capabilities for controlling real robots. SimEX operates in two stages. First, the agent conducts open-ended probe-and-optimize iterations in simulation, developing a robot toolbox with robust and generalizable capabilities. Second, the agent adapts the toolbox and the simulator together through only a few physical trials: each trial corrects the simulator, and the corrected simulator is used to diagnose failures and screen candidate repairs. We evaluate SimEX extensively in sim-to-sim settings and on physical robots. On challenging real-world manipulation tasks including towel folding, barcode scanning, and plate manipulation, SimEX enables coding agents to efficiently acquire robot skills without any demonstration and with only 10 minutes of real-robot interaction. These results suggest that simulation can be a critical component in achieving physical intelligence, not only as a source of training data that must closely replicate the real world, but also as a roughly correct laboratory where a coding agent develops the knowledge and procedures needed to act on the robot. More details and robot videos at https://robo-simex.github.io/

AI.tldr: SimEX is an autoresearch framework that integrates simulated experimentation to let LLM coding agents efficiently acquire real-robot manipulation skills, achieving results on tasks like towel folding with only 10 minutes of real-robot interaction.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents succeed in digital domains but struggle in the physical world: direct generation methods (e.g., Code as Policies) suffer from LLMs' poor understanding of robots and physical environments, while iterative trial-and-error tuning in the physical world (physical autoresearch) incurs high experimental cost and safety risks.
AI.method: SimEX operates in two stages. First, the agent runs open-ended probe-and-optimize iterations in simulation to build a robot toolbox with robust, generalizable capabilities. Second, the agent co-adapts the toolbox and simulator via a few physical trials: each trial corrects the simulator, and the corrected simulator is used to diagnose failures and screen candidate repairs.
AI.result: SimEX is evaluated extensively in sim-to-sim settings and on physical robots across challenging real-world manipulation tasks including towel folding, barcode scanning, and plate manipulation, enabling coding agents to acquire robot skills without demonstrations and with only 10 minutes of real-robot interaction.
AI.conclusion: Simulation can be a critical component of physical intelligence—not only as training data that closely replicates reality, but as a roughly correct laboratory where a coding agent develops the knowledge and procedures needed to act on a real robot.

title: Reasoning Externalization for Faithful Large Language Model Narratives of Stock Return Predictions
summary: In finance, interpreting machine learning predictions is essential, yet the numerical outputs of explainable AI can be difficult for non-experts to understand. While large language models (LLMs) can translate these outputs into natural language, they may produce errors when inferring numerical changes and feature relations. We propose an LLM narrative framework for cross-sectional stock return prediction that combines temporal Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) evidence with historical regime analogs. Temporal evidence tracks changes in the normalized global SHAP importance of an XGBoost model over six months. Historical analogs are past periods with similar changes in SHAP importance, their model performance and subsequent market returns are provided as comparative context. Using this framework, we conduct a controlled study of progressive reasoning externalization, sequentially providing raw SHAP sequences, deterministic temporal descriptors, and feature relations. Each generated claim is verified against provenance-linked evidence. Across Qwen3, externalizing numerical and relational reasoning improved evidence faithfulness as well as temporal and relational accuracy. Evidence faithfulness increased from 0.696 to 0.996 for Qwen3-32B-Instruct. While historical analogs did not improve structured automatic faithfulness, they received higher human-rated usefulness scores. These results suggest that externalizing verifiable reasoning enhances narrative faithfulness and that historical context adds interpretive value.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an LLM narrative framework for cross-sectional stock return prediction that combines temporal SHAP evidence with historical regime analogs, and shows that externalizing verifiable numerical and relational reasoning improves narrative faithfulness.
AI.motivation: Explainable AI numerical outputs in finance are hard for non-experts to interpret. LLMs can translate these outputs into natural language but tend to produce errors when inferring numerical changes and feature relations, creating a faithfulness problem.
AI.method: A framework combining temporal SHAP evidence (changes in normalized global SHAP importance of an XGBoost model over six months) with historical regime analogs (past periods with similar SHAP-importance changes, plus their model performance and subsequent market returns). A controlled study of progressive reasoning externalization sequentially supplies raw SHAP sequences, deterministic temporal descriptors, and feature relations; each generated claim is verified against provenance-linked evidence. Evaluated across Qwen3 models.
AI.result: Externalizing numerical and relational reasoning improved evidence faithfulness and temporal/relational accuracy. Evidence faithfulness rose from 0.696 to 0.996 for Qwen3-32B-Instruct. Historical analogs did not improve structured automatic faithfulness but received higher human-rated usefulness scores.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing verifiable reasoning enhances narrative faithfulness, and historical context adds interpretive value beyond what automatic metrics capture.

title: Sparse-WAM: Accelerating World Action Models via Action-Guided Sparse Imagination
comment: Xinling Xie and Haodong Wang contributed equally to this work
summary: World-action models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video models to improve generalization in robot control by jointly predicting future visual states and actions. This capability comes at a substantial inference cost, as dense future-frame tokens are repeatedly processed during denoising. Prior methods address this by token pruning that prioritizes visual fidelity to reduce denoising costs in video diffusion models. However, these methods do not use action relevance to determine which future-frame tokens to retain during joint denoising in WAMs. In this paper, we propose Sparse-WAM, a training-free framework for action-guided sparse imagination that selectively processes future-frame tokens to accelerate WAM inference. We observe substantial overlap in the spatial distribution of attention from action tokens to future-frame tokens (action-to-future attention) between consecutive denoising steps, despite continued updates to the future representations. Motivated by this, we develop Action-Guided Token Selection to retain frame-specific action-relevant regions together with cross-frame context. However, a naive implementation can incur attention-scoring and token-packing overhead that offsets the computational savings from pruning. We therefore introduce Pilot, an efficient engine that reduces sparse inference overhead through lightweight scoring and cross-step reuse of token selections. On LIBERO with FastWAM-Joint and RoboLab-120 with Cosmos 3 Edge, Sparse-WAM achieves inference speedups of approximately $2.0\times$ and $1.8\times$, respectively, over dense eager inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, while largely preserving task performance.

AI.tldr: Sparse-WAM is a training-free framework that accelerates world-action model inference via action-guided sparse imagination, selectively processing future-frame tokens based on action relevance, achieving ~2x speedup with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: World-action models (WAMs) improve robot control generalization by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, but suffer substantial inference cost from densely processing future-frame tokens during denoising. Prior token-pruning methods optimize for visual fidelity in video diffusion models, but ignore action relevance when deciding which future-frame tokens to retain during joint denoising in WAMs.
AI.method: Sparse-WAM is a training-free framework for action-guided sparse imagination. It exploits the observation that action-to-future attention spatial distributions overlap substantially across consecutive denoising steps despite continued updates to future representations. Based on this, it introduces Action-Guided Token Selection, which retains frame-specific action-relevant regions plus cross-frame context. To avoid attention-scoring and token-packing overhead offsetting savings, it adds Pilot, an efficient engine using lightweight scoring and cross-step reuse of token selections.
AI.result: On LIBERO with FastWAM-Joint and RoboLab-120 with Cosmos 3 Edge, Sparse-WAM achieves inference speedups of approximately 2.0x and 1.8x respectively over dense eager inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, while largely preserving task performance.
AI.conclusion: Action relevance is an effective criterion for pruning future-frame tokens in WAMs. Sparse-WAM's training-free, action-guided token selection combined with an efficient engine delivers significant inference acceleration with minimal degradation in task performance, demonstrating practical viability for accelerating joint denoising in world-action models.

title: STRATA: Self-Learning Through Role-Aligned Tiered Agents for Real-Time Strategy Games
summary: Real-time strategy (RTS) games require agents to coordinate economic development, production and construction, base defense, unit organization, and attack timing over long matches. Existing studies have applied large language models to command decision-making in RTS games, enabling agents to read textual game states and generate high-level plans. However, long inference latency can cause them to miss critical tactical events. The complexity and tactical diversity of full RTS matches also leave existing systems heavily dependent on manually written experience-based prompts, with limited ability to learn continuously from past games. We present STRATA, a role-aligned hierarchical system with cross-game self-learning for Red Alert. STRATA assigns in-game strategic, logistical, and tactical decisions to a Strategic Agent (SA), Logistics Agent (LA), and Tactical Agent (TA), respectively. The SA generates high-level directives based on the global game state and relevant experience cards, while the LA and TA handle logistics and tactical execution. After each match, a Review Agent (RA) derives candidate experience from game traces, validates and revises it using evidence from subsequent matches, and compresses strategic experience supported across multiple games into concise experience cards for SA retrieval. We evaluate STRATA through the formation of experience cards, full-match comparisons before and after learning, and experience learning against AI opponents with different play styles. Under a fixed scenario, using the learned experience cards increases the observed win rate from 30% to 100%. Sequential learning against AI opponents with different play styles also produces distinct long-term strategic experience.

AI.tldr: STRATA is a role-aligned hierarchical system with cross-game self-learning for Red Alert, where strategic, logistical, and tactical decisions are handled by separate agents and a Review Agent distills validated experience cards that raise win rate from 30% to 100%.
AI.motivation: Real-time strategy matches require coordinating economy, production, construction, base defense, unit organization, and attack timing over long horizons. Although large language models have been applied to RTS command decision-making, two key limitations persist: long inference latency can cause agents to miss critical tactical events, and the complexity and tactical diversity of full matches leave existing systems heavily dependent on manually written experience-based prompts with limited ability to learn continuously from past games.
AI.method: STRATA adopts a role-aligned hierarchical architecture: a Strategic Agent (SA) generates high-level directives from the global game state and retrieved experience cards, while a Logistics Agent (LA) and Tactical Agent (TA) handle logistics and tactical execution. After each match, a Review Agent (RA) derives candidate experience from game traces, validates and revises it using evidence from subsequent matches, and compresses strategic experience supported across multiple games into concise experience cards for SA retrieval.
AI.result: Evaluation covered experience card formation, full-match comparisons before and after learning, and experience learning against AI opponents with different play styles. Under a fixed scenario, using learned experience cards increased the observed win rate from 30% to 100%. Sequential learning against opponents with different play styles produced distinct long-term strategic experience.
AI.conclusion: STRATA demonstrates that role-aligned hierarchy combined with cross-game self-learning can overcome latency-induced tactical misses and reliance on handcrafted prompts in RTS command decision-making, enabling continual improvement and adaptation to diverse opponent styles.

title: Cue the Flow: Steering Flow-Matching Policies for Open-World Delivery Manipulation
summary: Open-world goods delivery requires mobile manipulators to follow free-form user instructions and manipulate potentially novel objects. Existing dual-system approaches use high-level grounding models to convert language into grounded visual prompts, but their low-level controllers can remain brittle under noisy perception, dynamic scenes, and contact-rich interactions. We instead use a pretrained flow-matching vision-language-action model as the low-level control interface, leveraging its reactivity and robustness to environmental changes while treating the grounding output as a spatial cue for policy steering. Our key insight is that the pretrained VLA already provides a strong manipulation prior, while the spatial cue supplies the missing target information needed to guide actions under novel language--object mappings. Concretely, we introduce a lightweight cue-conditioned adapter. The adapter is first trained with contrastive objectives to produce salient and spatially discriminative cue representations, and is then supervised to predict a diagonal affine transformation over the generated action chunk, aligning policy steering with the cued target. Across tabletop and mobile-base settings, our method improves instruction following and manipulation success on both in-domain and out-of-domain objects, achieving up to near $2\times$ improvement in average task success rate with negligible inference overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a pretrained flow-matching VLA model as a low-level control interface and adds a lightweight cue-conditioned adapter that turns grounding output into a spatial cue for policy steering, improving open-world instruction following and manipulation success.
AI.motivation: Open-world goods delivery requires mobile manipulators to follow free-form instructions and manipulate novel objects. Existing dual-system approaches ground language into visual prompts but their low-level controllers stay brittle under noisy perception, dynamic scenes, and contact-rich interaction.
AI.method: They treat a pretrained flow-matching vision-language-action model as the low-level control interface, keeping its reactivity and robustness, and use the grounding output as a spatial cue. A lightweight cue-conditioned adapter is first trained with contrastive objectives for salient, spatially discriminative cue representations, then supervised to predict a diagonal affine transformation over the generated action chunk to align policy steering with the cued target.
AI.result: Across tabletop and mobile-base settings, the method improves instruction following and manipulation success for both in-domain and out-of-domain objects, achieving up to near 2x improvement in average task success rate with negligible inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a pretrained VLA as a strong manipulation prior while a spatial cue supplies missing target information yields robust policy steering for novel language-object mappings, with large success-rate gains and minimal inference cost.

title: Consistent Plan-Act for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
summary: Long-horizon agentic tasks demand strong reasoning and efficient execution across successive interactions with dynamic environments. A common approach decouples high-level planning from low-level execution through separate planner and actor roles. To investigate coordination failures in these tasks, we prompt both agents for structured state assertions and compare their reports programmatically to detect explicit contradictions. Our analyses reveal systematic disagreement about the same task-relevant state facts, a phenomenon we term planner-actor state mismatch. We further find that providing agents with task-relevant state information reduces mismatch and improves coordination and task performance. Based on the systematic analysis of the state mismatch, we propose Consistent Plan-Act (ConPAct), which feeds detected contradictions back to both agents to form consistent state interpretations and fine-tunes them on curated consistent interactions for better coordination. ConPAct improves performance across various environments and model configurations, e.g., increasing MiniGrid success rate from 38.6% to 54.4% with GPT-5.6-sol/terra as planner and actor respectively, demonstrating that state consistency can guide both inference-time correction and coordination training.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "planner-actor state mismatch"—systematic disagreement between planner and actor agents about task-relevant state facts—as a key coordination failure in long-horizon agentic tasks, and proposes ConPAct to resolve it via contradiction feedback and fine-tuning on consistent interactions.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agentic tasks require strong reasoning and efficient execution across successive interactions with dynamic environments, which motivates decoupling high-level planning from low-level execution into separate planner and actor roles. However, coordination failures between these roles remain underexplored and degrade overall task performance.
AI.method: The authors prompt both planner and actor agents to produce structured state assertions and programmatically compare their reports to detect explicit contradictions. This analysis uncovers systematic disagreement about the same task-relevant state facts (planner-actor state mismatch). They then propose Consistent Plan-Act (ConPAct), which (1) feeds detected contradictions back to both agents to form consistent state interpretations and (2) fine-tunes them on curated consistent interactions to improve coordination.
AI.result: Providing agents with task-relevant state information reduces mismatch and improves coordination and task performance. ConPAct improves performance across various environments and model configurations, e.g., raising MiniGrid success rate from 38.6% to 54.4% with GPT-5.6-sol/terra as planner and actor respectively.
AI.conclusion: State consistency is a key factor in planner-actor coordination and can guide both inference-time correction and coordination training, offering a general route to improving long-horizon agentic task performance.

title: NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation
summary: Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website: https://nexus-humanoid.github.io/

AI.tldr: NEXUS is a perceptive whole-body control framework for humanoid teleoperation that fuses human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback, enabling terrain-adaptive behavior reproduction across mismatched terrains.
AI.motivation: Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid to reproduce an operator's behavior even when terrains differ, so the robot must perceive local terrain and adapt posture and contacts rather than copy motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains is scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control.
AI.method: The authors develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus of nearly 1,000 hours, they train a perceptive whole-body controller via teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains.
AI.conclusion: NEXUS enables whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains by combining human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback, and its generalization is validated through zero-shot real-world deployment.

title: Composing Task-specific Agent Harnesses at Test Time with Reusable Primitives
summary: Agent harnesses govern how large language models (LLMs) gather context, invoke tools, verify results, preserve state, and terminate, largely affecting agent performance. However, the value of each harness mechanism can differ across heterogeneous tasks: a mechanism that improves one task may impose overhead or context distraction on another, leading to the suboptimality of a global harness. We characterize this suboptimality as a mismatch induced by fixed mechanism choices, motivating task-specific harness construction. Nonetheless, generating harness code for each task introduces generation and debugging costs, with execution risks that can compound as more mechanisms are generated. To address those challenges, we introduce Harness Primitives, reusable harness mechanisms with clear application scope and composition contract mined from failed task trajectories. Based on Harness Primitives, we propose STITCH, a framework that Selects suitable primitives given Task Information and compiles them into Task-speCific Harnesses at test time. This separation enables task-specific harnesses without generating or repairing mechanism code at test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that STITCH not only improves harness adaptability and robustness, but also scales with the primitive library size, boosting task success rates by up to 12 points over fixed harness baselines, surpassing human-designed harnesses like Codex CLI while maintaining a minimal test-time harness composition overhead of only 2.7%, 638 times more efficient than generating task-specific harnesses from scratch. Ultimately, our work demonstrates that building task-adaptive harnesses can be beneficial for completing diverse tasks and that building reusable primitives can be a promising path towards this goal.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Harness Primitives and STITCH, a framework that selects and composes reusable harness mechanisms into task-specific agent harnesses at test time, improving task success while avoiding per-task code generation costs.
AI.motivation: A single global agent harness is suboptimal because the value of each harness mechanism varies across heterogeneous tasks; a mechanism that helps one task may add overhead or context distraction to another. This mismatch motivates task-specific harness construction. However, generating harness code per task incurs generation and debugging costs and execution risks that compound as more mechanisms are added.
AI.method: The authors mine Harness Primitives-reusable harness mechanisms with clear application scope and composition contracts-from failed task trajectories. They then propose STITCH, which Selects suitable primitives given Task Information and compiles them into Task-speCific Harnesses at test time, avoiding the need to generate or repair mechanism code at test time.
AI.result: Experiments show STITCH improves harness adaptability and robustness, and scales with the primitive library size. It raises task success rates by up to 12 points over fixed harness baselines and surpasses human-designed harnesses such as Codex CLI, while incurring only a 2.7% test-time harness composition overhead-638 times more efficient than generating task-specific harnesses from scratch.
AI.conclusion: Building task-adaptive harnesses is beneficial for completing diverse tasks, and reusable primitives offer a promising path toward this goal.

title: Function beyond Form: Functional Correspondence for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
summary: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation remains challenging because robotic hands differ substantially in geometry, topology, and kinematics. Existing approaches often lack explicit correspondences between structurally different hand regions that play similar functional roles in a grasp, a concept we refer to as functional correspondence. Consequently, their models tend to learn hand-specific interaction patterns rather than transferable grasp knowledge, limiting generalization to unseen hands. To address this limitation, we introduce FunCo-Grasp, which establishes functional correspondences across heterogeneous hand embodiments. Specifically, Functional Part Alignment aligns each hand to a canonical functional schema by mapping physical links to shared functional parts according to their grasping roles, while Canonical Frame Alignment expresses these parts in canonical local frames. These two alignments provide a consistent representation for inter-part and hand-object interactions, allowing the model to learn transferable grasp knowledge across hands. Conditioned on the aligned hand representation and object geometry, a diffusion model generates the target spatial arrangement of the functional parts, which are then converted into an executable joint configuration. Adapting FunCo-Grasp to an unseen hand requires only its geometric and kinematic models and a one-time lightweight functional annotation, without target-hand grasp data, fine-tuning, or learned retargeting. In simulation on held-out objects from the filtered CMapDataset, we achieves average success rates of 92.40% on three seen hands and 74.02% on four unseen hands. In real-world experiments, the same model achieves an overall success rate of 76.00% on two unseen hands without additional training or fine-tuning. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of FunCo-Grasp in transferring grasp knowledge to unseen hands.

AI.tldr: FunCo-Grasp introduces functional correspondence across heterogeneous robotic hands via Functional Part Alignment and Canonical Frame Alignment, enabling a diffusion model to generate transferable dexterous grasps that generalize to unseen hands without target-hand data or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation is hard because robotic hands vary greatly in geometry, topology, and kinematics. Existing methods lack explicit correspondences between structurally different hand regions serving similar functional roles (functional correspondence), so models learn hand-specific interaction patterns instead of transferable grasp knowledge, limiting generalization to unseen hands.
AI.method: FunCo-Grasp establishes functional correspondences across heterogeneous hands. Functional Part Alignment maps physical links to shared functional parts based on grasping roles within a canonical functional schema; Canonical Frame Alignment expresses these parts in canonical local frames. These alignments yield a consistent representation for inter-part and hand-object interactions. Conditioned on the aligned hand representation and object geometry, a diffusion model generates the target spatial arrangement of functional parts, which is converted into an executable joint configuration. Adaptation to an unseen hand needs only its geometric/kinematic models and a one-time lightweight functional annotation.
AI.result: In simulation on held-out objects from the filtered CMapDataset, FunCo-Grasp achieves average success rates of 92.40% on three seen hands and 74.02% on four unseen hands. In real-world experiments, the same model achieves 76.00% overall success on two unseen hands without additional training or fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Explicit functional correspondence enables transferable grasp knowledge across embodiments. FunCo-Grasp generalizes to unseen hands using only geometric/kinematic models and a lightweight functional annotation, requiring no target-hand grasp data, fine-tuning, or learned retargeting, demonstrating effective cross-embodiment grasp transfer.

title: Risk-Aware Adaptive Evaluation: Finding High-Impact Failures Under Limited Budgets
comment: Accepted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Evaluation of Interactive Agents
summary: Evaluating interactive agents is expensive. Agent behavior is stochastic, so reliability must be measured over repeated trials, but failures are rare and differ widely in how much they matter. Standard benchmarks spend this budget uniformly: a read-only lookup is sampled as often as an irreversible payment action. We instead formulate evaluation as a sequential allocation problem. Given a fixed trial budget and a set of scenarios whose failure behavior is unknown, which scenarios should be run, and run again? We propose a risk-aware contextual Thompson Sampling policy that combines a pre-execution scenario context vector and a fixed impact score with the failure outcomes observed during evaluation, and we test it by offline replay over 70 $τ$-bench airline scenarios and 824 recorded trials. Our main result is at the smallest budget: with only 50 trials ($6\%$ of the corpus), the policy recovers $86\%$ of the impact-weighted failures an oracle could find, compared to $25\%$ for uniform allocation. It discovers $3.5\times$ more impact-weighted failures (215.4 vs. 62.2) with the same number of trials, delivers $5\times$ the discovery per dollar, and cuts the budget wasted on scenarios that never fail from $34\%$ to $2.8\%$. The rest of our analysis demonstrates and qualifies this result: a budget sweep shows the advantage shrinks as the budget approaches the corpus size, and paired significance tests show that scenario context helps mainly at small budgets while posterior-based exploration helps at moderate ones. Risk-aware adaptive allocation therefore helps most exactly where evaluation budget is scarcest.

AI.tldr: Risk-aware contextual Thompson Sampling allocates limited evaluation trials toward high-impact failure scenarios, recovering 86% of oracle impact-weighted failures with only 6% of a trial budget.
AI.motivation: Evaluating interactive agents is expensive because behavior is stochastic and rare failures matter unevenly, yet standard benchmarks spend trial budgets uniformly—sampling a read-only lookup as often as an irreversible payment—wasting budget on scenarios that never fail.
AI.method: Evaluation is framed as a sequential allocation problem: given a fixed budget and scenarios with unknown failure behavior, decide which scenarios to run and re-run. The authors propose a risk-aware contextual Thompson Sampling policy that combines a pre-execution scenario context vector and a fixed impact score with observed failure outcomes, validated via offline replay over 70 τ-bench airline scenarios and 824 recorded trials.
AI.result: At only 50 trials (6% of the corpus), the policy recovers 86% of impact-weighted failures an oracle could find versus 25% for uniform allocation, discovering 3.5× more impact-weighted failures (215.4 vs. 62.2), delivering 5× the discovery per dollar, and cutting wasted budget from 34% to 2.8%. A budget sweep shows the advantage shrinks as budget approaches corpus size; paired significance tests show scenario context helps mainly at small budgets while posterior-based exploration helps at moderate ones.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware adaptive allocation helps most exactly where evaluation budget is scarcest, offering a principled way to prioritize high-impact scenario testing under tight trial constraints.

title: OccluDex: Hierarchical 3D Visuo-Tactile Representation Learning for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation under Self-Occlusion
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Reliable dexterous manipulation requires continuous estimation of object geometry and hand-object contact throughout interaction. With egocentric sensing, however, the manipulating hand frequently occludes task-relevant object surfaces and contact regions, reducing the visual evidence available for state estimation and thereby making robust closed-loop control and generalization to unseen object geometries particularly challenging. To address this, we present OccluDex, a hierarchical 3D visuo-tactile representation learning framework that integrates global geometric structure with local contact information for robust manipulation under dynamic self-occlusion during hand-object interaction. OccluDex adopts multi-scale masked autoencoding to progressively encode partial 3D geometry and fuses tactile contact tokens with high-level geometric features through cross-modal attention. The encoder is pretrained from synchronized human visuo-tactile demonstrations and transferred as a frozen perceptual backbone for downstream reinforcement learning. We evaluate OccluDex on a faucet rotation task, requiring one full clockwise handle revolution, and a tabletop object reorientation task, requiring a 180-degree tabletop object reorientation without toppling. In simulation experiments, OccluDex demonstrated 12.6% higher accuracy for unseen objects and 8.3% higher accuracy for previously seen objects than the strongest state-of-the-art baseline models. Physical experiments were further performed with a Shadow Hand to demonstrate successful zero-shot sim-to-real generalization on unseen physical objects. This results could enable humanoid egocentric object manipulation for seen and unseen objects even when the manipulating robotic hand occludes vision.

AI.tldr: OccluDex is a hierarchical 3D visuo-tactile representation learning framework that fuses partial 3D geometry with tactile contact tokens to enable robust dexterous manipulation under hand-induced self-occlusion, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines and achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Egocentric sensing during dexterous manipulation suffers from the manipulating hand occluding task-relevant object surfaces and contact regions, which reduces visual evidence for state estimation and makes closed-loop control and generalization to unseen object geometries difficult.
AI.method: OccluDex uses multi-scale masked autoencoding to progressively encode partial 3D geometry and fuses tactile contact tokens with high-level geometric features via cross-modal attention. The encoder is pretrained on synchronized human visuo-tactile demonstrations and transferred as a frozen perceptual backbone for downstream reinforcement learning.
AI.result: In simulation, OccluDex achieved 12.6% higher accuracy on unseen objects and 8.3% higher accuracy on previously seen objects than the strongest state-of-the-art baselines, evaluated on a faucet rotation task (one full clockwise handle revolution) and a tabletop object reorientation task (180-degree reorientation without toppling). Physical experiments with a Shadow Hand demonstrated successful zero-shot sim-to-real generalization on unseen physical objects.
AI.conclusion: OccluDex shows that integrating global geometric structure with local tactile contact information enables robust manipulation under dynamic self-occlusion, potentially supporting humanoid egocentric object manipulation for both seen and unseen objects despite robotic hand occlusion.

title: How Much Can Reliability Drift Under a Fixed Confidence Distribution?
summary: A classifier's conditional accuracy can change while its confidence distribution stays exactly the same. We study the worst-case movement of the reliability relation under covariate shifts that preserve the distribution of the confidence score, constraining the reweighting within each confidence level by a $χ^2$ budget; the resulting worst case, as a function of the budget, is a fragility profile. On an interval of budgets that can be computed from the source distribution, the profile equals exactly the square root of the budget times the within-level variance of the correctness propensity -- the grouping-loss term of calibration-refinement decompositions. Beyond this interval the profile is governed by the tails of the propensity law, and the entire upward profile determines the centred within-level law; consequently, calibration residual and grouping variance do not determine fragility in general, though they do when labels and predictions are deterministic. Since the propensity is not observed, we restrict reweightings to a learned finite readout within confidence bins, bound the part the restriction misses by the grouping variance remaining inside readout cells, estimate the restricted profile with role-separated labels, and provide a separate split-sample lower confidence bound. On ImageNet this bound is positive in both splits for four of six primary classifiers and nine of twelve additional ones as released, and for three of eighteen after temperature scaling. Held-out drift under optimised reweightings fitted without evaluation labels tracks the estimated profile; an exploratory label-permutation diagnostic yields near-zero agreement for this statistic while largely reproducing the correlation observed for unsigned random reweightings.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "fragility profiles": worst-case movements of the reliability relation under confidence-preserving covariate shifts constrained by a chi-squared reweighting budget, and provides an estimable, statistically valid bound for these profiles.
AI.motivation: A model's conditional accuracy (reliability relation) can degrade even when its confidence distribution is unchanged, so standard calibration diagnostics based on aggregate calibration residual and grouping variance may fail to capture worst-case fragility. The authors want to characterize and estimate how badly the reliability relation can move under distribution shifts that leave confidences intact.
AI.method: They define fragility as the worst-case movement of the reliability relation over within-confidence-level reweightings constrained by a chi-squared budget, yielding a budget-indexed fragility profile. They characterize it analytically: on a computable interval the profile equals sqrt(budget) * within-level variance of the correctness propensity (the grouping-loss term of calibration-refinement decompositions); outside it is governed by propensity tails; the upward profile determines the centered within-level law. Because the propensity is unobserved, they restrict reweightings to a learned finite readout within confidence bins, bound the missed part by within-cell grouping variance, estimate the restricted profile with role-separated labels, and add a split-sample lower confidence bound.
AI.result: On ImageNet, the split-sample lower confidence bound is positive in both splits for 4 of 6 primary classifiers and 9 of 12 additional classifiers as released, and for 3 of 18 after temperature scaling. Held-out drift under optimized reweightings fitted without evaluation labels tracks the estimated profile. An exploratory label-permutation diagnostic yields near-zero agreement for the fragility statistic while largely reproducing the correlation seen for unsigned random reweightings.
AI.conclusion: Calibration residual and grouping variance do not determine fragility in general, though they do when labels and predictions are deterministic; fragility captures a distinct, estimable worst-case sensitivity of the reliability relation. The proposed readout-based estimator with role-separated labels and a split-sample lower bound provides a practically viable, validated diagnostic, including under temperature scaling.

title: Make Code as Policy Great Again: Frontier Agents Write, Call, and Evolve Robot Tools
summary: Frontier models can control robots, but reasoning through every reach, grasp, and retreat makes manipulation slow and token-intensive. We revisit code as policy with a different division of labor: models build executable tools, code handles multi-phase motions, and models decide what to do next. We introduce URAI (Universal Robot-Agent Interface), which couples a programming agent that constructs robot tools with an execution agent that uses them in a feedback loop. The programming agent writes reusable and task-specific tools from task intent and refines them through execution feedback and human guidance. The execution agent selects and parameterizes these tools from current observations; each call runs a complete motion locally before returning control to the agent. Unlike delegating subsequent decisions to a generated program, this design retains model-level decision-making between tool executions. Validated tool revisions persist across episodes without updating foundation-model weights, and a shared GUI and API make the same tools available to humans and agents. Across five RoboDojo tasks and four frozen execution agents, URAI raises aggregate success from 18.0% to 53.0% relative to direct fingertip control, with the largest gain on Swap Blocks; with the same tools, a program written in advance reaches only 24% against 56% for two agents deciding after each call. Three of the four agents also finish episodes 1.3-1.5 times faster with 1.5-1.7 times fewer execution-agent output tokens; DeepSeek-V4-Flash's cost barely changes. We further evaluate URAI on seven real-world AgileX dual-arm tasks, spanning object manipulation, cloth folding, and human-interactive tic-tac-toe. URAI connects the coding and decision-making capabilities of frontier agents, organizing robot control around reusable tools that agents can both invoke and revise.

AI.tldr: URAI separates robot control into a programming agent that builds reusable executable tools and an execution agent that selects and parameterizes them, raising success across simulation and real dual-arm tasks while cutting tokens and time.
AI.motivation: Frontier models can control robots, but reasoning through every fine-grained motion (reach, grasp, retreat) makes manipulation slow and token-intensive. The paper seeks a more efficient division of labor for code-as-policy robot control.
AI.method: URAI (Universal Robot-Agent Interface) couples a programming agent, which writes reusable and task-specific robot tools from task intent and refines them via execution feedback and human guidance, with an execution agent that selects and parameterizes these tools from current observations. Each tool call executes a complete motion locally before returning control, preserving model-level decision-making between tool executions. Validated tool revisions persist across episodes without updating foundation-model weights, and a shared GUI and API expose the same tools to humans and agents.
AI.result: Across five RoboDojo tasks and four frozen execution agents, URAI raises aggregate success from 18.0% to 53.0% versus direct fingertip control, with the largest gain on Swap Blocks. With identical tools, a pre-written program reaches only 24% versus 56% for two agents deciding after each call. Three of four agents finish episodes 1.3-1.5x faster with 1.5-1.7x fewer execution-agent output tokens; DeepSeek-V4-Flash's cost barely changes. URAI is also evaluated on seven real-world AgileX dual-arm tasks spanning object manipulation, cloth folding, and human-interactive tic-tac-toe.
AI.conclusion: URAI connects the coding and decision-making capabilities of frontier agents, organizing robot control around reusable tools that agents can both invoke and revise, improving success, speed, and token efficiency in both simulated and real-world manipulation.

title: Prototype-guided Bilateral Alignment Multimodal Federated Learning
summary: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for leveraging distributed data to enhance model performance. However, existing methods predominantly rely on idealized assumptions of model homogeneity and balanced modality distributions, rendering them ill-suited for practical scenarios characterized by heterogeneous client architectures and severe modality imbalance. To address these challenges, we propose a \textbf{M}ultimodal \textbf{Fed}erated learning Prototype-guided Bilateral Alignment (MFedPBA) framework. MFedPBA facilitates robust knowledge synergy through a dual alignment mechanism: (i) at the feature level, it aligns heterogeneous feature spaces via a projection encoder optimized by contrastive learning and the Gromov-Wasserstein distance; (ii) at the decision level, it employs an entropy-weighted aggregation of naturally aligned logit prototypes. This novel design achieves robust MFL by jointly tackling heterogeneous feature spaces and collectively aggregating decisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under conditions of model heterogeneity and modality imbalance.

AI.tldr: MFedPBA is a multimodal federated learning framework that uses prototype-guided bilateral alignment to handle heterogeneous client architectures and modality imbalance.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal federated learning methods assume model homogeneity and balanced modality distributions, making them unsuitable for practical scenarios with heterogeneous client architectures and severe modality imbalance.
AI.method: MFedPBA employs a dual alignment mechanism: (i) feature-level alignment of heterogeneous feature spaces via a projection encoder optimized by contrastive learning and Gromov-Wasserstein distance; (ii) decision-level alignment via entropy-weighted aggregation of naturally aligned logit prototypes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that MFedPBA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under model heterogeneity and modality imbalance.
AI.conclusion: MFedPBA achieves robust multimodal federated learning by jointly tackling heterogeneous feature spaces and collectively aggregating decisions.

title: Looking Back to Move Forward: Temporal Verification for Generative Robot Policies
summary: Generative policies have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot learning, combining expressive generative action modeling with scalable imitation learning from large demonstration corpora. However, heterogeneous demonstrations can induce suboptimal action chunks whose errors compound over time, eventually driving the robot into out-of-distribution states from which recovery is difficult. Action verification offers a test-time scaling strategy for mitigating this failure mode by sampling multiple candidate actions and using a verifier to select one for execution. Existing approaches, however, remain temporally myopic and costly to train, evaluating candidates from the current observation alone without accounting for trajectory continuity and often relying on large verifiers and additional expert demonstrations. In this paper, we introduce Temporal Verification (TeV), an efficient temporally aware action verification framework for flow-matching VLAs. TeV first learns a temporal token that summarizes recent observation--action history, enabling candidate chunks to be evaluated as continuations of the execution trajectory rather than as isolated predictions. Conditioned on this token, TeV constructs positive--negative pairs without additional expert demonstrations or preference annotations and trains an energy-based verifier contrastively to assign lower energy to higher-quality, trajectory-consistent action chunks. Beyond post-hoc ranking, TeV further uses the learned energy landscape to guide intermediate flow samples toward lower-energy regions, improving candidates before final selection. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that TeV provides reliably ranks action candidates, improves task success rates, and produces smoother execution trajectories.

AI.tldr: TeV is a temporally aware action verification framework for flow-matching VLAs that learns a temporal token summarizing recent observation-action history, trains an energy-based verifier contrastively without extra expert data, and also guides intermediate flow samples toward lower-energy regions, improving success rates and trajectory smoothness in simulation and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Generative policies for robot learning suffer from heterogeneous demonstrations producing suboptimal action chunks whose errors compound, driving the robot into hard-to-recover out-of-distribution states. Existing action verification methods for test-time scaling are temporally myopic—evaluating candidates from the current observation alone—and costly to train, relying on large verifiers and additional expert demonstrations.
AI.method: TeV introduces a temporally aware action verification framework for flow-matching VLAs. It first learns a temporal token that summarizes recent observation-action history, so candidate chunks are evaluated as continuations of the execution trajectory rather than isolated predictions. Conditioned on this token, it constructs positive-negative pairs without additional expert demonstrations or preference annotations and contrastively trains an energy-based verifier to assign lower energy to higher-quality, trajectory-consistent action chunks. Beyond post-hoc ranking, TeV uses the learned energy landscape to guide intermediate flow samples toward lower-energy regions, refining candidates before final selection.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings show that TeV reliably ranks action candidates, improves task success rates, and produces smoother execution trajectories.
AI.conclusion: TeV addresses the temporal myopia and training cost of prior action verification by integrating temporal history awareness and energy-guided candidate refinement into flow-matching VLA policies, offering an efficient test-time scaling strategy for more robust and smoother robot execution.

title: Learning What to Forget: Distributional Unlearning for LLM Representation Spaces
summary: Machine learning systems increasingly face the need to remove the influence of entire data domains, such as toxic language, harmful behavior, or topical content, rather than isolated records. Recent work formalizes this problem as \emph{distributional unlearning}: selecting a subset of a forget domain whose removal moves the training distribution away from an unwanted population while preserving proximity to the desired one. However, existing analyses often impose parametric assumptions to obtain tractable selection rules. These assumptions may be poorly suited to high-dimensional language-model representations. We introduce \textsc{Mamushi}, a framework for non-parametric distributional unlearning that ranks forget examples using a probabilistic classifier whose Bayes-optimal logit equals the forget-to-retain log-density ratio (up to an additive class-prior constant). We show that thresholding the population log-density ratio yields the optimal fixed-budget selection rule for our removal--preservation objective and establish a non-asymptotic transfer guarantee relating score-estimation and threshold-calibration errors to degradation from the population-optimal selection rule. Our empirical evaluation spans real-world datasets on toxic-language removal and topical-domain removal regimes using different representations, with \textsc{Mamushi} achieving a more favorable removal--preservation trade-off than other baselines. Our work shows that \textsc{Mamushi} can serve as an efficient selection approach for downstream machine unlearning procedures, reducing the number of forget examples required to reach a fixed forgetting target.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mamushi, a non-parametric framework for distributional unlearning that ranks forget examples via a probabilistic classifier whose Bayes-optimal logit equals the forget-to-retain log-density ratio, achieving better removal–preservation trade-offs than existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Machine learning systems must often remove the influence of entire data domains (e.g., toxic language, harmful behavior, topical content) rather than isolated records. Prior work formalizes this as distributional unlearning but relies on parametric assumptions to derive tractable selection rules. These assumptions are ill-suited to high-dimensional language-model representations, motivating a more flexible, non-parametric approach.
AI.method: Mamushi ranks forget examples using a probabilistic classifier whose Bayes-optimal logit equals the forget-to-retain log-density ratio (up to an additive class-prior constant). The authors prove that thresholding the population log-density ratio yields the optimal fixed-budget selection rule for their removal–preservation objective, and derive a non-asymptotic transfer guarantee linking score-estimation and threshold-calibration errors to degradation relative to the population-optimal selection rule.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world toxic-language and topical-domain removal datasets, across different representations, shows Mamushi achieving a more favorable removal–preservation trade-off than competing baselines. It also reduces the number of forget examples needed to reach a fixed forgetting target.
AI.conclusion: Mamushi provides an efficient, theoretically grounded non-parametric selection method that can serve as a preprocessing step for downstream machine unlearning procedures, improving removal–preservation trade-offs and lowering data requirements for achieving fixed forgetting targets.

title: CLIPPER Beyond Shortlisting: Auditable Decision Support for Changing Municipal Micromobility Policies
comment: Author preprint. Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2nd ACM SIGSPATIAL International Workshop on Spatial Intelligence for Smart and Connected Communities (SpatialConnect 2026)
summary: In municipal planning workshops, planners and other stakeholders compare shared-micromobility parking policies by varying no-parking zones, retained sites, spacing, or area allocations. Each edit changes feasible sites and how much demand they cover, so the alternative must be reoptimized on the same spatial data. Full-set greedy, the transparent reference for this task, takes tens of seconds per alternative at city scale. We present Constraint-exact Low-latency Iterative Planning with Pooled Evaluation and Replay (CLIPPER), an optimizer with audit functions developed for requirements elicited with the City of Braunschweig. In each greedy round, it forms a deterministic candidate pool of bounded size, computes how much still-uncovered demand each candidate would add, and rejects candidates that violate an active constraint. An optional offline audit scans every remaining feasible candidate and records what the restricted pool omitted. We evaluate these functions on complete eleven-state edit chains ($E_0,\ldots,E_{10}$) in Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin. With $K=1024$ candidates per group, the fixed-width mode CLIPPER-F has mean coverage gaps to full-set greedy under the same policy of 0.245, 0.003, and 0.001 percentage points in Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin, respectively, while mean rollout time falls by factors of 13.6--28.9; no audited run terminates while a candidate outside the pool could still increase coverage. Plans computed from two checksummed versions of Braunschweig's official no-parking-zone data differ in 30 of about 540 selected sites although coverage moves by only about 0.1 percentage points. These changes still require municipal assessment and implementation. The findings inform a proposed municipal process that versions policy inputs, reports site changes beside coverage, and scans the full candidate set before a final decision.

AI.tldr: CLIPPER is a greedy optimizer with bounded candidate pools and optional audits that accelerates shared-micromobility parking policy comparison by 13.6–28.9× while keeping coverage gaps near 0.001–0.245 percentage points across three German cities.
AI.motivation: Municipal planning workshops require rapid reoptimization of shared-micromobility parking sites under frequently edited policy inputs (no-parking zones, retained sites, spacing, area allocations). Full-set greedy, the transparent baseline, is too slow at city scale (tens of seconds per alternative), and small input data differences can shift many selected sites even when coverage barely changes, complicating municipal decisions.
AI.method: CLIPPER (Constraint-exact Low-latency Iterative Planning with Pooled Evaluation and Replay) forms, in each greedy round, a deterministic bounded candidate pool, computes each candidate's added coverage of still-uncovered demand, and rejects constraint-violating candidates. An optional offline audit scans all remaining feasible candidates to record what the restricted pool omitted. Evaluation uses complete eleven-state edit chains (E0–E10) in Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin, with K=1024 candidates per group in fixed-width mode (CLIPPER-F), plus comparison of two checksummed versions of Braunschweig's official no-parking-zone data. Requirements were elicited with the City of Braunschweig.
AI.result: With K=1024, CLIPPER-F shows mean coverage gaps to full-set greedy under the same policy of 0.245, 0.003, and 0.001 percentage points in Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin, while mean rollout time drops by factors of 13.6–28.9. No audited run terminates while a candidate outside the pool could still increase coverage. The two checksummed Braunschweig datasets yield plans differing in 30 of about 540 selected sites, with coverage shifting only about 0.1 percentage points; these changes still require municipal assessment and implementation.
AI.conclusion: CLIPPER enables constraint-exact, low-latency policy comparison for micromobility parking at city scale with negligible coverage loss and large speedups, and its audits guarantee no missed coverage-improving candidates. The findings support a proposed municipal process that versions policy inputs, reports site changes alongside coverage, and scans the full candidate set before final decisions.

title: Routing Probes Can Improve Without New Information: An Exact-Null Audit of Uncertainty Beyond Model Outputs
summary: Routing signals of modern vision transformers -- expert gates, attention-residual weights and halting scores -- often improve probes that predict whether the model is correct, and the improvement is commonly read as evidence that routing carries information about errors beyond the model's outputs. We test this inference directly: keeping real output-routing pairs, we redraw correctness labels from a frozen output-only generator fitted on disjoint data, so that routing is uninformative by construction. Under this exact label null, a width-matched MLP comparison still reports a routing gain in 51.3% of confidence-only evaluations (308/600), while a linear comparison reports none. Holding each training trajectory fixed on a six-model panel and selecting the checkpoint by validation log loss instead of validation accuracy removes the detections (50/120 to 0/120, and 83/120 to 0/120 in an independently implemented probe), identifying accuracy-based checkpoint selection as the cause; across all output views the raw detection rate falls from 27.5% (528/1,920) to zero observed detections. The repaired comparison is not sensitive, detecting an implanted signal of about 0.005 nats in 0/20 replicates in each of two matched settings, whereas a conditional permutation test built on an estimated routing law detects it in 11/20 and 10/20 and rejects rarely under the null. On real correctness labels, the conditional analysis yields model-relative evidence in five DeiT attention-residual families; in four it persists under two specified variants of the conditional law, and no family passes an additional noise criterion. Fitting a better probe and testing for incremental information are different problems, and each needs its own validation.

AI.tldr: Apparent gains in correctness probes from routing signals can be artifacts of accuracy-based checkpoint selection; the paper identifies this cause and proposes a conditional permutation test.
AI.motivation: Routing signals (expert gates, attention-residual weights, halting scores) often improve probes predicting correctness, and this is commonly read as evidence that routing carries error information beyond the model's outputs. The paper tests whether this inference is valid.
AI.method: Keeping real output-routing pairs, correctness labels are redrawn from a frozen output-only generator fitted on disjoint data, making routing uninformative by construction. Comparisons (width-matched MLP vs. linear) are evaluated under this exact label null. A six-model panel holds each training trajectory fixed, and checkpoint selection uses validation log loss instead of validation accuracy. A conditional permutation test built on an estimated routing law is also proposed.
AI.result: Under the label null, the width-matched MLP reports a routing gain in 51.3% of confidence-only evaluations (308/600), while the linear comparison reports none. Loss-based checkpoint selection removes detections (50/120 to 0/120; 83/120 to 0/120 in an independent probe), identifying accuracy-based selection as the cause; raw detection rate falls from 27.5% (528/1,920) to zero observed. The repaired comparison is not sensitive (0/20 replicates for a ~0.005-nat implanted signal), whereas the conditional permutation test detects it in 11/20 and 10/20. On real labels, conditional analysis yields model-relative evidence in five DeiT attention-residual families; in four it persists under two variants of the conditional law, and no family passes an additional noise criterion.
AI.conclusion: Fitting a better probe and testing for incremental information are distinct problems, each requiring its own validation. Accuracy-based checkpoint selection drives spurious routing-gain detections.

title: SteerQuant: Steering Quantization Error with Action-Guided Scaling in World-Action Models
comment: Yunhan Wang and Haodong Wang contributed equally to this work
summary: World-action models (WAMs) jointly generate future world states and actions through iterative denoising, using shared weights to process heterogeneous semantic streams of video, proprioceptive, and action tokens. Quantization reduces inference cost, but comparable numerical errors in different streams can have markedly different effects on final actions, making numerical accuracy alone insufficient for reliable control. We introduce SteerQuant, a 4-bit quantization framework for WAMs that steers errors toward computations with less influence on final actions. It maps how each stream's quantization errors affect final actions and uses this map to guide shared channel scaling. Activation scaling is further calibrated for each stream and denoising step to accommodate changes in activation ranges and action impact. This adapts quantization to different stream requirements without duplicating weights or increasing bit-widths for selected streams. To reduce the extra kernel launches and memory traffic introduced by scaling, we develop Rudder, a 4-bit inference engine for WAMs that fuses scaling and output compensation into low-bit kernels. Under W4A8 and W4A4, SteerQuant maintains mean LIBERO success within 0.8 percentage points of full precision, while delivering up to $2.23\times$ denoising speedup over BF16 across three WAMs with reduced peak GPU memory usage. On a real dual-arm robot, W4A8 deployment achieves a $1.35\times$ end-to-end inference speedup while maintaining average task success relative to BF16.
