AI.tldr: SteerQuant is a 4-bit quantization framework for world-action models that steers quantization errors toward computations less influential on final actions, paired with Rudder, a fused 4-bit inference engine.
AI.motivation: WAMs jointly generate future states and actions via iterative denoising using shared weights over heterogeneous streams (video, proprioceptive, action tokens). Quantization cuts inference cost, but equal numerical errors in different streams affect final actions very differently, so numerical accuracy alone is insufficient for reliable control.
AI.method: SteerQuant maps how each stream's quantization errors affect final actions and uses this map to guide shared channel scaling. Activation scaling is calibrated per stream and per denoising step to handle changing activation ranges and action impact, adapting to stream-specific requirements without duplicating weights or raising bit-widths for selected streams. Rudder, a 4-bit inference engine, fuses scaling and output compensation into low-bit kernels to cut extra kernel launches and memory traffic.
AI.result: Under W4A8 and W4A4, SteerQuant keeps mean LIBERO success within 0.8 percentage points of full precision, with up to 2.23x denoising speedup over BF16 across three WAMs and reduced peak GPU memory. On a real dual-arm robot, W4A8 deployment yields a 1.35x end-to-end inference speedup while maintaining average task success versus BF16.
AI.conclusion: Error steering, rather than pure numerical accuracy, enables reliable 4-bit WAM inference; combined with fused low-bit kernels, it delivers substantial speed and memory gains without sacrificing control success.

title: Targeted Retrieval, Compact Representations: How CoT Reasoning Improves Long-Context Counting
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been rapidly improving in long-context tasks, powered by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, the internal mechanisms underlying this improvement remain unclear. We investigate these mechanisms through a needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) counting task, where an LLM is asked to count the number of records dispersed in a long text. Across twelve model comparison groups, Thinking (or reasoning) improves counting accuracy over Non-thinking, with pronounced gains at larger counts. This motivates our mechanistic analysis, which identifies two contrasting mechanisms: (i) broad retrieval, where Non-thinking models broadly attend to multiple needles; (ii) targeted retrieval, where Thinking models use enumeration in CoT traces to successively retrieve needles. Targeted retrieval concentrates attention on individual needles and is accompanied by more compact internal representations. Moreover, causal intervention analysis suggests that Thinking models use the CoT trace to maintain and update an internal counter as needles are successively retrieved, even without explicit numbering. In small controlled experiments, both retrieval mechanisms and counter states emerge under standard autoregressive training. Together, our results connect long-context retrieval with representation geometry of counting, supporting a state-tracking account of CoT reasoning.

AI.tldr: Thinking (CoT) improves long-context counting over Non-thinking by switching from broad retrieval to targeted, enumerated retrieval, which concentrates attention on individual needles and maintains an internal counter via the CoT trace.
AI.motivation: LLMs are rapidly improving at long-context tasks thanks to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet the internal mechanisms behind this improvement remain unclear. The authors seek to uncover these mechanisms.
AI.method: They use a needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) counting task requiring an LLM to count records dispersed in long text. They compare Thinking vs. Non-thinking across twelve model comparison groups and perform mechanistic analysis, including attention analysis, representational geometry, and causal intervention, supplemented by small controlled experiments under standard autoregressive training.
AI.result: Thinking improves counting accuracy over Non-thinking, with larger gains at higher counts. Two contrasting mechanisms emerge: broad retrieval (Non-thinking attends broadly to multiple needles) vs. targeted retrieval (Thinking uses enumeration in CoT traces to successively retrieve needles). Targeted retrieval concentrates attention on individual needles with more compact internal representations. Causal interventions suggest Thinking models use the CoT trace to maintain and update an internal counter as needles are successively retrieved, even without explicit numbering. Both retrieval mechanisms and counter states emerge under standard autoregressive training in small controlled experiments.
AI.conclusion: The results connect long-context retrieval with the representation geometry of counting, supporting a state-tracking account of CoT reasoning.

title: DiFF: Doppler-informed Flow Matching for Human Motion Flow
comment: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 2026. Code: https://github.com/keroseus/DiFF
summary: Perceiving human motion via privacy-preserving 4D millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is critical for next-generation human-robot interaction (HRI), where point cloud scene flow serves as a foundational motion representation. Yet the extreme sparsity and noise of 4D radar point clouds make non-rigid motion flow estimation severely ill-posed--a challenge that existing rigid-centric methods and prior works fail to adequately address, largely because they neglect the rich Doppler velocity cues inherent in 4D radar. We propose DiFF, a generative framework that marries Doppler-informed motion priors with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN)-based conditional flow matching model. At its core, a KAN-attention mechanism enables expressive feature extraction, while a prior-guided generative process harnesses Doppler cues to regularize the ill-posed solution space. Extensive experiments show that DiFF achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across diverse real-world datasets, reducing 3D endpoint error to the millimeter scale on the mmBody benchmark.

AI.tldr: DiFF is a generative framework that fuses Doppler-informed priors with a KAN-based conditional flow matching model to estimate non-rigid 4D mmWave radar scene flow, achieving SOTA accuracy (millimeter-scale 3D endpoint error on mmBody).
AI.motivation: 4D mmWave radar enables privacy-preserving motion perception for next-generation human-robot interaction, where point cloud scene flow is a foundational motion representation. However, the extreme sparsity and noise of 4D radar point clouds make non-rigid motion flow estimation severely ill-posed. Existing rigid-centric methods and prior works inadequately address this because they neglect the rich Doppler velocity cues inherent in 4D radar.
AI.method: DiFF is a generative framework combining Doppler-informed motion priors with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN)-based conditional flow matching model. A KAN-attention mechanism performs expressive feature extraction, and a prior-guided generative process leverages Doppler cues to regularize the ill-posed solution space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate SOTA performance across diverse real-world datasets, with 3D endpoint error reduced to millimeter scale on the mmBody benchmark.
AI.conclusion: By integrating Doppler-informed priors with KAN-based conditional flow matching, DiFF effectively resolves the ill-posedness of non-rigid scene flow estimation on sparse, noisy 4D radar point clouds, establishing a new SOTA for this task.

title: Alleviating Hallucination in Reasoning Tasks with Training-Free Uncertainty-Guided Steering
summary: Recent work on hallucination detection in large language models has shown that, for a fixed pre-trained model and reasoning task, it is possible to estimate the model's confidence in the correctness of its outputs. Such uncertainty estimates have primarily been used to improve truthfulness by detecting or filtering confabulations. In this work, we ask whether these signals can instead be used more proactively to directly improve the accuracy of model-generated answers. We propose USteer, a simple, training-free steering mechanism that adjusts a model's layer-wise activations during inference using the gradient of a confidence measure with respect to the activations. This procedure nudges generation toward outputs with lower uncertainty at inference time, without modifying model parameters or requiring additional supervision. We show that this approach consistently reduces hallucination across a range of tasks, demonstrating that confidence signals can be leveraged not only for detection, but also for effective inference-time control of model behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes USteer, a training-free inference-time steering method that uses the gradient of a confidence measure w.r.t. layer-wise activations to actively reduce hallucinations in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Prior work on hallucination detection estimates model confidence, but such uncertainty signals are used mainly reactively—to detect or filter confabulations. The authors ask whether these signals can be used more proactively to directly improve the accuracy of model-generated answers.
AI.method: USteer is a simple, training-free steering mechanism that adjusts a model's layer-wise activations during inference using the gradient of a confidence measure with respect to the activations. It nudges generation toward lower-uncertainty outputs without modifying model parameters or requiring additional supervision.
AI.result: The approach consistently reduces hallucination across a range of tasks.
AI.conclusion: Confidence signals can be leveraged not only for detection, but also for effective inference-time control of model behavior.

title: Occlusion-Aware, Quasi-Static, Stability-Oriented Trajectory Planning on Uneven Terrain
summary: Autonomous navigation in unstructured off-road environments requires reasoning about both vehicle--terrain interaction and environmental unknowns. We propose a model-based framework for generating quasi-static, stability-oriented reference trajectories for rigid, non-articulated four-wheeled vehicles on highly uneven terrain. Our work makes three primary contributions. First, we model blind spots caused by terrain occlusion as coverage-induced epistemic uncertainty in a fixed-feature Fourier terrain representation, quantified through a regularized inverse-Hessian estimate. Second, we propagate this uncertainty through the Nonlinear Least-Squares (NLS) pose/contact model using implicit differentiation and incorporate the resulting pose, contact-point, and per-wheel surface-normal uncertainty terms into trajectory optimization based on the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM). Third, we introduce a Flow Matching model that warm-starts terrain fitting, and we evaluate its fitting-accuracy--latency trade-off while retaining model-based refinement. Across six synthetic terrains with 30 matched start--goal pairs per terrain, the complete framework produced an observed failure rate of 18.9%, compared with 46.1% and 41.7% for two representative baselines and 34.4% for an ablation that removed the propagated-uncertainty scoring. Hardware evaluations span six distinct outdoor environments, with two representative executions presented in the paper and four additional executions included in the supplementary video. The evaluation also reports the accuracy--latency trade-off for the Flow Matching warm start.

AI.tldr: A model-based framework generates quasi-static, stability-oriented reference trajectories for four-wheeled vehicles on uneven off-road terrain, modeling terrain-occlusion blind spots as coverage-induced epistemic uncertainty and propagating it through the pose/contact model into CEM-based trajectory optimization, with a Flow Matching warm start for terrain fitting.
AI.motivation: Autonomous navigation in unstructured off-road environments requires reasoning about both vehicle-terrain interaction and environmental unknowns. Existing approaches often neglect the uncertainty arising from terrain occlusion (blind spots), which affects stability-oriented trajectory generation on highly uneven terrain.
AI.method: Three contributions: (1) blind spots from terrain occlusion are modeled as coverage-induced epistemic uncertainty in a fixed-feature Fourier terrain representation, quantified via a regularized inverse-Hessian estimate; (2) this uncertainty is propagated through the Nonlinear Least-Squares pose/contact model using implicit differentiation, and the resulting pose, contact-point, and per-wheel surface-normal uncertainty terms are incorporated into CEM-based trajectory optimization; (3) a Flow Matching model warm-starts terrain fitting, with its fitting-accuracy-latency trade-off evaluated while retaining model-based refinement.
AI.result: Across six synthetic terrains with 30 matched start-goal pairs per terrain, the complete framework achieved an observed failure rate of 18.9%, versus 46.1% and 41.7% for two baselines and 34.4% for an ablation removing the propagated-uncertainty scoring. Hardware evaluations span six outdoor environments, with two representative executions in the paper and four in the supplementary video; the Flow Matching warm start's accuracy-latency trade-off is also reported.
AI.conclusion: Modeling and propagating occlusion-induced epistemic uncertainty into trajectory optimization substantially reduces navigation failure rates versus baselines and an ablation, and Flow Matching warm-starting offers a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off for terrain fitting.

title: When Order Matters: First-Speaker Bias and Mitigation through Personality in Sequential Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate (MAD) is often used to improve large language model (LLM) reasoning, but sequential debate is rarely a neutral aggregator of agents' opinions. We show that sequential MAD suffers from a pronounced first-speaker bias: agents disproportionately shape the final answer when they speak first. As a result, placing a stronger model after weaker ones can substantially offset its reasoning advantage. We then focus on the disadvantaged strong-agent-last setting and ask whether personality prompting can mitigate this imbalance. Drawing on the Big Five model, we study agreeableness and extraversion as behavioral interventions applied to either the strong or weak side. We find that their effects are trait-specific. Influence consistently shifts in the direction of lower agreeableness, and assigning low agreeableness to the stronger agent helps restore its lost influence and improves final accuracy. Extraversion, by contrast, produces less systematic changes in influence and accuracy, with its clearest effect appearing in agents' verbosity. These findings show that effective MAD design depends not only on model capability, but also on how speaking order and induced interaction behavior shape the debate process.

AI.tldr: Sequential multi-agent debate (MAD) exhibits a first-speaker bias that erodes the advantage of a stronger model placed later; personality prompting—specifically low agreeableness on the strong agent—can partially restore its influence and improve final accuracy.
AI.motivation: MAD is widely used to improve LLM reasoning, but sequential debate is not a neutral aggregation of opinions. The authors aim to expose the first-speaker bias and to test whether behavioral (personality) interventions can correct the resulting imbalance in the disadvantaged "strong-agent-last" setting.
AI.method: The authors first demonstrate first-speaker bias in sequential MAD, showing that speaking first disproportionately shapes the final answer and that placing a stronger model after weaker ones offsets its reasoning advantage. They then target the strong-agent-last setting and apply Big Five personality prompting, manipulating agreeableness and extraversion on either the strong or weak agent, and measure effects on influence, final accuracy, and verbosity.
AI.result: Effects are trait-specific. Influence consistently shifts toward lower agreeableness, and assigning low agreeableness to the stronger agent restores its lost influence and raises final accuracy. Extraversion yields less systematic changes in influence and accuracy, with its clearest effect on agents' verbosity.
AI.conclusion: Effective MAD design depends not only on model capability but also on speaking order and induced interaction behavior, which jointly shape the debate process and outcomes.

title: LBDU-VIO: Learned Bias Dynamics and Uncertainty for Visual-Inertial Odometry with Unreliable Vision
summary: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) for aerial robots relies on high rate inertial measurement unit (IMU) propagation between visual updates. However, conventional multi state constraint Kalman filters (MSCKFs) use random walk bias assumptions and fixed noise parameters, which can limit robustness when visual information is unreliable. To address this problem, we propose LBDU-VIO, a learning-augmented MSCKF with learned continuous time bias dynamics and an IMU uncertainty model. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) models continuous time bias dynamics to propagate the filter's bias states, replacing their random walk model. The IMU uncertainty model predicts motion adaptive measurement noise covariances for covariance propagation. Both models are trained with pose supervision without direct labels. Experiments on real world EuRoC and TUM-VI benchmarks show lower errors than representative visual-inertial baselines, including a 25.1% reduction in mean relative position error compared with S-MSCKF on EuRoC sequences with 10s visual outage.

AI.tldr: LBDU-VIO augments an MSCKF with a neural ODE for continuous-time IMU bias dynamics and a learned motion-adaptive IMU noise model, both trained via pose supervision, improving robustness during visual outages.
AI.motivation: Conventional multi-state constraint Kalman filters (MSCKFs) for aerial VIO rely on random-walk bias assumptions and fixed noise parameters, which limits robustness when visual information is unreliable.
AI.method: A learning-augmented MSCKF is proposed: a neural ODE models continuous-time bias dynamics to propagate the filter's bias states (replacing the random walk model), and an IMU uncertainty model predicts motion-adaptive measurement noise covariances for covariance propagation. Both models are trained with pose supervision, without direct bias/noise labels.
AI.result: On real-world EuRoC and TUM-VI benchmarks, lower errors are obtained than representative visual-inertial baselines, including a 25.1% reduction in mean relative position error versus S-MSCKF on EuRoC sequences with 10 s visual outage.
AI.conclusion: Learning continuous-time bias dynamics and motion-adaptive IMU uncertainty enhances MSCKF robustness and accuracy, particularly under visual degradation, offering a label-free, pose-supervised alternative to fixed random-walk bias and noise assumptions.

title: RealWorldShop: Benchmarking and Improving Conversational Shopping Agents in Real-World E-commerce
summary: Large language models are reshaping ecommerce from static recommenders into interactive shopping assistants, yet real-world shopping requires session-level decision support: users reveal and revise constraints, coordinate multiple goals, and expect product-grounded recommendations over a full conversation. Existing benchmarks are mostly outcome-oriented or execution-oriented, leaving this evolving decision process under-evaluated. We introduce REALWORLDSHOP, a benchmark built on 3.28M grounded products, structured shopping episodes, a profile-grounded and actioncontrolled user simulator, and role-play evaluation. Our analysis shows that current systems produce locally plausible responses but struggle with state tracking, constraint updating, and grounded convergence, especially under ambiguous intent, bundle, and multi-intent scenarios. We further propose REALSHOP_AGENT, an executable session-control framework with explicit state management, shopping-flow control, catalog-grounded retrieval, and runtime guards. Experiments show that REALSHOP_AGENT consistently outperforms strong baselines on REALWORLDSHOP.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces REALWORLDSHOP, a benchmark with 3.28M grounded products and structured shopping episodes for evaluating session-level decision support in interactive e-commerce assistants, and proposes REALSHOP_AGENT, an executable session-control framework that outperforms strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Large language models are transforming e-commerce from static recommenders into interactive shopping assistants, but real-world shopping requires session-level decision support where users reveal and revise constraints, coordinate multiple goals, and expect product-grounded recommendations across a full conversation. Existing benchmarks are mostly outcome-oriented or execution-oriented, leaving this evolving decision process under-evaluated.
AI.method: The authors build REALWORLDSHOP on 3.28M grounded products, structured shopping episodes, a profile-grounded and action-controlled user simulator, and role-play evaluation. They also propose REALSHOP_AGENT, an executable session-control framework featuring explicit state management, shopping-flow control, catalog-grounded retrieval, and runtime guards.
AI.result: Analysis shows that current systems produce locally plausible responses but struggle with state tracking, constraint updating, and grounded convergence, especially under ambiguous intent, bundle, and multi-intent scenarios. Experiments show that REALSHOP_AGENT consistently outperforms strong baselines on REALWORLDSHOP.
AI.conclusion: Session-level decision support remains a key challenge for interactive shopping assistants, and explicit session-control frameworks such as REALSHOP_AGENT offer a consistent improvement over strong baselines on the proposed REALWORLDSHOP benchmark.

title: Drape-Compatible Tool-Tip Localization for Hand-Held Laparoscopic Instruments via UWB Carrier-Phase Ranging and Trocar-Constrained Geometry
summary: A surgical robot policy needs to know where each instrument's working end sits relative to the camera and to the other instrument, yet a laparoscopic operation leaves only the endoscope video, and a draped instrument hides every optical path on itself. We estimate the tool tips from distances and an IMU alone. The distances are measured by ultra-wideband carrier phase between antenna nodes on the handle side of the instruments: one per hand-held instrument, one on the endoscope, all outside the sterile barrier. Take the endoscope antenna as the reference. The two instrument antennas carry six coordinates while the three pairs give three distances, so the problem is short by three, and averaging cannot close that gap because what is missing is information, not precision. Carrier phase adds one more unknown per pair, an integer that leaves distance fixed only modulo lambda/2 = 23.1 mm. The trocar settles both difficulties: each shaft passes through a port whose position is known and whose direction the on-board IMU measures, so its antenna keeps a single degree of freedom, the insertion depth. Two unknowns now face three distances -- two fix the depths and the third is left over, and that spare equation exposes a wrong integer or a wrong mounting offset instead of absorbing it. The same solve returns both tool tips in the endoscope frame, without the second carrier frequency that integer resolution usually needs, so the link never leaves a single PLL lock. In an 11-hole phantom among metal instruments the three distances hold sigma = 0.10-0.33 mm at 35-46 Hz, a sterile drape pressed onto the antennas leaves the link unchanged where an optical path would be blocked, and the logger was carried into a live rabbit appendectomy.

AI.tldr: Tool-tip localization for laparoscopic instruments is achieved using ultra-wideband carrier-phase distances plus IMU-measured trocar directions, resolving the underdetermined geometry without a second carrier frequency.
AI.motivation: A surgical robot must know each instrument's working end relative to the camera and the other instrument, but endoscope video is the only available view, and a draped instrument blocks all optical paths on itself. Optical tracking is therefore unavailable.
AI.method: Ultra-wideband carrier-phase distances are measured between antenna nodes on the handle side of two hand-held instruments and the endoscope, all outside the sterile barrier, with the endoscope antenna as reference. Two instrument antennas carry six coordinates while three antenna pairs give three distances, leaving three missing coordinates; carrier phase also adds an integer unknown per pair (distance fixed only modulo lambda/2 = 23.1 mm). The trocar resolves both: each shaft passes through a known port whose direction is measured by an on-board IMU, reducing each antenna to one degree of freedom (insertion depth). Two unknowns then face three distances, so two determine the depths and the spare equation flags a wrong integer or mounting offset. The same solve returns both tool tips in the endoscope frame.
AI.result: In an 11-hole phantom among metal instruments, the three distances hold sigma = 0.10-0.33 mm at 35-46 Hz. A sterile drape pressed onto the antennas leaves the link unchanged where an optical path would be blocked, and the logger was carried into a live rabbit appendectomy.
AI.conclusion: Tool tips can be estimated from distances and an IMU alone, without the second carrier frequency normally required for integer resolution, so the link never leaves a single PLL lock and remains robust under draping.

title: C-STRIDE: An Observation-Driven AI Digital Twin for Predicting Basin-Wide Flood Fields from Sparse Stream-Gauge Histories
summary: Emergency managers need to know where floodwater is, how deep it is, and how it will change over the coming hours across an entire river basin. During a flood, however, real-time measurements come from only a handful of stream gauges, and high-resolution hydrodynamic models are too costly to rerun each time new data arrive or to run as large ensembles. We present C-STRIDE, an observation-driven AI digital twin that turns short records from a few stream gauges, together with terrain and rainfall, into basin-wide maps of water depth and extends these predictions up to a day ahead. It is trained on simulations from a calibrated two-dimensional hydrodynamic model and needs no separate data-assimilation step. In the Des Plaines River basin near Chicago, six gauges inform predictions over 4.2 million 30-m grid cells. Terrain improves the predictions most, rainfall keeps errors from growing over longer horizons, and together they reduce errors by about 40% compared with gauge records alone. When future rainfall is known, errors remain near 15% one day ahead, compared with nearly 40% without rainfall. Given real instead of simulated gauge records, the model shifts its predictions toward the observed hydrographs at three of six gauges without retraining, and it runs about 150 times faster than the hydrodynamic model. These results show how sparse gauges, terrain, and rainfall can be combined into fast, continuously updated flood predictions, a step toward operational flood digital twins that still requires testing with real-time data and rainfall forecasts.

AI.tldr: C-STRIDE is an observation-driven AI digital twin that converts sparse stream-gauge records, terrain, and rainfall into basin-wide, 30-m water-depth maps and forecasts up to 24 hours ahead, running ~150× faster than a 2D hydrodynamic model.
AI.motivation: Flood managers need basin-wide, real-time knowledge of water location, depth, and evolution, but real-time observations come from only a few stream gauges, and high-resolution hydrodynamic models are too expensive to rerun for each new observation or to run as large ensembles. A fast, continuously updatable surrogate is therefore needed.
AI.method: C-STRIDE is trained on simulations from a calibrated 2D hydrodynamic model and maps short records from a few stream gauges plus terrain and rainfall to basin-wide water-depth fields, extending predictions up to one day ahead. It requires no separate data-assimilation step. It is evaluated in the Des Plaines River basin near Chicago, where six gauges inform 4.2 million 30-m grid cells.
AI.result: Terrain contributes most to prediction skill, rainfall prevents error growth at longer horizons, and together they cut errors by ~40% versus gauge records alone. With known future rainfall, error stays near 15% at one day ahead versus nearly 40% without rainfall. Given real instead of simulated gauges, the model shifts predictions toward observed hydrographs at three of six gauges without retraining, and runs ~150× faster than the hydrodynamic model.
AI.conclusion: Sparse gauges, terrain, and rainfall can be combined into fast, continuously updated basin-wide flood predictions, advancing toward operational flood digital twins, though validation with real-time data and rainfall forecasts remains necessary.

title: Blackout vs. Freeze: Analyzing Physical Failure Modes of VLAs under Camera Faults
summary: Unreliable visual inputs can harm task performance and cause potential physical safety risks for vision-language-action (VLA) models. We analyze how $π0.5$ and GR00T models act under input faults such as image blackouts and freezing. We find that blackout and freezing produce distinct physical failure modes even when task-success rates are similarly low: freezing causes more extreme joint behavior, whereas blackout after gripper closure can cause more object drops, most markedly without proprioception. Selective intervention studies reveal that proprioception (current robot state) partly compensates for the removed robot depictions and reduces non-target contact. However, it cannot sufficiently restore task success when wrist-view object information is removed, even when aided by the remaining scene view. We then evaluate two mitigation approaches: camera-blackout training and training-free replacement of faulty visual embeddings. Both improve task success in selected conditions, but can increase unintended contact or disturbance to surrounding objects. Real-robot trials further show that successful execution under camera faults can still involve unintended physical interactions. These findings motivate designing VLA policies that use the robot and object information still available under camera faults to limit hazardous motion.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how VLA models (π0.5 and GR00T) behave under visual input faults (blackout, freezing), showing distinct physical failure modes, the partial compensatory role of proprioception, and the trade-offs of two mitigation strategies.
AI.motivation: Unreliable visual inputs can degrade task performance and pose physical safety risks for vision-language-action models, yet the specific physical failure modes and the role of available modalities under such faults remain underexplored.
AI.method: Analyze π0.5 and GR00T behavior under blackout and freezing faults; compare failure modes (joint behavior, object drops); conduct selective intervention studies isolating proprioception and view contributions (wrist vs. scene); evaluate camera-blackout training and training-free replacement of faulty visual embeddings; validate with real-robot trials.
AI.result: Blackout and freezing produce distinct failure modes even at similarly low success rates: freezing yields more extreme joint behavior; blackout after gripper closure causes more object drops, most markedly without proprioception. Proprioception partially compensates for removed robot depictions and reduces non-target contact but cannot restore success when wrist-view object information is removed. Both mitigations improve success in selected conditions yet can increase unintended contact or disturbance. Real-robot trials confirm successful execution under camera faults can still involve unintended physical interactions.
AI.conclusion: VLA policies should be designed to exploit still-available robot and object information under camera faults to constrain hazardous motion, rather than relying solely on task-success metrics.

title: Search Shapes Conclusions: Auditing Evidence Selection Bias in Deep Research Agents
summary: Deep Research agents synthesize evidence into cited reports, yet a well-cited report can still reach a misleading conclusion. Citation correctness checks whether cited sources support individual claims. It does not show whether adaptive search exposed a representative view of all documents made available for evaluation, which we call the candidate pool. Early findings redirect later queries, document choices, and stopping, so the documents an agent reads form a selective sample. Existing evaluations rarely account for this selection. We formulate the problem as adaptive evidence sampling and introduce Causal Evidence Selection Correction (CESS). CESS predicts each candidate document's evidence direction and corrects the candidate-pool average using the logged probabilities of selecting each document and reaching each search round. Shrinkage stabilizes short searches, while intervals replace point estimates when some documents cannot be sampled. We also prove that estimating the average evidence direction of a common pool differs from measuring how a change in search policy alters the evidence read. The latter requires intervention. On questions from the MS2 systematic-review benchmark, CESS reduces mean absolute error against the candidate-pool average by $9.2\%$ and reduces the estimate's change under opposing document rankings by $39.4\%$ relative to averaging the evidence scores of documents read. Across trajectories from a public Open Deep Research agent, the corresponding reductions reach $60.1\%$ and $87.2\%$. A further 4,800 trajectories under paired interventions confirm that correcting a pool estimate and measuring a policy effect are different tasks. CESS therefore audits whether the evidence direction underlying a report reflects the documents available for evaluation, while a separate intervention analysis measures the effect of search decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates the selective sampling in Deep Research agents as "adaptive evidence sampling" and introduces CESS, a method that corrects candidate-pool evidence estimates using logged selection probabilities, reducing bias versus naively averaging read documents.
AI.motivation: Deep Research agents produce cited reports, but citation-correctness checks only verify whether individual sources support individual claims. They do not reveal whether the agent's adaptive search surfaced a representative view of the entire candidate pool. Because early findings redirect later queries, document choices, and stopping, the documents an agent reads constitute a selective sample, a selection bias existing evaluations rarely account for.
AI.method: The authors formalize the issue as adaptive evidence sampling and propose Causal Evidence Selection Correction (CESS). CESS predicts each candidate document's evidence direction and corrects the candidate-pool average using logged probabilities of selecting each document and reaching each search round. Shrinkage stabilizes short searches, and intervals replace point estimates when some documents are unsamplable. They also prove that estimating the average evidence direction of a common pool is a distinct task from measuring how a policy change alters the evidence read, the latter requiring intervention.
AI.result: On MS2 systematic-review benchmark questions, CESS cuts mean absolute error against the candidate-pool average by 9.2% and reduces the estimate's change under opposing document rankings by 39.4% versus averaging evidence scores of read documents. Across trajectories from a public Open Deep Research agent, reductions reach 60.1% and 87.2%. A further 4,800 trajectories under paired interventions confirm that correcting a pool estimate and measuring a policy effect are different tasks.
AI.conclusion: CESS audits whether the evidence direction underlying a report reflects the documents available for evaluation, whereas a separate intervention analysis is needed to measure the effect of search decisions. The work separates pool estimation from policy-effect measurement in adaptive evidence sampling.

title: Linear Recurrent Memory Suffices to Distil a World-Model Policy for Robot Air Hockey
summary: Does memory-dependent control need nonlinear recurrent dynamics? We study simulated air-hockey defence under temporary loss of puck tracking. A DreamerV3 teacher outperforms a memoryless policy under tracking loss, while resetting the teacher's recurrent state sharply reduces performance, which demonstrates that the task requires memory. We distil this teacher into compact recurrent policies with a 64 dimensional state, with a combination of a diagonal linear recurrence and an optional rank-$k$ nonlinear innovation while retaining nonlinear observation encoders and action heads. Across five matched seeds, the purely linear recurrent model ($k=0$) matches both the GRU baseline and the teacher throughout the tested range of tracking loss. Increasing nonlinear innovation rank providing no measured benefits. This result is obtained on a fresh test split, which will be only opened after all models and analyses are frozen. The linear model requires fewer recurrent parameters and less computation than GRU, but performs comparably. These results suggest that, for this memory dependent control task, nonlinear representation learning around a simple linear memory mechanism can be sufficient, and that nonlinear recurrent dynamics are not necessarily required. These conclusions are limited to the simulated task, teacher, state dimension, and blackout horizon considered here, and to policies whose observation encoder and action head remain nonlinear.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether memory-dependent control requires nonlinear recurrent dynamics, using simulated air-hockey defence under temporary puck-tracking loss. Distilling a DreamerV3 teacher into compact recurrent policies shows that a purely linear recurrence (k=0) matches both a GRU baseline and the teacher, with nonlinear innovation providing no measurable benefit.
AI.motivation: The central question is whether memory-dependent control genuinely needs nonlinear recurrent dynamics, or whether a simple linear memory mechanism combined with nonlinear representation learning elsewhere suffices. The task requires memory, as demonstrated by the teacher's performance drop when its recurrent state is reset, making it a valid testbed for this question.
AI.method: Simulated air-hockey defence is studied under temporary loss of puck tracking. A DreamerV3 teacher, shown to outperform a memoryless policy under tracking loss, is distilled into compact recurrent policies with a 64-dimensional state. These policies combine a diagonal linear recurrence with an optional rank-k nonlinear innovation, while retaining nonlinear observation encoders and action heads. Evaluation spans five matched seeds and a range of tracking-loss conditions, with a fresh test split opened only after all models and analyses are frozen.
AI.result: Across five matched seeds, the purely linear recurrent model (k=0) matches both the GRU baseline and the teacher throughout the tested range of tracking loss. Increasing the nonlinear innovation rank yields no measured benefits. The linear model requires fewer recurrent parameters and less computation than GRU yet performs comparably.
AI.conclusion: For this memory-dependent control task, nonlinear representation learning around a simple linear memory mechanism can be sufficient, and nonlinear recurrent dynamics are not necessarily required. These conclusions are limited to the simulated task, teacher, state dimension, and blackout horizon considered, and to policies whose observation encoder and action head remain nonlinear.

title: Multi-LLM Collaborative Alignment via Stackelberg Games
summary: A pool of language models can collaborate and improve collectively by learning from one another's responses. These interactions depend on the instructions used during training. Existing methods typically sample instructions uniformly, even though their usefulness may change as the models improve: an instruction on which models' responses once differed in quality may later be answered equally well, while a previously difficult instruction may begin to provide a useful learning signal. We propose Stackelberg Alignment, a game-theory-inspired leader-follower framework that turns instruction selection into an adaptive curriculum. An EXP3 bandit acts as the leader, allocating a fixed sampling budget across instructions and updating its sampling distribution using a reward that combines instruction difficulty and response discriminability. The language models act as followers: they respond to the selected instructions, evaluate one another's responses, and learn from the resulting preference signals through DPO or GRPO. The framework uses Elo-style reputation-weighted peer judgment and reputation-based opponent matching to support reliable and competitive model interactions. Experiments across three heterogeneous model pools and 12 benchmarks spanning scientific discovery, reasoning, code, instruction following, and knowledge show that Stackelberg Alignment achieves the highest macro-average across three diverse model pools, outperforming the strongest training-time baseline by up to 7.4% and the best static inference baseline by 12-25%. Analysis confirms that the adaptive leader concentrates duels on the most informative instructions, and ablations show that both reputation-weighted judgment and reputation-based matching improve the effectiveness of multi-LLM evolution.

AI.tldr: Stackelberg Alignment is a leader-follower framework that adaptively selects training instructions for collaborative multi-LLM improvement, beating baselines by up to 7.4%.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-LLM collaboration methods sample instructions uniformly, ignoring that instruction usefulness shifts as models improve; instructions once discriminative may become trivial, while harder ones may later yield useful signals.
AI.method: A game-theory-inspired leader-follower (Stackelberg) design: an EXP3 bandit leader allocates a fixed sampling budget across instructions, updating its distribution via a reward combining instruction difficulty and response discriminability; language models act as followers responding to selected instructions, evaluating peers, and learning via DPO or GRPO. Includes Elo-style reputation-weighted peer judgment and reputation-based opponent matching.
AI.result: Across three heterogeneous model pools and 12 benchmarks (scientific discovery, reasoning, code, instruction following, knowledge), Stackelberg Alignment achieves the highest macro-average, outperforming the strongest training-time baseline by up to 7.4% and the best static inference baseline by 12-25%.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive leader concentrates duels on the most informative instructions, and ablations confirm that both reputation-weighted judgment and reputation-based matching improve multi-LLM evolution effectiveness.

title: Concurrent Semantic Search and Mission Execution for LTL Missions in Unknown Environments
summary:
Planning complex missions in unknown environments requires robots to reason simultaneously about what they should do and what they still need to discover. Existing approaches for solving LTLf missions typically assume a known environment, or separate the exploration of the environment from the execution of the mission, while semantic exploration methods look for one target at a time and ignore the mission being executed.
  To fill this gap, our main contribution is an adaptive high-level planning method that interleaves a task-driven semantic search with the execution of the mission, advancing both in a non-myopic manner.
  Our method leverages two representations built online, a metric-semantic scene graph, built with a Vision Language Model (VLM), that provides the evidence needed to locate the objects the mission refers to, and the deterministic finite automaton (DFA) encoding the mission, that indicates which of them matter at each mission state. At every planning stage, our planner selects the waypoints that are most valuable for both the semantic search and the advancement of the mission, valuing them over the remaining mission stages in order to avoid blocking states. The selected waypoints are then ordered in a single high-level plan, which is recomputed as new information arrives.
  In photorealistic indoor environments over five mission types, our method completes more missions than the compared approaches while having to cover less of the environment, and it does so with shorter paths and complying with the restrictions imposed by the mission.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive high-level planning method that interleaves task-driven semantic search with LTLf mission execution, using an online metric-semantic scene graph and a DFA encoding of the mission to select and order waypoints non-myopically, outperforming baselines in photorealistic indoor environments.
AI.motivation: Robots operating in unknown environments must simultaneously decide what to do and what to discover. Existing LTLf approaches either assume a known environment or decouple exploration from mission execution, while semantic exploration methods target one object at a time and ignore the mission, leaving a gap the paper aims to fill.
AI.method: The method interleaves task-driven semantic search with mission execution. It builds two online representations: a metric-semantic scene graph from a Vision Language Model, supplying evidence to locate mission-referenced objects, and a DFA encoding the mission, indicating which objects matter at each mission state. At each planning stage, the planner selects waypoints most valuable for both semantic search and mission advancement, valuing them over remaining mission stages to avoid blocking states, and orders them into a single high-level plan recomputed as new information arrives.
AI.result: Across five mission types in photorealistic indoor environments, the method completes more missions than compared approaches while covering less of the environment, using shorter paths and complying with mission-imposed restrictions.
AI.conclusion: Interleaving non-myopic, task-driven semantic search with LTLf mission execution via online scene graph and DFA representations yields more complete, more efficient, and constraint-compliant mission execution in unknown environments.

title: Beyond Prediction: Steering VLM Agents with Retrospective World Modeling
summary: Equipping VLM agents with world modeling capabilities has shown strong potential for complex reasoning and long-horizon planning, while reducing the dependence of policy learning on costly real-world interactions. Existing methods mainly rely on prospective simulation to predict the consequences of candidate actions. However, this forward-only paradigm focuses on what will happen next and provides limited constraints for verifying whether an action is causally consistent with the observed state transition, which can lead to plausible-looking but physically incoherent behaviors. In this paper, we challenge the view of world modeling as only prospective prediction and introduce Retrospective World Modeling, a new agent learning paradigm that enables agents to reason backward by estimating the retrospective attribution distribution $P(\hat{a}{t}|s_t, s{t+1})$ for the action that most likely caused a given transition. Based on this capability, we formulate the Self-Consistency Reward (SCR), an intrinsic signal that measures the probabilistic consistency between the policy action and the retrospective explanation. Integrating SCR into reinforcement learning provides dense transition-level feedback and steers agents toward behaviors that are both task-effective and physically grounded. Extensive experiments across diverse agentic tasks show that our method substantially improves policy robustness and generalization over prospective-only world modeling baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Retrospective World Modeling, letting VLM agents infer the action most likely to have caused an observed state transition, and uses this as a Self-Consistency Reward in RL to produce more physically grounded, robust, and generalizable behavior than prospective-only world modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM agent methods rely on prospective simulation to predict consequences of candidate actions. This forward-only paradigm focuses on what happens next and offers limited constraints for verifying whether an action is causally consistent with the observed state transition, leading to plausible-looking but physically incoherent behaviors. The authors challenge the view of world modeling as only prospective prediction.
AI.method: They propose Retrospective World Modeling, an agent learning paradigm enabling agents to reason backward by estimating the retrospective attribution distribution P(â_t | s_t, s_{t+1}) for the action that most likely caused a given transition. Based on this, they formulate the Self-Consistency Reward (SCR), an intrinsic signal measuring the probabilistic consistency between the policy action and the retrospective explanation. SCR is integrated into reinforcement learning to provide dense transition-level feedback.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse agentic tasks show that the method substantially improves policy robustness and generalization over prospective-only world modeling baselines.
AI.conclusion: Retrospective world modeling complements prospective prediction, and the Self-Consistency Reward steers agents toward behaviors that are both task-effective and physically grounded, reducing the need for costly real-world interactions.

title: Exploiting Vulnerabilities: Universal Adversarial Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models in Robotics
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2026), Vienna, Austria. 8 pages. (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes
summary: Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have revolutionized robotic manipulation by seamlessly integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation in an end-to-end learning framework. However, since these models are designed to interact directly with the physical world and humans, their security is critical, and even small vulnerabilities can lead to catastrophic failures. In this work, we propose the Universal Adversarial Object, a sphere with optimized surface texture that significantly degrades task success rates when placed within the robot's field of view. Specifically, our approach introduces a multi-level attack framework that jointly disrupts trajectory planning, task execution, and action control. We validate our method in both simulated and real-world robotic settings. Experimental results demonstrate that the adversarial object reduces the average task success rates by 31.2%-39.9% for two representative VLA models (Pi0 and RDT), with success rates dropping to near zero in complex scenarios. Index Terms--Vision-Language-Action models, adversarial attack, robotic security, universal adversarial object

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a "Universal Adversarial Object"—a sphere with an optimized surface texture that, when placed in a robot's field of view, severely degrades the success rates of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models via a multi-level attack framework.
AI.motivation: VLA models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation for robotic manipulation but interact directly with the physical world and humans, making their security critical—even small vulnerabilities can cause catastrophic failures. This motivates the study of adversarial threats against VLA-based robots.
AI.method: The authors design a sphere with an optimized surface texture serving as a universal adversarial object, and introduce a multi-level attack framework that jointly disrupts trajectory planning, task execution, and action control. The method is validated in both simulated and real-world robotic settings.
AI.result: The adversarial object reduces average task success rates by 31.2%–39.9% for two representative VLA models (Pi0 and RDT), with success rates dropping to near zero in complex scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The universal adversarial object constitutes a potent physical-world threat to VLA-based robotic manipulation, demonstrating the need for robust defenses in VLA systems deployed in real environments.

title: Reserve-Aware Contrast Certificates for Conservative Bandits with Uncertain Baselines
summary: Conservative bandits must improve an incumbent policy without exhausting a prescribed performance budget. When the incumbent is uncertain, separately bounding candidate and baseline rewards can charge twice for shared estimation error. We develop Reserve-C4B around the baseline-relative contrast itself. A shared confidence set yields an exact expression for this avoidable penalty and a tighter admissibility test at every fixed history. A reserve ledger separates statistical evidence from permitted performance deficit; a prefix-refresh extension recertifies accumulated decisions under the current confidence set without discarding previously certified credit. For linear rewards, self-normalized confidence sets provide simultaneous validity over time and adaptively generated candidates, and the resulting policy satisfies a conditional-mean performance constraint with high probability. Reproducible experiments isolate certificate coupling, prefix refresh, and historical information, showing large reductions in baseline fallback while exposing the limitations of frozen certificates.

AI.tldr: We develop Reserve-C4B, a conservative bandit policy built around the baseline-relative contrast, using a shared confidence set, reserve ledger, and prefix-refresh mechanism with self-normalized confidence sets, achieving a high-probability conditional-mean performance constraint and large reductions in baseline fallback.
AI.motivation: Conservative bandits must improve an incumbent policy without exhausting a prescribed performance budget. However, when the incumbent is uncertain, separately bounding candidate and baseline rewards can charge twice for shared estimation error.
AI.method: Reserve-C4B centers on the baseline-relative contrast itself. A shared confidence set yields an exact expression for the avoidable penalty and a tighter admissibility test at every fixed history. A reserve ledger separates statistical evidence from permitted performance deficit. A prefix-refresh extension recertifies accumulated decisions under the current confidence set without discarding previously certified credit. For linear rewards, self-normalized confidence sets provide simultaneous validity over time and adaptively generated candidates.
AI.result: The resulting policy satisfies a conditional-mean performance constraint with high probability. Reproducible experiments isolate certificate coupling, prefix refresh, and historical information, showing large reductions in baseline fallback while exposing the limitations of frozen certificates.
AI.conclusion: By formulating around the baseline-relative contrast with shared confidence sets, reserve ledgers, and prefix refresh, Reserve-C4B removes double-charging of shared estimation error, maintains a high-probability conditional-mean performance constraint, and substantially reduces baseline fallback, though frozen certificates remain a limitation.

title: LocoWM: High-Precision Locomotion through World-Model-Guided Residual Adaptation
summary: High-precision locomotion combines motion-command tracking with precise regulation of task-relevant physical states, enabling robots to interact reliably with their surroundings during motion. Joint end-to-end optimization can leave precision objectives insufficiently optimized, while reactive residual control adjusts actions only after deviations become observable. We present \textbf{LocoWM}, a world-model-guided preactive residual adaptation framework for high-precision locomotion. A base policy provides command-following locomotion, while an action-conditioned world model predicts a sequence of future physical states from proprioceptive history and the proposed base action. A residual adapter conditions on this predicted sequence to generate additive action corrections that compensate for anticipated deviations. Two-stage training first learns locomotion and action-conditioned dynamics, then freezes both modules while training the adapter, separating locomotion acquisition from precision adaptation. Experiments spanning terrain leveling, acceleration compensation, and push recovery demonstrate improved control precision and disturbance robustness over end-to-end and reactive residual baselines. Demos and code are available at: https://zhaozijie2022.github.io/LocoWM

AI.tldr: LocoWM is a world-model-guided preactive residual adaptation framework that improves high-precision locomotion by predicting future physical states and generating additive action corrections in advance.
AI.motivation: End-to-end optimization can under-optimize precision objectives, and reactive residual control only adjusts actions after deviations are observable, limiting precision for high-precision locomotion tasks.
AI.method: A base policy performs command-following locomotion; an action-conditioned world model predicts future physical states from proprioceptive history and proposed base actions; a residual adapter conditions on the predicted state sequence to output additive action corrections. Two-stage training first learns locomotion and action-conditioned dynamics, then freezes both modules and trains the adapter.
AI.result: Experiments on terrain leveling, acceleration compensation, and push recovery show improved control precision and disturbance robustness over end-to-end and reactive residual baselines.
AI.conclusion: Separating locomotion acquisition from precision adaptation via world-model-based preactive residual adaptation yields more precise and robust locomotion, with demos and code released.

title: MASCRDM: Multi-Agent System for Compliance Risk Detection and Mitigation in Training Process of Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been applied in various fields. However, ensuring compliance and safety of LLMs, such as avoiding discrimination and bias, still remains a challenge. Current efforts mainly focus on detecting and filtering inputs and outputs of the trained models, rather than studying the intrinsic architecture of the models in real-time. To tackle this challenge, we analyze the LLMs training process and discover two critical issues: 1) Most of the existing methods are predominantly static in their approach to detection and filtering, achieving only localized optimizations without systematically enhancing the compliance of LLMs. 2) Another issue with existing approaches is the lack of real-time risk detection and mitigation across the full training process, which leads to limited flexibility. Motivated by these, we propose MASCRDM (Multi-Agent System for Compliance Risk Detection and Mitigation) during the LLM training process. Firstly, we develop a set of compliance rules based on existing Artificial Intelligence (AI) laws and a compliance-specific LLM with the instruction of compliance law experts. Then, we deconstruct LLMs into several components and identify key nodes based on the compliance knowledge graph. During LLMs training, we implement our multiple agents in the whole process, giving compliance risk alerts and suggestions for LLM developers. Experiments on discrimination and bias benchmark demonstrate that our multi-agent system can effectively improve the compliance while maintaining reasonable semantic performance. The results indicate that our method provides an executable path for mitigating compliance risk from within the LLMs systematically.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MASCRDM, a multi-agent system that detects and mitigates LLM compliance risks in real-time throughout the training process, improving compliance on discrimination and bias benchmarks while preserving sensible semantic performance.
AI.motivation: Ensuring LLM compliance and safety (e.g., avoiding discrimination and bias) remains challenging. Existing efforts mainly detect and filter inputs/outputs of trained models rather than studying the intrinsic architecture in real-time, resulting in two issues: (1) detection/filtering is mostly static, achieving only localized optimizations without systematically enhancing compliance; (2) there is a lack of real-time risk detection and mitigation across the full training process, leading to limited flexibility.
AI.method: MASCRDM (Multi-Agent System for Compliance Risk Detection and Mitigation) operates during LLM training. It first develops a set of compliance rules based on existing AI laws and a compliance-specific LLM instructed by compliance law experts. It then deconstructs LLMs into several components and identifies key nodes based on a compliance knowledge graph. Multiple agents are implemented across the whole training process to provide compliance risk alerts and suggestions to LLM developers.
AI.result: Experiments on discrimination and bias benchmarks demonstrate that the multi-agent system effectively improves compliance while maintaining reasonable semantic performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method provides an executable path for mitigating compliance risk from within the LLMs systematically.

title: DSDyn-VLA: A Dual-Stream Dynamic Manipulation Framework with Motion Perception, Future Awareness, and Realtime Correction
summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in static tasks, they struggle in dynamic environments where objects are in motion (e.g., conveyor belt manipulation). We identify three fundamental limitations hindering current VLAs in these scenarios: the \textbf{perception gap}, where static visual inputs lack temporal motion cues; the \textbf{latency gap}, where inference delays render actions obsolete; and the \textbf{control gap}, caused by the open-loop action chunk execution without real-time adjustment. In this work, we propose \textbf{DSDyn-VLA}, a Slow-Fast \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{S}tream \textbf{Dyn}amic manipulation framework that integrates motion-aware foresighted planning with real-time residual correction. The slow \textbf{Flow-Planner} serves as a macro-planner. By enhancing the VLA with optical flow for temporal perception and a future state awareness mechanism to preemptively offset inference latency, it produces globally consistent, motion-aware action chunks. Complementing this, the fast \textbf{Res-Refiner} employs a lightweight RL policy to inject high-frequency, closed-loop corrections into the planned action chunks based on real-time observations. In addition, we introduce \textbf{DynBench}, a MuJoCo-based benchmark for dynamic object manipulation that comprises nine tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DSDyn-VLA reduces the failure rate by over 76\% compared to current SOTA method in high-latency setting on the Kinetix dynamic benchmark, while achieving about 6$\times$ the success rate of PI0.5 in real-world dynamic settings and about 5$\times$ on DynBench. We will open-source all the code and weights.

AI.tldr: DSDyn-VLA is a Slow-Fast Dual-Stream framework for dynamic manipulation that combines motion-aware foresighted planning with real-time residual correction, reducing failure rates by over 76% and improving success rates substantially over baselines like PI0.5.
AI.motivation: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in static tasks but struggle in dynamic environments with moving objects (e.g., conveyor belt manipulation). The authors identify three fundamental limitations: the perception gap (static visual inputs lack temporal motion cues), the latency gap (inference delays render actions obsolete), and the control gap (open-loop action chunk execution without real-time adjustment).
AI.method: A Slow-Fast Dual-Stream Dynamic manipulation framework integrating motion-aware foresighted planning with real-time residual correction. The slow Flow-Planner acts as a macro-planner, enhancing the VLA with optical flow for temporal perception and a future state awareness mechanism to preemptively offset inference latency, producing globally consistent motion-aware action chunks. The fast Res-Refiner uses a lightweight RL policy to inject high-frequency closed-loop corrections into planned action chunks from real-time observations. A MuJoCo-based benchmark, DynBench, with nine tasks is also introduced.
AI.result: DSDyn-VLA reduces the failure rate by over 76% compared to current SOTA in a high-latency setting on the Kinetix dynamic benchmark, achieves about 6x the success rate of PI0.5 in real-world dynamic settings, and about 5x on DynBench.
AI.conclusion: DSDyn-VLA effectively addresses perception, latency, and control gaps to enable robust dynamic object manipulation, with code and weights to be open-sourced.

title: BELIEFRAG: Making Adaptive RAG State-Aware under Evolving Evidence
summary: Adaptive RAG uses signals such as confidence, relevance, support, and retrieval quality to decide when to search or correct evidence. In multi-step retrieval, however, these local signals must be combined into a persistent view of what the current evidence supports, what remains missing, and which action should follow. Existing methods often use such signals as separate triggers, making it difficult to preserve a coherent evidence state across a trajectory; we call this problem evidence-state fragmentation. We introduce BELIEFRAG, a closed-loop controller that updates an explicit state over sufficiency, reliability, conflict, uncertainty, evidence gaps, and acquisition cost, then chooses among retrieval, query rewriting, verification, answering, stopping, and abstention. Across six QA benchmarks with gpt-oss-120b, BELIEFRAG reaches mean token F1 0.572 with 3.89k tokens per question, outperforming fixed iterative retrieval (0.555 F1) while using 39% fewer tokens. The same quality-cost pattern transfers to Qwen3-32B, where BELIEFRAG reaches 0.552 F1 versus 0.523 for iterative retrieval while using 35% fewer tokens. Analysis shows that the main gains come from corrective re-retrieval rather than pruning alone, while several belief dimensions are redundant and calibrated answerability plays the strongest operational role. Calibration improves threshold stability across related evidence sources, although source shift can still invalidate the same decision signal.

AI.tldr: BELIEFRAG is a closed-loop Adaptive RAG controller that maintains an explicit belief state (sufficiency, reliability, conflict, uncertainty, evidence gaps, acquisition cost) to decide among retrieval, rewriting, verification, answering, stopping, or abstention, avoiding evidence-state fragmentation across multi-step retrieval. It improves F1 while cutting token usage.
AI.motivation: Adaptive RAG relies on local signals (confidence, relevance, support, retrieval quality) to trigger search or correction, but in multi-step retrieval these signals must form a persistent view of what evidence supports, what is missing, and what action to take. Existing methods treat such signals as separate triggers, causing "evidence-state fragmentation"—failing to preserve a coherent evidence state across a trajectory.
AI.method: BELIEFRAG is a closed-loop controller that updates an explicit state over sufficiency, reliability, conflict, uncertainty, evidence gaps, and acquisition cost, then selects among retrieval, query rewriting, verification, answering, stopping, and abstention. Evaluated across six QA benchmarks with gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-32B.
AI.result: With gpt-oss-120b, BELIEFRAG achieves mean token F1 0.572 at 3.89k tokens/question vs. 0.555 F1 for fixed iterative retrieval, using 39% fewer tokens. With Qwen3-32B, 0.552 F1 vs. 0.523, using 35% fewer tokens. Gains stem mainly from corrective re-retrieval rather than pruning; several belief dimensions are redundant; calibrated answerability plays the strongest operational role. Calibration improves threshold stability across related evidence sources, though source shift can still invalidate the same decision signal.
AI.conclusion: Explicit belief-state control mitigates evidence-state fragmentation, delivering higher F1 at substantially lower token cost, with corrective re-retrieval as the key driver and calibrated answerability as the strongest practical component, though robustness to source shift remains limited.

title: Benchmarking EMlog Calibration for Autonomous Surface Vehicles
summary: Accurate velocity measurement is a fundamental requirement for autonomous surface and underwater vehicles. Commonly, velocity is provided by a Doppler velocity log (DVL) sensor, yet it becomes unavailable due to operational altitude constraints. In such situations, electromagnetic logs (EMLogs) provide a critically robust alternative for continuous velocity estimation. However, raw EMLog measurements are inherently corrupted by systematic errors, which need to be calibrated prior mission begins. Currently, a benchmarking comparative evaluation of how different calibration models perform under rapidly changing dynamic sea conditions is missing in the literature. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a comparative model-based calibration methodology that evaluates four distinct calibration models using two different estimation pipelines. The proposed framework is rigorously validated on a unique 221 minutes of continuous real-world telemetry collected from the MARVEL surface vehicle during dynamic sea trials. The dataset contains two different EMLogs and DVL recordings. Experimental results demonstrate that the bias and scale error model implemented with the Kalman filter improves the speed estimation by 71%. We also demonstrate that dynamical manoeuvres further improve the accuracy compared to standard straight-line paths, ultimately delivering a validated, real-time online calibration EMLog approach for autonomous surface vehicles.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comparative model-based calibration methodology for electromagnetic logs (EMLogs) using two estimation pipelines, validated on 221 minutes of real-world MARVEL surface vehicle telemetry. The bias and scale error model with a Kalman filter improves speed estimation by 71%, with dynamic manoeuvres yielding better accuracy than straight-line paths.
AI.motivation: Accurate velocity measurement is fundamental for autonomous surface and underwater vehicles, typically provided by DVL sensors. However, DVL becomes unavailable due to operational altitude constraints, making EMLogs a critically robust alternative for continuous velocity estimation. Raw EMLog measurements are corrupted by systematic errors requiring calibration, yet a benchmarking comparative evaluation of calibration models under rapidly changing dynamic sea conditions is missing in the literature.
AI.method: A comparative model-based calibration methodology evaluating four distinct calibration models using two different estimation pipelines. The framework is validated on 221 minutes of continuous real-world telemetry from the MARVEL surface vehicle collected during dynamic sea trials, containing two different EMLogs and DVL recordings.
AI.result: The bias and scale error model implemented with a Kalman filter improves speed estimation by 71%. Dynamic manoeuvres further improve accuracy compared to standard straight-line paths.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a validated, real-time online calibration EMLog approach for autonomous surface vehicles.

title: Schema: Discovering Unknown Environments via Agentic Program Induction
summary: Learning to complete tasks in unfamiliar environments with unknown rules remains a key challenge for LLM agents. Current LLM agents often record their discoveries in prose, which may not provide a compact, explicit account of how the environment works. Inspired by how scientists organize observations into testable, predictive theories, we introduce Schema, an agent harness that organizes learning and action through interactive program induction. The LLM agent decides what to investigate and how to act, expressing its evolving understanding of the environment as executable programs. The harness consists of a persistent program workspace and a small set of interfaces for checking these programs against the interaction history, planning within them, and executing plans under step-by-step verification. Schema raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE from 58.7% to 99.2% with the same base model, solves 100% of the public DiG-bench games, and reaches the median performance of the top-50 human players on MazeBench. Extensive analysis shows the effectiveness of Schema in unknown mechanism discovery, and ablations confirm the contribution of each component.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Schema, an agent harness that uses interactive program induction to help LLM agents learn and act in unfamiliar environments, raising ARC-AGI-3 RHAE from 58.7% to 99.2% and achieving strong results on DiG-bench and MazeBench.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to complete tasks in unfamiliar environments with unknown rules. Existing agents typically record discoveries in prose, which lacks a compact, explicit, and testable account of how the environment works.
AI.method: Inspired by scientific theory-building, Schema organizes learning and action through interactive program induction. The LLM agent decides what to investigate and how to act, expressing its evolving environmental understanding as executable programs. The harness comprises a persistent program workspace and a small set of interfaces for checking programs against interaction history, planning within them, and executing plans with step-by-step verification.
AI.result: With the same base model, Schema improves ARC-AGI-3 RHAE from 58.7% to 99.2%, solves 100% of public DiG-bench games, and reaches the median performance of top-50 human players on MazeBench. Analysis demonstrates effective unknown mechanism discovery, and ablations confirm each component's contribution.
AI.conclusion: Representing environmental understanding as verifiable executable programs, rather than prose, enables LLM agents to discover unknown mechanisms and act effectively in unfamiliar environments.

title: ASENA: Self-evolving Agents for Embodied Navigation
summary: We present ASENA, an embodied agent system that connects general-purpose coding agents to robot sensing, computation, supervised execution, and persistent experience. Agents can write and execute programs, inspect recorded outcomes, repair failures, and reuse notes and executable skills while keeping their model weights fixed. We further introduce ASENA-VLN, a 4B monocular navigation policy that serves as an optional tool within this programmable system. ASENA-VLN predicts body-frame trajectories for both extended routes and short-horizon behaviors using a shared vision-language decoder trained on route instructions, visual question answering, and a newly curated dataset of geometry-derived atomic navigation tasks. As a standalone policy, ASENA-VLN achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 68.7% on R2R and 70.2% on RxR. When integrated with a coding agent, learned navigation improves ASENA's success rate by 11 percentage points on both agentic benchmarks while reducing execution time. Through persistent workspace evolution and simulator feedback, ten passes over recurring 100-task subsets further improve success from 72% to 98% on R2R and from 65% to 89% on RxR. On embodied question answering, ASENA achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with fewer interaction steps. Finally, real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1 combine search, visual inspection, spatial reasoning, and synthesized gestures without a pre-built map, illustrating how online programming extends robot behavior beyond route following and predefined skills.

AI.tldr: ASENA is a programmable embodied agent system where fixed-weight coding agents control robots via code, supervised execution, and persistent experience; its optional 4B navigation policy (ASENA-VLN) sets state-of-the-art results and boosts agentic performance and real-world generalization.
AI.motivation: General-purpose coding agents are capable but disconnected from robot sensing, computation, and execution; the paper aims to bridge this gap so that agents can program robot behavior with persistent experience and improve through simulator feedback rather than weight updates.
AI.method: ASENA lets coding agents write/execute programs, inspect recorded outcomes, repair failures, and reuse notes and executable skills while keeping model weights fixed. ASENA-VLN is a 4B monocular navigation policy used as an optional tool, predicting body-frame trajectories for long routes and short-horizon behaviors with a shared vision-language decoder trained on route instructions, VQA, and a curated dataset of geometry-derived atomic navigation tasks. Persistent workspace evolution and simulator feedback refine performance.
AI.result: ASENA-VLN reaches 68.7% success on R2R and 70.2% on RxR standalone. Integrated with a coding agent, it improves ASENA by 11 percentage points on both agentic benchmarks and reduces execution time. Ten passes over recurring 100-task subsets raise success from 72% to 98% (R2R) and 65% to 89% (RxR). ASENA achieves state-of-the-art embodied QA accuracy with fewer interaction steps. Real-world demos on Unitree G1 handle search, visual inspection, spatial reasoning, and synthesized gestures without a pre-built map.
AI.conclusion: Online programming with persistent experience and an optional learned navigation tool extends robot behavior beyond route following and predefined skills, enabling flexible, real-world embodied tasks without fine-tuning model weights.

title: RefCon: Iterative Refinement and Contrastive Memory Extraction for Context-Evolving Agent
summary: Long-horizon agent interactions generate useful but noisy experience, and retraining models to absorb it is expensive. Context-evolving agents therefore need memory extraction methods that improve with more test-time compute without relying on gold labels. We propose RefCon, which combines sequential self-refinement with parallel self-contrast to extract higher-quality memories without gold labels. Evaluated on AppWorld and BFCL-V3 across multiple context-evolving agent frameworks, RefCon delivers strong and consistent gains, including relative improvements of 21.6% on ACE and 16.6% on ReMe over no-scaling baselines, while a diversity-focused variant (DivCon) achieves a 35.5% gain on ReasoningBank. RefCon consistently outperforms existing baselines without ground-truth labels, and generalizes across model scales and to software engineering tasks, where it surpasses even ground-truth baselines.
