We further analyze the accuracy-token trade-off and scaling behavior, showing RefCon maintains favorable efficiency and continues to improve as more trajectories are used, unlike diversity-only scaling which saturates earlier.

AI.tldr: RefCon is a label-free memory extraction method combining sequential self-refinement with parallel self-contrast to improve context-evolving agents, delivering consistent gains on AppWorld and BFCL-V3.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agent interactions produce useful but noisy experience, and retraining models to absorb it is expensive. Existing context-evolving agents need memory extraction methods that scale with test-time compute without gold labels.
AI.method: RefCon combines sequential self-refinement with parallel self-contrast to extract higher-quality memories without gold labels. A diversity-focused variant, DivCon, is also introduced.
AI.result: RefCon delivers strong, consistent gains across multiple context-evolving agent frameworks: 21.6% relative improvement on ACE and 16.6% on ReMe over no-scaling baselines; DivCon achieves 35.5% gain on ReasoningBank. It outperforms existing label-free baselines and generalizes across model scales and to software engineering tasks, surpassing even ground-truth baselines.
AI.conclusion: RefCon maintains favorable accuracy-token efficiency and continues improving as more trajectories are used, unlike diversity-only scaling which saturates earlier.

title: The Planning Limits of Latent World Models
summary: World models offer a promising way to help robots understand how the physical world evolves and plan complex behaviours through imagination. Yet existing studies mainly demonstrate what these models can accomplish, leaving unclear when their predictions remain useful for planning and where they fail. We study this question using action-conditioned predictors built on five frozen self-supervised visual backbones: V-JEPA 2, V-JEPA 2.1, VideoMAEv2, VideoPrism, and DINOv2. We use frozen backbones to test representations intended to transfer across environments. We evaluate these models on diverse Meta-World manipulation tasks and real-robot interactions from BridgeData V2. We find that a world model guides action selection reliably only when the goal lies within, or slightly beyond, the trajectory it imagines during planning. With five-step rollouts, the length the predictor was trained on, the world model ranks actions reliably only for targets five to ten control steps ahead, whereas task goals lie 16 to 53 steps away. Neither an 81-fold larger predictor nor longer-rollout training extends this range; the encoder affects both range and closed-loop success, with V-JEPA 2.1 performing most consistently. More fundamentally, the limit persists under perfect prediction: using the real simulator, success falls from 92% to 41% as the target moves from five to twenty steps ahead of a five-step rollout. Planning therefore requires either longer imagined trajectories or closer subgoals. For distant goals, pure imagination succeeds in 23% of episodes, planning with feedback (MPC) raises success to 30%, imagining as far as the goal to 47%, and nearby expert subgoals to 76%. Used within its plannable range, a world model can also improve a vision-language-action (VLA) policy: choosing among eight actions the VLA proposes raises its success from 65% to 77% across 16 different tasks.

AI.tldr: Action-conditioned world models reliably guide planning only within a short "plannable range" (~5-10 steps) around the rollout horizon they were trained on; this limit persists even with perfect prediction and larger models, so distant goals require longer imagined trajectories, closer subgoals, or MPC feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing world-model research mostly shows what these models can accomplish but leaves unclear when their predictions remain useful for planning and where they fail. The authors aim to characterize the boundary of a world model's usefulness for action selection and the factors that affect it.
AI.method: They build action-conditioned predictors on five frozen self-supervised visual backbones (V-JEPA 2, V-JEPA 2.1, VideoMAEv2, VideoPrism, DINOv2) to test transferable representations, evaluating on diverse Meta-World manipulation tasks and real-robot interactions from BridgeData V2. They probe rollout length, predictor scale (up to 81x larger), encoder choice, perfect-prediction controls with the real simulator, and planning strategies (pure imagination, MPC with feedback, imagining to the goal, expert subgoals), and test using the world model to rerank VLA-proposed actions.
AI.result: With five-step rollouts (the training length), the world model ranks actions reliably only for targets 5-10 control steps ahead, whereas task goals lie 16-53 steps away. Neither an 81x larger predictor nor longer-rollout training extends this range; the encoder affects both range and closed-loop success, with V-JEPA 2.1 most consistent. The limit persists under perfect prediction: simulator success falls from 92% to 41% as the target moves from 5 to 20 steps ahead of a five-step rollout.
AI.conclusion: Planning with world models requires either longer imagined trajectories or closer subgoals. For distant goals, pure imagination succeeds in 23% of episodes, MPC raises this to 30%, imagining to the goal to 47%, and nearby expert subgoals to 76%. Used within its plannable range, a world model can improve a VLA policy, raising success from 65% to 77% across 16 tasks by choosing among eight proposed actions.

title: MADBench: Benchmarking the Security of Multi-Agent Debate
summary:
Multi-agent debate (MAD) can improve large language model (LLM) reasoning by allowing multiple agents to exchange and critique their answers to the same task. However, the interactions that enable agents to correct mistakes can also spread adversarial errors and steer the agents toward an incorrect answer. Although some efforts have been made to examine particular attack types on MAD, systematic evaluation of MAD under diverse attacks remains limited. A central question is whether debate mitigates adversarial influence or amplifies it.
  In this paper, we present MADBench, a benchmark for evaluating the security of MAD. We organize attacks into a layered taxonomy following the MAD workflow, incorporating both established attacks and new strategies tailored to debate. We evaluate six attack families over 356 source tasks and 3,958 test cases, examining their effects on the final answer and the propagation of adversarial influence. Our results show that, under attacks, MAD does not necessarily improve LLM reasoning. Compared with a single-agent baseline, MAD can mitigate attacks on answer accuracy in question-answering tasks while amplifying unauthorized reads or writes in both question-answering and workspace tasks. Moreover, even when three out of five agents collude, the attack changes the final answer from correct to wrong on only 28.30\% of tasks answered correctly without attack, while only 3.26\% of initially correct honest agents switch to wrong answers during debate.

AI.tldr: MADBench is introduced as a benchmark to systematically evaluate multi-agent debate (MAD) security under diverse attacks, revealing that debate can both mitigate and amplify adversarial influence depending on task type.
AI.motivation: Prior work only examines particular attack types on MAD, leaving systematic evaluation under diverse attacks limited. A central open question is whether debate mitigates adversarial influence or amplifies it.
AI.method: The authors build a layered taxonomy of attacks following the MAD workflow, combining established attacks with new debate-tailored strategies. They evaluate six attack families across 356 source tasks and 3,958 test cases, measuring effects on the final answer and the propagation of adversarial influence.
AI.result: Under attacks, MAD does not necessarily improve LLM reasoning. Compared with a single-agent baseline, MAD can mitigate attacks on answer accuracy in question-answering tasks while amplifying unauthorized reads or writes in both question-answering and workspace tasks. Even with three of five agents colluding, the attack flips the final answer from correct to wrong on only 28.30% of tasks answered correctly without attack, and only 3.26% of initially correct honest agents switch to wrong answers during debate.
AI.conclusion: MAD's security effects are task-dependent: it can resist some attacks yet amplify others, and collusion-based attacks have limited success in flipping correct answers, suggesting debate provides partial robustness against adversarial influence.

title: ReWAM: Reciprocal World Action Models for Interactive Autonomous Driving
summary: In interactive scenarios, an autonomous driving system is required to generate ego actions under the influence of other agents' behaviors. Existing World Action Models (WAMs) typically model other agents as components of the world model rather than as decision-makers that fundamentally shape the action of the ego agent, which impairs their performance in dense interaction scenarios. We introduce Reciprocal World Action Models (ReWAM), a game-theoretic world action modeling framework that captures the reciprocal influence between the ego agent and other agents by representing them as conditional responders whose actions are mutually influenced. We instantiate this framework with a Level-$k$ response hierarchy, where role-specific ego and other action DiTs exchange compact strategy tokens through cross-agent attention while remaining grounded in a shared representation of the future driving world. To learn the response policy of the ego agent from demonstrations, we formulate expert actions as samples from the best response distribution and jointly optimize the entire hierarchy using conditional flow matching. Our framework is evaluated on the NAVSIM dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to baselines. The improvement is particularly significant in interactive scenarios, validating that modeling reciprocal responses provides a more effective foundation for interaction-aware world action generation.

AI.tldr: ReWAM is a game-theoretic world action modeling framework that captures reciprocal influence between ego and other agents via mutually conditioned responders, instantiated with a Level-k response hierarchy and trained with conditional flow matching, achieving state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM, especially in interactive scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing World Action Models (WAMs) treat other agents merely as components of the world model rather than as decision-makers that fundamentally shape the ego agent's actions. This impairs performance in dense interaction scenarios where mutual influence matters.
AI.method: The authors introduce Reciprocal World Action Models (ReWAM), a game-theoretic world action modeling framework representing ego and other agents as conditional responders whose actions mutually influence each other. It is instantiated with a Level-k response hierarchy, where role-specific ego and other action DiTs exchange compact strategy tokens via cross-agent attention while grounded in a shared future driving world representation. To learn the ego response policy from demonstrations, expert actions are formulated as samples from the best response distribution, and the whole hierarchy is jointly optimized using conditional flow matching.
AI.result: ReWAM is evaluated on the NAVSIM dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to baselines. The improvement is particularly significant in interactive scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Modeling reciprocal responses provides a more effective foundation for interaction-aware world action generation than treating other agents as passive world-model components.

title: Do Self-Evolving Skills Generalize to Held-Out Tasks?
summary: AI agents can externalize what they learn from past tasks into reusable \emph{skills}, such as procedures, checklists, code, or other executable artifacts, that can be retrieved and reused when solving new tasks. Self-evolving skill methods keep rewriting these skills after each round of practice on training tasks, and the skill is then used on new tasks of the same kind. We ask a question: does the improvement a skill shows on its training tasks carry over to new test tasks? We test five self-evolving methods and a one-shot skill on six benchmarks, with the same model, the same agent, and the same train/test split for every method. Of the 21 skills that improve on their training tasks, 5 keep all of that improvement on the test tasks, 13 keep part of it, and 3 keep none of it. No existing method is best everywhere. When we read the skills, the ones that carry over badly often fix details that should depend on the task, such as column names and output files, or turn a fix for one failure into a rule for every task. An LLM judge that reads the skill content can often see this: it ranks finished skills the same way the test results do in 86\% of pairs. But it predicts the effect of a single edit poorly, so edits still have to be tested by running them. Based on these findings, we describe Generalizable Skill Optimization (GSO), which keeps only a guide for writing skills and writes a new skill for each task; it scores highest on all six benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether improvements that self-evolving AI agent skills gain on training tasks transfer to new test tasks. Across five self-evolving methods plus a one-shot baseline, six benchmarks, and 21 improved skills, only 5 fully retain their training-task gains on test tasks, 13 partially, and 3 lose everything. Bad transfer stems from skills overfitting task-specific details, and while an LLM judge can rank finished skills well, it poorly predicts individual edit effects. The authors propose Generalizable Skill Optimization (GSO), which retains only a skill-writing guide and generates a fresh skill per task, achieving top scores on all six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving skill methods repeatedly rewrite skills after each round of practice on training tasks, and these skills are then applied to new tasks of the same kind. The paper questions a core implicit assumption: that a skill's measured improvement on its training tasks actually carries over to test tasks. Verifying this matters because poor generalization would mean reported gains reflect overfitting rather than genuine reusable capability.
AI.method: The study evaluates five self-evolving methods and a one-shot skill baseline under controlled conditions: the same model, the same agent, and identical train/test splits for every method, across six benchmarks. It then analyzes the 21 skills that improved on training tasks to measure retention on test tasks, qualitatively inspects skill content to identify causes of poor carryover, and tests an LLM judge that reads skill content to rank finished skills and predict the effect of individual edits.
AI.result: Of the 21 skills improving on training tasks, 5 retain all of that improvement on test tasks, 13 retain part of it, and 3 retain none. No single existing method is best everywhere. Skills that carry over badly tend to fix task-dependent details (e.g., column names, output files) or convert a fix for one failure into a universal rule. An LLM judge reading skill content matches test-result rankings in 86% of pairs, but predicts the effect of a single edit poorly, so edits must still be validated by execution. The proposed Generalizable Skill Optimization (GSO), which keeps only a guide for writing skills and writes a new skill for each task, scores highest on all six benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Training-task gains from self-evolving skills only partially transfer to test tasks, with widespread overfitting to task-specific details, and no existing method dominates across benchmarks. Skill content is informative enough for LLM judges to rank finished skills reliably, but not to predict edit effects without running them. Retaining only a reusable skill-writing guide and generating a per-task skill (GSO) is more generalizable, yielding the best results on all six benchmarks.

title: Scale and Selection: What Makes Automatic Harness Evolution Work for Visual-Interface Robot Agents
summary: When an off-the-shelf coding agent is used directly as a robot policy, observing a browser-based 3D interface through screenshots and acting by posing a virtual target gripper through a few tools, the agent's harness, its prompts, tools, and control rules, largely determines success, and until now it has been written by hand. We show that this harness can be improved automatically by another coding agent, the optimizer agent, and report two findings about what makes it work. First, the number of rollouts the optimizer agent sees per round governs whether the evolved harness is trustworthy, generalizes, and improves steadily. A single rollout is a noisy binary outcome, so with few rollouts per round a revision can be promoted on luck; enlarging the batch raises the signal-to-noise ratio of every promotion decision. Holding rounds fixed and growing the training set from 5 to 100 rollouts, held-out success rises from 47% to 67%, while small training sets overfit, reaching 70% on training tasks but only 54% held-out. Second, the optimizer agent must not be given free rein. With every revision it proposes accepted unconditionally, performance drifts downward within ten rounds as ill-judged edits accumulate; adding the most basic safeguard, Champion-Challenger selection that promotes a revision only if it strictly beats the incumbent on the same fixed evaluation set, turns the same loop into one that raises held-out success from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds. Automatic harness evolution for visual-interface robot agents is thus feasible, but its gains hinge on the rollout scale behind each decision and on how the optimizer agent's revisions are selected.

AI.tldr: A coding agent (the "optimizer agent") can automatically evolve the hand-written harness — prompts, tools, and control rules — of an off-the-shelf coding agent used as a visual-interface robot policy. Two factors determine success: the number of rollouts seen per round (more rollouts raise signal-to-noise and held-out success from 47% to 67%) and gating revisions with Champion-Challenger selection rather than accepting them unconditionally (51% to 67% over 30 rounds).
AI.motivation: When a coding agent is repurposed as a robot policy operating a browser-based 3D interface via screenshots and virtual gripper tools, the harness (prompts, tools, control rules) largely dictates success, yet it has always been hand-written. The paper asks whether this harness can be evolved automatically by another coding agent, and what conditions make such evolution reliable.
AI.method: An optimizer coding agent iteratively proposes revisions to the harness of a target coding-agent robot policy. The study manipulates two variables: (1) the rollout batch size observed per round — comparing 5 vs. 100 rollouts on training tasks, with held-out evaluation — and (2) the acceptance rule for proposed revisions — comparing unconditional acceptance against Champion-Challenger selection that promotes a revision only if it strictly beats the incumbent on a fixed evaluation set.
AI.result: Scaling rollouts from 5 to 100 (with rounds fixed) raised held-out success from 47% to 67%; small training sets overfit, hitting 70% on training tasks but only 54% held-out. Unconditional acceptance caused performance to drift downward within ten rounds as ill-judged edits accumulated, while adding Champion-Challenger selection raised held-out success from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds.
AI.conclusion: Automatic harness evolution for visual-interface robot agents is feasible, but its gains hinge on the rollout scale behind each promotion decision and on how the optimizer agent's revisions are selected. Trustworthy, generalizable, steady improvement requires sufficiently large per-round rollout batches and a safeguard such as Champion-Challenger selection.

title: Rep2Skill: Representation-Guided Skill Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
summary: Textual skills enable large language model (LLM) based agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. Yet existing skill evolution remains largely confined to the text space: an optimizer must diagnose success and failure patterns, and revise skills solely from long execution trajectories and sparse task outcomes. This text-only paradigm leaves the agent's internal representations, which contain rich records of its evolving execution state, outside the skill optimization loop. We ask whether an agent can improve its external textual skills by reflecting on its own internal representations. We introduce Rep2Skill, a representation-guided framework for self-evolution on agent skills. Specifically, upon the collected agent rollouts, Rep2Skill models their internal model representation trajectories to localize turns that deviate from successful execution dynamics, and it further interprets these signals alongside the execution contexts as actionable textual feedback for targeted skill revision. Experiments on two agent environments with two open-source LLMs show that Rep2Skill consistently outperforms text-only approaches in the self-evolution setting, where the same LLM serves as both executor and optimizer without a stronger external model. This establishes a promising direction moving agent self-improvement beyond text-only reflection.

AI.tldr: Rep2Skill is a framework that improves LLM agent skills by reflecting on internal model representations rather than only text, using representation trajectories to localize deviating turns and generate targeted textual feedback for skill revision.
AI.motivation: Existing skill evolution for LLM-based agents operates in text space: an optimizer diagnoses success/failure and revises skills solely from long execution trajectories and sparse task outcomes. This text-only paradigm excludes the agent's internal representations, which contain rich records of its evolving execution state, from the skill optimization loop. The authors ask whether an agent can improve its external textual skills by reflecting on its own internal representations.
AI.method: Rep2Skill is a representation-guided self-evolution framework for agent skills. On collected agent rollouts, it models internal model representation trajectories to localize turns that deviate from successful execution dynamics, then interprets these signals alongside execution contexts as actionable textual feedback for targeted skill revision.
AI.result: Experiments on two agent environments with two open-source LLMs show that Rep2Skill consistently outperforms text-only approaches in the self-evolution setting, where the same LLM serves as both executor and optimizer without a stronger external model.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a promising direction for moving agent self-improvement beyond text-only reflection, leveraging internal representations to guide external textual skill evolution.

title: FORTE: Forecasting Occupancy for Spatiotemporal Risk-Aware Planning in Dynamic Environments
summary: Safe navigation in dynamic environments requires anticipating future environmental states to account for spatiotemporal risks, specifically when and where collisions may occur. To this end, occupancy grid map (OGM) prediction has been widely adopted as an effective approach. However, existing OGM-based navigation methods often struggle to achieve accurate and efficient forecasting and fail to fully exploit the temporal information in predicted OGMs during planning. To address these challenges, we propose FORTE, a navigation framework that directly exploits the spatiotemporal evolution of predicted occupancy from the perspectives of spatiotemporal occupancy overlap and occupancy directivity. Based on these properties, FORTE evaluates multiple topology-distinct paths and selects the suitable one without explicit object detection or tracking. To support online planning, we formulate a latent diffusion model-based OGM predictor that generates the entire forecast horizon in a non-autoregressive manner while maintaining temporal consistency through temporal shift modules. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FORTE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. For prediction, FORTE achieves up to 215.3% higher IoU and 5.24x faster inference; for navigation, it yields up to a 3.5x higher success rate.

AI.tldr: FORTE is an OGM-based navigation framework that exploits the spatiotemporal evolution of predicted occupancy via overlap and directivity metrics, paired with a non-autoregressive latent diffusion OGM predictor, achieving large gains in prediction accuracy, speed, and navigation success.
AI.motivation: Safe navigation in dynamic environments requires anticipating future environmental states to capture spatiotemporal risks (when and where collisions occur). Existing OGM-based navigation methods struggle with accurate and efficient forecasting and fail to fully exploit temporal information in predicted OGMs during planning.
AI.method: FORTE directly exploits the spatiotemporal evolution of predicted occupancy from two perspectives: spatiotemporal occupancy overlap and occupancy directivity. Using these properties, it evaluates multiple topology-distinct paths and selects a suitable one without explicit object detection or tracking. For online planning, it uses a latent diffusion model-based OGM predictor that generates the entire forecast horizon non-autoregressively, maintaining temporal consistency via temporal shift modules.
AI.result: For prediction, FORTE achieves up to 215.3% higher IoU and 5.24x faster inference. For navigation, it yields up to a 3.5x higher success rate compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: FORTE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across both OGM prediction and navigation, validating the effectiveness of leveraging spatiotemporal occupancy properties with an efficient non-autoregressive diffusion predictor.

title: Beyond the Remembered World: Predictive 4D Belief for Persistent Navigation in Evolving Worlds
summary: Persistent spatial memory enables embodied agents to navigate familiar environments across repeated visits. However, targets may move while unobserved, including during navigation, making remembered locations unreliable by the time an agent arrives. Despite advances in memory retrieval and state prediction, accounting for continued hidden world evolution and revising beliefs under limited visibility remain challenging. We study Evolving-World Navigation, where agents infer target locations from intermittent observations, predict their states at inspection time, and revise beliefs using visual evidence. We propose EvolvingNav, which constructs a time-indexed belief from timestamped 3D object histories through a structured persistence-relocation model. The belief distinguishes persistence at the last observed location from relocation to alternative locations and retains probability mass outside the known candidate set. An event-driven filter propagates the current belief as time elapses, forecasts target occupancy at candidate inspection times, and incorporates new RGB-D evidence. Negative observations downweight location hypotheses according to calibrated, visibility-conditioned detection probabilities, while evidence tracking prevents repeated use of the same observations. A frozen, zero-shot vision-language controller uses the updated belief to choose actions and replan. We further introduce EvoWorld-Bench, a benchmark grounded in human activity traces, comprising 54 scenes and 803,680 tasks with controlled changes before and during navigation. In simulation and real-robot experiments, EvolvingNav improves navigation success and search efficiency over the evaluated baselines. Paired experiments show the clearest gains under learnable temporal patterns, while ablations demonstrate the value of preserving uncertainty and incorporating visibility-aware evidence.

AI.tldr: EvolvingNav maintains a time-indexed belief over target locations by combining a persistence-relocation model over timestamped 3D object histories, an event-driven filter that forecasts occupancy at future inspection times under limited visibility, and a frozen zero-shot vision-language controller; paired with the human-activity-grounded EvoWorld-Bench (54 scenes, 803,680 tasks), it improves navigation success and search efficiency in simulation and on a real robot.
AI.motivation: Persistent spatial memory lets embodied agents navigate familiar environments, but remembered target locations become unreliable when targets move while unobserved, including during navigation itself. Existing memory retrieval and state prediction methods struggle to account for continued hidden world evolution and to revise beliefs under limited visibility, so agents may arrive at stale locations.
AI.method: The paper formalizes Evolving-World Navigation, where agents infer target locations from intermittent observations, predict target states at inspection time, and revise beliefs with visual evidence. EvolvingNav builds a time-indexed belief from timestamped 3D object histories via a structured persistence-relocation model that separates persistence at the last observed location from relocation to alternative locations and retains probability mass outside the known candidate set. An event-driven filter propagates the belief over time, forecasts target occupancy at candidate inspection times, and integrates new RGB-D evidence. Negative observations downweight location hypotheses using calibrated, visibility-conditioned detection probabilities, and evidence tracking prevents reuse of the same observations. A frozen, zero-shot vision-language controller consumes the updated belief to select actions and replan. EvoWorld-Bench is introduced, grounded in human activity traces with 54 scenes and 803,680 tasks with controlled changes before and during navigation.
AI.result: In simulation and real-robot experiments, EvolvingNav improves navigation success and search efficiency over the evaluated baselines. Paired experiments show the clearest gains under learnable temporal patterns, and ablations confirm the value of preserving uncertainty and incorporating visibility-aware evidence.
AI.conclusion: Evolving-world navigation can be tackled by maintaining and updating a time-indexed belief that models both persistence and relocation of targets and explicitly preserves uncertainty, rather than relying on static remembered locations. Visibility-conditioned negative evidence and evidence tracking are important components, and the approach transfers from simulation to a real robot.

title: A Biophysically Detailed C. elegans Circuit as a Task-Agnostic Dynamical Core for Visually Robust Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot policies are usually trained for one task, one body and one visual environment, and generalize poorly beyond these conditions. Whether a nervous system can instead supply the sensorimotor computation through its evolved wiring and biophysics remains unresolved. Here we embed a biophysically detailed Caenorhabditis elegans sensorimotor circuit - 136 multicompartment neurons with realistic morphologies and electrophysiological characteristics - as the dynamical core of a visuomotor policy. Only thin task-specific adapters are trained; the core's synaptic weights stay fixed while its membrane voltages evolve freely. Across different MetaWorld tasks the core matches or exceeds diffusion-policy, action-chunking-transformer and neural-circuit-policy baselines, and degrades less under visual perturbations. Replacing the core with generic network models such as MLP, LSTM, transformer or reservoir networks removes the advantage. Furthermore, on a real robotic arm the core withstands diverse visual perturbations that collapse the baselines. Our results suggest that visual robustness can be inherited from biophysically detailed circuit dynamics rather than learned by task-specific controllers.

AI.tldr: A biophysically detailed C. elegans sensorimotor circuit (136 multicompartment neurons) with fixed synaptic weights serves as the dynamical core of a visuomotor policy, with only thin task-specific adapters trained. It matches or beats diffusion-policy, action-chunking-transformer and neural-circuit-policy baselines across MetaWorld tasks, degrades less under visual perturbations, and generalizes to a real robotic arm, whereas generic cores (MLP, LSTM, transformer, reservoir) lose the advantage.
AI.motivation: Robot policies are typically trained for a single task, body, and visual environment, generalizing poorly beyond these conditions. It remains unresolved whether a nervous system can instead supply sensorimotor computation through its evolved wiring and biophysics, motivating the use of a biological circuit as a reusable dynamical core.
AI.method: Embed a biophysically detailed Caenorhabditis elegans sensorimotor circuit (136 multicompartment neurons with realistic morphologies and electrophysiological characteristics) as the dynamical core of a visuomotor policy. Only thin task-specific adapters are trained; the core's synaptic weights stay fixed while membrane voltages evolve freely, tested across MetaWorld tasks and on a real robotic arm against diffusion-policy, action-chunking-transformer and neural-circuit-policy baselines.
AI.result: The biological core matches or exceeds diffusion-policy, action-chunking-transformer and neural-circuit-policy baselines across MetaWorld tasks and degrades less under visual perturbations. Replacing it with MLP, LSTM, transformer or reservoir networks removes the advantage. On a real robotic arm, the core withstands diverse visual perturbations that collapse the baselines.
AI.conclusion: Visual robustness can be inherited from biophysically detailed circuit dynamics rather than learned by task-specific controllers, indicating evolved neural wiring and biophysics can serve as a general-purpose sensorimotor core.

title: Reinforcing Multimodal Reasoning via Token-Level Perception-Grounded Advantage Estimation
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has improved the reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), yet existing frameworks rely on coarse, sequence-level reward signals that lack the fine-grained supervision over the visually-grounded steps within a multimodal reasoning chain. We investigate this gap through the lens of two token-level metrics: visual dependency (i.e. how much a token's prediction relies on the input image features) and predictive entropy. Our empirical analysis reveals two key findings: (1) correct reasoning chains exhibit a markedly sharper entropy reduction as visual grounding intensifies, compared to incorrect ones; (2) pivotal tokens, those whose misprediction triggers reasoning collapse, are statistical outliers in the joint distribution of visual dependency and predictive entropy derived from correct chains. Motivated by these findings, we propose token-level perception-grounded advantage estimation (TPAE), which estimates token-level advantages by measuring each token's statistical consistency with the vision-entropy patterns of correct rollouts. TPAE leverages this granular score to modulate the sequence-level advantage, producing a fine-grained supervision signal that can be integrated into various RLVR frameworks. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks show that TPAE consistently outperforms leading strong baselines, yielding more stable and efficient optimization for multimodal reasoning. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Zhihan72/TPAE.

AI.tldr: TPAE introduces token-level perception-grounded advantage estimation for RLVR in MLLMs, using visual dependency and predictive entropy patterns of correct rollouts to modulate sequence-level rewards, achieving consistent gains across seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR frameworks for MLLMs use coarse sequence-level rewards, lacking fine-grained supervision over visually-grounded steps within a multimodal reasoning chain.
AI.method: The authors analyze two token-level metrics: visual dependency (reliance on input image features) and predictive entropy. Two findings motivate TPAE: (1) correct chains show sharper entropy reduction as visual grounding intensifies versus incorrect ones; (2) pivotal tokens (misprediction triggers reasoning collapse) are statistical outliers in the joint visual-dependency/entropy distribution of correct chains. TPAE estimates token-level advantages by measuring each token's statistical consistency with vision-entropy patterns of correct rollouts, then uses this granular score to modulate the sequence-level advantage, yielding a fine-grained signal integrable into various RLVR frameworks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks show TPAE consistently outperforms leading strong baselines, yielding more stable and efficient optimization for multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Token-level, perception-grounded advantage estimation provides effective fine-grained supervision for RLVR in MLLMs, improving both stability and efficiency of multimodal reasoning optimization. Code is publicly available.

title: HiWE: Hierarchical World Knowledge Model with Visual Keypoint Enhancement for Zero-Shot 3D Path Planning
summary: Robot demonstration generation requires a system to identify where an interaction should occur, plan a feasible motion, and execute the required contact. HiWE connects these decisions through a point-based interface between visual grounding and language-based planning. PointVLM is instruction-tuned to associate task-relevant objects with image coordinates using a mixture of point annotations, segmentation-derived samples, robot observations, and visual question answering data. Depth measurements lift these predictions into a semantic 3D representation. A language planner, 3DLLM, uses this representation to specify end-effector waypoints and gripper commands, while a hybrid grasping module resolves local grasp poses. The evaluation covers 14 simulated manipulation tasks and four physical-robot tasks, together with ablations of the visual training data, spatial inputs, and grasp selection. Here, zero-shot execution refers to deployment without task-specific demonstration training; the visual model uses existing robot data during fine-tuning. This paper describes the original point-based formulation of the framework; its relationship to the subsequent GeneralVLA extension is detailed in the introduction.

AI.tldr: HiWE is a point-based robot demonstration generation framework that couples PointVLM (visual grounding to image coordinates) with 3DLLM (language planning over a semantic 3D scene), evaluated on 14 simulated and 4 physical manipulation tasks plus ablations.
AI.motivation: Robot demonstration generation requires solving three coupled problems: identifying where an interaction should occur, planning a feasible motion, and executing the required contact. The paper aims to connect these decisions through a unified point-based interface bridging visual grounding and language-based planning.
AI.method: PointVLM is instruction-tuned to associate task-relevant objects with image coordinates using a mixture of point annotations, segmentation-derived samples, robot observations, and visual question answering data. Depth measurements lift these predictions into a semantic 3D representation. A language planner, 3DLLM, consumes this representation to specify end-effector waypoints and gripper commands, while a hybrid grasping module resolves local grasp poses.
AI.result: Evaluation spans 14 simulated manipulation tasks and four physical-robot tasks, supplemented by ablations of the visual training data, spatial inputs, and grasp selection. Zero-shot execution denotes deployment without task-specific demonstration training, though the visual model uses existing robot data during fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the original point-based formulation of the framework; its relationship to the subsequent GeneralVLA extension is detailed in the introduction.

title: Learning Process Rewards via Reasoning State Propagation
summary: Process reward models (PRMs) have demonstrated notable effectiveness in test-time scaling and reinforcement learning by providing fine-grained signals for evaluating intermediate reasoning states, but their training relies heavily on costly process annotations. A natural way to alleviate this dependence is to complement limited process supervision with scalable outcome supervision. However, existing PRMs often model reasoning prefixes independently, providing no explicit mechanism for effectively using final outcome to guide the learning of intermediate reasoning states. We introduce Reasoning State Propagation (RSP), which represents each reasoning prefix with a binary validity state and models transitions between successive states across the reasoning trajectory. Specifically, RSP predicts a break probability that a valid state becomes invalid and a repair probability that an invalid state returns to valid. By propagating these transitions, RSP connects intermediate states to the final state, allowing process annotations to supervise intermediate states while outcome labels supervise the final state and can provide learning signals to preceding steps. Across reasoning search, response selection, and reinforcement learning, RSP consistently outperforms representative PRM baselines, with average improvements over Qwen2.5-Math-PRM of 5.6% in beam search and 2.1% in reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Reasoning State Propagation (RSP), a process reward model that represents each reasoning prefix with a binary validity state and models transitions (break/repair probabilities) across the trajectory, enabling outcome labels to supervise the final state and propagate learning signals back to intermediate steps. RSP outperforms PRM baselines across beam search, response selection, and RL.
AI.motivation: Existing PRMs model reasoning prefixes independently and lack an explicit mechanism to use final outcomes to guide learning of intermediate reasoning states. Training PRMs also depends heavily on costly process annotations. The goal is to complement limited process supervision with scalable outcome supervision while effectively linking intermediate states to final outcomes.
AI.method: RSP represents each reasoning prefix with a binary validity state and models transitions between successive states along the reasoning trajectory. It predicts a break probability (valid to invalid) and a repair probability (invalid to valid). By propagating these transitions, RSP connects intermediate states to the final state, so process annotations supervise intermediate states while outcome labels supervise the final state and provide learning signals to preceding steps.
AI.result: RSP consistently outperforms representative PRM baselines across reasoning search, response selection, and reinforcement learning. Average improvements over Qwen2.5-Math-PRM are 5.6% in beam search and 2.1% in reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Modeling reasoning states as a propagating binary validity process lets outcome supervision effectively shape intermediate reasoning states, improving PRM performance in test-time scaling and reinforcement learning while reducing reliance on costly process annotations.

title: MotionWeave: Learning Motion-Centered Future Dynamics for Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: 4 pages + 1 page references, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code: https://github.com/autu-mn/MotionWeave
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently incorporated world models to provide richer dynamic supervision beyond sparse action labels. However, explicitly predicting future images or videos may include control-irrelevant appearance, while guidance derived from holistic future visual representations and shared global action features may fail to establish timestep-specific correspondence between actions and local visual changes. To address this issue, we propose MotionWeave, a motion-centric future-dynamics framework for action-chunk prediction with two modules: the Action-Induced Motion Grounder (AIMG) and the Horizon Residual Composer (HRC). Specifically, AIMG conditions on action and proprioceptive representations to construct horizon-specific queries that localize interaction regions associated with each future action timestep from current visual tokens. HRC extracts differences between interaction representations at adjacent horizons, encodes them as temporal motion cues, and injects them into action tokens through a gated residual. During training, robot-arm masks rendered from future frames are used to construct KL-based motion-grounding supervision, while inference uses only the current observation. On six MetaWorld tasks, MotionWeave achieves a 75.3% average success rate, an absolute gain of 8.6% over π0 (66.7%), especially on sustained-interaction tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/autu-mn/MotionWeave.

AI.tldr: MotionWeave is a motion-centric future-dynamics framework for action-chunk prediction in VLA models, using action-conditioned motion grounding and horizon-residual motion cues to improve control-relevant future supervision, achieving 75.3% average success on six MetaWorld tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA world-model approaches predict future images/videos that contain control-irrelevant appearance, and rely on holistic future visual representations plus shared global action features, which fail to capture timestep-specific correspondence between actions and local visual changes.
AI.method: Two modules: (1) Action-Induced Motion Grounder (AIMG) conditions on action and proprioceptive representations to build horizon-specific queries that localize interaction regions for each future action timestep from current visual tokens; (2) Horizon Residual Composer (HRC) computes differences between interaction representations at adjacent horizons, encodes them as temporal motion cues, and injects them into action tokens via a gated residual. Training uses KL-based motion-grounding supervision built from robot-arm masks rendered from future frames; inference uses only the current observation.
AI.result: On six MetaWorld tasks, MotionWeave achieves 75.3% average success rate, an absolute improvement of 8.6% over π0 (66.7%), with particular gains on sustained-interaction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Motion-centric, timestep-specific future dynamics supervision improves action-chunk prediction in VLA models, outperforming strong baselines without requiring future observations at inference.

title: Fyan: A Human--AI Harness with Semantic Auditing for Document-Level Formalization
summary: We present FYAN, a human--AI harness for document-level mathematical formalization. Rather than treating theorems in isolation, FYAN coordinates an end-to-end workflow spanning specification, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof construction, knowledge curation, and validation, with support for independent supervision and human guidance. A central component is evidence-grounded semantic auditing, which assesses whether formal statements faithfully preserve their informal specifications. A language model constructs structured evidence over local correspondences, omissions, scope, and logical relations, while a deterministic validator checks this evidence and produces reproducible judgments. When a substantive but admissible deviation is accepted, FYAN requires an explicit proof-transfer obligation connecting the formal statement back to a source-facing interpretation. With the same model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) in every stage, FYAN proves 86 of 143 FormalTCS theorems under a strict Lean check, against 69 for a general agent harness, and raises the natural-language proof score from 0.501 to 0.851. On ConsistencyCheck, its semantic audit catches more inconsistent statements than a direct LLM judge, both on labels verified against the source (recall 0.777 vs. 0.636) and on the original labels (0.873 vs. 0.820), and localizes each mismatch it reports to a specific hypothesis, conclusion, or scope. FYAN also built ODENumLib, a 9,355-line Lean library for the numerical analysis of ordinary differential equation.

AI.tldr: FYAN is a human–AI harness for document-level mathematical formalization that integrates specification, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof construction, knowledge curation, and validation. Its evidence-grounded semantic auditing component checks whether formal statements preserve informal specifications, and when admissible deviations are accepted, it enforces an explicit proof-transfer obligation. With the same model across all stages, FYAN proves 86/143 FormalTCS theorems under strict Lean checking (vs. 69 for a general agent harness), improves the natural-language proof score from 0.501 to 0.851, outperforms a direct LLM judge on ConsistencyCheck, and produced ODENumLib, a 9,355-line Lean library for ODE numerical analysis.
AI.motivation: Document-level mathematical formalization is not merely a collection of isolated theorem-proving tasks. It requires coordinated specification, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof construction, knowledge curation, and validation. Existing approaches often treat theorems in isolation, lacking end-to-end workflow support, independent supervision, and human guidance. A key risk is that formal statements may fail to faithfully preserve their informal specifications, so there is a need for semantic auditing and reproducible validation.
AI.method: FYAN coordinates an end-to-end workflow spanning specification, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof construction, knowledge curation, and validation, with support for independent supervision and human guidance. Its central component is evidence-grounded semantic auditing: a language model constructs structured evidence over local correspondences, omissions, scope, and logical relations, while a deterministic validator checks this evidence and produces reproducible judgments. When a substantive but admissible deviation is accepted, FYAN requires an explicit proof-transfer obligation connecting the formal statement back to a source-facing interpretation.
AI.result: With the same model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) in every stage, FYAN proves 86 of 143 FormalTCS theorems under a strict Lean check, versus 69 for a general agent harness, and raises the natural-language proof score from 0.501 to 0.851. On ConsistencyCheck, its semantic audit catches more inconsistent statements than a direct LLM judge, both on labels verified against the source (recall 0.777 vs. 0.636) and on the original labels (0.873 vs. 0.820), and localizes each reported mismatch to a specific hypothesis, conclusion, or scope. FYAN also built ODENumLib, a 9,355-line Lean library for the numerical analysis of ordinary differential equations.
AI.conclusion: FYAN demonstrates that a human–AI harness with evidence-grounded semantic auditing can improve document-level mathematical formalization in both proof success and natural-language proof quality compared with a general agent harness, while providing more reliable and localized inconsistency detection than a direct LLM judge. It also shows the approach can support construction of a substantial Lean library (ODENumLib, 9,355 lines) for ODE numerical analysis.

title: Beyond the Current Scene: Event-Referential Grasping with Active View Selection
summary: A robot that observes people interacting with objects should be able to carry out later requests that refer back to those interactions. Such requests may specify a grasp target by the role it played in a past event rather than by its name or appearance. Moreover, the target may no longer be visible when the robot is asked to act. We present BeyondSCe, a zero-shot robotic grasping system for this event-referential setting. Given the event history and the current scene, the system identifies the requested object or part and localizes it for grasping. If the target is occluded, it combines an event prior recovered from the history with current scene geometry to select camera viewpoints likely to reveal the target. The system uses pretrained models without additional task-specific training. In real-robot experiments with a single wrist-mounted RGB-D camera, it achieves grasp success rates of 76% and 77% for initially visible and occluded targets, respectively, compared with 40% and 55% for the strongest baseline in each condition. On four additional scenes with heavy occlusion, it increases grasp success rates from 75% to 95% while reducing the mean number of views from 3.35 to 2.20, compared with an active-perception baseline given the target's ground-truth 3D bounding box.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BeyondSCe, a zero-shot robotic grasping system that resolves event-referential requests, including when the target is occluded, by combining an event prior from interaction history with current scene geometry to select revealing viewpoints, using only pretrained models.
AI.motivation: Robots observing people interacting with objects should later handle requests that refer to a grasp target by the role it played in a past event rather than by name or appearance, and the target may be invisible at request time. Existing grasping approaches generally assume targets are specified by appearance or name and are visible, leaving event-referential and occlusion-aware grasping unaddressed.
AI.method: BeyondSCe is a zero-shot system using pretrained models without task-specific training. Given the event history and current scene, it identifies the requested object or part by its event role and localizes it for grasping. When the target is occluded, it fuses an event prior recovered from the history with current scene geometry to select camera viewpoints likely to reveal the target; experiments use a single wrist-mounted RGB-D camera on a real robot.
AI.result: In real-robot experiments, BeyondSCe achieves grasp success rates of 76% for initially visible and 77% for occluded targets, versus 40% and 55% for the strongest baseline in each condition. On four additional heavily occluded scenes, it raises grasp success from 75% to 95% while reducing mean views from 3.35 to 2.20, compared with an active-perception baseline given the target's ground-truth 3D bounding box.
AI.conclusion: BeyondSCe enables zero-shot, event-referential robotic grasping and robustly handles occluded targets by integrating past-interaction priors with current scene geometry for viewpoint selection, outperforming strong baselines in both success rate and perception efficiency.

title: Effective Does Not Mean Useful: Conditional Functional Substitutability for Redundancy and Scaling in Transformers
summary: Modern neural networks scale predictably, yet the mechanisms behind these regularities remain unclear. Neural redundancy is typically characterized by component importance or representational similarity, both indirect proxies. We view redundancy as an input-conditioned, dynamic relation: intermediate computational states are functionally redundant when they induce similar downstream responses. We introduce Conditional Functional Substitutability (CFS) to directly characterize such functional substitution. CFS exposes functional relations and reduction potential missed by conventional importance- and similarity-based measures. Across modalities and Transformer families, CFS reveals systematic functional reorganization with scale. Controlled scaling further shows that performance gains need not track growth in substitutability, while fixed-capacity models with more independent functional structure perform better, providing a functional account of diminishing returns. Predicted CFS further enables dynamic computation with a better performance--computation trade-off than importance-based component selection, suggesting new directions for redundancy-aware computation and more efficient model scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Conditional Functional Substitutability (CFS), an input-conditioned, dynamic measure that identifies redundant intermediate computational states by whether they induce similar downstream responses, revealing functional reorganization with scale and enabling more efficient dynamic computation.
AI.motivation: Modern neural networks scale predictably, but the mechanisms behind these regularities are unclear. Existing notions of neural redundancy rely on indirect proxies—component importance or representational similarity—which fail to capture true functional relations and reduction potential.
AI.method: The authors formalize redundancy as an input-conditioned, dynamic relation and propose Conditional Functional Substitutability (CFS), which directly characterizes functional substitution by measuring whether intermediate computational states induce similar downstream responses.
AI.result: Across modalities and Transformer families, CFS exposes functional relations and reduction potential missed by importance- and similarity-based measures, and reveals systematic functional reorganization with scale. Controlled scaling shows performance gains need not track growth in substitutability, while fixed-capacity models with more independent functional structure perform better. Predicted CFS also yields a better performance–computation trade-off in dynamic computation than importance-based component selection.
AI.conclusion: CFS provides a functional account of diminishing returns and suggests new directions for redundancy-aware computation and more efficient model scaling.

title: RoboAssist: Interactive Human-Humanoid Planning for Long-Horizon Surgical Assistance
summary: Long-horizon surgical assistance requires humanoid robots to coordinate with evolving human activities while maintaining safety across planning and execution. We present RoboAssist, an agent-based framework for interactive human-humanoid planning that integrates workflow reasoning, task coordination, and cross-layer safety. At its core is an asymmetric dual-track representation that separates partially observed human process states from executable robot task sequences. By updating human-process estimates, scene context, and task dependencies online, RoboAssist revalidates the remaining task sequence and replans only the affected suffix when workflow requests change. A cross-layer safety architecture combines preventive navigation regulation, reactive regulation during close-range handover, and independent whole-body runtime supervision. This design couples online task coordination with safety constraints throughout execution. We demonstrate the framework on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot in long-horizon, multi-stage simulated surgical assistance scenarios encompassing multimodal interaction, instrument handling, medical material transport, navigation, and safe human-robot handover. Experiments show multi-stage task completion and adaptation to workflow-request changes. A targeted full-replanning ablation shows that residual replanning reduces plan-update latency and post-update token usage. Separate safety experiments demonstrate complementary protection across navigation, handover, and runtime supervision. Additional results and demonstrations are available online at https://roboassist.github.io.

AI.tldr: RoboAssist is an agent-based framework enabling interactive human-humanoid planning for long-horizon surgical assistance, combining workflow reasoning, task coordination, and cross-layer safety, validated on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon surgical assistance demands humanoid robots coordinate with evolving human activities while maintaining safety across both planning and execution, a challenge existing approaches do not fully address.
AI.method: The framework centers on an asymmetric dual-track representation separating partially observed human process states from executable robot task sequences. It updates human-process estimates, scene context, and task dependencies online, revalidating the remaining task sequence and replanning only the affected suffix when workflow requests change. A cross-layer safety architecture integrates preventive navigation regulation, reactive regulation during close-range handover, and independent whole-body runtime supervision.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid in long-horizon, multi-stage simulated surgical assistance scenarios (multimodal interaction, instrument handling, material transport, navigation, safe handover). Experiments show multi-stage task completion and adaptation to workflow-request changes; a full-replanning ablation shows residual replanning reduces plan-update latency and post-update token usage; separate safety experiments show complementary protection across navigation, handover, and runtime supervision.
AI.conclusion: RoboAssist effectively couples online task coordination with safety constraints throughout execution, achieving adaptive long-horizon humanoid surgical assistance with layered safety guarantees.

title: ANI: Adaptive Numerical Injection for Unifying Semantic and Arithmetic Representations in Numerical Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 16 pages, 7 figures. Code available at https://github.com/Jinsung-Jeon/ANI_EMNLP
summary: Precise numerical reasoning with Large Language Models (LLMs) is essential for expanding their applicability to complex real-world tasks. However, text-based tokenization often fragments numbers, significantly hindering precise arithmetic reasoning. Meanwhile, numerical embeddings, despite arithmetic precision, rely on context-agnostic substitution that disregards the semantic role of numbers as identifiers. To combine the complementary strengths, we propose \textbf{ANI (Adaptive Numerical Injection)}, a hybrid framework that governs the selective injection of numerical features based on the semantic context. By employing a context-aware gating mechanism, we selectively inject numerical embeddings (specifically FoNE) into the latent space, explicitly preserving nominal identifiers while enhancing quantitative operands. Through extensive evaluations across various LLMs, we demonstrate that ANI enhances MATH performance by 9.5 points over the official reference model, while maintaining robust performance on general linguistic benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ANI is a hybrid framework that selectively injects numerical embeddings (FoNE) into LLMs via context-aware gating, improving MATH performance by 9.5 points while preserving general linguistic ability.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with precise numerical reasoning: text-based tokenization fragments numbers and impedes arithmetic, while numerical embeddings, though arithmetically precise, use context-agnostic substitution that ignores numbers' semantic role as identifiers. The goal is to combine the complementary strengths of both approaches.
AI.method: The paper proposes ANI (Adaptive Numerical Injection), a hybrid framework that governs selective injection of numerical features based on semantic context. A context-aware gating mechanism selectively injects numerical embeddings (specifically FoNE) into the latent space, explicitly preserving nominal identifiers while enhancing quantitative operands.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across various LLMs show that ANI improves MATH performance by 9.5 points over the official reference model, while maintaining robust performance on general linguistic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ANI demonstrates that context-aware selective injection of numerical embeddings effectively enhances precise arithmetic reasoning in LLMs without sacrificing general language capabilities.

title: UniWAM Technical Report: Unified Mobile Manipulation via Mixed-Stream World-Action Modeling and Manipulation Anchor Pose Supervision
summary: Mobile manipulation requires precise navigation to a manipulation-ready pose followed by reliable object interaction. These two stages differ in action spaces and visual requirements, which complicates unified policy learning. In addition, collecting diverse real-world navigation data with explicit manipulation-ready pose supervision remains costly and difficult to scale. We introduce UniWAM, a unified mixed-stream world-action model with separate action encoders and output heads for navigation and manipulation, sharing a common backbone. This design supports joint representation learning on independently sampled navigation and manipulation data. UniWAM supports independent inference for either stream and batch-parallel inference for both. We further introduce Manipulation Anchor Pose (MAP) supervision for where to stop and how to orient for manipulation. An automated pipeline constructs MAP-Data from large-scale 3D scenes, yielding over 1.5 million episodes and 7,500 hours. MAP-Data provides per-frame target-object bounding boxes and image-plane MAP coordinates as auxiliary navigation supervision. Together with projected end-effector trajectories for manipulation, these prediction targets provide stream-specific image-plane supervision for action learning from egocentric observations. With large-scale MAP-Data, UniWAM outperforms the strongest external baselines on our MAP-Bench by 30.1\% in position error and 44.0\% in heading error. Across 24 real-robot tasks, UniWAM achieves leading results in MAP navigation and mobile manipulation, with competitive manipulation performance. We have released code, data, and benchmark.

AI.tldr: UniWAM is a unified mixed-stream world-action model with separate action encoders/heads for navigation and manipulation sharing a common backbone, trained on 1.5M+ auto-generated MAP-Data episodes, achieving leading results on MAP navigation and mobile manipulation across 24 real-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Mobile manipulation couples navigation to a manipulation-ready pose with reliable object interaction, but the two stages differ in action spaces and visual requirements, complicating unified policy learning. Additionally, collecting diverse real-world navigation data with explicit manipulation-ready pose supervision is costly and hard to scale.
AI.method: UniWAM uses a shared backbone with separate action encoders and output heads for navigation and manipulation, enabling joint representation learning on independently sampled data and supporting both independent and batch-parallel inference. It introduces Manipulation Anchor Pose (MAP) supervision (where to stop, how to orient), with an automated pipeline building MAP-Data from large-scale 3D scenes (1.5M+ episodes, 7,500 hours) that supplies per-frame target-object bounding boxes and image-plane MAP coordinates as auxiliary navigation supervision, alongside projected end-effector trajectories for stream-specific image-plane supervision from egocentric observations.
AI.result: On MAP-Bench, UniWAM beats the strongest external baselines by 30.1% in position error and 44.0% in heading error. Across 24 real-robot tasks, it achieves leading results in MAP navigation and mobile manipulation, with competitive manipulation performance. Code, data, and benchmark are released.
AI.conclusion: A unified mixed-stream world-action architecture with stream-specific encoders/heads plus large-scale MAP supervision enables effective joint learning of navigation and manipulation, delivering strong transfer to real-robot mobile manipulation.

title: MiniRep: Robust Reputation-Based Aggregation for Multi-Agent Debate
summary:
Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving into an open agentic ecosystem. To support trustworthy collaboration, industry initiatives increasingly assess agent reputation from past behavior and provide performance leaderboards. However, reputation derived from past performance may not reliably predict an agent's behavior on new tasks, particularly when malicious agents can adapt their behavior and influence other agents during collaboration.
  We study reputation in multi-agent debate (MAD), where multiple agents answer the same query, debate to improve their answers, and aggregate them into a final output. We present MiniRep, a reputation-based aggregation system for MAD under malicious agents. To ground our threat model in established research, we construct an attack taxonomy drawing on reputation-system attacks and software-testing mutation operators, covering strategic exploitation of reputation and subtle corruption of agent proposals. Guided by this taxonomy, MiniRep evaluates agents based on both their behavior on the current task and their reputation over time, while preventing groups of agents with highly similar responses from dominating the final decision. We assess MiniRep across diverse tasks, LLM-agent compositions, corruption placements, and attack types drawn from our taxonomy. Our experimental results show that, MiniRep outperforms both conventional MAD aggregation and conventional reputation-based approaches on MATH no matter being attacked or not. Also, under a heterogeneous 10-agent setting on MATH, MiniRep outperforms all baselines in all 28 attack conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MiniRep, a reputation-based aggregation system for multi-agent debate (MAD) that defends against malicious agents by combining current-task behavior with long-term reputation, and preventing highly similar response groups from dominating decisions.
AI.motivation: Agent reputation and leaderboards derived from past performance may fail to predict behavior on new tasks, especially when malicious agents adapt their strategies and influence collaborators. This gap motivates a more robust reputation mechanism for multi-agent collaboration.
AI.method: The authors ground their threat model in a taxonomy built from reputation-system attacks and software-testing mutation operators, covering strategic exploitation of reputation and subtle corruption of agent proposals. Guided by this taxonomy, MiniRep evaluates agents using both current-task behavior and reputation over time, while preventing groups of highly similar responses from dominating the final decision. Evaluation spans diverse tasks, LLM-agent compositions, corruption placements, and attack types.
AI.result: MiniRep outperforms conventional MAD aggregation and conventional reputation-based approaches on MATH, whether or not attacks occur. In a heterogeneous 10-agent setting on MATH, it outperforms all baselines across all 28 attack conditions.
AI.conclusion: Reputation in MAD should integrate dynamic, task-specific behavior with longitudinal signals and redundancy control to remain robust under adversarial conditions. MiniRep demonstrates consistent gains, suggesting taxonomy-guided reputation aggregation is a promising direction for trustworthy agent ecosystems.

title: IronMind: Scaling Humanoid Dexterous Manipulation via Camera-Space Ego-Centric Pretraining
summary: Egocentric human video offers a scalable data source for dexterous manipulation, yet using it to train humanoid robots presents two challenges: (1) an embodiment gap, as human hands differ structurally from robot end-effectors and low-cost egocentric recordings lack the torso kinematics required by conventional retargeting; and (2) heterogeneous data quality, including noisy hand-pose tracking and weakly aligned text annotations. We introduce IronMind, a vision-language-action (VLA) model that uses egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot data to pretrain policies for humanoid dexterous manipulation. To bridge the embodiment gap, IronMind bypasses explicit body-retargeting by using a camera-space action representation, the native reference space of egocentric video, and semantically aligning robot and human action dimensions. Across total pretraining budgets from 250 to 10,000 hours, validation loss decreases approximately log-linearly with data scale. Larger pretraining budgets also improve out-of-distribution real-robot manipulation after post-training: across six challenging tasks with unseen objects, affordances, and reasoning prompts, the 10,000-hour model achieves a 55.0% success rate, compared with at most 11.7% for every pretraining budget up to 5,000 hours and 5.0% without pretraining. At the same pretraining budget, the camera-space action representation also outperforms the torso-frame baseline. Together, these findings support pretraining with a camera-space action representation on large-scale human egocentric data as a scalable foundation for humanoid robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: IronMind is a VLA model that pretrains humanoid dexterous manipulation policies from egocentric human video plus heterogeneous robot data using a camera-space action representation, achieving 55.0% success on six challenging real-robot tasks after 10,000 hours of pretraining.
AI.motivation: Egocentric human video is a scalable data source for dexterous manipulation, but training humanoid robots from it faces two obstacles: an embodiment gap (human hands vs. robot end-effectors, plus missing torso kinematics in low-cost egocentric recordings that defeats conventional retargeting) and heterogeneous data quality (noisy hand-pose tracking, weakly aligned text annotations).
AI.method: IronMind bypasses explicit body-retargeting by adopting a camera-space action representation—the native reference space of egocentric video—and semantically aligning robot and human action dimensions. It is pretrained on egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot data across budgets of 250 to 10,000 hours, then post-trained to real-robot manipulation.
AI.result: Validation loss decreases approximately log-linearly with data scale. After post-training, the 10,000-hour model reaches 55.0% success across six challenging tasks with unseen objects, affordances, and reasoning prompts, versus at most 11.7% for budgets up to 5,000 hours and 5.0% without pretraining. At equal budget, camera-space actions outperform a torso-frame baseline.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining with a camera-space action representation on large-scale human egocentric data provides a scalable foundation for humanoid robot manipulation.

title: WorkGenesis: Building the Worlds That Teach Agents to Work
summary: The ability of Large Language Model (LLM) agents to complete daily and professional work is receiving increasing attention. Training such agents requires realistic work scenarios. Expert-authored occupational work is costly and slow to produce, while unconstrained synthesis often yields tasks with weak factual grounding or internally inconsistent requirements. To bridge this gap, we introduce WorkGenesis, a framework that constructs executable occupational work from real-world artifacts through two core technical innovations: (1) Evidence-Based Work Construction, which grounds each unit of work in real-world evidence by retrieving public files guided by O*NET occupational knowledge and synthesizing the surrounding context, companion materials, work request, and itemwise rubric around them; and (2) Execution-Guided Consistency Verification, which renders a reference deliverable inside the constructed work, attributes every unsatisfied rubric item to the agent, the task, or the rubric, and uses task and rubric defects as feedback to iteratively repair the work until it passes the audit. Experimental results demonstrate that Fx-Work-35B, trained with simple supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on only 20K units of work synthesized by WorkGenesis, achieves the highest scores among all comparable-scale baselines on the five reported metrics across GDPvalAA-v2, APEX-Agents-AA, and JobBench (31.00 versus 24.79 average score), and even surpasses frontier models such as the 1.6T DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview. These results show that WorkGenesis provides scalable training data for working agents.

AI.tldr: WorkGenesis synthesizes executable occupational work from real-world artifacts to train LLM work agents, using evidence-grounded task construction and execution-guided consistency verification; a 35B model trained on 20K such units outperforms comparable baselines and even frontier models.
AI.motivation: Training LLM agents for daily and professional work requires realistic work scenarios, but expert-authored occupational work is costly and slow, while unconstrained synthesis produces tasks with weak factual grounding or internally inconsistent requirements. A gap therefore exists between scalability and realism/consistency in agent training data.
AI.method: WorkGenesis builds executable occupational work from real-world artifacts via two innovations: (1) Evidence-Based Work Construction, which retrieves public files guided by O*NET occupational knowledge and synthesizes surrounding context, companion materials, work request, and itemwise rubric grounded in that evidence; and (2) Execution-Guided Consistency Verification, which renders a reference deliverable, attributes each unsatisfied rubric item to the agent, task, or rubric, and iteratively repairs the work using task and rubric defects as feedback until it passes the audit.
AI.result: Fx-Work-35B, trained with simple SFT on only 20K synthesized work units, achieves the highest scores among comparable-scale baselines across five reported metrics on GDPvalAA-v2, APEX-Agents-AA, and JobBench (31.00 vs. 24.79 average score), and surpasses frontier models such as the 1.6T DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview.
AI.conclusion: WorkGenesis provides scalable, realistically grounded training data for working agents, enabling substantial gains from modest supervised fine-tuning data.

title: Communication-Free Distributed Multi-Robot Task Allocation under Partial Observations Using Labeled Multi-Bernoulli Filtering
comment: This paper has been submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027 for possible publication
summary: This paper proposes a communication-free multi-robot task allocation framework based solely on local observations. In this study, tasks are defined as reaching target locations. Each robot estimates the positions of neighboring robots using a Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (LMB) filter and independently assigns tasks through a greedy auction-based strategy. By continuously updating state estimates and reallocating tasks during execution, the proposed method enables decentralized coordination without explicit communication. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the proposed method enables effective cooperative task allocation without inter-robot communication while remaining robust to measurement clutter and observation uncertainty.

AI.tldr: A communication-free multi-robot task allocation framework where each robot uses an LMB filter to estimate neighbor positions and performs greedy auction-based task assignment independently, achieving robust decentralized coordination through local observations only.
AI.motivation: Explicit inter-robot communication can be unreliable or unavailable in real deployments, yet effective cooperative task allocation typically relies on it. This work aims to remove that dependency by using local observations alone.
AI.method: Tasks are defined as reaching target locations. Each robot estimates neighboring robots' positions using a Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (LMB) filter and assigns tasks independently via a greedy auction-based strategy. Task allocation is repeatedly updated during execution based on continuously refreshed state estimates.
