AI.result: Monte Carlo simulations show the method achieves effective cooperative task allocation without inter-robot communication and remains robust to measurement clutter and observation uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized, communication-free coordination for multi-robot task allocation is feasible using LMB-based neighbor estimation combined with greedy auction assignment, providing robustness under noisy and cluttered sensing.

title: Understanding as No-Arbitrage: Bounded Dutch Books as a Definition and Training Objective for Language Models
summary: Does a language model merely predict tokens, or does it understand what it says? We make this question measurable by defining "understanding" through the lens of no-arbitrage. A model understands a vocabulary to a certain degree if a computationally bounded trader cannot extract guaranteed profit by betting against the model's probabilities on logically related claims (a "Dutch book"). We establish three theoretical results: first, because full logical coherence is computationally intractable, understanding is inherently graded, not absolute. Second, we prove that the exact optimum of standard next-token prediction is inherently incoherent across different question formats; the flaw lies in the training objective, not the architecture. Third, we show that uncertainty accumulates predictably along reasoning chains, making unjustified overconfidence an arbitrage opportunity in itself. To address this, we introduce Arbitr, a training framework where an adversarial trader penalizes the model for logical inconsistencies, paired with a calibration anchor to prevent uninformative collapse. Across five pre-registered experiments on Qwen2.5 and Phi-3.5 models, we demonstrate that standard models are highly exploitable across different phrasings. Arbitr reduces this exploitability by orders of magnitude without sacrificing task accuracy, and the effect successfully transfers to unseen logical patterns and new model families. Crucially, we uncover a scaling illusion: at 7B parameters, near-zero measured incoherence often coincides with extreme, unjustified confidence. We conclude that while Arbitr enforces rigorous logical consistency, coherence is a necessary condition for knowledge, but not a sufficient one

AI.tldr: The paper defines LM "understanding" via a no-arbitrage criterion (a bounded trader cannot build a Dutch book against the model) and proves three results: full coherence is intractable so understanding is graded; standard next-token training is inherently incoherent across question formats; and uncertainty accumulates along reasoning chains. It introduces Arbitr, an adversarial-trader training framework with a calibration anchor, which reduces exploitability by orders of magnitude on Qwen2.5 and Phi-3.5 without hurting accuracy, transfers to unseen patterns and new families, and reveals a "scaling illusion" where near-zero incoherence at 7B can mask extreme overconfidence.
AI.motivation: The question of whether a language model genuinely understands or merely predicts tokens is vague and hard to measure. The authors seek a rigorous, testable criterion for "understanding" that avoids vague introspection or behavioral anecdote, and they aim to locate whether failures of understanding stem from architecture or from the training objective.
AI.method: Understanding is operationalized through no-arbitrage: a model understands a vocabulary to a degree if a computationally bounded trader cannot extract guaranteed profit by betting against the model's probabilities on logically related claims (a Dutch book). The authors prove three theoretical results (graded understanding due to intractability of full coherence; incoherence across question formats is intrinsic to the standard next-token objective, not the architecture; predictable uncertainty accumulation along reasoning chains). They then propose Arbitr, a training framework in which an adversarial trader penalizes logical inconsistencies, paired with a calibration anchor to avoid uninformative collapse. Evaluation uses five pre-registered experiments on Qwen2.5 and Phi-3.5 models.
AI.result: Standard models are highly exploitable across different phrasings. Arbitr reduces exploitability by orders of magnitude without sacrificing task accuracy, and the effect transfers to unseen logical patterns and new model families. A "scaling illusion" is uncovered: at 7B parameters, near-zero measured incoherence often coincides with extreme, unjustified confidence.
AI.conclusion: Arbitr enforces rigorous logical consistency against adversarial arbitrage, but coherence is a necessary condition for knowledge, not a sufficient one—models can be made internally consistent without thereby possessing knowledge.

title: LIBERO-Agent: Evaluating General-Purpose Agents for Direct Embodied Manipulation
summary: General-purpose agents can plan, use tools, and revise their behavior from feedback, but it remains unclear whether these capabilities transfer from digital environments to embodied manipulation. To investigate this question, we introduce LIBERO-Agent, an agent-native benchmark for evaluating these agents in robot manipulation tasks. Rather than asking agents to submit task-level Python control programs or operate through high-level robot skills, LIBERO-Agent provides an interactive robotic environment where agents can select which observations to inspect, process them with their own tools, and issue native action commands. LIBERO-Agent integrates 200 tasks into a common interaction framework and provides a 30-task primary suite that separates perception, short-horizon execution, and long-horizon composition. Results reveal a pronounced reliability gap: while agents perform well on perception and easy short-horizon tasks, their performance degrades substantially on hard short-horizon and long-horizon tasks. Richer observations improve short-horizon manipulation, while demonstration benefits depend on the agent and format. Among these agents, GPT-6 Astra achieves the strongest overall performance. Further analysis shows its major advantage lies in mechanism interaction, especially when sustained physical contact is needed, while its remaining failures stem from cross-stage interference and geometric errors.

AI.tldr: LIBERO-Agent is an agent-native benchmark of 200 embodied manipulation tasks (with a 30-task core suite) that lets general-purpose agents interact directly with a robot environment by choosing observations, processing them with their own tools, and issuing native action commands, revealing a large reliability gap between perception and long-horizon manipulation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose agents can plan, use tools, and revise behavior from feedback, but it is unclear whether these capabilities transfer from digital environments to embodied manipulation. Existing evaluations either ask agents to submit task-level Python control programs or require operating through high-level robot skills, which does not test native agentic interaction in robotics.
AI.method: The authors introduce LIBERO-Agent, an interactive robotic environment where agents select which observations to inspect, process them using their own tools, and issue native action commands. It unifies 200 tasks in a common interaction framework and defines a 30-task primary suite that disentangles perception, short-horizon execution, and long-horizon composition.
AI.result: A pronounced reliability gap emerges: agents do well on perception and easy short-horizon tasks but degrade substantially on hard short-horizon and long-horizon tasks. Richer observations improve short-horizon manipulation, while demonstration benefits depend on the agent and format. GPT-6 Astra achieves the strongest overall performance, with its main advantage in mechanism interaction, especially when sustained physical contact is required; its remaining failures stem from cross-stage interference and geometric errors.
AI.conclusion: Agentic capabilities do not transfer uniformly to embodied manipulation: reliability breaks down as task horizon and execution difficulty increase. LIBERO-Agent provides an agent-native testbed for diagnosing these failures, and the analysis indicates that improving sustained contact interaction, reducing cross-stage interference, and correcting geometric errors are key directions for stronger embodied agents.

title: The Golden Path Hypothesis: Reusable Schedules in Diffusion Caching
summary: Diffusion caching accelerates generation by replacing transformer computation with cached or predicted features at selected denoising steps. We introduce the Golden Path Hypothesis (GPH): under fixed inference conditions, prompt-independent cache schedules can achieve final-output quality comparable to the best prompt-specific schedules across prompts. We investigate the GPH across ten caching methods, four image and video models, and three cache ratios. Prompt-adaptive methods repeatedly select a small number of schedules, and reusing their most frequent schedules on new prompts closely matches the quality of prompt-specific choices. Exhaustive evaluation of 1.4 million schedules on four examples further identifies prompt-independent schedules that remain competitive on unseen prompts. To explain this transfer, we analyze denoising trajectories and the accumulation of caching errors. Latent-state trajectories exhibit similar structures across datasets and seeds, while an exact error decomposition shows that accumulated effects of earlier errors predict final latent-state error better than local approximation errors. This motivates searching for end-to-end schedules using final-output quality. With only a small set of examples, the resulting golden paths transfer across prompts and datasets, and can be tuned to the desired quality objective, including reconstruction fidelity or perceptual similarity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Golden Path Hypothesis (GPH): under fixed inference conditions, prompt-independent cache schedules can match the quality of the best prompt-specific schedules. It validates this across ten caching methods, four image/video models, and three cache ratios, and explains the transfer via analysis of denoising trajectories and caching-error accumulation.
AI.motivation: Diffusion caching accelerates generation by replacing transformer computation with cached or predicted features at selected denoising steps. However, most high-quality schedules are prompt-specific, requiring per-prompt search or adaptive selection, which limits practical efficiency. The work asks whether a single prompt-independent schedule can achieve comparable quality, thereby simplifying deployment and removing prompt-level search overhead.
AI.method: The GPH is tested across ten caching methods, four image and video models, and three cache ratios. Prompt-adaptive methods are examined to show they repeatedly select a small number of schedules, and their most frequent schedules are reused on new prompts. An exhaustive evaluation of 1.4 million schedules over four examples identifies competitive prompt-independent schedules. To explain the transfer, the authors analyze denoising trajectories and perform an exact error decomposition, comparing the accumulated effects of earlier errors against local approximation errors. This motivates end-to-end schedule search using final-output quality.
AI.result: Reusing the most frequent schedules from prompt-adaptive methods closely matches the quality of prompt-specific choices. Exhaustive search over 1.4 million schedules yields prompt-independent schedules that remain competitive on unseen prompts. Latent-state trajectories exhibit similar structures across datasets and seeds, and accumulated earlier errors predict final latent-state error better than local approximation errors. Golden paths obtained from only a small set of examples transfer across prompts and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-independent golden paths are feasible and transferable, supporting the GPH. They can be tuned to a desired quality objective, including reconstruction fidelity or perceptual similarity, suggesting a practical route to efficient diffusion caching without per-prompt schedule search.

title: Discrete Forcing: Infusing Discrete Guidance into Continuous Denoising for Few-Step Action Experts
summary: Efficient action generation in vision-language-action (VLA) models requires capturing both coarse action structure and fine-grained details. Discrete action tokens provide compact structural representations but sacrifice precision, while continuous action tokens offer high precision but often require multiple denoising steps. We introduce Discrete Forcing, a flow-matching framework that combines these representations through an explicit coarse-to-fine generation process. It first predicts discrete action tokens to establish a coarse action structure, then uses them to guide continuous action refinement. The discrete and continuous components share a common diffusion transformer backbone with specialized branches, maintaining a parameter count comparable to a conventional single-branch model while requiring only one forward pass per branch. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate improved performance and faster inference over a parameter-matched continuous action expert, with consistent performance gains as model capacity increases. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improvements on high-precision and dynamic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Discrete Forcing is a flow-matching VLA framework that unifies discrete action tokens (coarse structure) and continuous action tokens (fine precision) via a coarse-to-fine process within a shared diffusion transformer backbone.
AI.motivation: Efficient action generation in VLA models must capture both coarse action structure and fine-grained details, but discrete tokens are compact yet imprecise, whereas continuous tokens are precise but need multiple denoising steps. A unified approach is needed to balance precision and efficiency.
AI.method: Discrete Forcing combines discrete and continuous action representations through an explicit coarse-to-fine generation process. It first predicts discrete action tokens to establish a coarse structure, then uses them to guide continuous action refinement. The discrete and continuous components share a common diffusion transformer backbone with specialized branches, keeping parameter count comparable to a single-branch model and requiring only one forward pass per branch.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks show improved performance and faster inference over a parameter-matched continuous action expert, with consistent gains as model capacity increases. Real-world experiments confirm improvements on high-precision and dynamic manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Discrete Forcing effectively unifies discrete and continuous action generation for VLA models, delivering a favorable precision-efficiency trade-off and scaling benefits, and validating practical gains in real-world manipulation.

title: On the Complexity of Preference-Based Bandits
summary: We study preference-based bandits with general reward function classes, where a learner sequentially selects pairs of arms and observes binary preference feedback governed by the Bradley--Terry model. This setting naturally arises in applications such as recommender systems, tournament ranking, and learning from human feedback, where relative preferences are easier to elicit than absolute rewards. The observation model inherits the logistic bandit challenge of handling the problem-dependent constant $κ$, which accounts for the non-linearity of the link function and can grow arbitrarily large. Moreover, prior work has predominantly focused on linear or kernelized reward models, precluding the use of richer function classes. To address these limitations, we consider general reward function classes and introduce the \emph{locally sensitive eluder dimension}, a novel complexity measure tailored to the logistic structure of preference feedback that yields fine-grained regret guarantees without unfavorable dependence on $κ$. Building on this notion, we propose \textbf{GINOP} (Generic INformative OPtimism), an algorithm that constructs log-loss confidence sets and jointly selects arm pairs to balance optimism and informative exploration. We establish a first-order regret bound that, in contrast with what previous results suggest, demonstrates that learning with preference feedback is as statistically efficient as learning from direct reward observation. Finally, we corroborate our theoretical findings with empirical evaluations against competitive baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper studies preference-based bandits with general reward function classes under the Bradley-Terry model, introduces a novel complexity measure (locally sensitive eluder dimension) and the GINOP algorithm, achieving first-order regret bounds without unfavorable dependence on the logistic constant κ, showing preference feedback can be as statistically efficient as direct reward observation.
AI.motivation: Preference feedback arises in recommender systems, tournament ranking, and learning from human feedback, where relative preferences are easier to elicit than absolute rewards. However, the logistic (Bradley-Terry) observation model suffers from the problem-dependent constant κ, which grows arbitrarily large and degrades regret. Moreover, prior work is largely restricted to linear or kernelized reward models, excluding richer function classes.
AI.method: The authors consider general reward function classes and introduce the locally sensitive eluder dimension, a complexity measure tailored to the logistic structure of preference feedback that yields fine-grained regret guarantees without unfavorable κ dependence. Building on this, they propose GINOP (Generic INformative OPtimism), which constructs log-loss confidence sets and jointly selects arm pairs to balance optimism and informative exploration.
AI.result: The paper establishes a first-order regret bound showing that learning with preference feedback is as statistically efficient as learning from direct reward observation, contrary to what previous results suggested. Theoretical findings are corroborated by empirical evaluations against competitive baselines.
AI.conclusion: Preference-based bandits with general reward function classes can be learned efficiently without unfavorable dependence on κ, and relative preference feedback is no harder, statistically, than absolute reward observation. The locally sensitive eluder dimension and GINOP provide a principled framework extending preference-based learning beyond linear/kernelized models.

title: General Performance Guarantee for Human Torque Estimation-Based Task-Agnostic Assistive Exoskeleton Control
summary: Accurate human torque estimation is crucial for enabling task-agnostic control in robotic exoskeleton systems. However, estimation errors may cause mismatches between the robot assistance and the human intention, degrading controllability and task performance. In this paper, we address this issue by formally defining matched assistance as scenarios in which the robot positively contributes to human movement. Based on this definition, we develop a theoretical framework to design the robot's desired interaction torque that guarantees a lower bound on the matched assistance probability. Importantly, the proposed guarantee holds over the entire torque distribution, including unseen data beyond the training tasks. This provides our method with strong reliability and generalization, both of which are critical for effective exoskeleton control. The proposed strategy is implemented on the ABLE upper-limb exoskeleton and evaluated in a multi-task setup. Experimental results validate the theoretical guarantees and demonstrate that the proposed strategy achieves effective general performance across several tasks, guaranteeing movement smoothness while reducing human physical effort.

AI.tldr: This paper tackles torque estimation errors in exoskeleton control by formally defining "matched assistance" and designing a desired interaction torque that guarantees a lower bound on matched assistance probability across the entire torque distribution, with validation on the ABLE upper-limb exoskeleton.
AI.motivation: Accurate human torque estimation is essential for task-agnostic control in robotic exoskeletons. Estimation errors can cause mismatches between robot assistance and human intention, degrading controllability and task performance. Existing approaches lack guarantees on assistance quality, especially for unseen data beyond training tasks.
AI.method: The authors formally define matched assistance as scenarios where the robot positively contributes to human movement. Based on this definition, they develop a theoretical framework to design the robot's desired interaction torque that guarantees a lower bound on the matched assistance probability. The guarantee holds over the entire torque distribution, including unseen data beyond the training tasks. The strategy is implemented on the ABLE upper-limb exoskeleton and evaluated in a multi-task setup.
AI.result: Experimental results validate the theoretical guarantees and demonstrate that the proposed strategy achieves effective general performance across several tasks, guaranteeing movement smoothness while reducing human physical effort.
AI.conclusion: By providing a probabilistic lower bound on matched assistance that generalizes beyond training data, the proposed framework offers strong reliability and generalization for exoskeleton control, enabling effective multi-task assistance that improves movement smoothness and reduces human effort.

title: Autoresearch in Mixed-Integer Linear and Nonlinear Programming
summary: Despite recent progress in autoresearch, applying it to practical operations research problems, typically formulated as NP-hard mixed-integer linear or nonlinear programs (MILPs or MINLPs), remains challenging because effective research requires systematically managing competing ideas and long-horizon experimental trajectories. We introduce AutoMIP, a reusable agent skill for organizing long-horizon autoresearch in mixed-integer programming through idea pooling and algorithm tree search. AutoMIP maintains a persistent pool of complementary candidate ideas while organizing executable experiments into an algorithm tree, enabling the agent to preserve unexplored hypotheses, refine promising algorithms, and switch to alternative methodological directions based on historical states. On MILP and MINLP benchmark cohorts, AutoMIP achieves the highest final success rates among the evaluated autoresearch frameworks. On MIPLib, AutoMIP discovers new best solutions for 31 of 60 instances, surpassing existing autoresearch frameworks. On MINLPLib, it achieves new best solutions for 52 of 60 instances. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary contributions of idea pooling and algorithm tree search, highlighting the importance of jointly maintaining diverse research ideas and structured experimental trajectories for long-horizon autoresearch.

AI.tldr: AutoMIP is a reusable agent skill that organizes long-horizon autoresearch for mixed-integer programming via idea pooling and algorithm tree search, achieving top success rates and new best solutions on MIPLib and MINLPLib benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Applying autoresearch to practical operations research problems (NP-hard MILPs/MINLPs) remains challenging because effective research requires systematically managing competing ideas and long-horizon experimental trajectories.
AI.method: AutoMIP maintains a persistent pool of complementary candidate ideas while organizing executable experiments into an algorithm tree, enabling the agent to preserve unexplored hypotheses, refine promising algorithms, and switch to alternative methodological directions based on historical states.
AI.result: On MILP and MINLP benchmark cohorts, AutoMIP achieves the highest final success rates among evaluated autoresearch frameworks. On MIPLib, it discovers new best solutions for 31 of 60 instances; on MINLPLib, it achieves new best solutions for 52 of 60 instances. Ablation studies show complementary contributions of idea pooling and algorithm tree search.
AI.conclusion: Jointly maintaining diverse research ideas and structured experimental trajectories is important for long-horizon autoresearch, and AutoMIP operationalizes this through idea pooling and algorithm tree search.

title: Sparse Planner: A Hybrid Planner for Efficient Sampling via a Conditional Variational Autoencoder
summary:
Trajectory planning is a core component of autonomous driving systems, where real-time performance and solution quality directly affect safety and reliability. Sample-Based Motion Planning (SBMP) is widely adopted for its ability to approximate near-optimal solutions through parameter space sampling. However, achieving high-quality trajectories typically requires dense sampling, leading to substantial computational overhead and significant runtime variability in complex traffic scenarios.
  To address this limitation, we propose a Sparse Planner (SP) that improves sampling efficiency by learning the conditional relationship between scene context and effective trajectory parameters using a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE). By modeling the structure of high-quality sampling distributions, SP directly generates cost-effective samples in the parameter space, significantly reducing the required sampling density while preserving solution quality.
  Experimental results show that SP achieves lower trajectory cost than the state-of-the-art FISS+ planner while using only one-eighth of the sampling density. In addition, SP demonstrates improved distance-keeping capability in obstacle-rich scenarios and maintains reduced and more stable runtime characteristics, indicating enhanced computational efficiency and predictable runtime behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Sparse Planner (SP) using a Conditional Variational Autoencoder to learn the mapping from scene context to effective trajectory parameters, generating cost-effective samples in parameter space and cutting sampling density to one-eighth while achieving lower trajectory cost than FISS+.
AI.motivation: Sample-Based Motion Planning offers near-optimal trajectories via parameter space sampling, but high-quality results require dense sampling, incurring heavy computation and unstable runtime in complex traffic. A method is needed to boost sampling efficiency while keeping solution quality and predictable runtime.
AI.method: SP models the structure of high-quality sampling distributions and learns the conditional relationship between scene context and effective trajectory parameters with a CVAE. It then directly generates cost-effective samples in the parameter space, reducing sampling density and avoiding wasteful uniform sampling.
AI.result: SP attains lower trajectory cost than the state-of-the-art FISS+ planner while using only one-eighth the sampling density. It also improves distance-keeping in obstacle-rich scenarios and yields reduced, more stable runtime, indicating higher computational efficiency and predictable runtime behavior.
AI.conclusion: Learning context-conditioned trajectory parameter distributions via a CVAE enables sparse yet high-quality sampling, delivering better cost, obstacle-aware distance-keeping, and more stable runtime than dense-sampling baselines like FISS+.

title: EHR-RobustGym: Benchmarking and Training Agents for Robust Clinical Reasoning
summary: In hospital workflows, electronic health records (EHRs) are often noisy, and may not contain the evidence needed to confirm events or measurements referenced in a clinical query. Even when database retrieval succeeds, clinical agents can overlook such discrepancies and return plausible but unsupported answers. We introduce EHR-RobustGym, a scalable and interactive environment for evaluating and training robust clinical agents grounded in noisy EHRs. Built on MIMIC-IV hospital records (365K patients, 31 tables, and over 500M records), EHR-RobustGym comprises 5,486 Clean-Noise pairs spanning six clinical intents and both patient-level and population-level queries. The pairs test robustness to Record-level, Value-level, and Query-level noise, while interactive SQL/Python execution and outcome verification support trajectory collection and training. Evaluating multiple LLMs reveals substantial robustness gaps: average task success across proprietary and large-scale open-weight models drops from 62.2% on Clean questions to 37.9% on Noise questions. At k=4, pass^k consistency falls below 50% for most evaluated models, exposing instability in clinical task completion. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in EHR-RobustGym improve performance, with gains generalizing to five external EHR benchmarks. Together, these results position EHR-RobustGym as a testbed for evaluating and improving the evidence-grounded robustness of clinical agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EHR-RobustGym, an interactive environment built on MIMIC-IV for evaluating and training clinical agents on noisy EHR data, revealing substantial robustness gaps in LLMs and showing that SFT/RL within the environment improves robustness with generalization to external benchmarks.
AI.motivation: EHRs in hospital workflows are often noisy and may lack evidence needed to confirm events or measurements referenced in clinical queries. Even when database retrieval succeeds, clinical agents can overlook these discrepancies and return plausible but unsupported answers, making robustness evaluation and training necessary.
AI.method: EHR-RobustGym is a scalable, interactive environment built on MIMIC-IV (365K patients, 31 tables, over 500M records). It contains 5,486 Clean-Noise pairs across six clinical intents and patient-/population-level queries, testing Record-level, Value-level, and Query-level noise. It supports interactive SQL/Python execution, outcome verification, trajectory collection, and training (SFT and RL).
AI.result: Evaluating multiple LLMs shows large robustness gaps: average task success drops from 62.2% on Clean questions to 37.9% on Noise questions. At k=4, pass^k consistency falls below 50% for most models, indicating instability. SFT and RL in EHR-RobustGym improve performance, with gains generalizing to five external EHR benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: EHR-RobustGym serves as a testbed for evaluating and improving the evidence-grounded robustness of clinical agents, addressing the critical gap between plausible and supported clinical answers in noisy EHR settings.

title: ECHO-G: Embodied Co-speech Humanoid mOtion Generation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://echo-g-project.github.io/
summary: Generating full-body co-speech motion for humanoid robots requires coordinating speech prosody, linguistic content, and embodiment-specific motion. To this end, we present ECHO-G, a framework jointly conditioned on speech audio and timed transcripts. Its Speech-Grounded Diffusion Transformer (SGDiT) combines frame-aligned acoustic features with token-level linguistic context, preserving their distinct granularities. Trained with rectified flow matching, it models one-to-many utterance-motion relationships directly in robot space. To support training and evaluation, we introduce a BEAT2-derived audio-text-robot dataset and a benchmark covering co-speech characteristics, robot-motion quality, and runtime efficiency. Comparative evaluation supports direct robot-space generation over the evaluated human-motion generation and retargeting pipelines, while modality ablations highlight the benefits of joint audio-text conditioning. We further demonstrate deployment on a physical humanoid robot. A complementary video-rating study also favors joint conditioning over the alternatives. The dataset and training, inference, and evaluation code are available through our project page.

AI.tldr: ECHO-G is a framework generating full-body co-speech motion for humanoid robots by jointly conditioning on speech audio and timed transcripts via a Speech-Grounded Diffusion Transformer trained with rectified flow matching, and is validated by a new dataset, benchmark, and physical robot deployment.
AI.motivation: Full-body co-speech motion for humanoid robots must coordinate speech prosody, linguistic content, and embodiment-specific motion dynamics, a multi-modal, one-to-many problem that prior human-motion generation and retargeting pipelines do not directly address in robot space.
AI.method: ECHO-G jointly conditions on speech audio and timed transcripts. Its Speech-Grounded Diffusion Transformer (SGDiT) combines frame-aligned acoustic features with token-level linguistic context while preserving their distinct granularities. It is trained with rectified flow matching to model one-to-many utterance-motion relationships directly in robot space. A BEAT2-derived audio-text-robot dataset and a benchmark spanning co-speech characteristics, robot-motion quality, and runtime efficiency are introduced.
AI.result: Comparative evaluation shows direct robot-space generation outperforms the evaluated human-motion generation and retargeting pipelines. Modality ablations confirm the benefit of joint audio-text conditioning. Deployment on a physical humanoid robot is demonstrated, and a video-rating study favors joint conditioning over alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Jointly conditioning on speech audio and timed transcripts and generating directly in robot space yields superior co-speech robot motion. Dataset and training, inference, and evaluation code are released via the project page.

title: SkillFM: Generating Skills for LLM Agents via Latent Flow Matching
summary: Textual skills provide reusable guidance for large language model agents, but existing approaches often rely on manually curated skill banks or reinforcement learning with indirect and delayed feedback. We introduce SkillFM (Skill Flow Matching), a generative framework that synthesizes task-conditioned textual skills directly without test-time skill retrieval. Our framework combines a codec for encoding and reconstructing textual skills in a continuous latent space with a conditional flow model trained using improved MeanFlow. At inference time, the learned velocity field enables single-step latent sampling, and an LLM-based decoder converts the sampled representation into textual guidance for a frozen downstream agent. We evaluate the framework on embodied tasks, question answering, and web shopping. On ALFWorld and Search-QA, our method achieves the best overall performance among the compared vector-based skill approaches. Our analyses further demonstrate that latent skill generation is an effective alternative to retrieval-based skill augmentation. Our code and training skill libraries are available at https://github.com/lulushang999/SkillFM.

AI.tldr: SkillFM is a generative framework that synthesizes task-conditioned textual skills directly in a continuous latent space via a conditional flow model, avoiding test-time retrieval and manual skill banks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for equipping LLM agents with reusable textual skills rely on manually curated skill banks or reinforcement learning with indirect and delayed feedback, which limits scalability and guidance quality.
AI.method: SkillFM combines a codec that encodes and reconstructs textual skills in a continuous latent space with a conditional flow model trained using improved MeanFlow. At inference, the learned velocity field enables single-step latent sampling, and an LLM-based decoder converts the sampled representation into textual guidance for a frozen downstream agent.
AI.result: Evaluated on embodied tasks, question answering, and web shopping, SkillFM achieves the best overall performance among compared vector-based skill approaches on ALFWorld and Search-QA. Analyses show latent skill generation is an effective alternative to retrieval-based skill augmentation.
AI.conclusion: Task-conditioned textual skills can be generated directly in latent space rather than retrieved, offering an effective alternative to retrieval-based skill augmentation. Code and training skill libraries are released.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Predicate Learning for Semantic Safe Robot Control
summary: As robots are increasingly deployed in everyday environments, ensuring their safety has become a central challenge. Existing methods often encode safety requirements as opaque mathematical/logical formulations or dense cost functions. While effective in specific tasks, they remain difficult to interpret, tightly coupled to individual tasks, and offer limited insight into why a robot action is considered safe or unsafe. To address this limitation, we propose ``Neuro-Symbolic Predicate Learning for Semantic Safe Robot Control'' (NEUPRO), which leverages a differentiable reasoner that can learn reusable safety representations from human-specified safety knowledge. NEUPRO allows practitioners to express task-related safety requirements as transparent symbolic rules, while enabling gradients to propagate through these rules to a feature extractor that maps raw observations to safety-relevant concepts. As a result, the learned feature extractor is (softly) grounded in human-understandable semantics, supports transparent constraint evaluation, and is transferable across tasks. By coupling interpretability with differentiability, NEUPRO moves beyond opaque cost design toward reusable safety reasoning. To evaluate NEUPRO's capability, we collect and release REASON, the first real robot benchmark dataset for interpretable robot safety specification. Experiments on REASON show that NEUPRO learns safety-critical features that generalize across tasks, mitigate the interpretability limitations of conventional black-box cost formulations, and provide explicit explanations of safety violation.

AI.tldr: NEUPRO is a neuro-symbolic framework that learns reusable, interpretable safety representations from human-specified symbolic rules via a differentiable reasoner, and is evaluated on REASON, a new real-robot benchmark for interpretable safety specification.
AI.motivation: Safety in everyday robot deployment is a central challenge. Existing methods encode safety as opaque mathematical/logical formulations or dense cost functions, which are hard to interpret, tightly coupled to individual tasks, and give little insight into why an action is safe or unsafe.
AI.method: NEUPRO uses a differentiable reasoner to learn reusable safety representations from human-specified safety knowledge. Practitioners express task-related safety requirements as transparent symbolic rules, and gradients propagate through these rules to a feature extractor mapping raw observations to safety-relevant concepts, softly grounding the extractor in human-understandable semantics.
AI.result: Experiments on REASON, the first real-robot benchmark dataset for interpretable robot safety specification (collected and released by the authors), show that NEUPRO learns safety-critical features that generalize across tasks, mitigates interpretability limitations of black-box cost formulations, and provides explicit explanations of safety violations.
AI.conclusion: By coupling interpretability with differentiability, NEUPRO moves beyond opaque cost design toward reusable safety reasoning, enabling transparent constraint evaluation and transferable safety representations across tasks.

title: Experimental Experience Modeling for Autonomous Research
summary: Autonomous research agents can generate hypotheses and conduct experiments, but experimentation remains a major source of computational cost. A fundamental challenge is deciding which experiments are worth running, particularly when prior evidence is insufficient to resolve uncertainty. Yet current research agents lack a systematic way to leverage experimental experience when making such decisions. We introduce Experimental Experience Modeling (EEM), a framework for making informed experimental decisions by acquiring, reusing, and accumulating experimental experience. EEM extracts decision-relevant records from earlier experimental trajectories, distills them into reusable experience, and organizes them in an experience library. For a new experimental decision, EEM retrieves relevant historical experience and assesses whether it provides sufficient support for deciding whether a candidate direction warrants further investment. When historical experience is insufficient, EEM conducts a targeted, low-cost pilot experiment to acquire the missing decision-relevant experience on demand. It then combines this newly acquired experience with retrieved historical experience to determine whether the direction warrants full-scale evaluation, which requires substantial resources. The resulting experimental outcomes are further distilled into reusable experience, allowing the library to continually grow through iterative accumulation. Experiments on autonomous research benchmarks show that EEM improves research performance while reducing model interaction overhead, demonstrating the value of reusing accumulated experience and acquiring additional experience only when needed.

AI.tldr: EEM is a framework that enables autonomous research agents to make experimental decisions by acquiring, reusing, and accumulating experimental experience, improving research performance while reducing model interaction overhead.
AI.motivation: Autonomous research agents face high computational costs in experimentation, and a key challenge is deciding which experiments are worth running, especially when prior evidence is insufficient to resolve uncertainty. Current agents lack a systematic way to leverage past experimental experience for such decisions.
AI.method: EEM extracts decision-relevant records from prior experimental trajectories, distills them into reusable experience, and organizes them in an experience library. For a new decision, it retrieves relevant historical experience and assesses whether it sufficiently supports deciding if a candidate direction warrants further investment. If insufficient, it runs a targeted low-cost pilot experiment to acquire the missing experience on demand, then combines new and retrieved experience to decide whether full-scale evaluation is warranted. Outcomes are distilled back into reusable experience, enabling iterative library growth.
AI.result: Experiments on autonomous research benchmarks show that EEM improves research performance while reducing model interaction overhead.
AI.conclusion: EEM demonstrates the value of reusing accumulated experience and acquiring additional experience only when needed for informed experimental decision-making.

title: MVP-SLAM: Multi-Camera Visual-Inertial Floorplan-Prior SLAM
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Indoor building construction sites are demanding environments for visual SLAM, where variable lighting and repetitive, low-textured structures make the system drift over long trajectories, though structural elements such as walls remain distinguishable despite these conditions. These buildings are constructed according to their as-planned floor plans, available from the design phase, and although the actual as-built site can differ from this design, floor plans still provide a metric reference, both to localize the system in the building and to correct drift. Existing methods often use the floor plan to correct an already-built trajectory offline, and those that instead correct it online typically rely on depth sensors. We instead present MVP-SLAM, an online visual-inertial SLAM on two opposite-facing fisheye cameras that corrects drift from cameras alone by matching walls detected in its map to the floor plan, through a drift-aware policy. A multi-stage integration then turns each matched pair incrementally into a persistent correction, so the trajectory stays corrected and localized within the floor plan as it is built. MVP-SLAM was validated on the multi-floor construction sites of the Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge 2026, ranking 2nd of 22 teams in the Localization task (0.29 m mean RMSE) and 5th of 62 teams in the SLAM task (0.24 m), the top-ranked one in both tasks among those that operate online, integrate the floor plan, and localize within it.

AI.tldr: MVP-SLAM is an online visual-inertial SLAM system using two opposite-facing fisheye cameras that corrects drift by matching detected walls to the as-planned floor plan via a drift-aware policy, achieving top online performance on the Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge 2026 construction sites.
AI.motivation: Indoor construction sites challenge visual SLAM due to variable lighting and repetitive, low-textured structures, causing drift over long trajectories. Although structural elements like walls remain distinguishable, existing floor-plan-based correction methods are either offline or rely on depth sensors, leaving a gap for an online, camera-only solution.
AI.method: MVP-SLAM performs online visual-inertial SLAM with two opposite-facing fisheye cameras, correcting drift from cameras alone by matching walls detected in its map to the as-planned floor plan through a drift-aware policy. A multi-stage integration incrementally converts each matched pair into a persistent correction, keeping the trajectory corrected and localized within the floor plan as it is built.
AI.result: Validated on multi-floor construction sites of the Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge 2026, MVP-SLAM ranked 2nd of 22 teams in the Localization task (0.29 m mean RMSE) and 5th of 62 teams in the SLAM task (0.24 m). It was the top-ranked among systems that operate online, integrate the floor plan, and localize within it in both tasks.
AI.conclusion: MVP-SLAM demonstrates that online, camera-only floor-plan-based drift correction is feasible and competitive in demanding indoor construction environments, achieving leading results among comparable online, floor-plan-integrating systems.

title: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones?
summary: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? To answer this question, we first conduct preliminary experiments showing that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To understand these effects, we use controlled replay to isolate internal state changes specific to each problem-history pairing. Across different histories, these changes preserve similar relationships among current problems. To improve reasoning under retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). STAIR captures keys and values from earlier response generation in a fixed bank. It learns to redirect current queries when they read this bank during prompt processing. The base model remains frozen; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.

AI.tldr: STAIR introduces a small, trainable attention-redirection module (12,288 params) that reuses keys/values from earlier responses in a fixed bank to improve later-turn reasoning under retained history, boosting average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 points across three Qwen models and four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs often handle independent problems within a single conversation, yet it is unclear whether computation from earlier problems helps or harms solving new ones. Preliminary experiments show that retained history can both raise and lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain, motivating a controlled study and a method to exploit beneficial history.
AI.method: The authors use controlled replay to isolate internal state changes specific to each problem-history pairing, finding that across different histories these changes preserve similar relationships among current problems. They then propose STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse), which captures keys and values from earlier response generation in a fixed bank and learns to redirect current queries when they read this bank during prompt processing. The base model stays frozen, with only 12,288 parameters trained.
AI.result: Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history retained.
AI.conclusion: Retained history has problem-specific internal effects that can be systematically exploited; a lightweight, frozen-backbone attention redirection achieves substantial later-turn reasoning gains.

title: Text-to-3D Policy: Fine-Grained Language-Behavior Alignment for Unseen Specification Generalization
summary: 3D visuomotor policies provide a strong foundation for spatially precise manipulation, yet current text-to-3D policies struggle to follow unseen fine-grained behavioral specifications beyond those covered by demonstrations. We study this challenge as unseen specification generalization, where language specifies behaviorally significant variations, such as target position, displacement, or articulated state, that are absent from policy training. We find that pretrained language representations and conventional global behavior-language alignment capture coarse task semantics but often blur nearby specifications that require distinct behaviors. We introduce T3DP, a Text-to-3D Policy framework for fine-grained language-behavior alignment. Rather than compressing each instruction and demonstration into a single global embedding, T3DP preserves their local structures and establishes bidirectional token-level correspondence between linguistic elements and behavioral segments. This directly grounds subtle linguistic variations in the behavior components they affect, preventing closely related specifications from collapsing in the representation space. The resulting specification-sensitive language representation conditions a point-cloud-based 3D diffusion policy, enabling more precise control over unseen behavioral specifications without modifying the underlying policy architecture. Across Meta-World, ManiSkill, and RoboTwin, T3DP improves average held-out-specification success over global language-behavior alignment by +11.0-14.2 points, with gains on all 15 task families; on real-robot tasks, it further raises average success from 47.5% to 65.0% (+17.5 points). Representation and action-probe analyses show that fine-grained alignment better preserves specification geometry and action-relevant variation, linking local behavior grounding to downstream control.

AI.tldr: T3DP is a Text-to-3D policy framework that achieves fine-grained language-behavior alignment via bidirectional token-level correspondence, substantially improving generalization to unseen fine-grained behavioral specifications.
AI.motivation: Current text-to-3D visuomotor policies, despite offering spatially precise manipulation, fail to follow unseen fine-grained behavioral specifications such as target position, displacement, or articulated state that are absent from policy training. Pretrained language representations and conventional global behavior-language alignment capture only coarse task semantics and tend to blur nearby specifications that demand distinct behaviors.
AI.method: T3DP preserves the local structures of instructions and demonstrations instead of compressing each into a single global embedding, and establishes bidirectional token-level correspondence between linguistic elements and behavioral segments. This grounds subtle linguistic variations directly in the behavior components they affect, avoiding representation collapse among closely related specifications. The resulting specification-sensitive language representation conditions a point-cloud-based 3D diffusion policy without altering the underlying policy architecture.
AI.result: Across Meta-World, ManiSkill, and RoboTwin, T3DP improves average held-out-specification success over global language-behavior alignment by +11.0 to +14.2 points, with gains across all 15 task families. On real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 47.5% to 65.0% (+17.5 points). Representation and action-probe analyses show that fine-grained alignment better preserves specification geometry and action-relevant variation, linking local behavior grounding to downstream control.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, token-level language-behavior alignment enables more precise control over unseen behavioral specifications without modifying the policy architecture, outperforming global alignment across simulated and real-robot benchmarks by preserving specification geometry and action-relevant variation.

title: Advancing Entropy-Level Credit Assignment in RLVR via Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization
summary: Value-model-free RLVR methods such as GRPO assign uniform advantages to all tokens in a rollout, ignoring that tokens contribute unequally. Recent methods use token entropy as an importance proxy but compute it globally across the batch, conflating importance with prompt difficulty and positional trends. We argue that importance should instead be measured relative to the local context of each token. We introduce proximal entropy, a local measure of token importance relative to neighboring tokens, and prove it is invariant to both confounders. Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization (PEPO) uses it to weight per-token advantages and outperforms GRPO and entropy-based baselines on mathematical reasoning across Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. We also show the formulation generalizes to other algorithms where substituting proximal entropy into existing methods improves, and applying it to single-stream RL succeeds where global entropy fails.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces proximal entropy, a local, context-relative measure of token importance for value-model-free RLVR methods, and proposes PEPO, which weights per-token advantages using this measure, outperforming GRPO and entropy-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Value-model-free RLVR methods like GRPO assign uniform advantages to all tokens in a rollout, ignoring unequal token contributions. Existing entropy-based proxies compute importance globally across the batch, conflating it with prompt difficulty and positional trends, so importance should instead be measured relative to each token's local context.
AI.method: The authors propose proximal entropy, a local measure of token importance relative to neighboring tokens, and prove it is invariant to both prompt difficulty and positional confounders. They then introduce Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization (PEPO), which uses proximal entropy to weight per-token advantages.
AI.result: PEPO outperforms GRPO and entropy-based baselines on mathematical reasoning across Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The formulation also generalizes to other algorithms, improving existing methods when proximal entropy is substituted in, and applying it to single-stream RL succeeds where global entropy fails.
AI.conclusion: Measuring token importance locally relative to neighboring tokens, rather than globally across the batch, yields a confounder-invariant signal that improves advantage weighting and generalizes across algorithms and model scales.

title: Towards Agile Vision-Based Multi-UAV Flight: Revisiting State Estimation
comment: This work has been accepted to the IEEE for possible publication (IROS 2026)
summary: Agile multi-UAV flight requires accurate and low-latency onboard estimation of the kinematic states of neighboring UAVs for collision avoidance, motion coordination, etc. Most vision-based approaches rely on position-only measurements, inferring velocity and acceleration indirectly from displacement. We show that this introduces a fixed structural delay in the estimation of higher-order states, which limits the achievable agility. To address this, we propose to integrate tilt measurements, provided by a state-of-the-art visual detector, which inform about the thrust direction of co-planar multirotor UAVs. We benchmark four position-only and five pose-aware estimators, including a novel formulation of a linear thrust-constraining Kalman filter, on two real-world and one high-fidelity photorealistic simulated dataset over different levels of agility (3-21 m/s^2). In our setup, pose-aware estimation consistently reduces the average velocity and acceleration estimation errors by 40% and 57% across the three datasets with the proposed KF formulation outperforming the other estimators. Position-only filters exhibit a constant ~300 ms delay in acceleration step response independent of agility, whereas the tilt-constrained estimators operate near the physical response limit given by the camera frame-rate by observing the change in thrust direction before the displacement accumulates. In a closed-loop leader-follower simulated experiment with NMPC control, position-only estimation of the leader's state fails to facilitate stable hovering of the follower, while the proposed estimator enables tracking of lateral maneuvers exceeding 2g of acceleration.

AI.tldr: Vision-based estimation of neighboring multirotor UAV states suffers a fixed ~300 ms structural delay when using position-only measurements; integrating visual tilt (thrust-direction) measurements through a thrust-constraining Kalman filter reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 40% and 57% and enables closed-loop tracking of maneuvers exceeding 2g.
AI.motivation: Agile multi-UAV flight depends on accurate, low-latency onboard estimation of neighbors' kinematic states for collision avoidance and coordination. Existing vision-based methods rely on position-only measurements, deriving velocity and acceleration indirectly from displacement, which the authors argue imposes a fixed structural delay in higher-order state estimation that caps achievable agility.
AI.method: The authors incorporate tilt measurements from a state-of-the-art visual detector, which reveal the thrust direction of co-planar multirotor UAVs. They benchmark four position-only and five pose-aware estimators—including a novel linear thrust-constraining Kalman filter formulation—across two real-world datasets and one high-fidelity photorealistic simulated dataset, spanning agility levels of 3–21 m/s². A closed-loop leader-follower simulation with NMPC control is also conducted.
AI.result: Pose-aware estimation consistently cuts average velocity and acceleration errors by 40% and 57% across the three datasets, with the proposed KF formulation outperforming the others. Position-only filters show a constant ~300 ms delay in acceleration step response regardless of agility, whereas tilt-constrained estimators operate near the physical limit set by camera frame-rate by detecting thrust-direction changes before displacement accumulates. In closed loop, position-only estimation fails to support stable follower hovering, while the proposed estimator tracks lateral maneuvers exceeding 2g.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting visual tilt measurements resolves the structural latency of position-only neighbor-state estimation, and the proposed thrust-constraining Kalman filter yields superior accuracy and closed-loop agility, enabling stable tracking of high-acceleration maneuvers that position-only methods cannot support.

title: Inferring Causal Relations between Two Sequences of Events with Language Models
summary: Causal AI is a branch of Artificial Intelligence which helps understand and reason about cause and effect relationships, not just patterns or correlations. Causal discovery aims to infer elements of the underlying causal structure--often represented as a directed graph--from observational and, when available, interventional data. While causal discovery is the fundamental step for moving beyond mere associations toward genuine understanding, and thus the basic building block of causal AI, it becomes intrinsically difficult when causal relations must be inferred from single observations. In such situations, standard causal discovery methods cannot be used and one has to identify causal relations from limited amount of information. This is typically the case for, e.g., sequences of events produced by different alarms which need to be analyzed on the fly to detect abnormal phenomena, which are usually rare. We show in this study that it is possible to leverage the predictive power of Large Language Models (LLMs) to infer causal relations between only two sequences of events. This approach, which is validated on both synthetic and real data, provides better results than standard causal discovery algorithms on several time series data, even though these data were converted into smaller, single observed sequences.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that Large Language Models can infer causal relations between just two event sequences, outperforming standard causal discovery algorithms on converted time series data, validated on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery is the fundamental building block of causal AI, moving beyond associations toward genuine understanding. However, it becomes intrinsically difficult when causal relations must be inferred from single observations, since standard causal discovery methods cannot be applied and causal relations must be identified from limited information. This is typical for sequences of events produced by different alarms that need on-the-fly analysis to detect abnormal, usually rare, phenomena.
AI.method: The authors leverage the predictive power of Large Language Models (LLMs) to infer causal relations between only two sequences of events. The approach is validated on both synthetic and real data.
AI.result: The LLM-based approach provides better results than standard causal discovery algorithms on several time series data, even though these data were converted into smaller, single observed sequences.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively infer causal relations from a single observation of two event sequences, offering a superior alternative to standard causal discovery methods in settings where only limited, single-sequence information is available.

title: TO-mdiSPAs: Topology Optimization of multi-directional Soft Pneumatic Actuators
summary: Soft pneumatic actuators (SPAs) are highly promising and have been extensively explored within the field of soft robotics. Under pneumatic pressure loads, an SPA undergoes bending deformation to perform specific tasks. A multi- or omni-directional SPA can bend and move in any direction within a 3D space, leveraging its multiple degrees of freedom to realize various mechanical functions. This work presents a systematic methodology using topology optimization (TO) to achieve an optimized design for a multi-directional SPAs. To ensure manufacturing robustness, a three-field TO formulation considering blueprint, dilated, and eroded designs is implemented. Additionally, Darcy's law, incorporating a drainage term, is used to model the design-dependent nature of the pneumatic loading. A min-max optimization problem is formulated based on the target output deformations of the SPA unit and solved using the Method of Moving Asymptotes. The optimization yields a high-performing, unconventional geometric design. Finally, numerical simulations demonstrate that the optimized SPA successfully achieves versatile multi-directional movements.

AI.tldr: This work develops a systematic topology optimization (TO) methodology for designing multi-directional soft pneumatic actuators (SPAs), yielding an unconventional high-performance geometry validated to achieve versatile multi-directional motion.
AI.motivation: Multi- or omni-directional SPAs can bend and move in any direction in 3D space via multiple degrees of freedom, enabling diverse mechanical functions. However, achieving an optimized design for such multi-directional actuation remains challenging.
AI.method: A systematic TO approach is proposed. A three-field TO formulation (blueprint, dilated, and eroded designs) ensures manufacturing robustness. Darcy's law with a drainage term models the design-dependent pneumatic loading. A min-max optimization problem is formulated based on target output deformations of the SPA unit and solved with the Method of Moving Asymptotes.
AI.result: The optimization yields a high-performing, unconventional geometric design. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the optimized SPA successfully achieves versatile multi-directional movements.
AI.conclusion: Topology optimization provides an effective systematic methodology for designing multi-directional SPAs, with the resulting design exhibiting unconventional geometry and validated multi-directional actuation capability.

title: Beyond the Shadows of Plato's Cave: Evaluating False Memory in Autonomous Agents via Counterfactual Reasoning
summary: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on memory to generalize beyond their training environments. However, agents are bounded by what they have seen and believed, and leveraging such memories in unseen environments can introduce biases into their internal beliefs. We formalize this phenomenon as \textit{false memory}, which can arise from spurious correlations, environment shifts, and knowledge conflicts. Despite its importance, false memory is difficult to evaluate because it stems from agent internal beliefs and is easily confounded with ordinary generalization failures. Therefore, we propose FAME, a training-free framework that evaluates false memory through the evolution of agent beliefs under counterfactual reasoning. Specifically, counterfactual scenarios reveal how beliefs change as the latent concept of memory shifts under hypothetical interventions; thus, measuring the resulting concept drift provides a signal for distinguishing faithful versus false memory. Such concepts can be estimated from agent hidden states before answer generation, avoiding the need for reward design or answer sampling. Empirical experiments reveal that simply monitoring answers often fails to detect false memory, while FAME achieves AUROCs of 76.2% - 96.7% across false-memory settings, and outperforms the best baseline by 3.4% - 23.3% across realistic benchmarks, spanning math reasoning (GSM-Symbolic), code generation (GitChameleon), and complex reasoning (BigBench-Hard). We further release corresponding counterfactual templates and facilitate future research on false memory.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "false memory" in autonomous agents—biases in internal beliefs from spurious correlations, environment shifts, and knowledge conflicts—and proposes FAME, a training-free framework that detects it via belief evolution under counterfactual reasoning without reward design or answer sampling.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on memory to generalize beyond training environments, but are bounded by what they have seen and believed. Leveraging such memories in unseen environments can introduce biases into internal beliefs. False memory is important yet difficult to evaluate because it stems from agent internal beliefs and is easily confounded with ordinary generalization failures.
AI.method: FAME is a training-free framework that evaluates false memory through the evolution of agent beliefs under counterfactual reasoning. Counterfactual scenarios reveal how beliefs change as the latent concept of memory shifts under hypothetical interventions; measuring the resulting concept drift provides a signal for distinguishing faithful versus false memory. Concepts are estimated from agent hidden states before answer generation, avoiding reward design or answer sampling.
AI.result: Simply monitoring answers often fails to detect false memory. FAME achieves AUROCs of 76.2%–96.7% across false-memory settings and outperforms the best baseline by 3.4%–23.3% across realistic benchmarks spanning math reasoning (GSM-Symbolic), code generation (GitChameleon), and complex reasoning (BigBench-Hard). Corresponding counterfactual templates are released.
AI.conclusion: FAME provides an effective, training-free method for detecting false memory via counterfactual belief evolution, distinguishing it from ordinary generalization failures. The release of counterfactual templates facilitates future research on false memory.

title: Prediction is Better than Detection: Traffic Congestion Control using Drones
summary: A central question in deploying teams of mobile robots for persistent monitoring is how task performance scales with fleet size, and whether this scaling holds once sensing drives downstream action rather than mere observation. We study this question for a team of drones performing traffic-jam detection and prediction in a simulated road network, whose reports drive an adaptive traffic-signal controller in closed loop. We build a multi-agent simulation, with vehicles following Nagel-Schreckenberg cellular-automaton dynamics and drones patrolling junctions via a round-robin policy, and sweep fleet size, traffic level, and network size to evaluate detection rate, detection delay, and prediction rate. We show how performance plateaus for fleet size approximating the number of junctions being monitored, and offer a general fleet-provisioning rule for persistent-monitoring deployments. More significantly, adapting the signal on a predicted jam, rather than a detected one, roughly doubles the resulting reduction in jam duration, showing that the value of onboard prediction in a sensing-to-action pipeline can exceed the value of adding more robots. Prediction accuracy, not sensing coverage, is now the binding constraint on further improvement, pointing to onboard inference, not fleet size, as the more promising direction for future work.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how the performance of a drone fleet for persistent traffic monitoring scales with fleet size, when sensing is closed-loop into an adaptive traffic-signal controller. Performance plateaus once fleet size approaches the number of monitored junctions; crucially, acting on predicted rather than detected jams roughly doubles the reduction in jam duration.
AI.motivation: A central question in deploying mobile robot teams for persistent monitoring is how task performance scales with fleet size, and whether this scaling still holds when sensing drives downstream action rather than mere observation. Prior work largely addresses observation-only pipelines, leaving the sensing-to-action setting underexplored.
AI.method: A multi-agent simulation is built in which vehicles follow Nagel-Schreckenberg cellular-automaton dynamics, and drones patrol road-network junctions via a round-robin policy. Drones perform traffic-jam detection and prediction, with their reports driving an adaptive traffic-signal controller in closed loop. The study sweeps fleet size, traffic level, and network size, and evaluates detection rate, detection delay, and prediction rate.
AI.result: Performance plateaus for fleet sizes approximating the number of monitored junctions, yielding a general fleet-provisioning rule for persistent-monitoring deployments. Adapting the signal on a predicted jam rather than a detected one roughly doubles the resulting reduction in jam duration, indicating that onboard prediction can contribute more value than adding further robots. Prediction accuracy, not sensing coverage, becomes the binding constraint on further improvement.
AI.conclusion: The value of onboard prediction in a sensing-to-action pipeline can exceed the value of adding more robots. As prediction accuracy is now the limiting factor, onboard inference rather than increased fleet size is the more promising direction for future work.

title: Who Owns That? Evaluating Ownership Intuitions in Large Language Models
summary: Ownership establishes rights over the use, control, and transfer of objects. Understanding these relations is essential for AI systems to interact appropriately with people and their resources. Yet how large language models (LLMs) attribute ownership under competing claims remains unclear. We introduce the Competing Ownership Attribution Task (COAT), comprising 42 scenarios, and compare ownership allocations from 24 LLM configurations with those of 108 human participants. Overall, human-model similarity is close to human-human similarity, but models show greater homogeneity in their ownership judgments. Within individual answers, models also divide ownership more evenly among claimants than humans do. Pooling responses across model configurations reveals more scenarios with a shared judgment and fewer with distinct viewpoint groups than in humans. When humans form distinct groups, models may converge on one viewpoint or between competing viewpoints. Further comparisons reveal different contextual sensitivities. As material value increases across scenarios, allocations to creators decline less sharply in models than in humans. Across scenarios differing in public recognition of later holders as owners, allocations to these holders increase in models but decrease slightly in humans. Together, these findings suggest that the evaluated LLM responses do not fully capture the diversity of participants' ownership judgments or how those judgments vary across situations. Developing socially capable AI therefore requires moving beyond overall similarity to capture the diversity and context dependence of human judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces COAT, a 42-scenario benchmark comparing ownership attribution under competing claims between 24 LLM configurations and 108 human participants, finding that despite near human-human similarity in overall allocation, LLMs are more homogeneous, divide ownership more evenly, and show divergent context sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Ownership governs rights over use, control, and transfer of objects, and appropriate AI interaction with people and their resources requires understanding these relations. However, how LLMs attribute ownership under competing claims is unclear, and aggregate similarity metrics may conceal important differences in diversity and context dependence.
AI.method: Introduce the Competing Ownership Attribution Task (COAT), comprising 42 scenarios, and compare ownership allocations from 24 LLM configurations against those of 108 human participants. Analyses include human-model versus human-human similarity, within-answer distribution of ownership across claimants, pooling responses to identify shared judgments versus distinct viewpoint groups, and contextual manipulations of material value and public recognition of later holders.
AI.result: Human-model similarity approaches human-human similarity, yet models show greater homogeneity in ownership judgments and divide ownership more evenly among claimants within individual answers. Pooling across model configurations yields more scenarios with a shared judgment and fewer with distinct viewpoint groups than in humans; when humans form distinct groups, models converge on one viewpoint or fall between competing viewpoints. Context sensitivity also differs: as material value increases, allocations to creators decline less sharply in models than in humans, and as public recognition of later holders increases, allocations to these holders rise in models but decline slightly in humans.
AI.conclusion: Evaluated LLM responses do not fully capture the diversity of participants' ownership judgments or how those judgments vary across situations. Developing socially capable AI requires moving beyond overall similarity to capture the diversity and context dependence of human judgments.

title: Making Waves: A Membrane-Coupled Delta Array for Manipulating Objects Below the Actuator Spacing
summary: Distributed manipulator systems manipulate objects through the coordinated motion of many actuators. However, an object must be supported by several actuators at once, so the centre-to-centre actuator spacing imposes a hard lower bound on manipulable object size. We remove this bound by coupling the end-effectors of an 8 x 8 array of three degrees-of-freedom delta robots with a stretchable fabric, turning 64 discrete contacts into a continuous surface capable of manipulating objects smaller than the actuator spacing. Viewing the array as a displacement field over that surface, we investigate local quasi-static and cyclic fields as manipulation primitives. These primitives can be applied globally across the array or locally confined around each tracked object to independently manipulate several objects in parallel. We then train a policy acting on low-order discrete cosine transform coefficients: at equal action dimension, commanding a nineteen-delta neighbourhood halves the placement error of commanding the whole array. The policy transfers to hardware without adaptation at 76% success. The platform manipulates objects from 15mm-90mm, a six-fold range spanning both sides of the actuator spacing, 43.3mm, on a single surface.

AI.tldr: Coupling an 8x8 delta-robot array's end-effectors with stretchable fabric creates a continuous manipulation surface, breaking the actuator-spacing lower bound on object size and enabling parallel manipulation of objects from 15mm to 90mm.
AI.motivation: In distributed manipulator systems, objects must be supported by multiple actuators simultaneously, so centre-to-centre actuator spacing imposes a hard lower bound on the size of manipulable objects. The paper aims to remove this bound.
AI.method: The end-effectors of an 8x8 array of 3-DOF delta robots are coupled with a stretchable fabric, converting 64 discrete contacts into a continuous surface. The array is viewed as a displacement field over the surface, and local quasi-static and cyclic fields are used as manipulation primitives, applied globally or locally around tracked objects for parallel manipulation. A policy acting on low-order discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients is trained.
AI.result: At equal action dimension, commanding a nineteen-delta neighbourhood halves the placement error versus commanding the whole array. The policy transfers to hardware without adaptation at 76% success. The platform manipulates objects from 15mm to 90mm—a six-fold range spanning both sides of the 43.3mm actuator spacing—on a single surface.
AI.conclusion: Coupling discrete actuators with a stretchable fabric yields a continuous manipulation surface that overcomes the actuator-spacing size bound and supports parallel, multi-scale object manipulation on one surface.

title: Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention
summary: Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the KL direction (reverse or forward), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions.
