We formalize a unifying framework to encompass all self-distillation methods vs classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to explain the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention; (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.

AI.tldr: Self-distillation with privileged context is decomposed into three axes—rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction—and studied via a unifying framework with 1,200 runs on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B, revealing distinct acquisition-retention trade-offs and a controlled model that reproduces them.
AI.motivation: Existing self-distillation methods vary along three entangled axes (rollout source, teacher coupling, KL direction) but are typically studied in fixed combinations, producing conflicting conclusions. A systematic, unified investigation is needed to disentangle their individual effects.
AI.method: A unifying framework encompassing all self-distillation methods and classic supervised fine-tuning. All combinations of the three axes are trained on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs. A controlled model of the same objective is proposed to explain acquisition-retention trade-offs.
AI.result: (i) Rollout source matters mainly on contradictory tasks: teacher rollouts raise acquisition far above student rollouts with almost no retention change. (ii) Teacher coupling affects acquisition most on every task: acquisition rises with coupling rate then falls past a task-specific rate. (iii) Switching KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other, so which axis to tune first is model-dependent. The controlled model reproduces all three trends.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling the three axes clarifies prior conflicting findings and provides practical guidance: the priority of axes to tune depends on the model, and the controlled model validates the observed acquisition-retention trade-offs.

title: From Local Whole-Body VLA Behaviors to Scene-Scale Aerial Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable task-conditioned interaction, but extending them to scene-scale aerial manipulation remains challenging due to costly whole-body demonstrations, latency-induced action-state misalignment, and cross-site behavior composition. We present a unified framework for synthetic policy training and scene-scale execution on articulated uncrewed aerial manipulators (UAMs). A scene-reconfigurable pipeline synthesizes task-conditioned, kinodynamically feasible trajectories and synchronized multiview observations for VLA training without physical-platform demonstrations. Measured-progress-aligned realization (MPAR) aligns asynchronously returned action chunks with measured execution progress and realizes them as continuous, dynamically feasible trajectories. A relational Scene Graph grounds language goals to object instances and feasible interaction regions, while topology-guided transfer connects local behaviors across sites. Local VLA skills achieve 39/60 successes (65.0%) in simulation under oracle target and feasible-handoff conditions. Under 500-ms added latency, with and without a transient command-update stall, MPAR reduces median takeover phase error by 0.212 s over nominal-time alignment. The complete system completes 21/50 simulated multi-site missions (42.0%) and is further validated on a physical articulated UAM.

AI.tldr: A unified framework enables scene-scale aerial manipulation with articulated uncrewed aerial manipulators by synthesizing VLA training data, aligning asynchronously returned actions to measured progress (MPAR), and transferring local skills across sites via a relational scene graph.
AI.motivation: Extending VLA models to scene-scale aerial manipulation is hard due to costly whole-body demonstrations, latency-induced action-state misalignment, and cross-site behavior composition.
AI.method: A scene-reconfigurable pipeline synthesizes task-conditioned, kinodynamically feasible trajectories and synchronized multiview observations without physical demonstrations. Measured-progress-aligned realization (MPAR) aligns asynchronously returned action chunks with measured execution progress. A relational Scene Graph grounds language goals to object instances and feasible interaction regions, and topology-guided transfer connects local behaviors across sites.
AI.result: Local VLA skills reach 39/60 successes (65.0%) in simulation under oracle target and feasible-handoff conditions. Under 500-ms added latency, MPAR cuts median takeover phase error by 0.212 s versus nominal-time alignment. The full system completes 21/50 simulated multi-site missions (42.0%) and is validated on a physical articulated UAM.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports synthetic VLA policy training and scene-scale execution on articulated UAMs, mitigating demonstration cost, latency misalignment, and cross-site transfer, with simulation and physical validation.

title: Referential Uncertainty in Human--AI Collaboration
summary: Effective human-AI collaboration requires partners to establish references through interaction, which becomes fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, similar referents compete, or partners see different things. We study referential uncertainty - uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to - in a collaborative puzzle task where a human Helper instructs an AI Worker to place pieces. The Worker must identify and communicate its uncertainty, and the Helper must recognize and act on it. We show that a separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces is better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better discriminates correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities, which are severely overconfident (0.97 mean confidence, ECE 0.44). Across three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5), this elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness, but not with competing referents in context, even when those increase errors. The models seldom externalize it, asking for clarification on only 3.5-16.7% of turns. In a controlled human study (N=210), participants given only the Worker's default message accept 78% of wrong placements and cannot tell right from wrong (AUC 0.50). Precise descriptions and, especially, well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36% while largely preserving correct-move acceptance, compensating for missing shared awareness such as not seeing the Worker's action. But this benefit depends on targeting: a deployable hedge derived from the model's own belief entropy inherits that signal's weakness and can do more harm than good. Externalized uncertainty helps a human partner only when it is accurately targeted.

AI.tldr: In a human-AI collaborative puzzle task, separately elicited belief distributions over candidate referents are better calibrated than raw action-token probabilities, but frontier VLMs rarely externalize this uncertainty; externalized uncertainty helps human partners only when accurately targeted.
AI.motivation: Human-AI collaboration requires partners to jointly establish references through interaction, but this process is fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, multiple similar referents compete, or partners observe different things. The paper aims to understand referential uncertainty—uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to—and whether AI Workers can identify, communicate, and enable human Helpers to act on it.
AI.method: The authors use a collaborative puzzle task in which a human Helper instructs an AI Worker to place pieces. They compare a separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces against raw action-token probabilities. They evaluate three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5), testing how elicited uncertainty responds to instruction vagueness and competing referents. They also conduct a controlled human study (N=210) manipulating Worker messages (default vs. precise descriptions vs. targeted hedges) and measure wrong-move and correct-move acceptance.
AI.result: Elicited belief distributions are better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better discriminate correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities, which are severely overconfident (0.97 mean confidence, ECE 0.44). Elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness but not with competing referents, even when those increase errors. Models rarely externalize uncertainty, asking for clarification on only 3.5–16.7% of turns. In the human study, participants given only the default Worker message accept 78% of wrong placements and cannot distinguish right from wrong (AUC 0.50). Precise descriptions and especially well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36% while largely preserving correct-move acceptance, and they compensate for missing shared awareness. However, a deployable hedge derived from the model's own belief entropy inherits that signal's weakness and can do more harm than good.
AI.conclusion: Externalized uncertainty benefits human partners only when it is accurately targeted. Separately elicited beliefs provide a stronger internal signal than action-token probabilities, but current VLMs seldom communicate it and entropy-based hedges may fail to align with the sources of error that matter.

title: RoboCoach: World Models as Active Coaches for Compositional Robot Skills
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation reuses skills across many task compositions, but improving these compositions with additional end-to-end demonstrations is costly. A practical self-improving system must decide both what to teach next and where to apply that supervision. We present ROBOCOACH, a world-model-guided coaching framework that uses imagined failures to guide demonstration requests and expert updates. Its Route-Imagine-Diagnose-Improve (RIDI) loop executes reusable skill experts inside COACHWORLD, our shared action-conditioned world model, and uses a progress judge to record the first subtask that fails to complete. Aggregated records select which subtask demonstrations to acquire and which expert adapters to update. Across two simulation suites and two real-robot platforms, imagined and deployed success correlate over 22 task-policy pairs (rho = 0.840). Controlled comparisons show that our coaching method outperforms matched baselines under matched data budgets and update schedules. With only 150 additional subtask demonstrations, success rises from 13.3% to 75.0% on Franka and from 40.0% to 83.8% on AgileX. The coached experts also transfer to four held-out compositions, achieving an average success of 35.0%, compared with 0% for a shared-policy baseline updated with uniformly acquired demonstrations. Together, these results show that world models can serve as active coaches, turning imagined failures into targeted supervision for modular policy improvement. Project Page: https://robocoach-ai.github.io/

AI.tldr: ROBOCOACH is a world-model-guided coaching framework that uses imagined failures in a shared action-conditioned world model to decide which subtask demonstrations to collect and which skill experts to update, achieving large success gains under tight data budgets.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robot manipulation reuses skills across task compositions, but improving these compositions via additional end-to-end demonstrations is expensive. A self-improving system must decide both what to teach next and where to apply supervision.
AI.method: The Route-Imagine-Diagnose-Improve (RIDI) loop executes reusable skill experts inside COACHWORLD, a shared action-conditioned world model, and uses a progress judge to record the first subtask that fails. Aggregated failure records guide which subtask demonstrations to acquire and which expert adapters to update.
AI.result: Across two simulation suites and two real-robot platforms, imagined and deployed success correlate over 22 task-policy pairs (rho = 0.840). With only 150 additional subtask demonstrations, success rises from 13.3% to 75.0% on Franka and from 40.0% to 83.8% on AgileX. Coached experts transfer to four held-out compositions with 35.0% average success versus 0% for a shared-policy baseline updated with uniformly acquired demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: World models can serve as active coaches, turning imagined failures into targeted supervision for modular policy improvement, outperforming matched baselines under matched data budgets and update schedules.

title: Growing an Agent/Prover Interface: Evolutionary Tool Design for Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving in Rocq and Lean
summary: Recent achievements in AI-assisted mathematics require intensive interaction of agents with proof assistants to generate machine-checked proof certificates. Agents interact with proof assistants such as Rocq or Lean through an interface that controls what the agent receives from the prover and the cost of these interactions. Today, these interfaces are adapted from tools designed for humans and not optimized for agents. We propose an evolutionary method where a frontier model incrementally proposes new features and only keeps the ones that improve the overall performance of smaller models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by growing, on a curated set of mathematical problems, \rme, a new MCP server for the Rocq prover. On the held-out \texttt{test} split of miniF2F-Rocq, an agent equipped with \rme outperforms both the baseline that only exposes the Rocq compiler and an established MCP server, across four models from two families, in success rate, cost per solve, and time per solve. Although evolved for Rocq, the resulting server transfers to Lean, improving cost and time per solve on a subset of PutnamBench. We release \rme and its port to Lean.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evolutionary method in which a frontier model iteratively designs agent-optimized prover interfaces, and uses it to grow \rme, an MCP server for Rocq that outperforms baselines and transfers to Lean.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted mathematics relies on intensive agent interaction with proof assistants like Rocq and Lean, but today's interfaces were adapted from human-facing tools rather than optimized for agents. This mismatch constrains agent performance in terms of success rate, cost, and time.
AI.method: An evolutionary procedure where a frontier model incrementally proposes new interface features and retains only those that improve the overall performance of smaller models. Applied on a curated set of mathematical problems, this procedure grows \rme, a new MCP server for the Rocq prover.
AI.result: On the held-out test split of miniF2F-Rocq, an agent equipped with \rme beats both the baseline exposing only the Rocq compiler and an established MCP server, across four models from two families, improving success rate, cost per solve, and time per solve. Though evolved for Rocq, \rme transfers to Lean, reducing cost and time per solve on a subset of PutnamBench.
AI.conclusion: Agent-optimized prover interfaces can be evolved automatically, yielding substantial gains over human-designed and existing MCP servers, and such evolved interfaces generalize across provers. The authors release \rme and its Lean port.

title: Beyond Policy Alignment: Closing the Planning-Learning Loop for Robot Control with Learned World Models
summary: Planning with learned world models combines online trajectory optimization with learned value and policy functions for high-dimensional control. Because the planner determines the experience used for learning, while the learned critic and actor in turn score and propose future plans, planning and learning form a closed feedback loop. TD-MPC is a prominent instance of this design. Recent policy-constrained variants strengthen one part of the loop by aligning the learned policy with planner behavior. We introduce PL-MPC (Planning-Learning MPC), which additionally modifies critic supervision and planner terminal-value estimation. Hybrid multi-step TD targets expose critic updates to more realized rewards before bootstrapping; disagreement-aware terminal estimates reduce the influence of uncertain critic values during MPPI planning; and return-weighted actor distillation emphasizes planner-executed actions from high-return episodes. The world-model architecture and MPPI optimizer are otherwise unchanged. On HumanoidBench, the largest gains occur on \texttt{balance-hard}, where Total Average Return (TAR) increases from $98\pm18$ to $387\pm255$, and \texttt{hurdle}, from $199\pm13$ to $466\pm200$; performance across the broader benchmark remains task dependent, and PL-MPC remains competitive on DMControl. Controlled ablations show different component interactions across the two tasks. We further demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on wrench-nut alignment with a 7-DoF KUKA IIWA14, obtaining higher observed success than TD-M(PC)^2 on the training object size and two unseen sizes. Code and data will be available at: https://pl-mpc-humanoid.github.io.

AI.tldr: PL-MPC enhances TD-MPC's planning-learning loop by modifying critic supervision with hybrid multi-step TD targets, introducing disagreement-aware terminal-value estimates in MPPI planning, and applying return-weighted actor distillation, improving HumanoidBench tasks and achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: In planning with learned world models, the planner collects experience while the learned critic and actor score and propose plans, forming a closed feedback loop. Policy-constrained variants like TD-M(PC)^2 strengthen only one part of this loop (policy alignment), leaving critic supervision and terminal-value estimation unaddressed.
AI.method: PL-MPC modifies three components on top of TD-MPC while leaving the world-model architecture and MPPI optimizer unchanged: (1) hybrid multi-step TD targets that expose critic updates to more realized rewards before bootstrapping; (2) disagreement-aware terminal-value estimation to reduce the influence of uncertain critic values during MPPI planning; and (3) return-weighted actor distillation that emphasizes planner-executed actions from high-return episodes.
AI.result: On HumanoidBench, largest gains occur on balance-hard (TAR from 98±18 to 387±255) and hurdle (199±13 to 466±200); broader benchmark performance is task-dependent and remains competitive on DMControl. Controlled ablations reveal differing component interactions across the two tasks. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on wrench-nut alignment with a 7-DoF KUKA IIWA14 achieves higher observed success than TD-M(PC)^2 on the training object size and two unseen sizes.
AI.conclusion: Strengthening both critic supervision and terminal-value estimation, in addition to policy alignment, improves the tightly coupled planning-learning loop of TD-MPC, yielding substantial gains on challenging HumanoidBench tasks and effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

title: RankEvolve: A Reliable Multi-Agent Auto-Research Harness for Evolving Ranking Models
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables, 1 algorithm; includes appendices
summary: Auto-research agents, LLM systems that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes across iterations, promise to automate applied ML's experimental loop. Over long horizons, execution accuracy is a binding constraint: a change can silently leak held-out data, omit normalization, disconnect a gradient, or leave a train/eval flag unwired, invalidating expensive runs and compounding error across iterations. We present RankEvolve, an auto-research framework for evolving generative ranking models. An Executable Operating Protocol (EOP) declares phases, gates, branches, and loops, and the runtime enforces the compiled state machine. A meta-meta-harness composes complete black-box coding-agent products, including Claude Code and Codex, as execution-graph nodes that review and repair one another's work. In a budget-matched evaluation, heterogeneous composition raises all-oracle execution accuracy from the best single-product baseline of 45.8 percent to 62.5 percent (paired +16.7 points, 95 percent CI [6.6, 26.7]) while achieving a 10.4 percent silent critical-defect rate. An implemented knowledge layer carries findings, including negative results, across iterations. In a twelve-iteration deployment on the open-source HSTU recommender, RankEvolve reported NDCG@10 of 0.2192 on MovieLens-20M LARGE (+4.48 percent over the published anchor) and 0.1948 on BASE (+2.80 percent). ExecML-HSTU, seeded by incidents from that deployment, provides the oracle benchmark for the execution-accuracy evaluation. A pre-specified LitGPT transfer split replicates the heterogeneous-composition effect beyond recommendation (+12.5 points, 95 percent CI [3.0, 22.0]), and a paired ablation isolates per-step from full-protocol instruction injection. These results characterize when runtime-controlled composition of coding-agent products improves execution accuracy.

AI.tldr: RankEvolve is an auto-research framework for evolving generative ranking models that uses an Executable Operating Protocol (state machine enforcing phases, gates, branches, loops) plus a meta-meta-harness composing black-box coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) as mutually reviewing/repairing nodes, raising oracular execution accuracy from 45.8% to 62.5% and yielding NDCG@10 gains on HSTU recommender benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon auto-research, execution accuracy is a binding constraint: silent protocol violations (held-out data leakage, missing normalization, disconnected gradients, unwired train/eval flags) invalidate costly runs and compound errors across iterations. Existing automation lacks runtime enforcement of experimental correctness, motivating a framework that structurally constrains agent execution.
AI.method: EOP declares phases, gates, branches, and loops; a runtime enforces the compiled state machine. A meta-meta-harness composes complete black-box coding-agent products (Claude Code, Codex) as execution-graph nodes that cross-review and repair each other's work. A knowledge layer propagates findings, including negative results, across iterations. Evaluation uses ExecML-HSTU as an oracle benchmark seeded by deployment incidents, with budget-matched comparisons, a pre-specified LitGPT transfer split, and a paired ablation separating per-step from full-protocol instruction injection.
AI.result: Heterogeneous composition raises all-oracle execution accuracy from 45.8% (best single-product baseline) to 62.5% (paired +16.7 pts, 95% CI [6.6, 26.7]), with a 10.4% silent critical-defect rate. A 12-iteration deployment on HSTU reports NDCG@10 of 0.2192 on MovieLens-20M LARGE (+4.48% over published anchor) and 0.1948 on BASE (+2.80%). The LitGPT split replicates the composition effect (+12.5 pts, 95% CI [3.0, 22.0]).
AI.conclusion: Runtime-controlled composition of heterogeneous coding-agent products reliably improves execution accuracy in automated ML research, with benefits transferring beyond recommendation tasks; the paired ablation clarifies the contribution of instruction-injection granularity. The results characterize the conditions under which such composition is effective.

title: ChunkTrust: Adapting Execution Horizons for Robot Policies with Action-Expert Evidence
summary: Robot foundation policies predict action chunks, but how many actions to execute before replanning depends on the current task phase. We introduce ChunkTrust, which treats the execution horizon as a latent variable inferred from action-expert evidence rather than a fixed hyperparameter. Its training-free Action-aware Horizon Selector (AHS) combines intra-chunk spectral stability of generation traces with inter-chunk continuity between executed history and predicted actions. An online Beta posterior with kernel forgetting tracks horizon preferences across replans. A lightweight Query-based Horizon Adapter (QHA) optionally learns a context-conditioned dense prior from complementary evidence, fused with current evidence and episode-local Beta memory while the base policy remains frozen. Across RoboTwin2.0 and RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop, AHS improves overall task-averaged success for each evaluated base-policy configuration, including gains of +6.80 percentage points on $π_{0.5}$ over all 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks and +9.67 percentage points on Qwen3GR00T in RoboCasa. AHS+QHA raises the gain over Base to +9.44 percentage points on the eight-task $π_{0.5}$ evaluation. On four real-world household tasks, AHS improves the equal-task mean normalized process score from 50.4% to 57.5%. Ablations examine the contributions of both evidence terms, temporal memory, and the learned prior. Project page is https://hf618.github.io/ChunkTrust.github.io/

AI.tldr: ChunkTrust treats action-chunk execution horizon as a latent variable inferred from action-expert evidence, using a training-free selector (AHS), online Beta memory, and an optional learned adapter (QHA), improving success across simulated and real robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Robot foundation policies predict action chunks, but the number of actions to execute before replanning is task-phase dependent. Existing approaches treat this execution horizon as a fixed hyperparameter rather than an adaptive, context-sensitive quantity.
AI.method: ChunkTrust infers the execution horizon from action-expert evidence. A training-free Action-aware Horizon Selector (AHS) combines intra-chunk spectral stability of generation traces with inter-chunk continuity between executed history and predicted actions. An online Beta posterior with kernel forgetting tracks horizon preferences across replans. A lightweight Query-based Horizon Adapter (QHA) optionally learns a context-conditioned dense prior from complementary evidence, fused with current evidence and episode-local Beta memory, while the base policy stays frozen.
AI.result: On RoboTwin2.0 and RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop, AHS raises task-averaged success for every evaluated base-policy configuration, including +6.80 pp on π_0.5 over all 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks and +9.67 pp on Qwen3GR00T in RoboCasa. AHS+QHA increases the gain over Base to +9.44 pp on the eight-task π_0.5 evaluation. On four real-world household tasks, AHS lifts the equal-task mean normalized process score from 50.4% to 57.5%. Ablations assess both evidence terms, temporal memory, and the learned prior.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, evidence-driven horizon selection improves robot foundation policy performance over fixed-horizon replanning, with consistent gains in simulation and real-world settings; both evidence terms, temporal memory, and the optional learned prior contribute to these improvements.

title: Divide and Collapse: MAPF-Collapse via Exact Decomposition into Independent Sub-Instances
summary: In this work we study the problem of MAPFC, a post-optimization step for Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) plans where we are given a feasible plan produced by a modern MAPF solver and are tasked with removing avoidable moves while preserving feasibility. This NP-hard problem naturally arises when using learning-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) solvers which construct plans that contain redundant moves that can be removed. Recently, Tang et al. presented Judgelight, which uses Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to solve MAPFC. Importantly, the ILP is constructed over all agents jointly, so its cost is governed by the full instance rather than by the small coupled residue that actually requires joint reasoning. Our key insight, motivating this work, is that MAPFC instances naturally decompose into independent sub-problems, most of which involve a single agent and can be solved without any inter-agent reasoning. To this end, we first identify which agents need to coordinate their motion and partition the instance into sub-problems accordingly. For the cases where no coordination is required, we introduce an extremely lightweight solver that is $\approx\!1{,}900\times$ faster than Judgelight. For cases where coordination is required, Judgelight can be used but we introduce an alternative CBS-like solver which is more efficient on easier problems. The resulting framework is exact, uses no commercial ILP solver, and matches Judgelight's quality while running substantially faster on the coordination-light majority of instances; on the coordination-heavy instances we propose a regime-aware hybrid planner that falls back to Judgelight. Over all benchmarks tested, this planner achieves a median $10.5\times$ per-instance speedup over Judgelight.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses MAPFC (removing avoidable moves from feasible Multi-Agent Path Finding plans). The key insight is that MAPFC decomposes into independent sub-problems, most requiring no inter-agent reasoning. The proposed framework partitions agents into coordination groups, solves single-agent cases with a lightweight solver (~1900x faster than Judgelight), and uses a CBS-like solver for coordination cases, with a hybrid planner falling back to Judgelight. It achieves a median 10.5x speedup while matching Judgelight's quality.
AI.motivation: MAPFC is an NP-hard post-optimization step that naturally arises with learning-based SOTA MAPF solvers, which produce plans containing redundant, removable moves. The prior method, Judgelight (Tang et al.), uses ILP constructed jointly over all agents, so its cost is governed by the full instance rather than the small coupled residue that actually requires joint reasoning—making it inefficient.
AI.method: The authors exploit the insight that MAPFC instances decompose into independent sub-problems. They first identify which agents need to coordinate their motion and partition the instance into sub-problems accordingly. For cases requiring no coordination (single-agent), they introduce an extremely lightweight solver (~1900x faster than Judgelight). For cases requiring coordination, they introduce a CBS-like solver that is more efficient on easier problems, while Judgelight can still be used. The framework is exact and uses no commercial ILP solver. They also propose a regime-aware hybrid planner that falls back to Judgelight for coordination-heavy instances.
AI.result: The single-agent lightweight solver is approximately 1900x faster than Judgelight. The overall framework matches Judgelight's quality while running substantially faster on the coordination-light majority of instances. Over all benchmarks tested, the regime-aware hybrid planner achieves a median 10.5x per-instance speedup over Judgelight.
AI.conclusion: MAPFC naturally decomposes into independent sub-problems, enabling an exact, ILP-free framework that handles coordination-light instances much faster than Judgelight and falls back to Judgelight for coordination-heavy cases, delivering a median 10.5x speedup while preserving solution quality.

title: Experience-Driven Continual Learning of Terrain Traversability for Quadruped Robots
summary: Safe and efficient quadruped navigation over unfamiliar terrain requires predicting terrain-robot interaction before contact: geometry and visual appearance alone cannot reveal how the robot will slip, load its feet, or expend energy. This paper presents a continual learning pipeline that uses locomotion experience to learn these interaction outcomes from pre-contact images and continually updates the predictions as new contacts are observed. Pre-contact descriptors, produced by a DINOv3 backbone model frozen during training, are mapped to five proprioceptive indicators weighted according to measurement reliability: planar foot slip, mean normal ground-reaction force, traction index, cost of transport, and touchdown loading rate. A compact evidential regressor allows us to predict these indicators together with aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from the visual descriptors. Continual adaptation combines bounded experience replay with a validation gate: candidate models replace the deployed predictor only when they improve performance on recent held-out data while keeping degradation on historical held-out data within a prescribed tolerance. Predictions and epistemic uncertainty are projected into a local multilayer map and combined into a conservative traversability score map whose property weights can be adjusted without retraining. The resulting map is used for downstream navigation tests. The ROS2 implementation supports evaluation on a Unitree Go2 in simulation and on hardware, with models trained separately in each domain. On a sequential hardware stream over three previously unseen terrains, gated replay reduces final anchor negative log-likelihood (NLL) degradation by 23.1% relative to replay without the gate while attaining similar new-terrain adaptation.

AI.tldr: A continual learning pipeline predicts robot-terrain interaction outcomes (slip, load, energy) from pre-contact images using a frozen DINOv3 backbone and an evidential regressor, with gated experience replay preventing catastrophic forgetting, feeding a conservative traversability map for quadruped navigation.
AI.motivation: Safe, efficient quadruped navigation over unfamiliar terrain requires predicting terrain-robot interaction before contact, since geometry and visual appearance alone cannot reveal slipping, foot loading, or energy expenditure. Existing approaches cannot leverage accumulated locomotion experience to continually refine such predictions as new contacts are observed.
AI.method: Pre-contact descriptors from a frozen DINOv3 backbone are mapped to five reliability-weighted proprioceptive indicators (planar foot slip, mean normal ground-reaction force, traction index, cost of transport, touchdown loading rate). A compact evidential regressor predicts these indicators plus aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Continual adaptation uses bounded experience replay with a validation gate that accepts candidate models only if they improve on recent held-out data while staying within tolerance on historical held-out data. Predictions and epistemic uncertainty are projected into a local multilayer map and fused into a conservative traversability score map with adjustable weights, used for downstream navigation. Implemented in ROS2, evaluated on a Unitree Go2 in simulation and hardware.
AI.result: On a sequential hardware stream over three previously unseen terrains, gated replay reduces final anchor negative log-likelihood degradation by 23.1% relative to replay without the gate, while achieving similar new-terrain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Gated replay effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in continual terrain-interaction prediction without sacrificing adaptation to new terrains, and the resulting uncertainty-aware traversability map supports safe quadruped navigation on the Unitree Go2 in both simulation and hardware.

title: A2Z GameSpec-Bench: How Faithfully Can Coding Agents Generate Games from Game Design Specifications?
summary: Delegating complete application development to coding agents requires preserving the intended design rather than simply producing plausible outputs through naive prompting. Game development provides a demanding testbed, as long-form Game Design Documents (GDDs) describe requirements that must work together across game logic, visual rendering, and player interactions. However, existing game-development benchmarks typically use compact specifications and provide limited support for evaluating interdependent requirements across these aspects in long-form GDDs. We introduce A2Z GameSpec-Bench, a benchmark of 100 long-form GDDs for evaluating end-to-end game development by agents. We measure faithfulness by checking whether the game satisfies the GDD requirements and preserves the relationships among them. Each GDD is turned into a dependency-aware contract that contains rules, constraints, and prerequisite relations. Following game-development practices, we combine source-code inspection with agent-generated test policies for scenario-based replay and adaptive playtesting. The contract remains fixed across agents and revision rounds, while judgments and evidence linked to the same requirements support consistent comparison and failure detection. Our evaluations show that current agents struggle to jointly satisfy interdependent requirements across code implementation and actual play. Requirement-specific feedback improves GDD Fidelity by 10.9% relative to self-revision after two rounds. A2Z GameSpec-Bench assesses end-to-end specification-following ability beyond implementation judgments and provides targeted feedback to support more faithful game development. Code and datasets are available at https://a2z-gamespec-bench.github.io.

AI.tldr: A2Z GameSpec-Bench is a benchmark of 100 long-form Game Design Documents (GDDs) that evaluates whether coding agents can faithfully develop complete games that satisfy interdependent requirements across logic, rendering, and interaction, rather than just producing plausible outputs.
AI.motivation: Delegating full application development to coding agents requires preserving the intended design, but naive prompting only yields plausible outputs. Game development is a demanding testbed because long-form GDDs describe requirements that must cohere across game logic, visual rendering, and player interactions. Existing game-development benchmarks rely on compact specifications and offer limited support for evaluating interdependent requirements in long-form GDDs.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark of 100 long-form GDDs. Each GDD is converted into a dependency-aware contract capturing rules, constraints, and prerequisite relations. Faithfulness is measured by checking whether the game satisfies the GDD requirements and preserves the relationships among them. Evaluation combines source-code inspection with agent-generated test policies for scenario-based replay and adaptive playtesting. The contract is fixed across agents and revision rounds, so judgments and evidence tied to the same requirements enable consistent comparison and failure detection.
AI.result: Current agents struggle to jointly satisfy interdependent requirements across both code implementation and actual play. Providing requirement-specific feedback improves GDD Fidelity by 10.9% relative to self-revision after two rounds.
AI.conclusion: A2Z GameSpec-Bench assesses end-to-end specification-following ability beyond implementation judgments and provides targeted feedback to support more faithful game development. Code and datasets are available at the project page.

title: DiffWAM: A Fast and Efficient Navigation World Action Model
summary: Pretrained video foundation models encode rich semantic and spatiotemporal priors for embodied navigation, yet converting these priors into UAV motion typically requires expensive future-video synthesis and geometric reconstruction. We investigate whether the motion implicit in future visual prediction can instead be recovered directly from the predictive representations of a frozen video model. To this end, we present DiffWAM, a geometry-conditioned navigation world-action model that directly transforms multi-level predictive features into continuous camera trajectories. Its Grid-Motion module preserves spatial-temporal motion associations, while Latent2Pose grounds them with first-frame geometry to recover metrically meaningful 3D motion. Complete video rollouts and geometric reconstruction are required only for offline supervision, eliminating future-video decoding and multi-frame reconstruction during deployment. We further introduce FastDreamer, which overlaps predictive and geometric computation with ongoing flight and performs timestamp-aware asynchronous trajectory handoff for continuous UAV execution. DiffWAM achieves a trajectory RMSE of 0.3492 m and an endpoint success rate of 74.40% on the 1,000-sample DiffWAM-1000 benchmark, while representative real-world experiments demonstrate complex behaviors including constrained traversal, orbiting, S-shaped flight, and multi-stage navigation. An onboard DiffWAM-Flash implementation further reaches 1.08 s model-pipeline latency on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor. These results demonstrate that predictive video representations can be efficiently grounded into continuous 3D motion, providing a direct alternative to generate-then-reconstruct navigation pipelines. Project page: https://zzmmzzm.github.io/diffwam.github.io/.

AI.tldr: DiffWAM converts multi-level predictive features from a frozen video foundation model directly into continuous UAV camera trajectories, avoiding future-video synthesis and geometric reconstruction at deployment. It achieves 0.3492 m trajectory RMSE and 74.40% endpoint success on DiffWAM-1000, with real-world complex flight demonstrations and 1.08 s onboard latency on Jetson AGX Thor.
AI.motivation: Pretrained video foundation models encode rich semantic and spatiotemporal priors useful for embodied navigation, but turning these priors into UAV motion typically demands costly future-video synthesis and geometric reconstruction. The work investigates whether the motion implicit in future visual prediction can be recovered directly from predictive representations of a frozen video model, eliminating the generate-then-reconstruct pipeline.
AI.method: DiffWAM is a geometry-conditioned navigation world-action model that transforms multi-level predictive features directly into continuous camera trajectories. Its Grid-Motion module preserves spatiotemporal motion associations, while Latent2Pose grounds these associations with first-frame geometry to recover metrically meaningful 3D motion. Full video rollouts and geometric reconstruction are used only for offline supervision. FastDreamer overlaps predictive and geometric computation with ongoing flight and performs timestamp-aware asynchronous trajectory handoff for continuous UAV execution.
AI.result: DiffWAM reaches a trajectory RMSE of 0.3492 m and an endpoint success rate of 74.40% on the 1,000-sample DiffWAM-1000 benchmark. Real-world experiments show complex behaviors including constrained traversal, orbiting, S-shaped flight, and multi-stage navigation. An onboard DiffWAM-Flash implementation attains 1.08 s model-pipeline latency on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor.
AI.conclusion: Predictive video representations can be efficiently grounded into continuous 3D motion, offering a direct alternative to generate-then-reconstruct navigation pipelines. The results suggest frozen video foundation models can serve as practical motion priors for UAV navigation without deployment-time video decoding or multi-frame reconstruction.

title: AVERT-VLN: Abstention-aware Visual Error Recovery and Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Deploying vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents in unseen environments remains challenging because unfamiliar layouts and visual conditions can cause execution to go off track. Rather than relying on continuous human supervision, a practical strategy is to selectively request corrective guidance, recover the ongoing task, and reuse corrective interactions to improve subsequent navigation. We propose Abstention-aware Visual Error Recovery and Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation (AVERT-VLN), a closed-loop framework that uses a plug-in vision-language Monitor for online human-assisted recovery and offline preference learning. The Monitor operates separately from navigation decision generation and assesses instruction-execution consistency from the instruction, visual history, and current observation. To train the Monitor for deviation recognition, we construct LOSTNAV DATASET with 20K counterfactual risk trajectories and rule-based deviation labels. The Monitor is first fine-tuned on 40K normal trajectories to assess instruction progress and then jointly fine-tuned on normal and risk trajectories to recognize semantic deviations. At runtime, Asynchronous Sidecar Monitoring evaluates execution alongside the navigation model. When the controller accepts a LOST verdict, it suspends autonomous execution and requests human guidance for recovery. For offline policy improvement, Trajectory-Anchored Preference Learning converts deviation-associated failures into decision-level preference pairs under shared decision contexts, restricting supervision to the decisions targeted for correction. Under human-assisted evaluation, the full AVERT-VLN system achieves success rates of 76.2% and 66.3% on the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, respectively. The same monitoring and human-assisted recovery interface also improves success rates across the three evaluated navigation architectures.

AI.tldr: AVERT-VLN is a closed-loop VLN framework that uses a plug-in vision-language Monitor for online human-assisted recovery and offline preference learning, boosting unseen-environment success rates.
AI.motivation: VLN agents struggle in unseen environments where unfamiliar layouts and visual conditions cause execution to go off track; continuous human supervision is impractical, so selective corrective guidance that is recovered and reused is desirable.
AI.method: A plug-in vision-language Monitor runs separately from navigation decision generation, assessing instruction-execution consistency from instruction, visual history, and current observation. It is trained on the LOSTNAV DATASET (20K counterfactual risk trajectories with rule-based deviation labels), first fine-tuned on 40K normal trajectories and then jointly fine-tuned on normal and risk trajectories. Runtime uses Asynchronous Sidecar Monitoring; on a LOST verdict the controller suspends execution and requests human guidance. Offline improvement uses Trajectory-Anchored Preference Learning, converting deviation-associated failures into decision-level preference pairs under shared decision contexts.
AI.result: Under human-assisted evaluation, full AVERT-VLN achieves 76.2% and 66.3% success rates on val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE. The monitoring and human-assisted recovery interface also improves success rates across all three evaluated navigation architectures.
AI.conclusion: Selective, abstention-aware human-assisted recovery combined with preference-based offline learning provides an effective, architecture-agnostic solution for robust VLN in unseen environments.

title: Tool-Policy Co-Design for Powder Weighing in Laboratory Automation
comment: Paper video can be found at https://youtu.be/BEUT70hX9LM
summary: Autonomous powder weighing is one of many bottlenecks in laboratory automation due to the complex, non-linear dynamics of heterogeneous materials. Robot chemists performing this task utilise standard tools shaped for the dexterity of human hands, whose fixed geometry sets the dynamics that the control policy needs to regulate. This work introduces a tool-policy co-design framework that concurrently optimises the morphology of a dispensing tool and its control policy for use by robots in chemistry laboratories, formulated as a bi-level optimisation that minimises dispensing error over a target distribution of powder flowabilities. The outer loop varies tool-design parameters such as tool depth, width and rim spike topology using Bayesian optimisation and hyperband, while an inner loop optimises a control policy for each candidate morphology. We also introduce a geometric similarity metric that warm-starts policy training from cached policies of structurally similar designs, exploring 28% more configurations under the same compute budget. The proposed framework is evaluated on a robotic powder weighing task across seven materials with distinct physical dynamics in a flowability-informed robot-material simulation framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our co-designed tool morphology reduces real-world weighing errors by 45% relative to a standard tool, including on previously unseen materials. These results demonstrate our method can adapt both the control policy and the physical tool to the dynamics of the target material, bringing a new paradigm for material manipulation to the field of laboratory automation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a tool-policy co-design framework that jointly optimizes a powder dispensing tool's morphology and its control policy via bi-level optimization, reducing real-world weighing errors by 45% versus a standard tool.
AI.motivation: Autonomous powder weighing is a bottleneck in laboratory automation due to complex, non-linear dynamics of heterogeneous materials. Existing robot chemists use standard human-oriented tools with fixed geometry, leaving the dynamics that the control policy must regulate unoptimized.
AI.method: A bi-level optimization framework minimizing dispensing error over a target distribution of powder flowabilities. The outer loop varies tool-design parameters (tool depth, width, rim spike topology) using Bayesian optimization and hyperband; the inner loop optimizes a control policy for each candidate morphology. A geometric similarity metric warm-starts policy training from cached policies of structurally similar designs.
AI.result: Evaluated on a robotic powder weighing task across seven materials with distinct physical dynamics in a flowability-informed robot-material simulation. The geometric similarity metric explores 28% more configurations under the same compute budget. Co-designed tool morphology reduces real-world weighing errors by 45% relative to a standard tool, including on previously unseen materials.
AI.conclusion: The method can adapt both the control policy and the physical tool to target material dynamics, offering a new paradigm for material manipulation in laboratory automation.

title: Why Do Conventional World Models Fail to Learn Cellular Automata?
comment: 35 pages, 18 figures. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/guoshaoyang-pku/momentum-induction
summary: Although conventional world models - auto-regressive or diffusion models based on transformers or convolutional networks - may learn surface statistics of world dynamics, can they learn the exact world dynamics from its observed history? Leveraging cellular automata as a simple testbed, we find the answer to be no in many cases. Conventional architectures predict most pixels correctly yet rarely complete a rollout: a CNN predicts 96.3% of cells but completes 18.9% of rollouts; a joint diffusion model completes none. We trace the gap to three failure modes of these world models - namely, they fail to exactly capture spatial locality, temporal locality or temporal stability. Simple changes repair each: (1) for spatial locality, two-dimensional rotary positions lift a transformer from 39.1% to 100% on the Game of Life; (2) for temporal locality, handing each token its cell's previous-frame neighbourhood lifts the same transformer from 25.8% to 99.9% on unseen rules; (3) for temporal stability, causal freezing lifts the same diffusion weights from 42.2% to 99.9%. None of the three changes touches the architectural backbone; each only modifies the information flow within it. We also compare joint and ordered sampling on billiards and, in an exploratory study, on a simulated Burgers equation.

AI.tldr: Conventional world models (autoregressive/diffusion, transformer/CNN) grasp surface pixel statistics but fail to reproduce exact world dynamics; cellular automata reveal three failure modes—spatial locality, temporal locality, temporal stability—each fixable by a minimal information-flow change without altering the backbone.
AI.motivation: The paper questions whether world models that learn surface statistics of dynamics can actually learn exact dynamics from observed history, using cellular automata as a minimal, verifiable testbed.
AI.method: Cellular automata are adopted as a testbed. Standard architectures (CNN, transformer, joint diffusion) are evaluated on rollout completion versus per-pixel accuracy. Three targeted, backbone-preserving interventions are introduced: 2D rotary positional embeddings (spatial locality), per-token previous-frame neighbourhood tokens (temporal locality), and causal freezing (temporal stability). Joint vs. ordered sampling is also compared on billiards and a simulated Burgers equation.
AI.result: High pixel accuracy coexists with poor rollout success: CNN 96.3% cells vs 18.9% rollouts; joint diffusion completes none. 2D rotary positions raise a transformer from 39.1% to 100% on Game of Life; previous-frame neighbourhood lifts it from 25.8% to 99.9% on unseen rules; causal freezing lifts the same diffusion weights from 42.2% to 99.9%. Each change only modifies internal information flow.
AI.conclusion: Exact world-dynamics learning requires explicit spatial locality, temporal locality, and temporal stability in information flow, not larger backbones; minimal structural edits close the rollout gap.

title: Learning from Runtime Feedback through Failure-Bank Self-Evolution for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Runtime-feedback-driven self-evolution for safer VLA policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize broadly across robotic manipulation tasks, but complex environments require balancing task success with unintended contact. Runtime shields can correct individual actions, but they leave the underlying policy unchanged, so repeated disagreements may create a persistent policy-shield mismatch that blocks task progress. To address this challenge, we introduce FailBank, a four-stage self-evolving framework that converts runtime feedback into persistent policy improvement. During collection, a fixed CBF-based safety module serves as an observe-only teacher, producing counterfactual corrections while the policy remains in control. Outcome-aware admission then converts useful proposals into corrective targets and retains successful uncorrected actions as quiet anchors for guarded LoRA updates. We evaluate FailBank on the VLA-Arena benchmark across two difficulty levels and two VLA backbones. Compared with the base policies, FailBank improves the joint success-cost operating point. Across the two backbones, FailBank improves task success rate by 8.5 and 6.9 percentage points, while reducing policy-induced cumulative cost by 35.6\% and 23.8\%, respectively. Compared with runtime shielding, FailBank raises task success rate by 25.4 and 9.5 percentage points, while maintaining comparable policy-induced cumulative cost. These results show that runtime feedback can serve as persistent policy supervision rather than only as a temporary action constraint.

AI.tldr: FailBank is a four-stage self-evolving framework that turns runtime safety feedback into persistent policy improvement for VLA models, improving both success rate and safety cost over base policies and runtime shielding.
AI.motivation: VLA models must balance task success against unintended contact in complex environments. Runtime shields can correct individual actions, but they leave the underlying policy unchanged, so repeated disagreements create a persistent policy-shield mismatch that blocks task progress.
AI.method: FailBank is a four-stage self-evolving framework. (1) Collection: a fixed CBF-based safety module acts as an observe-only teacher, producing counterfactual corrections while the policy remains in control. (2) Outcome-aware admission converts useful proposals into corrective targets. (3) Successful uncorrected actions are retained as quiet anchors. (4) Guarded LoRA updates are performed using these targets and anchors.
AI.result: Evaluated on the VLA-Arena benchmark at two difficulty levels with two VLA backbones. Versus base policies, FailBank improves task success rate by 8.5 and 6.9 percentage points and reduces policy-induced cumulative cost by 35.6% and 23.8%. Versus runtime shielding, it raises task success rate by 25.4 and 9.5 percentage points while maintaining comparable policy-induced cumulative cost.
AI.conclusion: Runtime feedback can serve as persistent policy supervision rather than only as a temporary action constraint, yielding a better joint success-cost operating point.

title: ChronoGraph: Functional 4D Scene Graphs with Vision-Language Models for Interaction Understanding and Grounded Planning
summary: Embodied agents must determine where to act, anticipate the resulting scene changes, and interpret observed outcomes to guide subsequent actions. This requires connecting 4D interaction understanding, which explains how past actions changed the scene, with spatially grounded planning, which determines how and where to act toward a goal and anticipates the resulting scene changes. We introduce ChronoGraph, a functional 4D scene graph that links actions on affordance parts to semantic and geometric state changes. By representing observed and anticipated transitions in the same form, it provides a shared basis for understanding and planning. We construct ChronoGraphBench through an automatic data engine that converts human-interaction videos and simulated robot trajectories into graph-annotated questions for training and evaluating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on both tasks. Using these annotations, we train ChronoGraphVLM by adapting pretrained VLMs in two stages. Graph-as-Chain-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning teaches the models to reconstruct observed transitions and predict future ones as graph traces before answering. Subsequent joint 4D graph reinforcement learning directly rewards graph properties and answer correctness. Experiments across model scales show improvements over the corresponding pretrained baselines and zero-shot transfer to VLM4D. Real-world demonstrations further show that graph-based planning and affordance grounding support mobile manipulation through existing robot skills without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ChronoGraph, a functional 4D scene graph linking actions on affordance parts to semantic and geometric state changes, enabling a shared representation for 4D interaction understanding and spatially grounded planning. It also builds ChronoGraphBench and trains ChronoGraphVLM via graph-as-chain-of-thought SFT and joint 4D graph RL, showing gains over pretrained baselines and zero-shot transfer to VLM4D.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents need to decide where to act, anticipate resulting scene changes, and interpret observed outcomes. This requires connecting 4D interaction understanding (explaining how past actions changed the scene) with spatially grounded planning (determining how/where to act toward a goal while anticipating scene changes). However, these two capabilities are typically studied separately, lacking a unified representation.
AI.method: The authors propose ChronoGraph, a functional 4D scene graph that links actions on affordance parts to semantic and geometric state changes, representing observed and anticipated transitions in the same form. They build ChronoGraphBench via an automatic data engine converting human-interaction videos and simulated robot trajectories into graph-annotated questions for training/evaluating VLMs. They then train ChronoGraphVLM by adapting pretrained VLMs in two stages: (1) graph-as-chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning to reconstruct observed transitions and predict future ones as graph traces before answering, and (2) joint 4D graph reinforcement learning directly rewarding graph properties and answer correctness.
AI.result: Experiments across model scales show improvements over corresponding pretrained baselines and zero-shot transfer to VLM4D. Real-world demonstrations show that graph-based planning and affordance grounding support mobile manipulation through existing robot skills without additional fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: ChronoGraph provides a unified 4D graph representation that bridges interaction understanding and spatially grounded planning, and ChronoGraphVLM trained with graph-based CoT SFT and 4D graph RL outperforms pretrained baselines and transfers zero-shot to VLM4D, while enabling real-world mobile manipulation without extra fine-tuning.

title: Toward Real-Time VLAs: Stage-Aware Two-Step Flow Denoising and System-Level Evaluation
comment: 31 pages, 21 figures (including 10 supplementary figures), and 10 tables (including 3 supplementary tables). Project page: https://embodied.magiclab.top/works/inference/index.html. Code: https://github.com/MagiclabRobotics/Inference
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models face a timing gap between low-rate inference and high-rate robot execution. We characterize this gap through end-to-end latency measurements of model inference and the robot execution chain. Repeated Flow Matching denoising contributes substantially to inference cost, while robot-side delays mainly arise from perception acquisition, communication scheduling, and physical response. Analysis of the velocity field shows relatively stable magnitude and direction in early integration, followed by stronger directional correction near the terminal steps. Based on this stage heterogeneity, we propose two-stage non-uniform denoising, reducing the number of steps from 10 to 2 and model-inference time from 61.557 ms to 21.956 ms. We also develop a distributed real-time VLA framework with independent inference, action-publication, and robot-control rates, modular observation acquisition, and action-provenance logging. Using π0.5 as the baseline, we evaluate six real-time execution methods on a long-horizon physical garment-folding task. Legato performs best overall among training-based methods, while Temporal Smoothing leads among training-free methods; both perform strongly in task success, completion time, action continuity, and acceleration smoothness. Combining two-step denoising with representative execution methods substantially reduces inference cost with a small reduction in task performance. These results motivate joint optimization of model-inference efficiency and robot-system timing.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the timing gap between low-rate VLA inference and high-rate robot execution, proposes a two-stage non-uniform denoising scheme cutting flow-matching steps from 10 to 2 (61.557 ms → 21.956 ms), and builds a distributed real-time VLA framework to evaluate six execution methods on a garment-folding task.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) models suffer from a timing mismatch: model inference runs at a low rate while robot execution demands a high rate, creating end-to-end latency that harms real-time control. Repeated Flow Matching denoising dominates inference cost, and robot-side delays add further overhead, yet these two sources are typically not analyzed jointly.
AI.method: The authors measure end-to-end latency across model inference and the robot execution chain (perception acquisition, communication scheduling, physical response). They analyze the Flow Matching velocity field, finding stable magnitude/direction in early integration and stronger directional correction near terminal steps. Leveraging this stage heterogeneity, they design two-stage non-uniform denoising. They also build a distributed real-time VLA framework with independent inference, action-publication, and robot-control rates, modular observation acquisition, and action-provenance logging.
AI.result: Two-stage non-uniform denoising reduces denoising steps from 10 to 2 and model-inference time from 61.557 ms to 21.956 ms. Using π0.5 as baseline, six real-time execution methods are evaluated on a long-horizon physical garment-folding task. Legato performs best among training-based methods; Temporal Smoothing leads among training-free methods; both excel in task success, completion time, action continuity, and acceleration smoothness. Combining two-step denoising with representative execution methods substantially cuts inference cost with only a small drop in task performance.
AI.conclusion: Model-inference efficiency and robot-system timing should be optimized jointly rather than in isolation, as the proposed two-stage denoising and distributed real-time framework demonstrate effective latency reduction with minimal performance loss on a long-horizon manipulation task.

title: Values as Style: Disentangling Values from Semantics with One-Way Mixing for Low-Damage LLM Steering
summary: Value steering should change an LLM's normative priorities while preserving the scenario, facts, and task constraints underlying its answer. Conventional activation edits often change both. We introduce an editable semantic-value interface on frozen residual states, with a one-way semantic-to-value pathway that grounds value recognition in context. Stop-gradient blocks feedback through this pathway; swap consistency, topic de-confounding, and decorrelation encourage selective codes. At inference, editing the value code produces a residual delta while holding the semantic code fixed. On two instruction-tuned backbones, this interface improves semantic preservation and reduces benign refusals at comparable value alignment. A matched mixing-by-gating ablation separates representation learning from selective edit activation, and dimension-matched probes establish improved code selectivity. Against validation-selected prompting on LLaMA-3.1-8B, the method achieves comparable alignment (0.750 vs. 0.748), higher BERTScore (0.938 vs. 0.923), and fewer contradictions (5.1% vs. 7.6%). Human ratings and cross-taxonomy controls provide complementary evidence for low-damage value steering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an editable semantic-value interface on frozen residual states that enables value steering of LLMs by editing a value code while holding semantics fixed, improving semantic preservation and reducing benign refusals at comparable value alignment.
AI.motivation: Conventional activation edits for value steering typically change both an LLM's normative priorities and the scenario, facts, and task constraints underlying its answer. The paper aims to achieve value steering that changes normative priorities while preserving semantic content, i.e., low-damage value steering.
AI.method: The method builds an editable semantic-value interface on frozen residual states with a one-way semantic-to-value pathway grounding value recognition in context. Stop-gradient blocks feedback through this pathway, while swap consistency, topic de-confounding, and decorrelation encourage selective codes. At inference, editing the value code produces a residual delta while the semantic code is held fixed. Evaluated on two instruction-tuned backbones.
AI.result: On two instruction-tuned backbones, the interface improves semantic preservation and reduces benign refusals at comparable value alignment. A matched mixing-by-gating ablation separates representation learning from selective edit activation, and dimension-matched probes show improved code selectivity. Against validation-selected prompting on LLaMA-3.1-8B, it achieves comparable alignment (0.750 vs. 0.748), higher BERTScore (0.938 vs. 0.923), and fewer contradictions (5.1% vs. 7.6%).
AI.conclusion: The proposed editable semantic-value interface enables low-damage value steering, as supported by human ratings and cross-taxonomy controls, achieving value alignment comparable to prompting while better preserving semantics and reducing contradictions and benign refusals.

title: RL-Guided PAC-NMPC for Probabilistically-Safe Perception-Based Navigation in Unknown Environments
summary: In this paper, we present an approach for combining stochastic nonlinear model predictive control (SNMPC) and reinforcement learning (RL) to enable probabilistically-safe perception-based navigation in unknown environments. Our method first uses RL to train probabilistic actor-critic and sensor prediction models. We then leverage these probabilistic models in a sampling-based SNMPC framework known as Probably Approximately Correct (PAC)-NMPC, which uses hard constraints to enforce finite-time statistical guarantees on the probability of collision and value function improvement. By ensuring that our finite-horizon SNMPC policies decrease the value function in expectation, we can approach the long-horizon performance of the RL approach while satisfying probabilistic safety constraints. Through simulation experiments, we show that our approach can improve the safety of perception-based RL navigation policies and scale to high dimensional systems with large sensor input spaces and complex nonlinear dynamics. We also demonstrate our approach through hardware experiments, showing improved performance for vision-based navigation with an agile fixed-wing aerial vehicle in unknown environments.

AI.tldr: The paper combines stochastic nonlinear MPC with reinforcement learning to achieve probabilistically-safe, perception-based navigation in unknown environments, validated in simulation and on a fixed-wing aerial vehicle.
AI.motivation: RL navigation policies can achieve strong long-horizon performance but lack safety guarantees, especially under perception uncertainty in unknown environments. The paper aims to add probabilistic safety to such policies while retaining their performance.
AI.method: RL is first used to train probabilistic actor-critic and sensor prediction models. These probabilistic models are then embedded in a sampling-based stochastic nonlinear MPC framework (PAC-NMPC), which applies hard constraints to enforce finite-time statistical guarantees on collision probability and value function improvement.
AI.result: Simulation experiments show improved safety of perception-based RL navigation policies and scalability to high-dimensional systems with large sensor input spaces and complex nonlinear dynamics. Hardware experiments show improved vision-based navigation performance with an agile fixed-wing aerial vehicle in unknown environments.
AI.conclusion: Guaranteeing expected value function decrease for finite-horizon SNMPC policies lets the method approach RL's long-horizon performance while satisfying probabilistic safety constraints.

title: A helps B while B hurts A: directed transfer in instruction-tuning mixture
summary: Adapting a language model to a specialized corpus means choosing which instruction-tuning tasks to train on under a fixed budget, and testing one choice costs a fine-tuning run. Common heuristics add more source tasks or pick sources similar to the target. The first assumes transfer is never negative; the second, that it is symmetric. We show that both assumptions fail: task $A$ can help task $B$ while $B$ hurts $A$, so helpfulness is a signed property of ordered source--target pairs. We introduce the transfer map, a signed estimate of how much each source helps or hurts each held-out target. We fit the map in hundreds of fine-tuning runs on Qwen3 and Mistral models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, with all sources drawn from one corpus and no training examples from the target. The map predicts a held-out target's accuracy on unseen mixtures: recorded before those runs, its predictions have less than half the error of a mixture-agnostic baseline. The map is specific to its target and corpus but transfers across model scale: a mixture selected in advance at one size beats training on all source tasks at every other size we tested. Transfer is thus a property of the data. The map selects the tasks that help and drops the one that interferes: accuracy on the reasoning targets (causal explanation, multi-hop questions and methodological critique) rises by up to 14 percentage points over training on all source tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "transfer map," a signed, ordered source-target estimate of task helpfulness, empirically fit via hundreds of fine-tuning runs, showing that optimal task mixtures can be selected in advance and transfer across model scales, improving target accuracy by up to 14 points.
AI.motivation: Adapting a language model to a specialized corpus requires choosing instruction-tuning tasks under a fixed budget, where each choice costs a fine-tuning run. Prevailing heuristics assume transfer is never negative (more source tasks help) and symmetric (similarity implies mutual benefit). The authors argue both assumptions fail, since helpfulness is a signed property of ordered source-target pairs.
AI.method: The authors define the "transfer map" as a signed estimate of how much each source task helps or hurts each held-out target. They fit this map through hundreds of fine-tuning runs on Qwen3 and Mistral models ranging from 0.6B to 32B parameters, drawing all sources from a single corpus and using no training examples from the target.
AI.result: Recorded before the evaluation runs, the map predicts a held-out target's accuracy on unseen mixtures with less than half the error of a mixture-agnostic baseline. The map is target- and corpus-specific yet transfers across model scale: a mixture chosen in advance at one size outperforms training on all source tasks at every other tested size. Accuracy on reasoning targets (causal explanation, multi-hop questions, methodological critique) rises by up to 14 percentage points over training on all sources.
AI.conclusion: Transfer is a property of the data rather than the model. Treating helpfulness as an ordered, signed relationship and using the transfer map lets practitioners select beneficial tasks and drop interfering ones, achieving substantial gains within a fixed budget.

title: Magic-W0: A Structured World-Action Foundation Model for Physical Intelligence
comment: 29 pages, 15 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://embodied.magiclab.top/works/wam/magic-w0/index.html; Code: GitHub - MagiclabRobotics/Magic-W0
summary: World-action models (WAMs) augment robot policies with action-conditioned environment dynamics, yet existing approaches largely rely on future observation reconstruction or generic latent prediction and lack structured, control-oriented world representations tightly coupled with action generation. We introduce Magic-W0, a world-action foundation model that jointly models structured physical state evolution and continuous actions. Magic-W0 represents interaction as a Structured World Transition consisting of Current State, Transition, and Future State. Current State combines vision-language context with Current 3D Geometry; Transition is represented by 3D Motion capturing action-induced three-dimensional changes; and Future State is represented by Future Semantics describing task-relevant outcomes. To couple prediction and control, we propose a layer-aligned world-action interaction architecture in which evolving action hypotheses condition world-transition prediction, while predicted world representations continuously inform action generation. Magic-W0 is pre-trained on large-scale egocentric human manipulation, UMI, real-robot, and simulation data, with latent supervision for geometry, 3D motion, and future semantics from pre-trained visual models. Inference-time interventions show that structured world representations respond systematically to changes in candidate actions and that action-related information propagates through shared 3D representations into future semantic predictions. On RoboDojo-Sim, Magic-W0 achieves an average Score of 27.10, the highest among the compared WAMs. Across multiple real-robot tasks, it also demonstrates strong downstream performance after fine-tuning with limited downstream data, supporting generalization and rapid adaptation.

AI.tldr: Magic-W0 is a world-action foundation model that jointly models structured physical state evolution and continuous actions via a Structured World Transition (Current State, Transition, Future State), using a layer-aligned world-action interaction architecture and large-scale multimodal pre-training.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models augment robot policies with action-conditioned dynamics but mostly rely on future observation reconstruction or generic latent prediction, lacking structured, control-oriented world representations tightly coupled with action generation.
AI.method: Magic-W0 represents interaction as a Structured World Transition: Current State (vision-language context + Current 3D Geometry), Transition (3D Motion capturing action-induced 3D changes), and Future State (Future Semantics describing task-relevant outcomes). A layer-aligned world-action interaction architecture couples prediction and control: evolving action hypotheses condition world-transition prediction, while predicted world representations inform action generation. Pre-training uses large-scale egocentric human manipulation, UMI, real-robot, and simulation data with latent supervision for geometry, 3D motion, and future semantics from pre-trained visual models.
AI.result: Inference-time interventions show structured world representations respond systematically to candidate-action changes, and action-related information propagates through shared 3D representations into future semantic predictions. On RoboDojo-Sim, Magic-W0 achieves an average Score of 27.10, the highest among compared WAMs. On multiple real-robot tasks, it shows strong downstream performance after fine-tuning with limited data, supporting generalization and rapid adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Magic-W0 provides a structured, control-oriented world-action foundation model that tightly couples world prediction and action generation, yielding state-of-the-art performance among comparable WAMs and effective generalization and rapid adaptation on real-robot tasks with limited fine-tuning data.

title: ArchitectureIQ: On the Measure of Training Intuition
comment: 29 pages, 10 figures. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/renrua52/ArchitectureIQ
summary: Top researchers have good intuition, but do language models have as good intuition about model training as top AI researchers? To measure model intuition of LLMs and humans, we introduce the ArchitectureIQ benchmark. Each question presents a synthetic dataset and several training recipes, and the test-taker is asked to predict the recipe yielding the best test metric. Overall, we find that LLMs' model intuition is good but has four limitations: (1) The intuition is imperfect, or even sub-human in some cases. Frontier models achieve around 76% accuracy (random choice 33%) vs best human researcher (66.0%), yet remain far from perfect. For architecture-only questions, best human achieves 65% while GPT-6 Astra only has 38%. (2) The intuition is empirical, not structured, supported by the fact that more CoT compute does not lead to substantial improvement. Unlike math, we still lack a "Science of AI" language that enables structured reasoning on AI. (3) The intuition is not maximally condensed, and can be further compressed into a knoledge base. Our constructed knowledge base with only 20 items yields large gains for weak models: GPT-4o equipped with the accumulated knowledge almost matches the performance of Claude Opus 5.
