(4) The intuition is insensitive to dataset properties, but the best model should in general depend on data properties. This suggests that data is the real "dark matter" in AI -- LLMs (so do human researchers) understand too little about data, even less than model architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ArchitectureIQ, a benchmark measuring LLMs' and humans' intuition about model training by asking them to predict which of several training recipes yields the best test metric on synthetic datasets. LLMs show good but imperfect intuition, with four identified limitations.
AI.motivation: Top AI researchers rely on strong intuition when choosing among training recipes, but it is unknown whether LLMs possess comparable model-training intuition. The authors aim to systematically measure this intuition in both LLMs and humans to characterize its nature and limitations.
AI.method: ArchitectureIQ presents each test-taker with a synthetic dataset and several training recipes, requiring them to predict the recipe that will yield the best test metric. The benchmark is applied to both frontier LLMs and human researchers, with analyses probing accuracy, CoT scaling, knowledge-base compression, and sensitivity to dataset properties.
AI.result: (1) Intuition is imperfect and sometimes sub-human: frontier models reach ~76% vs 33% random and 66.0% for the best human, yet on architecture-only questions the best human scores 65% while GPT-6 Astra scores only 38%. (2) The intuition is empirical rather than structured, since more CoT compute yields no substantial improvement. (3) It can be compressed into a knowledge base of only 20 items, which boosts GPT-4o to nearly match Claude Opus 5. (4) It is insensitive to dataset properties, though the optimal model should depend on the data.
AI.conclusion: LLMs' model-training intuition is good but limited: empirically grounded rather than structured, compressible into a small knowledge base, and insensitive to data properties. The authors argue data is the real "dark matter" of AI, as both LLMs and human researchers understand data far less than architectures, and call for a "Science of AI" language enabling structured reasoning.

title: SplineWAM: Adaptive Action Horizons for World Action Models via B-Spline Representations
summary: World action models (WAMs) are large embodied policies that jointly predict future video and the actions to execute, emitting a fixed-length action chunk per inference call. Such a policy allocates its computational budget uniformly in time, unable to execute for longer over free-space motion or to spend more inference on contact-rich manipulation, which limits the throughput a WAM can reach when served in the cloud. We present SplineWAM, which adaptively compresses the action trajectory into a fixed-size window of cubic B-spline parameters, fitting the knot times to the characteristics of the motion. One parameter budget then decodes into chunks of varying temporal resolution and duration, and both the executed span and the interval until the next policy call follow from the prediction itself. Aligning the video supervision to the fitted knot times of the demonstration rather than to a uniform grid concentrates the supervised frames where the action trajectory is complex. For asynchronous deployment we introduce Jacobian-Pullback Real-Time Chunking (JP-RTC), which imposes chunk continuity on the decoded raw actions the robot executes rather than on the spline parameters, and corrects the parameters through the decoder so that the executed prefix agrees with the actions already committed. On LIBERO-Plus and RoboCasa, SplineWAM improves success rate over an action chunking WAM by $8.2$ and $4.4$ points while cutting policy calls per episode by 22% and 26%. On three bimanual real-robot tasks under asynchronous execution, it leads or matches the baseline while decoding 1.2 to 1.6 times as much executed motion per call.

AI.tldr: SplineWAM replaces the fixed-length uniform action chunk of world action models with a fixed-size window of cubic B-spline parameters whose knot times adapt to the motion, enabling variable-resolution chunks and self-determined re-inference timing; a Jacobian-Pullback Real-Time Chunking scheme maintains continuity for asynchronous deployment. It improves success rate by 8.2/4.4 points on LIBERO-Plus and RoboCasa while reducing policy calls by 22%/26%, and leads or matches baselines on three bimanual real-robot tasks with 1.2-1.6x more executed motion per call.
AI.motivation: World action models emit a fixed-length action chunk per inference, allocating computation uniformly in time. This prevents the policy from executing longer over free-space motion or spending more inference on contact-rich manipulation, limiting cloud-served throughput.
AI.method: Represent the action trajectory as a fixed-size window of cubic B-spline parameters, fitting knot times to motion characteristics so one parameter budget decodes into chunks of varying temporal resolution and duration, with both executed span and next-call interval derived from the prediction. Video supervision is aligned to fitted knot times instead of a uniform grid to concentrate supervised frames on complex trajectory segments. For asynchronous deployment, Jacobian-Pullback Real-Time Chunking (JP-RTC) enforces chunk continuity on decoded raw actions and corrects spline parameters through the decoder so the executed prefix matches committed actions.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Plus and RoboCasa, success rate improves by 8.2 and 4.4 points over an action-chunking WAM while policy calls per episode drop by 22% and 26%. On three bimanual real-robot tasks under asynchronous execution, it leads or matches the baseline while decoding 1.2 to 1.6 times more executed motion per call.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive spline-based action compression with motion-aware knot placement yields non-uniform temporal allocation, improving throughput and success rate over uniform action chunking, and transfers effectively to asynchronous real-robot bimanual deployment.

title: Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Ancillary files: decision log, executable transition model, LLM-labelled synthetic holdout. Synthetic mechanism study; no deployment claim
summary: Benchmarks, audits, and agent protocols describe performance, permissions, and repair, but not how observed evidence should change an agent's authority during a consequential task. We call this the assurance-transition gap. We propose a Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), a policy-level formal schema binding autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, evidence state, transition policy, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory gates. Under RAC, soft metrics may inform routing, whereas a failed or unknown mandatory gate forces retry, switch, escalation, deferral, or stop; aggregate performance cannot authorize action. We define the contract, an evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants, and illustrate them in clinical, industrial, and judicial failure probes. We then report a deterministic failure-injection study in agentic coding: 280 constructed cases evaluated by a gate conjunction, a score-only rule, and a restricted protocol baseline. At the published example weights and threshold, the score rule admits 80 of 100 block-required injections and all 40 review-required injections. Tuned in hindsight, it matches the conjunction on this corpus. For positive weights, a positive threshold, binary risk signals, zero-signal controls, and an injected case firing each signal alone, we show that exact agreement holds if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight. A separate set of 18 hand-authored traces checks version-pinned evidence and review transitions against simpler policy variants. In a further prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes, two blinded LLM judges assign identical labels to all 72 action attempts; RAC and a separately implemented full stateful baseline both match these labels. These studies test mechanisms on synthetic cases; they establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), a formal policy schema that binds autonomy boundaries, evidence state, and non-compensatory gates so that observed evidence, not aggregate performance, governs an agent's authority transitions; it is illustrated with failure probes and validated by deterministic failure-injection and synthetic holdout studies.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks, audits, and agent protocols characterize performance, permissions, and repair, but they do not specify how observed evidence should change an agent's authority during a consequential task. The authors identify this as the assurance-transition gap and aim to close it with a policy-level formal schema.
AI.method: The authors define the Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), binding autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, evidence state, transition policy, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory gates, along with an evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants. They illustrate these in clinical, industrial, and judicial failure probes and conduct a deterministic failure-injection study in agentic coding with 280 constructed cases evaluated by a gate conjunction, a score-only rule, and a restricted protocol baseline. They also analyze threshold agreement conditions and check 18 hand-authored traces for version-pinned evidence and review transitions, plus a prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes judged by two blinded LLM judges.
AI.result: Soft metrics may inform routing under RAC, but a failed or unknown mandatory gate forces retry, switch, escalation, deferral, or stop, and aggregate performance cannot authorize action. At published weights and threshold, the score rule admits 80 of 100 block-required injections and all 40 review-required injections; tuned in hindsight, it matches the conjunction on this corpus. For positive weights, positive threshold, binary risk signals, zero-signal controls, and single-signal injected cases, exact agreement holds if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight. In the 24-episode holdout, two blinded LLM judges assign identical labels to all 72 action attempts, and RAC and a full stateful baseline both match these labels.
AI.conclusion: The studies test mechanisms on synthetic cases and establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness; their contribution is conceptual and mechanistic rather than evidential of real-world assurance.

title: Active Mapping of Underwater Litter Using Camera-Sonar Fusion
summary: Marine litter is a growing threat to the underwater ecosystem, driving demand for autonomous survey methods that can locate debris efficiently over large areas. Existing survey methods typically follow predefined paths or operate with a single sensing modality, typically a camera (with image quality suffering in poor-visibility conditions) or sonar (usually noisy and low-resolution). We present an active mapping framework in which a forward-looking sonar and a camera both feed into a shared Bayesian occupancy map, and an optimization problem is solved at each step to decide on the next best view. Candidate viewpoints are scored by a two-term utility that balances exploration of uncertain regions via voxel entropy against exploitation of likely objects. Each sensor is characterized by range- and bearing-dependent detection and false-alarm probability tables determined from data. We evaluate the approach in a realistic underwater simulator, demonstrating that active mapping finds objects faster than a lawnmower coverage pattern, and that the dual-sensor approach works better than using either of the individual sensors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an active mapping framework for efficient underwater marine litter survey, fusing forward-looking sonar and camera into a shared Bayesian occupancy map, with a two-term entropy/exploitation utility driving next-best-view optimization; validated in simulation.
AI.motivation: Marine litter threatens the underwater ecosystem, creating demand for autonomous survey methods that efficiently locate debris over large areas. Existing surveys follow predefined paths or use a single sensing modality, which is limited: cameras degrade in poor visibility, while sonar is noisy and low-resolution.
AI.method: The authors build an active mapping framework in which a forward-looking sonar and a camera both feed a shared Bayesian occupancy map. An optimization problem is solved at each step to select the next best view. Candidate viewpoints are scored by a two-term utility balancing exploration of uncertain regions (voxel entropy) against exploitation of likely objects. Each sensor uses range- and bearing-dependent detection and false-alarm probability tables learned from data.
AI.result: Evaluation in a realistic underwater simulator shows that active mapping finds objects faster than a lawnmower coverage pattern, and that the dual-sensor approach outperforms either sensor used individually.
AI.conclusion: Active, dual-sensor mapping with entropy- and exploitation-based next-best-view planning improves the efficiency of underwater marine litter surveys relative to predefined coverage paths and single-sensor approaches.

title: OverForge: Reasoning Through Strategies and Tactics Helps Cooperative Lifelong Adaptation
summary: Cooperative language-model agents must coordinate over long horizons and adapt to changing environments and to partners with unfamiliar conventions, yet existing agents map observations to actions without separating persistent coordination strategies from their tactical execution. We introduce OverForge, a training-free hierarchical architecture that separates strategic reasoning over roles and divisions of labour from tactical reasoning over actions within each agent's private, partner-conditioned world model. A metacognitive Prefrontal Cortex Module couples the two levels by forming strategy-action branches, imagining their consequences with a forward model, and committing when confident. In OvercookedV2, OverForge delivers 7 soups in a connected kitchen versus 3 for each flat LLM baseline, retains agreed roles, and adopts roles proposed by unfamiliar partners. Ablations and a fixed-strategy probe show that persistent strategies guide tactical adaptation while each reasoning level contributes to coordination. Memory restarts show that cross-episode partner knowledge supports task performance and partner prediction, linking the hierarchy to continual adaptation.

AI.tldr: OverForge is a training-free hierarchical LLM agent architecture that separates persistent strategic reasoning (roles, division of labour) from tactical action execution via partner-conditioned world models, coupled by a metacognitive Prefrontal Cortex Module. It outperforms flat LLM baselines in OvercookedV2 (7 vs 3 soups) and generalizes to unfamiliar partners.
AI.motivation: Existing cooperative LM agents map observations directly to actions, conflating persistent coordination strategies with their tactical execution. This makes them poorly suited to long-horizon coordination and to adapting when environments or partners' conventions change.
AI.method: A training-free hierarchical architecture with two levels: strategic reasoning over roles and divisions of labour, and tactical reasoning over actions inside each agent's private, partner-conditioned world model. A metacognitive Prefrontal Cortex Module bridges the levels by forming strategy-action branches, imagining consequences with a forward model, and committing when confident.
AI.result: In OvercookedV2, OverForge achieves 7 soups in a connected kitchen versus 3 for each flat LLM baseline; it retains agreed roles and adopts roles proposed by unfamiliar partners. Ablations and a fixed-strategy probe show persistent strategies guide tactical adaptation and both levels contribute to coordination. Memory-restart experiments show cross-episode partner knowledge supports task performance and partner prediction.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling persistent strategies from tactical execution, mediated by metacognitive branching and a forward model, yields stronger long-horizon coordination and partner adaptation, linking the hierarchy to continual adaptation via cross-episode memory.

title: Magnetic based In-situ Self 3D Pose Estimation for a Modular Soft Tendon-Driven Continuum Robot via IMU-Fusion
summary: Continuum robots are well suited for gentle manipulation because of their inherent compliance and ability to adapt to complex environments. However, their continuously deformable structure makes accurate configuration estimation challenging, particularly when external vision systems are unavailable or obstructed. In this work, we present an embedded pose sensing framework that combines inertial measurement units (IMUs) and active magnetic fields to estimate the robot configuration without relying on external cameras. The angular measurements from the IMU and magnetic-field references are fused to improve local orientation estimation and reduce accumulated orientation error during operation. This pose sensing scheme achieves an update rate of 16.7~Hz, allowing real-time feedback. The proposed system is experimentally validated through closed-loop control, where the estimated robot configuration is used to maintain the end-effector at a desired position while interacting with an object. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed magnetic--inertial sensing for real-time pose estimation and closed-loop control of continuum robots.

AI.tldr: An embedded pose sensing framework fusing IMUs and active magnetic fields enables real-time configuration estimation and closed-loop control of continuum robots without external cameras.
AI.motivation: Continuum robots offer gentle manipulation due to inherent compliance and adaptability, but their continuously deformable structure makes accurate configuration estimation difficult, especially when external vision systems are unavailable or obstructed.
AI.method: The authors combine inertial measurement units (IMUs) with active magnetic fields. Angular measurements from the IMU and magnetic-field references are fused to improve local orientation estimation and reduce accumulated orientation error during operation, achieving a 16.7 Hz update rate for real-time feedback.
AI.result: The system is experimentally validated through closed-loop control, where the estimated configuration maintains the end-effector at a desired position while interacting with an object.
AI.conclusion: Distributed magnetic–inertial sensing shows potential for real-time pose estimation and closed-loop control of continuum robots, overcoming the need for external cameras.

title: Safety of Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Latent communication enables multi-agent systems to exchange information directly in internal representation space, reducing the token, computation, and latency overhead of text-based communication. To this end, lightweight trainable links are introduced to map the sender's representations into the receiver's input space. In this work, we show that even benign link training can increase harmful compliance relative to text-based communication while the underlying safety-aligned agents remain unchanged. An attacker can amplify this effect by optimizing the links on harmful query--response pairs or poisoning otherwise benign training data. We further develop a reinforcement-learning attack that rewards harmful compliance alongside benign task performance without requiring harmful target responses. Across three communication topologies and four safety benchmarks, this attack raises the mean harmful-compliance score from 27.9 with benignly trained links to 76.9. Compared with direct supervised optimization, it also achieves higher average accuracy on two benign utility benchmarks. Adapting the rewards toward safer behavior also enables repair of compromised links, substantially reducing harmful compliance across all evaluated attacks without updating the agents. Overall, our results show that safety alignment requires considering the multi-agent system as a whole.

AI.tldr: Latent communication links between safety-aligned agents can be trained (even benignly) to increase harmful compliance; a reinforcement-learning attack amplifies this effect, but reward-shaping can repair compromised links without updating the agents.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems using latent communication (trainable links mapping sender representations to receiver input space) reduce token, computation, and latency overhead versus text-based communication. The authors aim to show that safety of such systems cannot be assessed by the alignment of individual agents alone, since the trainable links introduce a new attack surface.
AI.method: The authors introduce lightweight trainable links between agents and show that link training alone (even benign) raises harmful compliance while agents remain unchanged. They amplify this via (1) optimizing links on harmful query-response pairs, (2) poisoning otherwise benign training data, and (3) a reinforcement-learning attack rewarding harmful compliance alongside benign task performance without requiring harmful target responses. They also explore reward-shaping toward safer behavior to repair compromised links.
AI.result: Across three communication topologies and four safety benchmarks, the RL attack raises mean harmful-compliance from 27.9 (benignly trained links) to 76.9, and outperforms direct supervised optimization on two benign utility benchmarks. Adapting rewards toward safer behavior repairs compromised links, substantially reducing harmful compliance across all evaluated attacks without updating the agents.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment must treat the multi-agent system as a whole: latent communication links are a distinct vulnerability that can subvert aligned agents, and link-level reward shaping offers an effective repair mechanism without retraining the underlying agents.

title: TACTIC: Temporal and Context-Aware LLM Tactical Planning for Roadside LiDAR Attacks
summary: Physical LiDAR attacks are often evaluated using fixed primitives and manually selected parameters, despite their strong dependence on surrounding traffic. We present TACTIC, a scene-aware framework that uses a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to coordinate state-adaptive roadside LiDAR attacks. Under a gray-box threat model, TACTIC relies only on an attacker-operated roadside perception stack, without accessing the victim LiDAR's native point clouds or internal processing. Local perception provides metric vehicle states, while the MLLM combines these measurements with roadside imagery to infer relational traffic context and construct a semantic scene graph. Based on this representation, TACTIC selects and configures two complementary primitives: \emph{push-away}, which shifts the perceived range of a lead vehicle, and \emph{phantom-obstacle braking}, which triggers emergency braking through obstacle injection. Measured traffic states and empirically calibrated constraints ground the generated tactics in physically feasible operating regions. To accommodate MLLM latency, TACTIC overlaps reasoning and execution asynchronously while high-rate local perception detects scene changes and triggers replanning. Across 280 randomized CARLA trials, the full policy achieves a 100% collision rate, compared with 35% for a fixed rule, 60% for random selection, and 75% for a restricted LLM using mode selection with default parameters. Joint physical-and-image input achieves 100% success, versus 65% with physical measurements alone and 75% with imagery alone, while asynchronous $Δ$ refresh reduces scene-mutation response from 7.4 s to 2.0 s. These results show that scene-dependent tactical planning can expose context-sensitive LiDAR failure modes that fixed attack policies may miss.

AI.tldr: TACTIC is a scene-aware framework that uses a multimodal large language model to coordinate state-adaptive roadside LiDAR attacks, achieving 100% collision rate in CARLA trials.
AI.motivation: Physical LiDAR attacks are often evaluated using fixed primitives and manually selected parameters, despite their strong dependence on surrounding traffic. This limits realism and misses context-sensitive failure modes.
AI.method: Under a gray-box threat model relying only on an attacker-operated roadside perception stack, local perception provides metric vehicle states, while an MLLM combines these with roadside imagery to infer relational traffic context and build a semantic scene graph. TACTIC selects and configures two primitives: push-away (shifts perceived range of a lead vehicle) and phantom-obstacle braking (triggers emergency braking via obstacle injection). Measured states and calibrated constraints ground tactics in feasible regions. Asynchronous overlap of reasoning and execution handles MLLM latency, with high-rate perception triggering replanning on scene changes.
AI.result: Across 280 randomized CARLA trials, the full policy achieves 100% collision rate vs. 35% for a fixed rule, 60% for random selection, and 75% for a restricted LLM. Joint physical-and-image input yields 100% success vs. 65% (physical only) and 75% (imagery only). Asynchronous Δ refresh reduces scene-mutation response from 7.4 s to 2.0 s.
AI.conclusion: Scene-dependent tactical planning can expose context-sensitive LiDAR failure modes that fixed attack policies may miss.

title: Learning Steganography Is Easy, Learning Steganographic Reasoning Is Hard
comment: Accepted as an oral at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD). 41 pages. Code: https://github.com/stegano-ai/steg-reasoning-is-hard
summary:
Chain-of-thought monitoring as an approach for AI oversight and control is threatened by the possibility of steganographic reasoning, where LLMs conceal their reasoning inside innocuous-looking text. Two neighbouring capabilities, steganographic messaging (passing a concealed message) and encoded reasoning (reasoning in an illegible but unconcealed format), have already been shown to emerge under training pressures that occur in real pipelines, such as reinforcement learning against monitors. This suggests that steganographic reasoning too might arise as an unintended side effect of training. Here, we compare how easily models learn steganographic reasoning and these two neighbouring capabilities across three elicitation methods: reinforcement learning, in-context learning, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
  For most tasks, models learn steganographic reasoning only under SFT, while they learn steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning under all three elicitation methods. Even under SFT, steganographic reasoning requires at least twice as much training as messaging, and for several model-task combinations it is not learned at all. However, on a cover task that makes hiding information especially convenient, steganographic reasoning can be successfully learned under all three elicitation methods. Steganographic reasoning is thus much harder than steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning, and learning the latter two does not imply learning the former. Yet it lies within reach: an easy version is learned under every elicitation method, when the cover task is convenient for hiding information.

AI.tldr: Steganographic reasoning (concealing reasoning in innocuous text) is much harder for LLMs to learn than steganographic messaging or encoded reasoning, arising mostly only under SFT and requiring at least 2x more training—yet it becomes learnable under all elicitation methods when the cover task conveniently allows hiding information.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a key AI oversight technique, but it is threatened by steganographic reasoning, where models hide their reasoning in innocuous-looking text. Since neighbouring capabilities (steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning) have already been shown to emerge under realistic training pressures like RL against monitors, steganographic reasoning might also arise as an unintended training side effect. The authors therefore investigate how easily models acquire this capability relative to its neighbours.
AI.method: The authors compare how easily models learn steganographic reasoning versus steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning across three elicitation methods: reinforcement learning, in-context learning, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). They measure learnability across multiple model-task combinations, including a cover task designed to make information hiding especially convenient.
AI.result: For most tasks, models learn steganographic reasoning only under SFT, whereas they learn steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning under all three elicitation methods. Even with SFT, steganographic reasoning needs at least twice as much training as messaging, and for several model-task combinations it is not learned at all. However, on a cover task that makes hiding information especially convenient, steganographic reasoning is successfully learned under all three elicitation methods.
AI.conclusion: Steganographic reasoning is substantially harder to acquire than steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning, and learning the latter two does not imply learning the former. Nevertheless, it remains within reach: an easy version can be learned under every elicitation method when the cover task is convenient for hiding information.

title: PhasePlan: Ordered Future-Phase Planning for Robot Brain Models
summary: Robot brain models integrate vision, language, and robot state to generate actions for complex manipulation tasks. Most predict fixed-length action chunks that may span multiple task phases. This can obscure phase transitions and favor frequent action patterns, compromising action timing in dynamic environments. We propose \method, an ordered future-phase planning method for robot brain models. From current multimodal observations, it predicts the task phase at each future action position. The resulting planning representations condition the corresponding actions, preserving temporal alignment between task progress and action generation. Training first learns the planner, then freezes it during action-model adaptation to maintain stable phase representations. We instantiate \method on pretrained $π_{0.5}$ and AcrossWAM1.0 robot brain models. Detailed quantitative evaluation uses the $π_{0.5}$ implementation. On conveyor-belt manipulation, \method reduces offline joint-action error by approximately 22.5\% relative to the original $π_{0.5}$ model. It also improves phase-transition modeling and cross-phase action prediction. These results demonstrate the value of ordered future-phase planning for continuous action generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ordered future-phase planning method (\method) for robot brain models, predicting task phases at each future action position to condition action generation and improve phase-transition handling and action timing.
AI.motivation: Most robot brain models predict fixed-length action chunks spanning multiple task phases, which obscures phase transitions and biases toward frequent action patterns, harming action timing in dynamic environments.
AI.method: \method predicts the task phase at each future action position from current multimodal observations. The resulting planning representations condition corresponding actions, preserving temporal alignment between task progress and action generation. Training first learns the planner, then freezes it during action-model adaptation to keep phase representations stable. It is instantiated on pretrained π_{0.5} and AcrossWAM1.0 robot brain models.
AI.result: On conveyor-belt manipulation using the π_{0.5} implementation, \method reduces offline joint-action error by about 22.5% relative to the original π_{0.5} model, and improves phase-transition modeling and cross-phase action prediction.
AI.conclusion: Ordered future-phase planning is valuable for continuous action generation in robot brain models.

title: FIGS: Evaluating Multi-Turn Sycophancy Without Penalizing Empathy
summary: Large language models frequently fail to balance staying truthful with being supportive. They often exhibit sycophancy in responses to users, agreeing with false claims, offering unwarranted flattery, and giving advice skewed toward users' expressed views. In reality, sycophancy rarely happens in a single exchange; it may emerge organically as users repeatedly insist or subtly steer the dialogue over time. Current evaluations, however, rely on rigid, single-turn tests or fixed scripts that fail to capture these natural dynamics. Furthermore, these benchmarks often mistake showing basic empathy for yielding, penalizing models for acknowledging a user's feeling. This view may drive future models to over-correct into cold, dismissive rigidity. To address this gap, we introduce FIGS (Factual Integrity and Grounded Support), a dual-axis evaluation framework built around extended, realistic dialogue. We use an adaptive 10-turn conversational simulator that dynamically challenges the target model, reflecting how users repeat requests, push back, or steer a conversation toward a preferred answer. To accurately evaluate these trajectories, we apply a taxonomy that strictly separates Sycophancy (whether the model holds firm to the truth and keeps its praise proportional) from Calibrated Validation (showing empathetic understanding of the user's feelings without overdoing it). We release our complete testing environment, including 500 diverse multi-turn scenarios and an automated judge. Our evaluation of leading models reveals a consistent trade-off: over the course of a sustained interaction, current systems either slowly drift to sycophancy or over-correct into robotic detachment. This demonstrates that balancing honesty with appropriate support throughout a natural conversation remains a critical, unsolved challenge.

AI.tldr: FIGS is a dual-axis, multi-turn evaluation framework (500 adaptive 10-turn scenarios + automated judge) that separates Sycophancy from Calibrated Validation, revealing that leading LLMs either drift toward sycophancy or over-correct into robotic detachment over sustained dialogue.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to balance truthfulness with supportiveness, often showing sycophancy (agreeing with false claims, unwarranted flattery, advice skewed to user views). Sycophancy typically emerges across repeated insistence and subtle steering, yet existing evaluations use rigid single-turn tests or fixed scripts that miss these dynamics. They also conflate basic empathy with yielding, penalizing appropriate acknowledgment of user feelings—risking future models that over-correct into cold, dismissive rigidity.
AI.method: The authors introduce FIGS (Factual Integrity and Grounded Support), a dual-axis evaluation framework based on extended, realistic dialogue. It uses an adaptive 10-turn conversational simulator that dynamically challenges the target model, mimicking how users repeat requests, push back, or steer toward a preferred answer. A taxonomy strictly separates Sycophancy (holding firm to truth, keeping praise proportional) from Calibrated Validation (empathizing with user feelings without overdoing it). The complete testing environment is released, including 500 diverse multi-turn scenarios and an automated judge.
AI.result: Evaluating leading models reveals a consistent trade-off: over sustained interaction, current systems either slowly drift into sycophancy or over-correct into robotic detachment.
AI.conclusion: Balancing honesty with appropriate support throughout a natural conversation remains a critical, unsolved challenge, highlighting a persistent tension between factual integrity and grounded support that current models fail to resolve.

title: When Instructions Retrieve Trajectories: Diagnosing and Mitigating Generalization Failures in VLA Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can exceed 90% success on in-distribution tasks and withstand nuisance changes that preserve the required action, yet fail under counterfactual changes that demand a different action. Aggregate robustness scores can therefore conceal a more specific failure, in which a policy responds to both language and vision yet does not combine them to select the action the task requires. We call this failure instruction-action binding. Instructions cue familiar trajectory families, and visual feedback adjusts their execution. Behavioral analyses of fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T-N1.7 policies reveal that failed rollouts often retain the source behavior or switch to another demonstrated task. These switches show that language is not simply ignored. Readouts and interventions connect these choices to task-conditioned internal states. Our analysis of the imitation objective shows how narrow conditional action support can leave grounded and instruction-keyed solutions indistinguishable on the demonstrations. This motivates Equivariant Counterfactual Training (ECT), which acts at two levels. ECT data supply valid demonstrations in which the same instruction requires different actions in distinguishable scenes, while the ECT loss trains each demonstration with its counterpart in the same update. In a controlled LIBERO-PRO comparison, full ECT raises $π_{0.5}$'s mean position-swap success from 36% to 59%. On CALVIN, where counterparts already occur in the original data, the ECT loss improves five-task completion without new demonstrations. On a real UR5e under a fixed demonstration budget, full ECT raises unseen-position success from 8% to 88%.

AI.tldr: VLA models that appear robust can still fail at "instruction-action binding"—using both language and vision but not combining them to select the required action; the paper diagnoses this and proposes Equivariant Counterfactual Training (ECT) to fix it.
AI.motivation: Aggregate robustness scores hide a specific failure mode: policies respond to language and vision yet fail under counterfactual changes that demand a different action. Instructions cue familiar trajectory families while visual feedback only adjusts execution, so the policy may not truly bind instruction to action. This failure is termed instruction-action binding.
AI.method: Behavioral analyses of fine-tuned π0.5 and GR00T-N1.7 policies show failed rollouts retain source behavior or switch to another demonstrated task, indicating language is not simply ignored. Readouts and interventions link these choices to task-conditioned internal states. Analysis of the imitation objective shows narrow conditional action support leaves grounded and instruction-keyed solutions indistinguishable on demonstrations. This motivates Equivariant Counterfactual Training (ECT), operating at two levels: ECT data provide valid demonstrations where the same instruction requires different actions in distinguishable scenes, and the ECT loss trains each demonstration with its counterpart in the same update.
AI.result: In a controlled LIBERO-PRO comparison, full ECT raises π0.5's mean position-swap success from 36% to 59%. On CALVIN, where counterparts already exist in the original data, the ECT loss improves five-task completion without new demonstrations. On a real UR5e under a fixed demonstration budget, full ECT raises unseen-position success from 8% to 88%.
AI.conclusion: ECT effectively addresses instruction-action binding failures in VLA models, improving counterfactual robustness across simulated benchmarks (LIBERO-PRO, CALVIN) and real-robot settings (UR5e), with substantial gains even under fixed demonstration budgets.

title: Completion-Aware Cross-Fidelity Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Line Bus Holding
summary: Exploratory reinforcement learning (RL) on an operating bus fleet is impractical,while policies trained only from historical data cannot acquire new experience. Hybrid Offline-and-Online (H2O) RL combines fixed target replay with simulator interaction, but the inexpensive online simulator can differ from the target in transition and event-duration dynamics. We study this cross-fidelity problem for multi-line bus holding and address a failure mode in which lower generalized passenger time coexists with incomplete passenger journeys.

AI.tldr: This paper studies cross-fidelity Hybrid Offline-and-Online (H2O) reinforcement learning for multi-line bus holding, addressing a failure mode where generalized passenger time improves but some passengers fail to complete their journeys.
AI.motivation: Exploratory RL directly on a live bus fleet is impractical, and purely offline policies trained on historical data cannot gain new experience. H2O RL, combining fixed target replay with simulator interaction, is a promising alternative, but the low-cost online simulator can differ from the real target in both transition dynamics and event-duration dynamics. This cross-fidelity mismatch creates reliability issues that must be understood before deployment.
AI.method: The authors formulate the cross-fidelity problem for multi-line bus holding and analyze a specific failure mode of H2O RL in this setting. The analysis links the simulator-target fidelity gap in transition and event-duration dynamics to the observed phenomenon of reduced generalized passenger time alongside incomplete passenger journeys.
AI.result: A failure mode is identified in which lower generalized passenger time coexists with incomplete passenger journeys, indicating that standard aggregate performance metrics can mask service failures under cross-fidelity H2O RL.
AI.conclusion: Cross-fidelity mismatch between simulator and target must be explicitly accounted for in H2O RL for bus holding; aggregate metrics alone are insufficient, and journey-completion criteria are needed to detect and avoid this failure mode.

title: EWAM: Emergent Depth-Wise Specialization in a Unified Embodied Model -- From Semantic Understanding through Visual Foresight to Action
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies emphasize semantic understanding, whereas world-action models (WAMs) learn predictive representations of environment dynamics. Systems that expose a policy to both sources often still concentrate action computation on a single expert. We present EWAM, an action-centric unified embodied model whose asymmetric joint attention lets action tokens read semantic, current-visual, predicted-future, and action information at every layer while the perceptual experts retain their distinct roles. Without layer-wise supervision, EWAM develops an emergent depth-wise specialization: action queries attend mainly to vision-language features in shallow layers, to predicted future frames in intermediate layers, and to action tokens themselves in deep layers. This handoff replicates across tasks and is stable across denoising steps. Checkpoint tracking and causal interventions show that it is learned and that action generation depends on it. EWAM is pretrained in two separate regimes, one on cross-embodiment robot trajectories and one on human egocentric video. In simulation and real-robot experiments, it surpasses existing VLA, WAM, and hybrid baselines. Human egocentric data improve both cross-embodiment transfer and real-robot robustness, and subtask-phase supervision improves long-horizon completion. Together, these results suggest that unified embodied learning can induce an ordered internal progression from semantic understanding, through visual foresight, to action formation.

AI.tldr: EWAM is an action-centric unified embodied model that uses asymmetric joint attention to let action tokens read semantic, current-visual, predicted-future, and action information at every layer. Without explicit layer-wise supervision, it develops an emergent depth-wise specialization in which action queries shift from vision-language features in shallow layers, to predicted future frames in intermediate layers, to action tokens in deep layers. This ordered progression is stable, causally necessary, and yields state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches are split between Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, which emphasize semantic understanding, and World-Action Models (WAMs), which learn predictive representations of environment dynamics. Systems that expose a policy to both sources typically still concentrate action computation on a single expert, failing to exploit the complementary structure of semantic and predictive information in an integrated way.
AI.method: EWAM is an action-centric unified embodied model built on asymmetric joint attention, in which action tokens attend to four information sources—semantic, current-visual, predicted-future, and action—at every layer, while the perceptual experts retain their distinct roles. It is pretrained in two regimes: one on cross-embodiment robot trajectories and one on human egocentric video. The authors analyze the learned attention structure via checkpoint tracking and causal interventions, and additionally apply subtask-phase supervision.
AI.result: Without layer-wise supervision, EWAM exhibits an emergent depth-wise specialization: action queries attend mainly to vision-language features in shallow layers, predicted future frames in intermediate layers, and action tokens in deep layers. This handoff replicates across tasks and remains stable across denoising steps. Checkpoint tracking and causal interventions show the pattern is learned and that action generation depends on it. In simulation and real-robot experiments, EWAM surpasses existing VLA, WAM, and hybrid baselines; human egocentric data improve cross-embodiment transfer and real-robot robustness, and subtask-phase supervision improves long-horizon completion.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that unified embodied learning can induce an ordered internal progression from semantic understanding, through visual foresight, to action formation, with emergent architectural specialization arising from the joint attention design rather than explicit supervision.

title: GrammarRL: Effective Grammar-Constrained Decoding via Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Grammar-constrained generation guarantees syntactic validity, but can substantially degrade semantic quality when the model's preferred outputs are poorly aligned with the imposed grammar. This trade-off is particularly severe when the prompt is underspecified or the model has limited instruction-following ability. Beam search can partially mitigate these failures by exploring multiple valid sequences, but its computational cost grows with beam width, while sequence-level probability is only an imperfect proxy for semantic quality.
  We introduce GrammarRL, a label-free reinforcement learning method that adapts language models to grammar constraints without requiring annotated data. GrammarRL optimizes the model using two complementary self-supervised rewards derived from its own likelihoods: a direct reward, measuring how likely the constrained output is given the input, and a reverse reward, measuring how well the input can be reconstructed from the generated output. We optimize these rewards with a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) objective over groups of grammar-constrained rollouts, augmented with the top-1 beam-search hypothesis and regularized towards a frozen base model.
  We evaluate GrammarRL on sign language gloss translation, hierarchical text classification, and named entity recognition using Llama models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters. GrammarRL consistently outperforms constrained greedy decoding, with an average improvement of 9.8 points and gains of up to 22.8 BLEU. It matches or outperforms beam search on two of the three tasks while preserving greedy-decoding inference cost. Ablations further show that the two rewards are complementary: either reward alone can underperform the untrained baseline, whereas their combination consistently improves upon it.

AI.tldr: GrammarRL is a label-free RL method that adapts language models to grammar constraints using two self-supervised rewards (direct and reverse likelihood), optimized with RLOO over constrained rollouts, improving semantic quality while keeping greedy-decoding inference cost.
AI.motivation: Grammar-constrained generation guarantees syntactic validity but can substantially degrade semantic quality when the model's preferred outputs misalign with the imposed grammar. This trade-off is severe with underspecified prompts or weak instruction-following. Beam search partially mitigates this but its cost grows with beam width, and sequence-level probability is an imperfect proxy for semantic quality.
AI.method: GrammarRL is a label-free RL method that adapts LMs to grammar constraints without annotated data. It optimizes the model with two complementary self-supervised rewards from its own likelihoods: a direct reward (likelihood of the constrained output given the input) and a reverse reward (reconstructability of the input from the output). Rewards are optimized with a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) objective over groups of grammar-constrained rollouts, augmented with the top-1 beam-search hypothesis and regularized toward a frozen base model.
AI.result: On sign language gloss translation, hierarchical text classification, and named entity recognition with Llama models (1B–8B), GrammarRL consistently outperforms constrained greedy decoding, averaging +9.8 points and up to +22.8 BLEU. It matches or beats beam search on two of three tasks while preserving greedy-decoding inference cost. Ablations show the two rewards are complementary: either alone can underperform the untrained baseline, while their combination consistently improves upon it.
AI.conclusion: GrammarRL resolves the validity-quality trade-off of grammar-constrained generation by training a model to produce semantically strong yet grammatically valid outputs, achieving beam-search-level quality at greedy-decoding cost without annotated data, and demonstrating that direct and reverse likelihood rewards must be combined to be effective.

title: Multi-Link Safety Filtering for VLA Policies Around Moving Hazards
summary: A vision-language-action (VLA) policy can finish a manipulation task while knocking over objects unrelated to it, so task success alone does not show that the policy is safe to deploy in clutter. We study how to keep a pretrained VLA policy clear of such hazards at run time without retraining it, which requires guarding more of the arm than the end effector, following the hazard as it moves, and sharing onboard compute with the policy. Our training-free shield covers the gripper, wrist, and forearm with five ellipsoids and filters every commanded motion through one barrier program against a keep-out ellipsoid fitted from RGB-D perception at reset. Sparse optical flow then carries that ellipsoid's center along with the hazard, with no repeated detection or refitting. Over six simulated hazard-motion conditions, the shield lowers collision from $65.62\%$ to $27.27\%$ and raises safe-success, task completion without collision, from $29.35\%$ to $50.43\%$. Ablations show that guarding the arm links protects beyond end-effector shielding, and that tracking recovers most of the protection lost when the hazard estimate is frozen at reset. On heterogeneous edge hardware, the five-ellipsoid barrier runs on the CPU in $2.2$~ms at the 99th percentile, and trimming the vision--language prefix and taking fewer flow-matching steps shortens each $π_{0.5}$ policy call on the integrated GPU from $343$ to $177.3$~ms. On a physical SO-101 arm across four tasks, the arm touched the hazard in 3 of 16 shielded episodes versus 11 of 16 unshielded ones. Project page: https://yathag.github.io/multilink-safety-filter/

AI.tldr: A training-free run-time shield keeps a pretrained VLA policy clear of task-unrelated hazards by covering the gripper, wrist, and forearm with five ellipsoids and filtering commanded motions through a single barrier program against a keep-out ellipsoid, which is tracked by sparse optical flow. It cuts collisions from 65.62% to 27.27% and raises safe-success from 29.35% to 50.43% across six simulated conditions, runs within real-time budgets on edge hardware, and reduces hazard contact on a physical SO-101 arm.
AI.motivation: Task success alone does not demonstrate that a VLA policy is safe to deploy in clutter, since a policy can complete a manipulation task while knocking over unrelated objects. The goal is therefore to keep a pretrained VLA policy clear of such hazards at run time without retraining it. This is challenging because it requires guarding more of the arm than just the end effector, following the hazard as it moves, and sharing onboard compute with the policy itself.
AI.method: The approach is a training-free shield. It covers the gripper, wrist, and forearm with five ellipsoids and filters every commanded motion through one barrier program against a keep-out ellipsoid fitted from RGB-D perception at reset. Sparse optical flow then carries the ellipsoid's center along with the hazard, avoiding repeated detection or refitting. For onboard efficiency, the vision-language prefix is trimmed and fewer flow-matching steps are used to shorten each policy call.
AI.result: Over six simulated hazard-motion conditions, the shield lowers collision from 65.62% to 27.27% and raises safe-success (task completion without collision) from 29.35% to 50.43%. Ablations show that guarding the arm links protects beyond end-effector shielding, and that tracking recovers most of the protection lost when the hazard estimate is frozen at reset. On heterogeneous edge hardware, the five-ellipsoid barrier runs on the CPU in 2.2 ms at the 99th percentile, and trimming the vision-language prefix and taking fewer flow-matching steps shortens each π0.5 policy call on the integrated GPU from 343 to 177.3 ms. On a physical SO-101 arm across four tasks, the arm touched the hazard in 3 of 16 shielded episodes versus 11 of 16 unshielded ones.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, multi-link shield that tracks a keep-out ellipsoid and shares compute with the policy can substantially reduce collisions and improve safe-success for a pretrained VLA policy, while remaining within real-time onboard budgets and transferring to physical hardware.

title: OSWorld-Science: A Benchmark of Computer Use Agents for Learning and Using Scientific Software
comment: 62 pages. Website: https://discoailab.github.io/osworld-science-page/ Public contributions welcome: https://forms.gle/htxY5snyANJ4moVEA
summary: Scientific software presents a demanding test for computer-using agents based on visual language models (VLMs): completing a research workflow requires interpreting specialized interfaces, manipulating scientific objects, and producing verifiable results. We thus introduce OSWorld-Science, a benchmark and evaluation environment that combines scientifically meaningful tasks, artifact-based evaluation, and an efficient agent harness for studying computer use in the scientific domain. The benchmark contains 12 VLMs and 146 high-quality tasks across several scientific domains and software configurations, covering workflows such as molecular drawing and retrosynthesis, pathology image analysis, statistical computing, and physical simulation. Tasks are developed through expert proposals and iterative human--AI co-design, with selection guided by scientific value and difficulty. Task-specific execution-based evaluators inspect application states and generated artifacts, including molecular structures, segmentation masks, plots, and numerical results, and award partial credit for incomplete outcomes. Our special harness integrates model adapters, interaction-loop control, and trajectory logging to support comparisons of models and interaction strategies. Our results show that current state-of-the-art VLMs with a strong harness still face challenges in addressing key questions in the scientific domains. We also analyze the benchmarking results across multi-linguistics, reasoning efforts, context length and other factors and derive several important conclusions and directions to assist future development. Overall, we provide an integrated framework connecting expert-defined scientific goals to verifiable software outcomes, enabling systematic evaluation of both agent capabilities and harness design in scientific workflows.

AI.tldr: OSWorld-Science is a new benchmark and evaluation environment for testing VLMs as computer-using agents on scientifically meaningful software tasks, using artifact-based execution evaluators and a specialized agent harness.
AI.motivation: Scientific software poses a demanding test for VLM-based computer-using agents, since research workflows require interpreting specialized interfaces, manipulating scientific objects, and producing verifiable results—yet no integrated benchmark existing for this domain.
AI.method: The authors build OSWorld-Science with 146 high-quality tasks across multiple scientific domains and software configurations (molecular drawing, retrosynthesis, pathology image analysis, statistical computing, physical simulation), developed via expert proposals and human–AI co-design. Task-specific execution-based evaluators inspect application states and generated artifacts (molecular structures, segmentation masks, plots, numerical results) with partial credit. A special harness integrates model adapters, interaction-loop control, and trajectory logging.
AI.result: Evaluating 12 VLMs shows that even state-of-the-art models with a strong harness still face challenges on key scientific questions. Analyses across multi-linguistics, reasoning effort, context length, and other factors yield several conclusions and directions for future development.
AI.conclusion: OSWorld-Science provides an integrated framework linking expert-defined scientific goals to verifiable software outcomes, enabling systematic evaluation of both agent capabilities and harness design in scientific workflows.

title: Identifiable Decomposition of Submovements in Human Hand Trajectories
summary: Voluntary movements have long been hypothesised to be comprised of discrete primitives called submovements, as a descriptive model of human motor behaviour. However, existing methods scale poorly, and no principled method exists to determine whether a decomposition is informative. We propose a spatiotemporal kernel correlation between primitive pairs as an identifiability criterion. Submovement-Identifiable Decomposition (Sub-ID) embeds this criterion in its adaptive-ridge regularisation, biasing the optimiser toward low-correlation solutions. Identifiability is lost when primitives become collinear and recovered when they diverge spatially. On synthetic data, Sub-ID recovers ground-truth parameter distributions where existing methods fail; furthermore, when primitives overlap too heavily to be distinguished, the method explicitly detects this ambiguity rather than outputting misleading results. Sub-ID extracts submovements from real three-dimensional, long-horizon movements, a regime no prior method addresses. This method has the potential to identify physiologically grounded primitives for motor control research and imitation learning.

AI.tldr: Sub-ID introduces a spatiotemporal kernel correlation as an identifiability criterion, embedded in adaptive-ridge regularization, to decompose voluntary movements into discrete submovement primitives.
AI.motivation: Voluntary movements are hypothesized to be built from discrete primitives called submovements, but existing decomposition methods scale poorly and lack a principled way to judge whether a decomposition is informative.
AI.method: The authors propose a spatiotemporal kernel correlation between primitive pairs as an identifiability criterion. Submovement-Identifiable Decomposition (Sub-ID) embeds this criterion into its adaptive-ridge regularization, biasing the optimizer toward low-correlation solutions.
AI.result: On synthetic data, Sub-ID recovers ground-truth parameter distributions where existing methods fail, and it explicitly detects ambiguity when primitives overlap too heavily. It also extracts submovements from real three-dimensional, long-horizon movements, a regime no prior method addresses.
AI.conclusion: Sub-ID offers a principled, scalable approach that can identify physiologically grounded primitives for motor control research and imitation learning.

title: ConflictGuide: AutoResearch Improves When Competing Behaviors Are Made Visible
summary: When designing machine learning models, desirable properties are often in tension: improving one behavior can impair another, so task progress can depend on alleviating the conflict. LLM-based AutoResearch systems, which iteratively edit model code and retain edits based on scalar task-performance feedback, have largely ignored this trade-off. We find that scalar feedback supports broad exploration early in search, but it does not reveal how edits affect competing behaviors. In matched-budget experiments, introducing competing-behavior feedback as task gains diminish increases the share of proposals that improve both behaviors and sustains progress beyond scalar-only plateaus. Obtaining this feedback for a given model requires identifying its competing behaviors and designing probes to measure them. To make competing-behavior feedback actionable, we introduce ConflictGuide. Its reusable ConflictGuide-Skill combines a literature-grounded taxonomy with model-specific evidence to identify competing behaviors and specify probes for a code agent to implement as metrics. Evolution proceeds in two stages: Stage I explores with task feedback; Stage II uses probe feedback to steer proposals toward conflict alleviation and retains marginal-gain edits only when probes indicate sufficient alleviation. Across five diverse model families, ConflictGuide reduces task and conflict-related errors by up to 28% and 14%, respectively, relative to scalar-only AutoResearch, with gains extending to other code agents.

AI.tldr: ConflictGuide enables LLM-based AutoResearch systems to detect and alleviate competing behaviors during model design by replacing pure scalar task feedback with probe-based competing-behavior feedback, reducing task errors up to 28% and conflict errors up to 14%.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models often face tensions where improving one desirable property impairs another, so progress depends on resolving these conflicts. Existing LLM-based AutoResearch systems iteratively edit model code and rely solely on scalar task-performance feedback, which supports broad early exploration but fails to reveal how edits affect competing behaviors, causing plateaus.
AI.method: Matched-budget experiments show that introducing competing-behavior feedback as task gains diminish increases the share of proposals improving both behaviors. The authors introduce ConflictGuide, featuring a reusable ConflictGuide-Skill that combines a literature-grounded taxonomy with model-specific evidence to identify competing behaviors and specify probes, implemented by a code agent as metrics. Evolution has two stages: Stage I explores with task feedback; Stage II uses probe feedback to steer proposals toward conflict alleviation and retains marginal-gain edits only when probes show sufficient alleviation.
AI.result: Across five diverse model families, ConflictGuide reduces task and conflict-related errors by up to 28% and 14%, respectively, compared to scalar-only AutoResearch, with gains extending to other code agents.
AI.conclusion: Competing-behavior feedback, operationalized through ConflictGuide's two-stage probe-steered search, reliably alleviates design tensions and sustains progress beyond scalar-only plateaus, generalizing across model families and code agents.

title: BatSLAM 2.0: Sequence-Verified Sonar Place Recognition in a Robust Pose Graph
summary: Echolocating bats can navigate dark and cluttered spaces using echolocation. Over a decade ago, BatSLAM showed that a robot with a biomimetic binaural sonar can build a topological map of the environment, by recognizing places from the received acoustic signals. Sonar place recognition, however, is ambiguous by nature: corridors produce nearly identical echo trains, and wrong loop closure can collapse the topological map. In this paper, we introduce BatSLAM 2.0, a novel sonar-only SLAM system built from three elements: an updated acoustic front-end, a sequence verifier that tracks and verifies loop closure candidates and a pose graph implemented on a high performance factor graph framework. The system was thoroughly evaluated both in simulated as well as real world recordings. In both cases, the BatSLAM2.0 algorithm shows the capability of robust topological map creation, countering map collapse, and robust scaling of map size.

AI.tldr: BatSLAM 2.0 is a sonar-only SLAM system built from an updated acoustic front-end, a sequence verifier for loop closure candidates, and a pose graph on a factor graph framework, enabling robust topological mapping and map scaling, validated in simulation and real world.
AI.motivation: Echolocating bats navigate dark and cluttered spaces via echolocation. BatSLAM demonstrated over a decade ago that a robot with biomimetic binaural sonar can build a topological map by recognizing places from acoustic signals. However, sonar place recognition is inherently ambiguous: corridors yield nearly identical echo trains, and incorrect loop closures can collapse the topological map.
AI.method: The proposed BatSLAM 2.0 consists of: (1) an updated acoustic front-end; (2) a sequence verifier that tracks and verifies loop closure candidates; and (3) a pose graph implemented on a high-performance factor graph framework. The system was evaluated on both simulated and real-world recordings.
AI.result: In both simulation and real-world evaluations, BatSLAM 2.0 demonstrated robust topological map creation, countering map collapse, and robust scaling of map size.
AI.conclusion: BatSLAM 2.0 achieves robust sonar-only SLAM by verifying loop closures and using a factor-graph pose graph, enabling reliable topological mapping and scalability in ambiguous acoustic environments.

title: Coverage Before Control: Route-Instruction Grounding and Steering for Controllable Retrosynthesis
summary: Single-step retrosynthesis models are commonly evaluated by their ability to recover recorded reactions. In practice, chemists may need to choose among several precursor sets for the same product, for example to preserve a particular motif. Recovering a recorded answer alone does not establish this ability to follow a preference. Satisfying such requests requires both coverage of relevant alternatives and control over which alternatives are favored. We introduce Route-Instruction Grounding and Steering (RIGS), a two-stage framework for instruction-conditioned retrosynthesis. Stage A trains a language projector, teaching it which alternatives an instruction favors or discourages. Stage B uses the projector learned in Stage A to steer a frozen generative model through lightweight residual adapters. We construct nested one-to-many training supports by pairing each product with increasing numbers of candidate precursor sets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that broader support helps the model generate a wider range of alternatives, and RIGS can learn to guide generation according to instructions. The relationship between coverage and control is consistent across model scales but non-monotone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RIGS, a two-stage framework for instruction-conditioned retrosynthesis that lets chemists steer a generative model toward preferred precursor sets, rather than only recovering a single recorded reaction.
AI.motivation: Single-step retrosynthesis models are typically evaluated only on recovering recorded reactions. In practice, chemists often need to choose among several precursor sets for the same product (e.g., to preserve a particular motif). Simple answer recovery does not demonstrate the ability to follow such preferences, which requires both coverage of relevant alternatives and control over which alternatives are favored.
AI.method: RIGS (Route-Instruction Grounding and Steering) is a two-stage framework. Stage A trains a language projector to learn which alternatives an instruction favors or discourages. Stage B uses that projector to steer a frozen generative model through lightweight residual adapters. The authors also construct nested one-to-many training supports by pairing each product with increasing numbers of candidate precursor sets.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that broader support helps the model generate a wider range of alternatives, and that RIGS can learn to guide generation according to instructions. The relationship between coverage and control is consistent across model scales but non-monotone.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-following retrosynthesis benefits from broad training support for coverage and from learned steering for control. RIGS achieves instruction-conditioned guiding of a frozen generative model, while the coverage–control trade-off remains non-monotone across scales.

title: Passive Stiffness Shaping in Cable-Suspended Aerial Manipulation via Movable Compliant Anchors
summary: Cable-suspended aerial manipulation offers a lightweight architecture for cooperative transportation and physical interaction, yet the passive mechanical response perceived at the load remains insufficiently understood and systematically exploited. This work interprets aerial vehicles as movable compliant anchors and develops a gravity-aware quasi-static theory for predicting and shaping the passive Cartesian stiffness of a suspended load. The formulation applies to an arbitrary number of aerial vehicles connected to a point load by taut, straight, inextensible cables. At a selected gravity-loaded equilibrium, aerial-anchor compliance and transverse cable geometric compliance combine in series within each leg, while the leg stiffnesses act in parallel on the load. For isotropic aerial-anchor behavior, each leg is exactly equivalent to a virtual unilateral elastic cable, revealing an axial--transverse stiffness decomposition governed by the equilibrium tension. These results define a nonlinear map from commanded-anchor configuration to passive load stiffness, whose differential enables local constraint-preserving shaping through anchor repositioning. A dynamic rigid-body validation framework with nonlinear vehicle control, elastic-damped tendons, and environmental contact is defined to assess when and to what extent the derived stiffness remains predictive beyond the assumptions of the analytical model.

AI.tldr: This work develops a gravity-aware quasi-static theory that predicts and shapes the passive Cartesian stiffness of a point load suspended by taut, inextensible cables from multiple aerial vehicles treated as movable compliant anchors.
AI.motivation: Cable-suspended aerial manipulation is a lightweight approach for cooperative transportation and physical interaction, but the passive mechanical response perceived at the load is poorly understood and not systematically exploited.
AI.method: The formulation applies to an arbitrary number of aerial vehicles connected to a point load by taut, straight, inextensible cables. At a gravity-loaded equilibrium, aerial-anchor compliance and transverse cable geometric compliance act in series per leg, while leg stiffnesses act in parallel on the load. Under isotropic anchor behavior, each leg is shown to be exactly equivalent to a virtual unilateral elastic cable, yielding an axial-transverse stiffness decomposition governed by equilibrium tension. This defines a nonlinear map from commanded-anchor configuration to passive load stiffness, whose differential enables local constraint-preserving shaping via anchor repositioning. A dynamic rigid-body validation framework with nonlinear vehicle control, elastic-damped tendons, and environmental contact is specified.
AI.result: The model establishes a nonlinear map from anchor configuration to passive load stiffness and a differential enabling local constraint-preserving stiffness shaping; the dynamic validation framework assesses when and to what extent the derived stiffness remains predictive beyond the analytical assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Aerial vehicles can be interpreted as movable compliant anchors, and the resulting gravity-aware quasi-static theory predicts and shapes passive load stiffness; the theory's validity beyond its assumptions is to be evaluated via the dynamic rigid-body framework with elastic-damped tendons and contact.

title: Better Deck or Different Judge? Evaluating Agentic Harness Gains in Corporate and Investment Banking
summary: Corporate and investment banking teams use presentations to support credit decisions and advise clients on financing and transactions. Producing these decks requires reconciling financial data, tracing sources and turning analysis into a recommendation. We retrospectively study the development of an agentic harness combining a 27B language model, financial calculations, narrative templates and validation checks. LLM judges guide engineering changes and assess the resulting decks, raising the question of whether higher scores reflect better documents or changes in grading. In shared-session text-only grading with template markers removed, five judges score the complete system 20.4 to 33.6 points out of 95 above the same model generating directly from a short prompt. Every judge scores the system higher on all seventeen development deliverables. Margins against direct Opus generation from a short prompt range from -4.7 to +0.8 points. Judges agree on broad progress across development rounds but agree less on final-deck rankings than on pooled scores. Repeated grading also shifts scores on unchanged decks, making small improvements difficult to distinguish from judge variability.

AI.tldr: An agentic harness (27B LLM + financial calculations + narrative templates + validation checks) is retrospectively evaluated for corporate/investment banking decks. Five LLM judges, using shared-session text-only grading with template markers removed, score the full system 20.4–33.6 points (of 95) above the same model prompted directly, and higher on all 17 development deliverables; margins vs. direct Opus generation range from −4.7 to +0.8 points. Judge agreement is stronger on broad, pooled progress than on final-deck rankings, and repeated grading shifts scores of unchanged decks.
AI.motivation: Corporate and investment banking teams rely on presentations for credit decisions and client financing/transaction advice. Building such decks requires reconciling financial data, tracing sources, and converting analysis into a recommendation—tasks that are error-prone and labor-intensive. The paper investigates whether an agentic, tool-augmented system can improve the quality of these deliverables, and critically, whether LLM-judge scores can be trusted as evidence of that improvement.
AI.method: Retrospective study of an agentic harness combining a 27B language model with financial calculations, narrative templates, and validation checks. Five LLM judges guide engineering changes and evaluate the resulting decks using shared-session, text-only grading with template markers removed. Comparisons include the full system vs. the same model generating directly from a short prompt, and vs. direct Opus generation from a short prompt. Judge reliability is probed via cross-judge agreement, score stability under repeated grading of unchanged decks, and agreement on pooled scores vs. final-deck rankings.
AI.result: The full system scores 20.4–33.6 points higher (out of 95) than the same model generating directly from a short prompt, and every judge scores it higher on all seventeen development deliverables. Margins relative to direct Opus generation from a short prompt range from −4.7 to +0.8 points. Judges agree on broad progress across development rounds but agree less on final-deck rankings than on pooled scores. Repeated grading shifts scores even for unchanged decks, so small improvements are hard to distinguish from judge variability.
AI.conclusion: The agentic harness yields substantial, consistently detected gains over direct short-prompt generation by the same model, though it only roughly matches direct Opus generation. Because LLM judges show limited ranking agreement and score instability on unchanged decks, judge-based scores warrant caution: measured improvements must be interpreted against grading variability, and higher scores may partly reflect grading changes rather than strictly better documents.

title: Tactile Curiosity Drives Robot Interaction
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Preprint, under review
summary: Mastering robot manipulation skills via reinforcement learning (RL) remains largely sample-inefficient. The most common RL algorithms rely on random action sampling to discover new strategies, resulting in agents that allocate most of their training budget to motions in free space, away from the contacts from which manipulation skills emerge. Existing intrinsic motivation methods based on model disagreement or epistemic uncertainty improve on isotropic noise, but they can also reward uncertainty in functionally irrelevant transitions, such as erratic motions in free space. In this work, we argue that tactile feedback provides a natural signal for exploration, and introduce TacEx, a framework that incorporates touch into epistemic uncertainty-driven exploration by decomposing model uncertainty across sensory modalities and directing curiosity toward the tactile channel. By anchoring curiosity to the sense of touch, TacEx drives the robot to discover complex contact dynamics, learning to manipulate and grasp objects without task rewards or expert demonstrations during exploration. The interaction-dense dataset collected through this tactile-driven curiosity supports offline learning of downstream pick-and-place policies without additional environment interaction. We further use tactile-driven exploration to post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. Although the VLAs are initially pre-trained without tactile feedback, post-training with TacEx substantially improves downstream performance while remaining highly sample-efficient.

AI.tldr: TacEx is a reinforcement learning exploration framework that uses tactile feedback as an intrinsic reward signal, enabling sample-efficient discovery of contact-rich manipulation skills without task rewards or demonstrations, and supporting downstream offline policy learning and VLA post-training.
AI.motivation: RL for robot manipulation is highly sample-inefficient. Standard algorithms rely on random action sampling, wasting most of the training budget on free-space motions far from the contacts where manipulation skills actually emerge. Existing intrinsic motivation methods (model disagreement, epistemic uncertainty) partially address this but still reward uncertainty in functionally irrelevant transitions such as erratic free-space motion.
AI.method: TacEx incorporates touch into epistemic uncertainty-driven exploration.
