It decomposes model uncertainty across sensory modalities and directs curiosity specifically toward the tactile channel, anchoring exploration to contact signals. Exploration proceeds without task rewards or expert demonstrations, collecting an interaction-dense dataset. This dataset then supports offline learning of downstream pick-and-place policies without further environment interaction.
AI.result: TacEx drives the robot to discover complex contact dynamics and learn to manipulate and grasp objects during exploration. The collected tactile-driven dataset enables offline learning of pick-and-place policies without additional environment interaction. When used to post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models that were initially pre-trained without tactile feedback, it substantially improves downstream performance while remaining highly sample-efficient.
AI.conclusion: Tactile feedback provides a natural and effective signal for exploration. Anchoring curiosity to the sense of touch yields sample-efficient discovery of contact-rich manipulation skills and generalizes to improving VLA models, even when those models were not pre-trained with tactile input.

title: AIMS: An Agentic AI Framework for Sim-to-Real Multi-Modal ISAC
summary: Multi-modal integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception and reliable connectivity for intelligent wireless networks. Data-driven multi-modal ISAC models depend heavily on annotated real-world data to learn relationships across sensing and wireless observations, thereby constraining scalable deployment. Although synthetic data generation reduces the burden, adapting existing simulation pipelines to a target deployment requires consistent scene, sensing, wireless, and learning configurations, while mismatches among these coupled components impair sim-to-real transferability. To address the challenge, we propose an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for sim-to-real multi-modal ISAC, named AIMS. Given a natural-language deployment request specifying the target task, deployment conditions, and real-data budget, AIMS derives a deployment-specific sim-to-real configuration and coordinates its execution to produce a deployment-specific task model. A two-agent architecture coordinates scene construction with task learning. A scene construction agent generates geographically grounded, synchronized sensing and wireless records from shared physical states, while a scene understanding agent configures task-relevant modalities and mixture-of-experts (MoE) learning for zero-shot inference or few-shot adaptation. Structured domain knowledge guides dependency-aware planning, while validation evidence supports feedback-driven revision of affected decisions. Experiments on the real-world DeepSense~6G dataset demonstrate improved vehicle detection and beam prediction over the considered simulation and fusion baselines. A separate orchestration benchmark evaluates task interpretation, dependency reasoning, and feedback-driven replanning across diverse deployment requests, showing improved plan correctness with structured domain knowledge and validation feedback.

AI.tldr: AIMS is an agentic AI framework for sim-to-real multi-modal ISAC that, given a natural-language deployment request, derives and executes a deployment-specific configuration using two coordinating agents to produce a task model.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal ISAC enables environmental perception and reliable connectivity, but data-driven models rely on scarce annotated real-world data. Synthetic data generation helps, yet aligning coupled scene, sensing, wireless, and learning configurations for sim-to-real transfer remains hard, and mismatches harm transferability.
AI.method: AIMS takes a natural-language deployment request (task, conditions, real-data budget) and constructs a deployment-specific sim-to-real configuration. A two-agent design couples scene construction and task learning: a scene construction agent produces geographically grounded, synchronized sensing and wireless records from shared physical states; a scene understanding agent selects task-relevant modalities and MoE learning for zero-shot or few-shot use. Structured domain knowledge drives dependency-aware planning, and validation evidence enables feedback-driven revision.
AI.result: On the real-world DeepSense 6G dataset, AIMS improves vehicle detection and beam prediction over simulation and fusion baselines. An orchestration benchmark shows improved plan correctness from task interpretation, dependency reasoning, and feedback-driven replanning, aided by structured domain knowledge and validation feedback.
AI.conclusion: AIMS addresses sim-to-real multi-modal ISAC by agentically deriving and executing deployment-specific configurations, yielding gains on real-world ISAC tasks and improved planning correctness under varied deployment requests.

title: Dream4ACT: A Shared Visual Action Interface for Multi-Embodiment Video-Action Modeling
summary: Video generation models (VGMs) offer strong spatiotemporal priors for embodied observation--action modeling. However, joint-space action vectors lack explicit image-space structure and vary in dimensionality and semantics across embodiments, making it challenging to directly leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors of VGMs. End-effector visualizations provide an alternative but do not specify the full articulated configuration needed for robot execution. We present Dream4ACT, a world model built for joint video-action modeling across embodiments. To unify action representations across embodiments, we introduce a shared visual action interface, called action views, which render target joint configurations from four prescribed virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics. This shared visual representation preserves embodiment-specific articulated geometry while allowing observation and action sequences to share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Through masked flow-matching, our model supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and joint observation--action generation within a single jointly trained model by varying which future sequences are corrupted. To recover executable action sequences from predicted action views, we propose a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview recovery mechanism, without a learned embodiment-specific decoder. Dream4ACT achieves an average success rate of 88.98\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and an overall score of 65.66 on TriWorldBench, supporting effective closed-loop manipulation and competitive action-conditioned multiview prediction through the visual action interface.

AI.tldr: Dream4ACT is a world model for joint video-action modeling across embodiments. It unifies action representations via "action views"—rendering joint configurations from four virtual cameras using URDF forward kinematics—letting observation and action sequences share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Via masked flow-matching it supports forward/inverse dynamics and joint generation, and recovers executable actions through a training-free URDF-constrained multiview recovery. It achieves 88.98% avg success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 65.66 on TriWorldBench.
AI.motivation: Video generation models provide strong spatiotemporal priors useful for embodied observation-action modeling, but joint-space action vectors lack explicit image-space structure and differ in dimensionality and semantics across embodiments, hindering direct use of these priors. End-effector visualizations are an alternative but do not specify the full articulated configuration required for robot execution. A shared, embodiment-agnostic action representation is thus needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce a shared visual action interface called "action views," which render target joint configurations from four prescribed virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics, preserving embodiment-specific articulated geometry while allowing observation and action sequences to share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Using masked flow-matching, a single jointly trained model supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and joint observation-action generation by varying which future sequences are corrupted. Executable actions are recovered from predicted action views via a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview recovery mechanism, without any learned embodiment-specific decoder.
AI.result: Dream4ACT achieves an average success rate of 88.98% on RoboTwin 2.0 and an overall score of 65.66 on TriWorldBench, supporting effective closed-loop manipulation and competitive action-conditioned multiview prediction through the visual action interface.
AI.conclusion: By unifying action representations across embodiments through a shared visual action interface, Dream4ACT effectively leverages video model spatiotemporal priors for cross-embodiment joint video-action modeling, enabling closed-loop manipulation and competitive multiview prediction without embodiment-specific decoders.

title: What Can Component-Replacement Evidence Establish? A Critical Scoping Review of Local Decisions in LLM Agents
comment: 36 pages, 3 figures. The authors contributed equally
summary: Background. A component replacement in a language-model agent changes an execution trajectory, potentially altering later observations, resource use, and recovery opportunities. Different evidence is needed to assess its task-level benefit and the contribution of local decision quality. Methods. This critical scoping review maps 348 studies and examines 90 comparison records: 88 from 40 included studies and two from supplementary studies. Eight purposively selected cases structure the synthesis around the replaced decision, executed conditions, measurement comparability, controls, and remaining explanations. Results. Of 222 studies reporting local decision metrics, 142 also report measured task endpoints and 49 report proxies. These counts identify studies that report both types of measurement, without establishing that the measurements come from matched comparisons. Outcome Monitors reports a package-level completion gain whose attribution to detector quality remains limited; First-chunk selection reports a local improvement assessed against an offline proxy endpoint; Evidence-Carrying Termination reports fewer premature unsupported terminations and completion non-inferiority, without establishing completion superiority. Cross-case analysis identifies three candidate mechanisms involving recovery and disruption, intervention timing, and downstream use. Attribution and deployment depend on the comparison controls, label definitions, and information available to the controller. Conclusions. The review distinguishes the task-level benefit of a component replacement from the contribution of local decision quality and derives eight claim-specific reporting items. Neither online execution nor simultaneous gains in local and task metrics alone establish that better local decisions explain the task-level gain.

AI.tldr: This critical scoping review of 348 studies (90 comparison records from 40 included studies plus supplementary work) distinguishes a language-model agent component replacement's task-level benefit from the contribution of local decision quality, using eight purposively selected cases, and derives eight claim-specific reporting items.
AI.motivation: A component replacement in a language-model agent alters the execution trajectory, potentially changing later observations, resource use, and recovery opportunities, so different evidence is required to assess its task-level benefit separately from the contribution of local decision quality.
AI.method: Critical scoping review mapping 348 studies and examining 90 comparison records (88 from 40 included studies, two from supplementary studies). Eight purposively selected cases structure the synthesis around the replaced decision, executed conditions, measurement comparability, controls, and remaining explanations. Counts of studies reporting local decision metrics, measured task endpoints, and proxies are used to identify co-reporting, not matched comparisons.
AI.result: Of 222 studies reporting local decision metrics, 142 also report measured task endpoints and 49 report proxies, without establishing matched comparisons. Outcome Monitors shows a package-level completion gain with limited attribution to detector quality; First-chunk selection shows a local improvement assessed against an offline proxy endpoint; Evidence-Carrying Termination shows fewer premature unsupported terminations and completion non-inferiority but no completion superiority. Cross-case analysis identifies three candidate mechanisms: recovery and disruption, intervention timing, and downstream use.
AI.conclusion: The review separates the task-level benefit of a component replacement from the contribution of local decision quality and derives eight claim-specific reporting items. Neither online execution nor simultaneous gains in local and task metrics alone establish that better local decisions explain the task-level gain; attribution and deployment depend on comparison controls, label definitions, and the information available to the controller.

title: Rethinking Legibility in Social Robot Hallway Navigation: Impact of Intent Representation and Human Distraction
summary: We focus on legible robot motion generation in social navigation settings. Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently infer the robot's intent. While mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, social robot navigation presents a new challenge: the robot must clearly convey its intent while ensuring human safety in dynamic pedestrian environments where human attention is often divided. With the goal of enabling robots to generate legible motion in dynamic and constrained spaces, we investigate how the choice of representation and the level of human attention shape navigation performance and human impressions. Focusing on the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, we conduct two controlled user studies involving alternative legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) investigates the role of intent representation, showing that passing-side legibility, particularly when adaptively updated, leads to smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion allows for smooth human motion even under distraction, even if this is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI.

AI.tldr: Two controlled user studies (N=45 each) in hallway navigation show that interaction-level, adaptively updated passing-side legibility yields smoother human motion with better perceived competence, and preserves smooth human motion even under pedestrian distraction, within a shared MPC framework.
AI.motivation: Legible robot motion is well studied with static observers, but social robot navigation requires conveying intent while ensuring human safety in dynamic pedestrian environments where human attention is divided. It remains unclear how the choice of intent representation and the level of human attention affect navigation performance and human impressions.
AI.method: Focus on hallway navigation. Two controlled user studies with alternative legibility formulations implemented in a shared model predictive control (MPC) framework. Study 1 (N=45) manipulates intent representation, comparing passing-side legibility (including an adaptively updated variant) against destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2 (N=45) manipulates pedestrian attention (including distraction) to test whether legibility supports smooth human motion when attention is divided, alongside subjective ratings.
AI.result: Study 1: passing-side legibility, especially when adaptively updated, produces smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2: legible motion enables smooth human motion even under distraction, although this benefit is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings.
AI.conclusion: Effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with certain benefits persisting even when human attention is divided. Code available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI.

title: Who Verifies the Graph? Misspecification Attacks on Causal Action Verification for Language Agents
comment: Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "Who Verifies the Agents?"
summary: Causal action verifiers gate an agent's state-changing tool calls by checking whether each proposed intervention is identifiable against a committed action-state graph, and they issue a certificate that carries the identification argument and a one-sided lower confidence bound. One such verifier, CIVeX, reports zero false executions on a confounded tool-use benchmark. We red-team it by corrupting only the committed graph. Omitting a single bidirected edge takes it from zero false executions to 15.3% at the benchmark's published confounding strength, with 91% of its executions harmful and utility falling from +2.27 to +0.35. Reversing one arrowhead, so that a mediator is committed as a confounder, gives 48.9% false executions and no correct ones. Every one of these actions carries an internally valid certificate. An attestation step that tests each observationally certified execution against a bounded randomised sample detected both attacks, with 2 false alarms in 555 executions on a truthful graph; refusing what fails the test, or cannot be tested, gave zero false executions in every setting we measured. It does not restore beneficial execution: at the published strength 97.1% of beneficial actions are still never executed, because the same misspecification rejects them before attestation runs. Those rejections carry certificates too, and auditing them works, but its cost scales with the number of rejections rather than the number of executions. Recovering safety costs 127 experiments per 1,050 actions; recovering the lost value costs 614 more, at which point the audited verifier makes the honest graph's decisions on every instance and spends exactly its experiment budget. An audit that inspects only executions protects against wrongful action. Wrongful inaction has to be paid for separately.

AI.tldr: Corrupting only the committed action-state graph lets CIVeX produce internally valid certificates for harmful tool calls: omitting one bidirected edge yields 15.3% false executions (91% harmful) and reversing one arrowhead yields 48.9% false executions with zero correct ones. A bounded-sample attestation step detects both attacks (2 false alarms in 555 truthful-graph executions), and refusing untestable actions gives zero false executions, but does not restore beneficial execution—97.1% of beneficial actions remain unexecuted at the published confounding strength. Auditing rejections recovers value but costs experiments proportional to rejections, requiring 614 extra experiments beyond the 127 already needed to recover safety.
AI.motivation: Causal action verifiers such as CIVeX are trusted to gate state-changing tool calls using certificates that carry an identification argument and a one-sided lower confidence bound, and CIVeX reports zero false executions on a confounded tool-use benchmark. The paper red-teams this guarantee to test whether certified safety survives corruption of the committed causal graph, and to separate the problem of wrongful action from the distinct problem of wrongful inaction.
AI.method: The authors attack CIVeX by modifying only the committed action-state graph: (1) omitting a single bidirected edge (removing a confounder), and (2) reversing one arrowhead so a mediator is committed as a confounder. They evaluate false executions, harm rate, and utility at the benchmark's published confounding strength, then add an attestation step that tests each observationally certified execution against a bounded randomised sample, refusing actions that fail or cannot be tested. They also audit the certificates attached to rejected (beneficial) actions and measure the experiment cost of recovering safety versus recovering lost value.
AI.result: Omitting one bidirected edge moves CIVeX from zero false executions to 15.3%, with 91% of executions harmful and utility dropping from +2.27 to +0.35. Reversing one arrowhead (mediator committed as confounder) produces 48.9% false executions and no correct ones. All these actions carry internally valid certificates. The attestation step detects both attacks with 2 false alarms in 555 executions on a truthful graph; refusing what fails or cannot be tested yields zero false executions in every measured setting. However, it does not restore beneficial execution: at the published strength, 97.1% of beneficial actions are never executed because the same misspecification rejects them before attestation. Auditing rejections works, but its cost scales with the number of rejections rather than executions. Recovering safety costs 127 experiments per 1,050 actions; recovering the lost value costs 614 more, after which the audited verifier reproduces the honest graph's decisions on every instance and spends exactly its experiment budget.
AI.conclusion: Certificate validity is not robustness to graph misspecification: a verifier can be fully sound relative to a wrong committed graph and still approve systematic harm. An execution-only attestation audit can protect against wrongful action at low cost, but wrongful inaction must be paid for separately, since rejection certificates are valid yet their audit cost scales with rejections. Safety and value recovery are distinct expenditures, and full restoration of the verifier's behaviour is achievable only by auditing rejections in addition to executions.

title: PrefPI: Preference-Guided Steering into Out-of-Distribution Behaviors
summary: We present PrefPI (Preference-Guided Policy Iteration), an iterative framework for steering pretrained generative robot policies using only relative preferences over self-generated trajectories. Unlike prior preference-learning methods that primarily sharpen modes already represented by the policy, we study steering beyond the initial effective support, where desired behaviors are rarely or never observed under the initial policy. Our key idea is to formulate preference learning as preference-conditioned generative modeling: preferred trajectories define a conditional distribution, whose density ratio with the broader behavior prior provides an implicit preference signal amplified by classifier-free guidance (CFG). Repeating this preference-conditioned modeling and guidance step yields a form of preference-guided policy iteration, turning incremental improvements toward previously inaccessible behaviors. Across diffusion policies and the PI0.5 flow- matching VLA in simulation and the real world, PrefPI produces substantial behavioral shifts with limited feedback. In particular, PrefPI increases object transport height from 10.7 cm to 19.8 cm on real hardware with only 150 preference-labeled trajectories.

AI.tldr: PrefPI steers pretrained generative robot policies toward behaviors outside their initial support using only relative preferences, by casting preference learning as preference-conditioned generative modeling and amplifying the implicit signal with classifier-free guidance in an iterative policy-iteration loop.
AI.motivation: Prior preference-learning methods mainly sharpen modes already present in the policy's effective support, so they cannot elicit behaviors that are rarely or never observed under the initial policy. The paper targets steering beyond the initial effective support with limited human feedback.
AI.method: Preference-conditioned generative modeling: preferred self-generated trajectories define a conditional distribution whose density ratio to the broader behavior prior yields an implicit preference signal, amplified by classifier-free guidance (CFG). Repeating this preference-conditioned modeling and guidance forms a preference-guided policy iteration scheme.
AI.result: Validated on diffusion policies and the PI0.5 flow-matching VLA in simulation and the real world; PrefPI produces substantial behavioral shifts with limited feedback, e.g., increasing real-hardware object transport height from 10.7 cm to 19.8 cm using only 150 preference-labeled trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Formulating preference learning as preference-conditioned generative modeling with CFG enables iterative steering of pretrained generative robot policies beyond their initial support, achieving significant behavioral change under scarce preference feedback.

title: PTNO: Training Neural Operators with Noisy Monte Carlo Estimates for Particle Transport Problems
summary: Particle transport under multiple scattering is central to radiative transfer and plasma physics, yet high-fidelity Monte Carlo (MC) simulations must trace prohibitively many particles. Learning-based surrogates can amortize this cost, but typically train on expensive, well-converged MC solutions. We propose the Particle Transport Neural Operator (PTNO), a neural operator that learns particle transport surrogates directly from noisy, low-cost MC labels. Such labels pose two challenges: (1) high variance, which destabilizes standard supervised learning, and (2) a high dynamic range (HDR) spanning many orders of magnitude. For the first, we learn the solution operator from noisy labels of many configurations, amortizing MC cost and generalizing to unseen configurations. Because MC labels are unbiased, we show that the squared loss on them shares its minimizer with the loss on converged solutions, and our budget-allocation study over training scenes $M$, MC samples per render $N$, and independent renders per scene $K$ shows that many noisy scenes beat fewer converged ones. For the second, a nonlinear transform such as the logarithm biases noisy supervision. Instead, PTNO keeps labels in physical space and enforces positivity with a softplus output layer that represents small values effectively. We further train with a pointwise relative $L_2$ loss (PRelL2), the stop-gradient relative loss of HDR denoising and neural rendering, which normalizes each residual by the stop-gradient prediction instead of the noisy label. We demonstrate PTNO on neutron transport in fusion reactors and radiative transfer in participating media. On the two neutronics tasks, PTNO is $10^4$-$10^5\times$ faster than converged MC on the same CPU and $10^3$-$10^5\times$ cheaper than MC at matched accuracy; on the two radiative-transfer tasks, MC at matched accuracy costs $0.8$-$11\times$ as much as PTNO.

AI.tldr: The Particle Transport Neural Operator (PTNO) learns particle transport surrogates directly from noisy, low-cost Monte Carlo labels, addressing high variance and high dynamic range via amortized operator learning, a softplus output layer, and a pointwise relative L2 loss, achieving large speedups and cost reductions over converged MC on neutronics and radiative-transfer tasks.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity Monte Carlo (MC) simulation of particle transport under multiple scattering is prohibitively expensive due to the many particles that must be traced. Existing learning-based surrogates can amortize this cost but typically require expensive, well-converged MC solutions for training. The goal is to remove this reliance by learning directly from cheap, noisy MC labels.
AI.method: PTNO learns the solution operator from noisy labels across many configurations to amortize MC cost and generalize to unseen configurations. Since MC labels are unbiased, the squared loss on noisy labels shares its minimizer with the loss on converged solutions. A budget-allocation study varies training scenes M, MC samples per render N, and independent renders per scene K. To handle high dynamic range, PTNO keeps labels in physical space, enforces positivity with a softplus output layer, and trains with a pointwise relative L2 loss (PRelL2) that normalizes each residual by the stop-gradient prediction rather than the noisy label.
AI.result: Many noisy scenes outperform fewer converged ones. On two neutronics tasks (neutron transport in fusion reactors), PTNO is 10^4-10^5x faster than converged MC on the same CPU and 10^3-10^5x cheaper than MC at matched accuracy. On two radiative-transfer tasks (participating media), MC at matched accuracy costs 0.8-11x as much as PTNO.
AI.conclusion: PTNO enables efficient learning of particle transport surrogates from cheap noisy MC labels, combining unbiased-label theory, a softplus output for HDR positivity, and a stop-gradient relative loss to deliver substantial speed and cost advantages over converged MC across neutronics and radiative-transfer applications.

title: Social-WM: Safety-Aware Latent World Models for Robot Social Navigation
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: Safe social navigation requires a robot to anticipate not only the future consequences of its actions, but also whether a nominal action can actually be executed under surrounding physical and social constraints. We present Social-WM, an efficient latent world-model planning framework trained from egocentric RGB video sequences. Our key observation is that social-navigation experience contains a systematic discrepancy between the nominal action and the realizable action: a nominal forward action may be fully executed in free space, but needs to be constrained when heading towards a pedestrian or obstacle. Social-WM learns these safety-relevant consequences directly through action-conditioned future prediction, where the target is the actual observed future following each command. We further introduce a realizable inverse-dynamics objective that associates observed latent transitions with the action actually realized rather than the nominal one. At deployment, candidate actions are imagined through the latent world model, and the inverse dynamics model estimates their realizability; nominal--realizable discrepancy then provides a safety signal before execution. The learned dynamics and realizability model remain goal-independent and support both position- and image-goal navigation. On Social-HM3D, Social-WM achieves 63.77% success while reducing human collisions to 21.67%, and maintains strong performance under zero-shot transfer to Social-MP3D, without explicit pedestrian tracking, privileged human state, or online reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: Social-WM is a latent world-model planning framework for safe social navigation trained from egocentric RGB video, learning the discrepancy between nominal and realizable actions to provide a pre-execution safety signal, without pedestrian tracking, privileged human state, or online RL.
AI.motivation: Safe social navigation requires the robot to anticipate both the future consequences of its actions and whether a nominal action is actually executable under physical and social constraints. Prior approaches often rely on explicit pedestrian tracking, privileged human state, or online reinforcement learning, which are costly or impractical.
AI.method: Social-WM trains a latent world model from egocentric RGB video via action-conditioned future prediction, where targets are the actually observed futures following each command. A realizable inverse-dynamics objective associates observed latent transitions with the action actually realized rather than the nominal one. At deployment, candidate actions are imagined through the world model, and the inverse dynamics model estimates their realizability; the nominal-realizable discrepancy serves as a safety signal before execution. The learned dynamics and realizability model are goal-independent and support both position- and image-goal navigation.
AI.result: On Social-HM3D, Social-WM achieves 63.77% success while reducing human collisions to 21.67%, and maintains strong performance under zero-shot transfer to Social-MP3D.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the discrepancy between nominal and realizable actions through latent world-model planning yields an effective, efficient safety signal for social navigation, generalizing across datasets and goal modalities without explicit pedestrian tracking, privileged human state, or online reinforcement learning.

title: Agent Error Dataset: Scaling 50,000 Error--Diagnosis Pairs for Failure Analysis and Error-Aware Post-Training
summary: An unsuccessful LLM agent rollout contains more information than its final reward: the observations available to the agent, the actions it chose, and the environment's responses. Reusing this experience for learning requires identifying a decision to revise and testing a concrete alternative. We introduce the Agent Error Dataset (AED), comprising 50,228 error-diagnosis pairs from 9,961 source tasks across 33 environments, 19 harness families, and 23 policy models in text-based agent systems. We retain source traces and execution metadata to support cross-setting failure analysis and re-diagnosis without repeating the original rollout. Our five-stage Agentic Error-to-Training (AET) pipeline collects natural failures, generates diagnoses and proposed corrections, and checks them against recorded evidence. Where replay is supported, we compare corrections with original-action retries from the same checkpoint under matched execution settings. We then construct separate training views for diagnosis and actor recovery. Across 3,062 matched replay pairs, first-proposal corrections raise verifier pass rates from 18.4% to 51.1%, a gain of 32.7 percentage points. Using a separately frozen diagnosis release, full-diagnosis fine-tuning on 1,656 source tasks raises Qwen3-8B's exact-step agreement with internal teacher labels from 47.2% to 63.6%, averaged over three seeds on a 943-case holdout. The strongest prompted reference in this comparison scores 54.7%, and mean agreement improves at each of four increasing training-set sizes. In a single-seed comparison of actor-training recipes, action-only repair training scores 6.67 percentage points higher on WebShop-lite than success-only training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Agent Error Dataset (AED) of 50,228 error-diagnosis pairs and an Agentic Error-to-Training (AET) pipeline that converts failed LLM agent rollouts into diagnoses and corrected actions, then trains models on them, substantially improving verifier pass rates and diagnosis accuracy.
AI.motivation: An unsuccessful LLM agent rollout contains more information than its final reward—observations, chosen actions, and environment responses. Reusing this experience for learning requires identifying a decision to revise and testing a concrete alternative, which prior work does not systematically exploit.
AI.method: They build AED from 9,961 source tasks across 33 environments, 19 harness families, and 23 policy models, retaining source traces and execution metadata. A five-stage AET pipeline collects natural failures, generates diagnoses and proposed corrections, and checks them against recorded evidence. Where replay is supported, corrections are compared with original-action retries from the same checkpoint under matched execution settings. Separate training views are constructed for diagnosis and actor recovery.
AI.result: Across 3,062 matched replay pairs, first-proposal corrections raise verifier pass rates from 18.4% to 51.1% (+32.7 pp). Full-diagnosis fine-tuning on 1,656 source tasks raises Qwen3-8B's exact-step agreement with internal teacher labels from 47.2% to 63.6% (three seeds, 943-case holdout), versus 54.7% for the strongest prompted reference, and improves at each of four training-set sizes. In a single-seed actor-training comparison, action-only repair training scores 6.67 pp higher on WebShop-lite than success-only training.
AI.conclusion: Failed agent rollouts can be systematically converted into diagnostic and corrective training signals. The AED dataset and AET pipeline enable cross-setting failure analysis and re-diagnosis without repeating original rollouts, and yield substantial gains in correction verification and model diagnosis agreement.

title: Non-Invasive Inspection of Water Canals Using Dronar
summary: Open concrete canals play a vital role in water transportation, serving as primary water infrastructure for millions of people across the Phoenix, Arizona, metro area. Over time, the concrete canals can experience a range of issues, including canal lining deformation, cracked concrete, and sediment buildup on the canal floor. Identifying such critical issues is a resource-intensive process, which currently happens only during four-year dry-up cycles. This prevents the maintenance crew from prioritizing operations on the most affected canal segments. To address this issue, the research team has developed and verified an easily deployable and non-invasive method to inspect canal beds without draining the water. This inspection system integrates affordable, off-the-shelf drone and sonar technology (termed dronar). This dronar system includes a consumer-grade sonar system integrated into an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) that carries the sonar transducer just under the surface of the canal water. This paper presents a proof-of-concept demonstration of the dronar system across three field tests on the Arizona Canal in Phoenix. DownScan depth profiles from the sedimented canal segment were consistently shallower than profiles from the same segment after cleaning, with offsets of up to 15 cm observed along the track. Repeated runs over the clean segment produced closely overlapping DownScan depth profiles, confirming that the dronar yields repeatable measurements across the natural variation of the canal bed. These results establish the dronar as a viable proof-of-concept tool for non-invasive canal bed inspection.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a proof-of-concept "dronar" system that integrates a consumer-grade sonar on an unmanned surface vehicle to inspect concrete canal beds without draining water, validated through three field tests on the Arizona Canal.
AI.motivation: Open concrete canals in the Phoenix, Arizona metro area serve as primary water infrastructure for millions but degrade over time through lining deformation, cracked concrete, and sediment buildup. Current inspection is resource-intensive and limited to four-year dry-up cycles, preventing maintenance crews from prioritizing the most affected segments. A non-invasive, easily deployable inspection method is needed.
AI.method: The team developed a "dronar" system combining affordable, off-the-shelf drone and sonar technology: a consumer-grade sonar integrated into an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) that carries the sonar transducer just below the canal water surface. The system was tested across three field tests on the Arizona Canal in Phoenix, generating DownScan depth profiles.
AI.result: DownScan depth profiles from the sedimented canal segment were consistently shallower than profiles from the same segment after cleaning, with offsets up to 15 cm along the track. Repeated runs over the clean segment produced closely overlapping depth profiles, confirming repeatable measurements amid natural canal bed variation.
AI.conclusion: The dronar system is established as a viable proof-of-concept tool for non-invasive canal bed inspection, enabling inspection without water drainage.

title: Unlearnable, or Unmeasured? On the Reliability of Difficulty Labels in RLVR
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training. Project page: https://syed-nazmus-sakib.github.io/Unlearnable-RLVR/
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach for improving reasoning during post-training. Recent work suggests that some difficult prompts remain resistant to learning even when they occasionally produce correct solutions. We revisit this unlearnability phenomenon and find that the affected prompts do improve, at roughly one third of the learnable rate, while the difficulty-defined set used to study them is much less reproducible than expected. These difficulty labels are estimated from a limited number of sampled responses. Combining them across seeds can further change which prompts are selected instead of simply reducing measurement noise. We develop a sampling-based framework for quantifying this instability and determining how much evaluation is required for difficulty assignments to reproduce reliably. We also revisit the gradient-similarity evidence proposed to explain unlearnability and show that part of the observed separation arises because difficult prompts provide fewer correct rollouts from which their gradients can be estimated. Matching this sample count weakens the gradient difference but does not remove it. Overall, the slow-learning phenomenon survives our reanalysis, while both the prompts used to define it and the evidence used to explain it require more careful measurement.

AI.tldr: The paper reanalyzes "unlearnable" prompts in RLVR, showing they do learn slowly (~1/3 the learnable rate), that difficulty labels are highly unstable and not simply denoised by seed combination, and that gradient-similarity evidence for unlearnability is partly confounded by fewer correct rollouts; the slow-learning phenomenon persists but needs more careful measurement.
AI.motivation: Prior work reports that some difficult prompts in RLVR resist learning despite occasionally yielding correct solutions, and explains this via gradient-similarity evidence. The authors question whether the difficulty-defined prompt set is reproducible and whether the explanatory evidence is sound, motivating a re-examination of both the phenomenon and its measurement.
AI.method: The authors revisit the unlearnability phenomenon by re-measuring learning rates for affected prompts, testing the reproducibility of difficulty labels, and introducing a sampling-based framework to quantify label instability and determine the amount of evaluation needed for reliable difficulty assignment. They also reanalyze the gradient-similarity evidence, controlling for the number of correct rollouts used to estimate gradients.
AI.result: Affected prompts do improve, at roughly one third of the learnable rate. Difficulty-defined sets are much less reproducible than expected: labels are estimated from limited samples, and combining them across seeds changes which prompts are selected rather than merely reducing noise. Matching sample counts weakens the reported gradient difference but does not eliminate it.
AI.conclusion: The slow-learning phenomenon survives reanalysis, but both the prompt sets used to define it and the gradient-based evidence used to explain it require more careful measurement.

title: Centralized Multi-UAV Exploration and 3D Reconstruction Using Single-UAV Planners
comment: Presented at the IEEE International Conference on Advanced Robotics and Mechatronics (ICARM 2026). To appear in IEEE Xplore
summary:
Extending single Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) exploration methods to multi-UAV teams can improve coverage speed and robustness, but introduces challenges such as consistent mapping, safe navigation, and deployment strategy. In this work, we present a centralized multi-UAV exploration framework that enables the use of existing single-UAV sampling-based planners in a multi-UAV setting.
  The proposed architecture allows multiple UAVs to collaboratively explore unknown environments using a shared global Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) map and centralized planning. Building on the voxblox library, we adapt its mapping pipeline to support real-time fusion of depth measurements from multiple UAVs into a common TSDF representation. In addition, inter-UAV collision avoidance and robot self-filtering mechanisms are integrated into the system to ensure safe navigation and prevent reconstruction of other UAVs as static obstacles.
  The framework is evaluated in simulation using four sampling-based exploration planners - RH-NBVP, KRH-NBVP, AEP, and KAEP - whose core sampling logic is preserved, with only system-level adaptations for multi-UAV operation. Experiments are conducted across multiple environments and under two deployment configurations: Joint Start (JS), where UAVs are initialized in close proximity, and Separated Start (SS), where UAVs are initialized in distinct locations. Results show that SS deployments consistently achieve faster exploration and improved coverage across all planners, highlighting the importance of the deployment strategy in multi-UAV exploration performance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a centralized multi-UAV exploration framework that reuses existing single-UAV sampling-based planners via a shared global TSDF map and centralized planning, and shows that separated-start deployments yield faster and more complete exploration.
AI.motivation: Extending single-UAV exploration to multi-UAV teams can improve coverage speed and robustness, but introduces challenges including consistent mapping, safe navigation, and deployment strategy.
AI.method: A centralized architecture enables multiple UAVs to collaboratively explore unknown environments using a shared global TSDF map and centralized planning. Building on voxblox, the mapping pipeline is adapted for real-time fusion of multi-UAV depth measurements into a common TSDF. Inter-UAV collision avoidance and robot self-filtering are integrated to ensure safety and prevent other UAVs from being reconstructed as static obstacles. Four sampling-based planners (RH-NBVP, KRH-NBVP, AEP, KAEP) are preserved in core logic, with only system-level adaptations for multi-UAV operation.
AI.result: Simulation experiments across multiple environments and two deployment configurations—Joint Start (JS, UAVs initialized in close proximity) and Separated Start (SS, UAVs initialized in distinct locations)—show that SS consistently achieves faster exploration and improved coverage across all planners.
AI.conclusion: Deployment strategy is critical to multi-UAV exploration performance, with separated starts outperforming joint starts. The framework allows existing single-UAV sampling-based planners to be reused effectively in a multi-UAV setting.

title: Learning from Research: Toward Lifelong Agent Harness Evolution
summary: Language agents are expected to solve increasingly complex tasks, creating a growing need for continual improvement. One promising approach is to evolve the agent harness, the software that governs tool use, memory management, and task execution, while keeping the underlying language model fixed. Recent methods automate this process by using a meta coding agent to modify the harness based on execution feedback. However, relying on that agent's existing knowledge and observed failures can restrict exploration and make adaptation reactive. Inspired by how human experts learn from the research literature for new solutions, we introduce ScholarEvolve, a framework that automatically draws on state-of-the-art research to guide harness evolution. ScholarEvolve organizes the harness evolution directions into functional modules and uses topic modeling to identify distinct improvement strategies for each module. It implements these strategies and evaluates their combinations to improve task performance. Moreover, the framework is designed to incorporate new publications over time, allowing research advances to drive proactive lifelong evolution. Experiments demonstrate improvements on AppWorld and Tau2-Bench. ScholarEvolve raises Qwen3.5-27B task goal completion from 49.6% to 63.6% on AppWorld Challenge, and raises GPT-5.4-mini pass@1 from 72.7% to 81.9% on Tau2-Bench Telecom.

AI.tldr: ScholarEvolve evolves language-agent harnesses by mining research literature (via topic modeling) into modular improvement strategies, outperforming purely failure-driven meta-agent approaches and supporting lifelong evolution.
AI.motivation: Language agents must handle increasingly complex tasks, so continual improvement is needed. A promising route is to evolve the agent harness (tool use, memory, task execution) while keeping the base model fixed. Existing automated methods let a meta coding agent modify the harness using only execution feedback, which constrains exploration and makes adaptation reactive rather than proactive.
AI.method: Inspired by how human experts learn from the research literature, ScholarEvolve automatically draws on state-of-the-art research to guide harness evolution. It organizes evolution directions into functional modules, applies topic modeling to identify distinct improvement strategies per module, implements these strategies, and evaluates their combinations for task performance. The framework is also designed to ingest new publications over time, enabling proactive lifelong evolution.
AI.result: Experiments show gains on AppWorld and Tau2-Bench. ScholarEvolve raises Qwen3.5-27B task goal completion from 49.6% to 63.6% on AppWorld Challenge, and raises GPT-5.4-mini pass@1 from 72.7% to 81.9% on Tau2-Bench Telecom.
AI.conclusion: Grounding harness evolution in research literature rather than only observed failures broadens exploration and enables proactive, lifelong improvement, yielding substantive gains across benchmarks.

title: STARS: From Spatiotemporal Dynamics to Social Representations in Human-Robot Interaction
comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. First two authors contributed equally. Project site: https://larg.github.io/stars/
summary: Robot navigation in dynamic, human-centered environments requires socially-compliant decisions grounded in robust scene understanding. Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit promising capabilities such as object recognition, common-sense reasoning, and contextual understanding, capabilities that align with the nuanced requirements of social robot navigation. However, it remains unclear whether VLMs can accurately understand complex social navigation scenes (e.g., inferring the spatial-temporal relations among agents and human intentions), which is essential for safe and socially compliant robot navigation. While some recent works have explored the use of VLMs in social robot navigation, no existing work systematically evaluates their ability to meet these necessary conditions. In this paper, we introduce the Social Navigation Scene Understanding Benchmark (SocialNav-SUB), a Visual Question Answering (VQA) dataset and benchmark designed to evaluate VLMs for scene understanding in real-world social robot navigation scenarios. SocialNav-SUB provides a unified framework for evaluating VLMs against human and rule-based baselines across VQA tasks requiring spatial, spatiotemporal, and social reasoning in social robot navigation. Through experiments with state-of-the-art VLMs, we find that while the best-performing VLM achieves an encouraging probability of agreeing with human answers, it still underperforms simpler rule-based approach and human consensus baselines, indicating critical gaps in social scene understanding of current VLMs. Our benchmark sets the stage for further research on foundation models for social robot navigation, offering a framework to explore how VLMs can be tailored to meet real-world social robot navigation needs. An overview of this paper along with the code and data can be found at https://larg.github.io/socialnav-sub.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SocialNav-SUB, a VQA benchmark for systematically evaluating Vision-Language Models on scene understanding in real-world social robot navigation, finding that current VLMs underperform rule-based and human baselines.
AI.motivation: Social robot navigation in dynamic, human-centered environments requires socially-compliant decisions based on robust scene understanding. VLMs show promising object recognition, common-sense reasoning, and contextual understanding, but it is unclear whether they can accurately understand complex social navigation scenes (e.g., spatiotemporal relations among agents and human intentions). No prior work systematically evaluates these necessary capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose the Social Navigation Scene Understanding Benchmark (SocialNav-SUB), a Visual Question Answering dataset and benchmark for evaluating VLMs on scene understanding in real-world social robot navigation. It offers a unified framework to assess VLMs against human and rule-based baselines across VQA tasks requiring spatial, spatiotemporal, and social reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments with state-of-the-art VLMs show that the best-performing model achieves an encouraging probability of agreeing with human answers, yet still underperforms simpler rule-based approaches and human consensus baselines, revealing critical gaps in social scene understanding of current VLMs.
AI.conclusion: SocialNav-SUB sets the stage for further research on foundation models for social robot navigation and provides a framework to explore how VLMs can be tailored to meet real-world social robot navigation needs.

title: Belief-Aware Multi-Agent Path Finding under Map Uncertainty
summary: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) aims to find collision-free paths for multiple agents in a shared environment. Classical MAPF assumes that all static obstacles are known in advance, but real-world environments can change unexpectedly due to fallen objects, spills, or other local disturbances. When such changes are spatially correlated, an observation can inform traversability estimates beyond the observed location. Prior approaches address uncertainty in traversability through contingent plans or replanning based on direct observations, but do not leverage this spatial dependence to infer the traversability of nearby unobserved locations. As a result, they cannot use one observation to anticipate nearby unobserved obstacles that may cause costly rerouting later. We focus on Belief-Aware MAPF, where map discrepancies are fixed during execution but initially unknown, and observations can be informative beyond the observed location. We propose Multi-Agent Gaussian belief Inference for Coordination (MAGIC), a framework that updates a shared belief about traversability online based on agents' observations. MAGIC uses a Gaussian Markov Random Field and Gaussian Belief Propagation to approximately infer traversability and construct detour-aware costs for standard MAPF planners. Our experiments on MAPF benchmarks show that MAGIC reduces the executed sum of costs compared to existing approaches on 96.3% of instances, across several planner families and teams of up to 800 agents, demonstrating its applicability to large-scale MAPF problems.

AI.tldr: MAGIC is a framework that maintains a shared online belief over map traversability using a Gaussian Markov Random Field and Gaussian Belief Propagation, enabling MAPF planners to exploit spatially correlated observations and build detour-aware costs.
AI.motivation: Classical MAPF assumes all static obstacles are known a priori, but real environments change unexpectedly (fallen objects, spills). Existing approaches handle traversability uncertainty via contingent plans or replanning from direct observations, yet they ignore spatial dependence, so a single observation cannot inform traversability of nearby unobserved locations. This prevents anticipating unobserved obstacles that later cause costly rerouting.
AI.method: The paper targets Belief-Aware MAPF: map discrepancies are fixed during execution but initially unknown, and observations are informative beyond the observed location. MAGIC updates a shared belief over traversability online from agents' observations, using a Gaussian Markov Random Field with Gaussian Belief Propagation to approximately infer traversability and derive detour-aware costs for standard MAPF planners.
AI.result: Experiments on MAPF benchmarks show MAGIC reduces the executed sum of costs compared to existing approaches on 96.3% of instances, across several planner families and teams of up to 800 agents.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging spatial correlation in observations through probabilistic belief inference improves MAPF execution cost, and the approach scales to large-scale problems.

title: GPU-Accelerated Path-Dependent Marginal Information Gain for Autonomous Exploration
comment: Submitted for review to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: Autonomous exploration demands that robots continuously evaluate candidate viewpoints based on their expected information gain and execution cost. Sampling-based planners estimate this gain by volumetric raycasting and, due to its computational cost, evaluate candidates under an assumption of mutual independence, ignoring the overlap between viewpoints along the same path. This work presents a GPU-accelerated method for computing path-dependent marginal information gain, where instead of storing and merging the observed unknown voxels along each candidate path, previous observations are represented using depth buffers. Candidate rays are projected into the depth buffers of their ancestors to identify observation overlap and exclude regions expected to be observed. The planning tree is evaluated in depth order to maintain the dependency between viewpoints and their optimized yaws, while candidate nodes and rays at each level are processed in parallel on the GPU. The proposed method stays within 5-10% of the exact marginal gain computed using voxel hash maps, with speed-ups of up to 118x on a desktop GPU and 28x on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The method was integrated into two sampling-based exploration planners and evaluated in three simulation environments, where marginal gain reduced the time to 95% coverage in five of the six evaluated planner-environment combinations. Real-world experiments also showed a 30% reduction in the time to 95% coverage, as well as earlier exploration termination times.

AI.tldr: A GPU-accelerated method computes path-dependent marginal information gain using depth buffers to capture viewpoint overlap, achieving near-exact accuracy with large speed-ups and improved exploration efficiency.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based exploration planners estimate information gain via volumetric raycasting and, due to computational cost, assume mutual independence among candidate viewpoints, ignoring overlap along paths. This leads to inaccurate gain estimates and inefficient exploration.
AI.method: Instead of storing and merging observed unknown voxels along each candidate path, previous observations are represented using depth buffers. Candidate rays are projected into ancestors' depth buffers to identify observation overlap and exclude regions expected to be observed. The planning tree is evaluated in depth order to preserve dependency between viewpoints and optimized yaws, while candidate nodes and rays at each level are processed in parallel on the GPU.
AI.result: The method stays within 5-10% of exact marginal gain computed via voxel hash maps, with speed-ups up to 118x on a desktop GPU and 28x on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. Integrated into two sampling-based exploration planners across three simulation environments, marginal gain reduced time to 95% coverage in five of six planner-environment combinations. Real-world experiments showed a 30% reduction in time to 95% coverage and earlier exploration termination.
AI.conclusion: Depth-buffer-based path-dependent marginal gain provides an accurate and highly efficient alternative to independence assumptions, improving exploration efficiency in both simulation and real-world settings.

title: PivotOPD: Learning to Recover from Pivotal Mistakes in Multi-Turn Agents
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for training language agents, providing dense teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, in multi-turn interaction, an incorrect action changes the states the student encounters later, so errors compound across turns. In preliminary experiments across three Qwen3 models (8B to 235B), we find that more than half of the failed rollouts contain a pivotal mistake, an action that moves the agent farther from completing the task, and this mistake typically occurs early. These pivotal mistakes often remain recoverable: guiding the model for only a few turns after the pivotal turn can restore task success. We therefore propose PivotOPD, an on-policy distillation framework that jointly trains the student to prevent pivotal mistakes and to recover from the states they create. At each pivotal mistake, a teacher model provides a gold action and then names a recovery action at each of the next few turns. Preventive distillation uses the gold action with reverse KL to steer the student away from the pivotal mistake, while recovery distillation uses the recovery actions with forward KL to transfer recovery behaviors that the student rarely samples. Against 13 baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA, PivotOPD achieves the strongest average performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B students, improving over the strongest baseline on ALFWorld by +5.5% with the 1.7B student. The gains also transfer to another model family on the software engineering domain, where PivotOPD raises the resolve rate of a Nemotron-3.5 student on SWE-Bench Verified by +3.2%. Project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/pivotopd/

AI.tldr: PivotOPD is an on-policy distillation framework for training multi-turn language agents that identifies pivotal mistakes (early errors that compound) and jointly trains the student to both prevent them via reverse-KL gold-action distillation and recover from them via forward-KL recovery-action distillation, achieving top performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA and transferring to SWE-Bench Verified.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn agent interaction, a single incorrect action alters the states the student later encounters, causing errors to compound across turns. Preliminary experiments across three Qwen3 models (8B–235B) show that more than half of failed rollouts contain a pivotal mistake—an action moving the agent farther from task completion—and this mistake typically occurs early. Crucially, these mistakes often remain recoverable: guiding the model for only a few turns after the pivotal turn can restore task success. Existing on-policy distillation offers dense teacher supervision but does not explicitly address preventing and recovering from such pivotal errors.
AI.method: PivotOPD is an on-policy distillation framework that jointly trains the student to prevent pivotal mistakes and to recover from the states they create. At each pivotal mistake, a teacher model provides a gold action and then names a recovery action at each of the next few turns. Preventive distillation uses the gold action with reverse KL to steer the student away from the pivotal mistake, while recovery distillation uses the recovery actions with forward KL to transfer recovery behaviors that the student rarely samples.
AI.result: Against 13 baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA, PivotOPD achieves the strongest average performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B students, improving over the strongest baseline on ALFWorld by +5.5% with the 1.7B student. The gains also transfer to another model family in the software engineering domain, where PivotOPD raises the resolve rate of a Nemotron-3.5 student on SWE-Bench Verified by +3.2%.
AI.conclusion: PivotOPD demonstrates that explicitly targeting pivotal mistakes—both preventing them and learning to recover from the states they create—is an effective strategy for on-policy distillation of multi-turn language agents. It yields strong, transferable gains across diverse benchmarks, model sizes, and domains, including software engineering.

title: DynaHarness: A Dynamic Physical Harness for Self-Evolving Robot Agents
summary: Pretrained robot policies provide useful action priors, but long-horizon manipulation still requires coordination between semantic reasoning and physical execution. Semantic reasoning operates at a coarser timescale than physical interaction, while episode-level failures provide limited guidance on which system component should be revised. We propose DynaHarness, a dynamic physical harness that couples semantic reasoning with physical governance through a shared execution contract and turns failure evidence into validated capability revisions. To be more specific, the slow brain proposes capabilities and symbolic arguments, while the fast brain grounds and monitors commands, refuses unresolved actions, substitutes capabilities, and requests replans when needed. The physical execution contract bounds each accepted command and records execution evidence across analytic skills, recovery skills, and the frozen VLA. Failure attribution localizes faults in these records and directs targeted revisions of reusable capabilities or execution mechanisms. Paired regression checks govern admission or rejection, closing the self-evolution loop. On LIBERO-Pro, DynaHarness achieves 75.2% on 800 newly sampled initial states, compared with 17.5% for the frozen policy. With the same capability library, full dynamic execution reaches 74.0% versus 63.9% under nominal one-step replanning. This demonstrates the value of DynaHarness as a dynamic physical harness that governs how existing capabilities are grounded, monitored, and coordinated during execution. Our project page is at https://denghaoyuan123.github.io/Dynaharness_page/.

AI.tldr: DynaHarness is a dynamic physical harness that couples slow semantic reasoning with fast physical governance via a shared execution contract, converting failure evidence into validated capability revisions and lifting LIBERO-Pro performance from 17.5% (frozen policy) to 75.2%.
AI.motivation: Pretrained robot policies offer useful action priors, but long-horizon manipulation demands coordination between semantic reasoning and physical execution. These operate at mismatched timescales, and episode-level failures give little signal about which component should be revised.
AI.method: DynaHarness separates a slow brain (proposing capabilities and symbolic arguments) from a fast brain (grounding and monitoring commands, refusing unresolved actions, substituting capabilities, requesting replans). A physical execution contract bounds accepted commands and records execution evidence across analytic skills, recovery skills, and a frozen VLA. Failure attribution localizes faults in these records, directing targeted revisions of reusable capabilities or execution mechanisms, with paired regression checks governing admission or rejection to close the self-evolution loop.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Pro with 800 newly sampled initial states, DynaHarness reaches 75.2% versus 17.5% for the frozen policy; with the same capability library, full dynamic execution achieves 74.0% versus 63.9% under nominal one-step replanning.
AI.conclusion: DynaHarness is valuable as a dynamic physical harness that governs how existing capabilities are grounded, monitored, and coordinated during execution.

title: How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?
summary: Recent autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made significant progress on public leaderboards. Often motivated by progress stagnation over long-horizon cycles and limited Large Language Model (LLM) primitives, modern MLE agents are deployed on top of increasingly elaborate machinery: multi-agent orchestrators, dedicated retrieval subagents, and more. While such harnesses expand, the use of more primitive but improved coding agents - where LLMs have direct access to the execution environment through read, write, and bash primitives - has received little attention in the field. In this paper we find that, under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art harnesses provide no advantages over a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent baseline, pointing to the backbone as the primary driver for performance. Via a series of large-scale systematic ablation studies, we argue that the machinery layers become redundant in the coding agent setting. We conclude that the effort spent elaborating hand-crafted harnesses around strong models yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Under equal time budgets and the same frontier LLM, elaborate MLE agent harnesses show no advantage over a minimal coding agent with read/write/bash access, suggesting the LLM backbone—not the harness—drives performance.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon stagnation and limited LLM primitives have driven MLE agents toward increasingly complex machinery (multi-agent orchestrators, retrieval subagents). Meanwhile, the simpler approach of coding agents with direct environment access via basic primitives has been underexplored.
AI.method: Large-scale systematic ablation studies comparing open-source state-of-the-art harnesses against a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent, holding time budget and frontier LLM backbone constant.
AI.result: The elaborate harnesses provide no performance advantage over the minimal coding agent baseline, indicating the backbone is the primary performance driver and that machinery layers become redundant in the coding agent setting.
AI.conclusion: Effort spent elaborating hand-crafted harnesses around strong models yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks.

title: Ego4WAM: What Matters When Scaling Egocentric Human Data for Robot Learning?
summary: Egocentric human data provides a scalable source of experience for robot learning, but varies substantially in human-robot alignment, behavioral coverage, and available supervision. Existing work shows favorable scaling with increasing human data, but it remains unclear which data properties drive downstream robot gains and how to use such data throughout the training pipeline. We present a systematic study of egocentric human data with different alignment and supervision under a unified world-action model framework. With the model backbone fixed, we disentangle the effects of human-robot alignment, data duration and task diversity, action supervision, and data usage strategies. We find that aligned human demonstrations substantially improve out-of-distribution generalization and reduce target-task robot data requirements; data duration and task diversity affect downstream capabilities differently; and video-only supervision remains effective without action labels, providing a strong foundation for subsequent video-action training. We validate these findings through closed-loop policy evaluation on both real robots and RoboDojo. Rather than treating data duration as the sole scaling axis, Ego4WAM shows how alignment, task diversity, available supervision, and usage strategy jointly shape the value of egocentric human data for robot learning.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies how different properties of egocentric human data—alignment, duration, task diversity, supervision, and usage strategy—affect robot learning within a unified world-action model (Ego4WAM), finding that alignment and task diversity matter more than sheer data volume.
AI.motivation: Egocentric human data is a scalable source of robot learning experience, yet it varies widely in human-robot alignment, behavioral coverage, and supervision. Prior work demonstrates favorable scaling with more human data but does not clarify which data properties actually drive downstream robot gains, nor how to best leverage such data across the training pipeline.
AI.method: Under a unified world-action model framework (Ego4WAM) with a fixed model backbone, the authors conduct a systematic, controlled study that disentangles the effects of human-robot alignment, data duration, task diversity, action supervision (including video-only supervision), and data usage strategies.
AI.result: Aligned human demonstrations substantially improve out-of-distribution generalization and reduce target-task robot data requirements; data duration and task diversity affect downstream capabilities differently; and video-only supervision remains effective even without action labels, providing a strong foundation for subsequent video-action training. Findings are validated via closed-loop policy evaluation on real robots and RoboDojo.
AI.conclusion: Rather than treating data duration as the sole scaling axis, Ego4WAM shows that alignment, task diversity, available supervision, and usage strategy jointly shape the value of egocentric human data for robot learning.

title: Cogentic: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Automated Proof Discovery
summary: We present Cogentic, a multi-agent harness for automated proof discovery on open research problems. While frontier language models can generate strong mathematical ideas in a single shot, single-shot generation is often insufficient for open problems that require exploring multiple competing conjectures, overcoming subtle technical obstructions, and retaining intermediate progress over a long horizon. Cogentic addresses these challenges through an iterative prove--verify loop in which an orchestrator allocates a population of independent provers across distinct proof directions, subjects their output to adversarial verification by several specialized components, and promotes confirmed intermediate results into a persistent verified ledger that later rounds build on. The harness is designed to be able to solve research-level math and theoretical computer science problems. Using Gemini as the base model, Cogentic produced novel results on five open problems across online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design. Each result was independently verified by domain experts and is developed in full in companion papers. We list these results, and new ones as they are verified, at https://sites.google.com/view/cogentic .

AI.tldr: Cogentic is a multi-agent harness for automated proof discovery that uses an iterative prove-verify loop with an orchestrator, independent provers, adversarial verifiers, and a persistent verified ledger. Using Gemini as the base model, it produced novel, expert-verified results on five open problems in online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design.
AI.motivation: Frontier language models can generate strong mathematical ideas in a single shot, but single-shot generation is often insufficient for open research problems that require exploring multiple competing conjectures, overcoming subtle technical obstructions, and retaining intermediate progress over a long horizon.
AI.method: Cogentic employs an iterative prove-verify loop in which an orchestrator allocates a population of independent provers across distinct proof directions, subjects their output to adversarial verification by several specialized components, and promotes confirmed intermediate results into a persistent verified ledger that later rounds build on. The harness is designed to be capable of solving research-level mathematics and theoretical computer science problems.
AI.result: Using Gemini as the base model, Cogentic produced novel results on five open problems across online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design. Each result was independently verified by domain experts and is developed in full in companion papers. Results are listed, along with newly verified ones, at https://sites.google.com/view/cogentic.
AI.conclusion: Cogentic demonstrates that a multi-agent prove-verify harness with independent provers, adversarial verification, and a persistent verified ledger can solve research-level open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, yielding expert-verified novel results.

title: WorldAuditBench: Interactive 3D World Auditing with Multimodal Agents
summary: As interactive 3D worlds are increasingly used to study intelligent behavior, it becomes important to develop efficient pipelines for identifying anomalies in these simulated environments, such as floating objects, traversable walls, or objects inconsistent with the surrounding scene. Multimodal AI systems, including vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs), have shown potential for automating this task. However, 3D world auditing is complex, requiring the close coupling of two distinct capabilities: action, to navigate the 3D world and search for anomalies systematically and efficiently; and visual reasoning, to understand the environment and identify anomalies from multimodal observations. It remains largely unexplored whether multimodal agents can effectively couple these two capabilities, using visual reasoning to identify potential anomalies while taking actions to validate them. In this paper, we introduce WorldAuditBench, a benchmark for 3D world auditing comprising 213 anomaly tasks across 13 environments built with Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js, spanning five anomaly families. We evaluate five frontier models under a fixed exploration budget using two auditing paradigms: VLA-based exploration followed by VLM-based anomaly identification, and an end-to-end VLM agent in which visual reasoning directly guides action selection. Across the evaluated models and two paradigms, success rates range from 6.6% to 42.3%, substantially below human performance (83.4%). Through the task of world auditing, WorldAuditBench provides a testbed for studying how multimodal agents couple action and visual reasoning in interactive 3D environments, while highlighting current limitations in their ability to gather and interpret evidence during exploration.

AI.tldr: WorldAuditBench is introduced as a benchmark of 213 anomaly-auditing tasks across 13 Unreal Engine 5/Three.js 3D environments, evaluating whether multimodal agents can couple action and visual reasoning; frontier models achieve only 6.6%–42.3% success versus 83.4% human performance.
AI.motivation: Interactive 3D worlds are increasingly used to study intelligent behavior, creating a need for efficient pipelines to detect anomalies such as floating objects, traversable walls, or scene-inconsistent objects. Multimodal AI systems (VLMs and VLAs) are promising for automating this, but 3D world auditing demands tight coupling of systematic, efficient action (navigation/search) and visual reasoning (identifying anomalies from multimodal observations). Whether multimodal agents can effectively couple these capabilities—using visual reasoning to spot anomalies while acting to validate them—remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors build WorldAuditBench, a 3D world auditing benchmark with 213 anomaly tasks across 13 environments created in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js, covering five anomaly families. They evaluate five frontier models under a fixed exploration budget using two paradigms: (1) VLA-based exploration followed by VLM-based anomaly identification, and (2) an end-to-end VLM agent where visual reasoning directly guides action selection.
AI.result: Across the five models and two paradigms, success rates range from 6.6% to 42.3%, well below the 83.4% human performance baseline.
AI.conclusion: WorldAuditBench offers a testbed for studying how multimodal agents couple action and visual reasoning in interactive 3D environments, exposing current limitations in their ability to gather and interpret evidence during exploration.

title: Turbo Harness: Instance-Adaptive Harness Optimization
summary: Automating the search for effective harnesses is an important step toward enabling agents to recursively self-improve. Existing harness optimizations typically produce a single global harness that is applied uniformly across task instances. However, a harness that works well on average may not be optimal for every instance. We introduce Turbo Harness, a framework that can adapt a globally optimized harness to each instance by reusing information generated during the original optimization process. Specifically, Turbo Harness recycles artifacts produced during a completed global harness optimization run, and summarizes them into a structured playbook. We train a harness editor to leverage this prior optimization experience to generate instance-specific patches to the global harness. At inference time, the editor uses the instance and the playbook to construct a tailored harness in which the execution model operates. Through numerical experiments, we show that Turbo Harness consistently outperforms existing harness optimization baselines across seven benchmarks spanning interactive agent tasks, software engineering, and long-horizon terminal tasks.

AI.tldr: Turbo Harness adapts a globally optimized agent harness to individual task instances by recycling artifacts from the original optimization run into a structured playbook, then training an editor to generate instance-specific harness patches, outperforming global-harness baselines across seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing harness optimization methods yield a single global harness applied uniformly to all task instances. Since a harness that performs well on average may be suboptimal for specific instances, there is a need for instance-level adaptation of harnesses to improve agent performance.
AI.method: Turbo Harness reuses artifacts generated during a completed global harness optimization run and summarizes them into a structured playbook. It trains a harness editor that leverages this prior optimization experience to produce instance-specific patches to the global harness. At inference, the editor takes the instance and the playbook to construct a tailored harness that hosts the execution model.
AI.result: Turbo Harness consistently outperforms existing harness optimization baselines across seven benchmarks covering interactive agent tasks, software engineering, and long-horizon terminal tasks.
AI.conclusion: Adapting a global harness per instance via recycled optimization artifacts and a trained editor is an effective approach, yielding consistent gains over global harness optimization baselines, and represents a step toward enabling agents to recursively self-improve.
